Ascertained from them what time the star had appeared. He asked carefully, because he wanted to calculate the child’s age. This explains why he later killed boys up to two years old (v. 16): the star had probably appeared some time before, perhaps a year or more.

Go and search diligently for the child. Herod uses the magi as unknowing spies.

That I too may come and worship him. A lie. He wanted to kill the child. Herod uses the language of worship to hide murder. Religious words can cover evil intentions.

What it does not mean. Not that the magi were foolish to trust him at first. They had no reason to suspect a king. God protected them by warning them later (v. 12).

In a sentence. Herod hid a murderous plan behind a pretence of worship, using the magi to find the child.

On a Tuesday. Be wary of anyone, including yourself, who uses pious words to cover selfish aims. God sees the heart.

parallels.desc: rulers take counsel against the LORD’s Anointed

verseByVerse.quote: After listening to the king, they went on their way. And behold, the star that they had seen when it rose went before them until it came to rest over the place where the child was. When they saw the star, they rejoiced exceedingly with great joy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The magi set out, and the star they had seen went ahead of them and stopped over the place where the child was. When they saw it, they were overwhelmed with joy.

After listening to the king, they went on their way. They went alone. No one from Jerusalem, not even the scholars, came with them.

The star … went before them until it came to rest over the place where the child was. No ordinary star or planet moves before travellers and stops over a single house. This was God’s guiding sign, like the pillar of cloud and fire that went before Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 13:21).

They rejoiced exceedingly with great joy. Matthew piles up words: literally “they rejoiced a great joy exceedingly”. After a long journey, and the disappointment of Jerusalem, they find God guiding them again. Their joy contrasts with the fear of Herod and Jerusalem (v. 3). The same news brings fear to some and joy to others, depending on whether they want the King.

What it does not mean. Not that God usually guides by signs in the sky. Here he gave a unique sign for a unique event. He guides his people today chiefly through his word (Psalm 119:105).

In a sentence. God led the magi to the child, and finding him filled them with overwhelming joy.

For worship. Thank God for the ways he has led you to Christ, and ask for the magi’s joy in finding him.

verseByVerse.quote: And going into the house, they saw the child with Mary his mother, and they fell down and worshiped him. Then, opening their treasures, they offered him gifts, gold and frankincense and myrrh. And being warned in a dream not to return to Herod, they departed to their own country by another way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Entering the house, the magi saw the child with his mother, fell down and worshipped him, and offered him costly gifts: gold, frankincense and myrrh. Warned in a dream not to return to Herod, they went home another way.

Going into the house. Not a stable. By now, perhaps months later, the family was living in a house in Bethlehem. Nativity scenes that put the magi at the manger with the shepherds combine two separate events.

They saw the child with Mary his mother. Matthew always mentions the child first (vv. 13, 14, 20, 21). Mary is honoured, but the child is the centre.

And they fell down and worshipped him. They worshipped the child, not Mary. Wealthy, learned foreigners lay face down on the floor before a child of an ordinary family. Worship is the right response to Jesus, even as an infant, because of who he is (1:23).

Opening their treasures. Their treasure chests: gifts fit for a king. In the ancient world one did not approach a king empty-handed.

Gold. The gift for a king.

Frankincense. A fragrant resin from trees in Arabia and Somalia, burned as incense in worship, including in the temple (Exodus 30:34–38). A gift associated with God and worship.

Myrrh. Another fragrant resin, used in perfume, medicine and for preparing bodies for burial (John 19:39). It was offered to Jesus again on the cross, mixed with wine (Mark 15:23).

The meaning of the gifts. From early times, Christians have seen the gifts as pointing to who Jesus is: gold for a king, frankincense for God, myrrh for one who would die. Matthew does not say this, and the magi probably intended simply to give the most precious gifts they had. But the gifts fit, and Isaiah had spoken of the nations bringing gold and frankincense to the Lord (Isaiah 60:6; Psalm 72:10–11). Practically, the gifts may have funded the family’s flight to Egypt.

Being warned in a dream not to return to Herod. God protected the child and the magi. God speaks in dreams five times in Matthew 1–2, always to guide and protect.

They departed to their own country by another way. They avoided Jerusalem. Matthew says no more about them. They returned home, having worshipped the King.

What it does not mean. Not that worship is measured by the size of the gift. The widow’s two small coins were worth more than the gifts of the rich (Mark 12:41–44). The magi gave their best; so should we, whatever it is.

In a sentence. The magi bowed in worship before the child King and gave him their most precious treasures.

On a Tuesday. What is your best that you could give to Christ this week: your time, your money, your skill, your attention?

For worship. Bow before Christ as the magi did, and give him your best.
verseByVerse.note: By now the family is in a house, not a stable. Frankincense was a resin burned in worship; myrrh a fragrant resin also used in burial.

parallels.desc: kings bring gifts to the king

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–23 — The Flight to Egypt and the Return to Nazareth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The holy family flees to Egypt to escape Herod's massacre of Bethlehem's infant boys, returns after Herod's death, and settles in Nazareth — each movement fulfilling a specific Old Testament text. Matthew sees in these events not merely historical geography but the recapitulation of Israel's story: Jesus relives the Exodus (out of Egypt), the Exile (the weeping of Rachel), and Israel's wilderness sojourn (settling in a despised region). The Son of God is doing in himself what Israel failed to do: he is the true Israel, perfectly faithful where the nation was not. Three items the summary passes over. Verses 19-20 contain a quiet oddity: "those who sought the child's life are dead" is plural, though only Herod had died — because Matthew is quoting Exodus 4:19 almost word for word, God's word to Moses in Midian, with the direction of travel reversed. Herod died at Jericho in the spring of 4 BC, which is why Jesus was born several years before the year we number 1 — an error not in Scripture but in the sixth-century monk who built the calendar. Verses 21-22 are the fifth dream in two chapters (1:20; 2:12, 13, 19, 22), and the verse-by-verse takes up the question readers actually carry: whether God still guides this way, and what to do with a vivid dream. Note that Joseph's fear of Archelaus was reasonable on its own terms and the dream confirmed his ordinary judgement rather than overruling it. Verse 23 is the hardest fulfilment quotation in the Gospel, because no Old Testament verse says the Messiah will be called a Nazarene — and Matthew signals as much by writing "prophets" in the plural, naming nobody and quoting nothing. The strongest reading is Isaiah 11:1, where the shoot from Jesse's stump is a netser; the theme of the despised one (Isa. 53:2-3) very likely stands behind it too. And the name stuck: it is what Pilate wrote over his head, how the angel identified him at the tomb, and what the risen Christ called himself from heaven on the Damascus road (Acts 22:8).
verseByVerse.theology: Matthew's three fulfillment quotations here (Hos. 11:1; Jer. 31:15; and possibly Isa. 11:1 or Judg. 13:5 for "Nazarene") reveal his typological reading of history: Israel's great narrative events were not merely past occurrences but prophetic templates waiting for their ultimate fulfillment in Christ. Jesus does not merely happen to visit Egypt; he is the true Son whom God calls out of Egypt. The slaughter of the innocents does not merely echo Rachel's weeping; it is the event that makes the older weeping fully intelligible. This is not proof-texting but fulfillment theology.
verseByVerse.examples: The massacre of Bethlehem's infants is the event that silences easy answers about suffering. Matthew does not explain it; he quotes Jeremiah's lament and moves on. Rachel weeping for her children who are no more: there are moments when the only honest response to evil is grief, not explanation. The Messiah's birth caused suffering for the innocent. His death would be the answer to that suffering — not by explaining it away, but by entering it and overcoming it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when they had departed, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream and said, "Rise, take the child and his mother, and flee to Egypt, and remain there until I tell you, for Herod is about to search for the child, to destroy him." And he rose and took the child and his mother by night and departed to Egypt
verseByVerse.commentary:
After the magi left, an angel warned Joseph in a dream to take the child and his mother and flee to Egypt, because Herod was about to search for the child to kill him. Joseph obeyed that very night.

An angel of the Lord appeared to Joseph in a dream. The second of four dreams (1:20; 2:13, 19, 22). Each time God guides Joseph, he obeys at once.

Rise, take the child and his mother. Joseph is responsible for protecting the family.

And flee to Egypt. Egypt was outside Herod’s territory, under direct Roman rule, about eighty miles (130 kilometres) from Bethlehem to the border, perhaps a week or more of travel. Large Jewish communities lived there, especially in Alexandria. Egypt had long been a refuge for God’s people: Abraham went there in famine (Genesis 12:10), and Jacob’s family went there under Joseph (Genesis 46). It was also the land of Israel’s slavery, from which God rescued them.

For Herod is about to search for the child, to destroy him. The first attempt on Jesus’ life. From the beginning, the world’s powers set themselves against God’s King (Psalm 2:1–2; Revelation 12:4).

And he rose and took the child and his mother by night. Immediate obedience, the same night. No questions recorded, no delay.

The pattern. Jesus relives Israel’s story. Like Israel, he goes down into Egypt; like Israel, he will be called out of Egypt (v. 15); like Israel, he will pass through water (3:16) and be tested in the wilderness (4:1–11). But where Israel failed, he will be faithful. He is the true Israel, God’s faithful Son.

What it does not mean. Not that fleeing danger shows a lack of faith. God himself commanded it. Trusting God includes using the means of safety he provides. Jesus later told his disciples to flee persecution when they could (10:23).

In a sentence. God warned Joseph to flee to Egypt to protect the child from Herod, and Joseph obeyed at once.

On a Tuesday. Refugees fleeing violence are not strangers to the story of Jesus: he was one. Pray for refugees, and welcome them as you would welcome him.
verseByVerse.note: Egypt had long been a refuge; large Jewish communities lived there.

parallels.desc: Jacob’s family goes down to Egypt

verseByVerse.quote: and remained there until the death of Herod. This was to fulfill what the Lord had spoken by the prophet, "Out of Egypt I called my son." Then Herod, when he saw that he had been tricked by the wise men, became furious, and he sent and killed all the male children in Bethlehem and in all that region who were two years old or under, according to the time that he had ascertained from the wise men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The family stayed in Egypt until Herod died, fulfilling God’s word through Hosea, “Out of Egypt I called my son”. Meanwhile Herod, furious at being tricked, ordered the killing of all the boys in and around Bethlehem aged two and under.

And remained there until the death of Herod. Herod died in 4 BC, after a painful illness. The family may have stayed in Egypt for a few months up to a year or two.

Out of Egypt I called my son. From Hosea 11:1. In Hosea, the verse looks back on the exodus: God called his son Israel out of Egypt. God had called Israel his firstborn son (Exodus 4:22). How can Matthew say this is fulfilled in Jesus?

How Matthew reads Hosea. Matthew is not saying that Hosea predicted this event directly. He is saying that Israel’s history was a pattern that Jesus completes. Israel was God’s son but was unfaithful; Hosea goes on to say that the more God called them, the more they went away and sacrificed to the Baals (Hosea 11:2). Jesus is the true and faithful Son, who lives out Israel’s story perfectly. What happened to Israel as a nation happens to Jesus as its representative. This is called typology: Old Testament people and events as patterns pointing to Christ. Matthew places the quotation here, before the return, because the point is that the child is safe in Egypt in order to be called out.

Then Herod, when he saw that he had been tricked by the wise men. The magi had not returned (v. 12).

Became furious. Herod’s rage was infamous. Shortly before he died he reportedly ordered that leading men be executed at his death so that there would be mourning in the land.

And he sent and killed all the male children in Bethlehem and in all that region who were two years old or under. Bethlehem was a small town of perhaps one thousand people, so the number of boys killed may have been around ten to twenty. No other ancient historian records this event, but it is exactly in character for Herod, who murdered on a much larger scale, and the killing of a few village children would have seemed minor beside his other crimes.

According to the time that he had ascertained from the wise men. He allowed a wide margin to be sure.

The parallel with Moses. Matthew’s readers would think of Pharaoh, who ordered the Hebrew baby boys to be killed, and of Moses, who was saved (Exodus 1:22–2:10). Jesus is the new Moses, saved from a murderous king to become his people’s deliverer. Later Jewish tradition even said that Pharaoh had been warned by his wise men of a coming deliverer.

What it does not mean. Not that God did not care about the children of Bethlehem. He did not cause Herod’s evil. Why God protected Jesus and not the others is not explained, and we should not pretend to know. But the same child who escaped would later die, innocent, at the hands of rulers, to defeat evil itself.

In a sentence. Jesus, the true Son, was sheltered in Egypt to be called out like Israel, while Herod murdered the boys of Bethlehem.

On a Tuesday. The world into which Jesus came was a world of violence against children. He did not come to a safe world; he came to save a broken one. Stand against violence toward the vulnerable.
verseByVerse.note: Bethlehem was a small town; the number of boys killed was probably small, but the act fits Herod’s known cruelty.

parallels.desc: “Out of Egypt I called my son”
Pharaoh orders the Hebrew boys killed

verseByVerse.quote: Then was fulfilled what was spoken by the prophet Jeremiah: "A voice was heard in Ramah, weeping and loud lamentation, Rachel weeping for her children; she refused to be comforted, because they are no more."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Herod’s massacre fulfilled the words of Jeremiah: Rachel weeping for her children, refusing to be comforted. Matthew does not hide the grief. But in Jeremiah, the weeping comes just before the promise of a new covenant, and in Jesus that hope has arrived.

Then was fulfilled. Matthew changes his usual wording. Elsewhere he says that something happened “to fulfil” Scripture, suggesting God’s purpose. Here he says “then was fulfilled”. He avoids saying that God intended the massacre. Herod’s evil was his own, though it fitted the pattern Scripture described.

What was spoken by the prophet Jeremiah. Jeremiah 31:15.

A voice was heard in Ramah. Ramah was a town about five miles (eight kilometres) north of Jerusalem, in the territory of Benjamin. In 586 BC the Babylonians gathered the captives of Judah there before marching them into exile (Jeremiah 40:1).

Rachel weeping for her children. Rachel was Jacob’s beloved wife, the mother of Joseph and Benjamin, and so a mother of Israel. She died giving birth to Benjamin and was buried on the way to Bethlehem (Genesis 35:16–20). Jeremiah pictures her weeping from her tomb as her descendants are led away into exile. Matthew hears the same weeping in Bethlehem, near her tomb, as mothers mourn their murdered sons.

She refused to be comforted, because they are no more. Scripture does not hurry grief. It gives voice to it. There is a grief so deep that it refuses easy comfort.

The context in Jeremiah. Jeremiah 31 is a chapter of hope. Immediately after this verse, God tells Rachel to stop weeping, because her children will come back (Jeremiah 31:16–17). And a little later comes the promise of the new covenant, in which God will forgive his people’s sin (Jeremiah 31:31–34). Matthew’s readers would know the context. The weeping of Bethlehem marks the moment just before God’s greatest comfort: the child who escaped will establish the new covenant in his blood (26:28).

What it does not mean. Not that grief is a lack of faith. Rachel’s weeping is recorded in Scripture without rebuke. Christians grieve, though not as those without hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13).

In a sentence. The grief of Bethlehem echoed Rachel’s weeping over exile, a grief that Scripture honours, on the edge of the new covenant’s comfort.

On a Tuesday. If you are grieving, you do not have to pretend. Bring your tears to God. And sit with those who grieve, without rushing them toward comfort.
verseByVerse.note: Ramah lay north of Jerusalem, on the road into exile. Rachel, Jacob’s wife, was buried near Bethlehem.

parallels.desc: Rachel buried on the way to Bethlehem

verseByVerse.quote: But when Herod died, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt, saying, "Rise, take the child and his mother and go to the land of Israel, for those who sought the child's life are dead."
verseByVerse.commentary:
After Herod died, the angel again appeared to Joseph in Egypt and told him to return to the land of Israel, because those who had tried to kill the child were dead.

But when Herod died. The tyrant who tried to kill God’s King died, and the King lived. Every enemy of Christ passes; he remains.

An angel of the Lord appeared in a dream to Joseph in Egypt. The third dream. God had promised to tell Joseph when to return (v. 13), and he did.

Go to the land of Israel. “The land of Israel” is a phrase used only here in the New Testament. It recalls God’s promise of the land to Abraham, and the exodus journey back to it. Like Israel, Jesus is called out of Egypt into the land.

For those who sought the child’s life are dead. These words echo almost exactly what God told Moses in Midian: all the men who were seeking your life are dead (Exodus 4:19). Jesus is the new Moses, returning to deliver his people.

What it does not mean. Not that every danger had passed: Herod’s son would be a new threat (v. 22). God guides one step at a time.

In a sentence. God called Joseph back from Egypt when Herod was dead, as he had once called Moses back to deliver Israel.

On a Tuesday. God keeps his word about timing: he told Joseph to wait until he spoke, and he spoke. Wait for him, and act when he makes the way clear.

parallels.desc: “all the men who were seeking your life are dead”

verseByVerse.quote: And he rose and took the child and his mother and went to the land of Israel. But when he heard that Archelaus was reigning over Judea in place of his father Herod, he was afraid to go there, and being warned in a dream he withdrew to the district of Galilee.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joseph obeyed and returned. But when he heard that Herod’s son Archelaus ruled Judea, he was afraid, and, warned in another dream, he went north to Galilee instead.

And he rose and took the child and his mother and went to the land of Israel. The same immediate obedience (vv. 14, 21).

Archelaus was reigning over Judea in place of his father Herod. When Herod died, Rome divided his kingdom among three of his sons. Archelaus received Judea, Samaria and Idumea. He began his reign by massacring about three thousand people at the temple during Passover. He was so brutal and incompetent that Rome removed him in AD 6 and sent him into exile, putting Judea under Roman governors, of whom Pontius Pilate was later one.

He was afraid to go there. Joseph’s fear was reasonable. Bethlehem, in Judea, was under Archelaus.

Being warned in a dream. The fourth and last dream. God confirms and directs Joseph’s caution.

He withdrew to the district of Galilee. Galilee, the northern region, was ruled by another of Herod’s sons, Herod Antipas, who was less violent (he later executed John the Baptist, 14:1–12). Galilee had a mixed population of Jews and Gentiles and was looked down on by people in Judea. Isaiah had spoken of Galilee of the nations, where those in darkness would see a great light (Isaiah 9:1–2; Matthew 4:15–16).

What it does not mean. Not that Joseph’s fear was faithlessness. God did not rebuke him; he confirmed his judgment and guided him. Fear can be a wise response to real danger, and God works through it.

In a sentence. Fearing Herod’s brutal son, and guided by God, Joseph took the family to Galilee.

On a Tuesday. God often guides through ordinary prudence as well as through clear words. Use the wisdom he gives, and trust him to correct your course.
verseByVerse.note: Archelaus, Herod’s son, ruled Judea so brutally that Rome removed him in AD 6. Galilee was ruled by his brother Herod Antipas.

verseByVerse.quote: And he went and lived in a city called Nazareth, so that what was spoken by the prophets might be fulfilled, that he would be called a Nazarene.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The family settled in Nazareth, a small and despised village in Galilee. Matthew sees in this the fulfilment of what the prophets had said, that the Messiah would be called a Nazarene: lowly, rejected, and yet the true Branch of David.

He went and lived in a city called Nazareth. Nazareth was a tiny village in the hills of lower Galilee, probably with a few hundred inhabitants. It is never mentioned in the Old Testament, in the Jewish historian Josephus, or in early rabbinic writings. When Nathanael heard that Jesus came from Nazareth, he asked whether anything good could come from there (John 1:46). Luke tells us that Joseph and Mary had lived there before (Luke 1:26; 2:39); Matthew focuses on God’s guidance there.

So that what was spoken by the prophets might be fulfilled. Notice “prophets”, plural. Elsewhere Matthew names a specific prophet. Here he refers to a theme found in several prophets, not to one verse. No Old Testament verse says, “He shall be called a Nazarene.”

That he would be called a Nazarene. What did Matthew mean? There are three main suggestions, and they may work together.

1. The despised one. To be called a Nazarene was to be called a nobody from nowhere. Many prophets said the Messiah would be despised and rejected (Isaiah 53:3; Psalm 22:6–8). Being from Nazareth fitted that pattern: the Messiah would be looked down on.

2. The Branch. The Hebrew word for “branch” is netser, which sounds like Nazareth. Isaiah 11:1 promises that a branch (netser) will grow from the stump of Jesse, David’s father: a new shoot from a fallen royal line. Other prophets also call the Messiah the Branch (Jeremiah 23:5; Zechariah 3:8; 6:12, using a related word). The village name echoes the messianic title.

3. A Nazirite. Some connect it with the Nazirite, a person set apart by a vow (Numbers 6). But Jesus was not a Nazirite (he drank wine, 11:19), and the spelling is different, so this is less likely.

Verdict: the first two together. Matthew uses a wordplay on the Branch (netser) to show that the despised village of Nazareth fits what the prophets said of the Messiah: a humble shoot from David’s line, despised by men.

What it does not mean. Not that Matthew invented a prophecy. He signals that he is summarising the prophets’ teaching, not quoting one text. And it does not mean that Jesus’ humble origin was an accident or embarrassment that had to be explained away. It was part of God’s plan: the King came in lowliness.

In a sentence. Jesus grew up in despised Nazareth, fulfilling the prophets’ picture of the Messiah as the humble Branch of David, scorned by men.

On a Tuesday. If you come from somewhere others look down on, so did your Lord. God’s greatest work often begins in places people dismiss.
verseByVerse.note: No single prophecy says “he shall be called a Nazarene”; Matthew speaks of “the prophets” in general. Nazareth was a despised backwater, and the prophets foretold a despised Messiah.

parallels.desc: a branch from the stump of Jesse
“Can anything good come out of Nazareth?”

2.theology:
Typology and the Unity of Scripture. Matthew 2 demonstrates the Reformed doctrine of the unity of the two Testaments through typological fulfilment. When Matthew reads “Out of Egypt I called my son” as fulfilled in Jesus, he is not wresting Hosea from its context. He is reading with the grain of Scripture’s own logic: Israel was God’s son (Exod. 4:22), whose history was a pattern that pointed forward to the Son of God. The Old Testament is not a collection of proof texts waiting to be claimed; it is a single story moving toward a single climax.

Reformed biblical theology, developed through scholars like Geerhardus Vos and continued by Edmund Clowney, has called this “redemptive-historical” interpretation: reading every text in the light of its place in the one story of God’s redemptive purpose. Matthew 2 is a masterclass in this method. Every Old Testament quotation is not forced but organic — the story was always moving here, toward the child in Bethlehem, the flight to Egypt, the return to the land, the settlement in Galilee of the nations (Isa. 9:1–2).
2.examples:
Then: The Magi represent the first fruits of the Gentile mission that will be formally commissioned in Matthew 28. They come from outside the covenant, guided by general revelation (the star), and are brought to special revelation (the Scriptures) and to the King himself. This is the pattern of mission throughout Acts: Cornelius, the Ethiopian eunuch, the Philippian jailer — each guided by a mixture of seeking and sovereign orchestration to the one who is the answer to every longing.

Now: In our world, the contrast of chapter 2 repeats daily: people with no theological background travelling great distances (literally and metaphorically) to find Jesus, while those with full access to Scripture never move toward him. Church membership without worship, theological knowledge without seeking — this is Jerusalem troubled but not travelling. The question Matthew 2 poses is not “how much do you know?” but “are you moving toward the King?” The Magi found him because they went. That remains the condition of finding him today.

3.title: The Voice and the Voice
3.text: <sup>1</sup>In those days John the Baptist came preaching in the wilderness of Judea, <sup>2</sup>“Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.” <sup>3</sup>For this is he who was spoken of by the prophet Isaiah when he said, “The voice of one crying in the wilderness: ‘Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.’” <sup>4</sup>Now John wore a garment of camel's hair and a leather belt around his waist, and his food was locusts and wild honey. <sup>5</sup>Then Jerusalem and all Judea and all the region about the Jordan were going out to him, <sup>6</sup>and they were baptized by him in the river Jordan, confessing their sins. <sup>7</sup>But when he saw many of the Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his baptism, he said to them, “You brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come? <sup>8</sup>Bear fruit in keeping with repentance. <sup>9</sup>And do not presume to say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father,’ for I tell you, God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham. <sup>10</sup>Even now the axe is laid to the root of the trees. Every tree therefore that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire. <sup>11</sup>I baptize you with water for repentance, but he who is coming after me is mightier than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire. <sup>12</sup>His winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will clear his threshing floor and gather his wheat into the barn, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire.” <sup>13</sup>Then Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan to John, to be baptized by him. <sup>14</sup>John would have prevented him, saying, “I need to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?” <sup>15</sup>But Jesus answered him, “Let it be so now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.” Then he consented. <sup>16</sup>And when Jesus was baptized, immediately he went up from the water, and behold, the heavens were opened to him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming to rest on him; <sup>17</sup>and behold, a voice from heaven said, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased.”
3.overview:
Chapter 3 is a chapter of two voices. The first voice is John’s: rough, wilderness-forged, prophetic, urgent. He wears the clothes of Elijah (2 Kgs. 1:8) and preaches with Elijah’s directness. Repent. The kingdom is not arriving on your terms. Your ancestry will not protect you. Bear fruit — now, because the axe is already laid to the root. John’s preaching is the sound of the law doing its proper work: exposing the bankruptcy of religious privilege and the urgency of genuine turning.

The second voice is the Father’s: tender, declarative, public. This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased. It comes from heaven, over the Jordan, spoken in Matthew's account as a declaration to those watching: This is my beloved Son. The Father is not waiting to see how the ministry goes before rendering his verdict; he speaks it before the first sermon, before the first miracle, before the temptation is overcome. The approval is unconditional, grounded not in performance but in person and covenant.

Between the two voices stands the baptism — and the question it raises: why does the sinless one need a baptism of repentance? Jesus answers it: to fulfil all righteousness. He is not confessing sin; he is identifying with sinners. The one who needs no baptism submits to it on behalf of those who need it most. This is the logic of substitution, enacted in water before it is enacted in blood. The baptism of Jesus is the first act of the atonement.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–17 — John the Baptist and the Baptism of Jesus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: John the Baptist appears in the wilderness preaching repentance, fulfilling Isaiah's prophecy of a voice preparing the way. His ministry draws crowds from Jerusalem and all Judea, but he reserves his sharpest words for the Pharisees and Sadducees — those who came for baptism without repentance. Jesus then comes from Galilee to be baptized by John, and at his baptism the heavens open, the Spirit descends as a dove, and the Father speaks: "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased." The Trinity is present at the inauguration of the Son's public ministry. Several things the summary passes over, all treated in full below. Verse 4's clothing and diet are not a costume: camel's hair and a leather belt are Elijah's uniform (2 Kgs. 1:8), whose return was promised before the day of the LORD (Mal. 4:5); locusts were among the few insects the law permitted (Lev. 11:22) and wild honey is what the wilderness gives away, so John lives on what God provides and takes nothing from anybody — which is precisely why nobody can buy him. The Jordan itself matters: it is where Israel crossed into the land (Josh. 3), where Elijah was taken up (2 Kgs. 2), and where Naaman went down a leper and came up clean (2 Kgs. 5:14). Note the direction of travel — the crowds go out of the towns to the river, leaving the land the way their ancestors entered it and coming back in through the water. John is asking Israel to start again from the beginning. Verse 9 contains a pun English cannot show: in Aramaic, stones are abanim and children are banim — take away a letter and the rubble becomes the family of God — and he says it standing at the river where Joshua set up twelve stones from the riverbed as a memorial to the twelve tribes (Josh. 4:1-7). Verses 13-14: Nazareth to the Jordan is sixty to eighty miles, three or four days on foot; and behind that walk lie eighteen years of which Scripture says nothing at all, since Luke last showed him at twelve and now says he was about thirty. The Son of God spent roughly nine-tenths of his life on earth doing work nobody recorded — and that was not preparation for obedience, it was obedience. John's protest is an imperfect verb, "he kept trying to prevent him", and his theology in it is impeccable while his conclusion is wrong: right premises do not guarantee a right conclusion about what God will do next. Verse 15's "to fulfil all righteousness" is the answer and the hinge of the chapter — not personal repentance but substitution enacted in water before it is enacted in blood.
verseByVerse.theology: John's baptism is a baptism of repentance, anticipating the one who will baptize with the Holy Spirit and fire. He is the last of the old-covenant prophets and the first herald of the new. His insistence on fruit worthy of repentance cuts against every form of religious privilege — ancestry, tradition, institutional membership. You cannot inherit faith; you must repent. Jesus's baptism is not a baptism of personal repentance (he has no sin) but an act of identification and consecration: he enters the waters of judgment on behalf of sinners and emerges declared righteous by the Father. The Spirit's descent and the Father's voice confirm him as the inaugurator of the new age.
verseByVerse.examples: John confronted the religious establishment with their false security: "Do not presume to say to yourselves, 'We have Abraham as our father.'" The same temptation runs through every tradition — to substitute membership for repentance, heritage for faith, attendance for transformation. John's question to each worshiper is still the right one: is there fruit? Not feeling, not knowledge, not ancestry — fruit. The tree is known by what it produces.

verseByVerse.quote: In those days John the Baptist came preaching in the wilderness of Judea, "Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
About thirty years later, John the Baptist appeared in the desert of Judea with one urgent message: turn back to God, because God’s promised reign is about to arrive.

In those days. A loose time marker. Matthew jumps from Jesus’ childhood to the start of his ministry, about AD 27–29 (Luke 3:1–2, 23). Nearly thirty years pass in silence.

John the Baptist. “The Baptist” means “the one who baptises”. John was the son of the priest Zechariah and Elizabeth, a relative of Mary, born about six months before Jesus (Luke 1). He was the first prophet in Israel for about four hundred years, since Malachi. His appearance meant that God was speaking again.

Came preaching. “Preaching” (kēryssō) means proclaiming like a herald, a royal messenger announcing the king’s decree in the town square. John is not offering ideas for discussion; he is announcing news from God.

In the wilderness of Judea. The dry, rocky land between Jerusalem and the Dead Sea, falling steeply to the Jordan valley. In Israel’s history the wilderness was the place of new beginnings. Israel was formed there after the exodus; God met Moses and Elijah there; and the prophets promised that God would lead his people through the wilderness in a new exodus (Isaiah 40:3; Hosea 2:14). John’s location says: God is starting again.

Repent. Metanoeite: literally “change your mind”. But in the Bible repentance is more than changing an opinion. It translates the Hebrew idea of “turning” (shuv): turning around, turning back to God from sin. It includes a change of thinking (seeing sin as God sees it), a change of heart (sorrow for sin and hatred of it), and a change of direction (forsaking sin and turning to God in obedience). It is not merely feeling sorry, nor merely doing better, but a turning of the whole person.

For the kingdom of heaven is at hand. “The kingdom of heaven” means the kingdom of God. Matthew, writing for Jews, usually says “heaven” in place of “God”, following the Jewish habit of reverently avoiding God’s name (as in “heaven help us”). It does not mean a place, heaven where people go when they die. “Kingdom” here means reign, rule, kingship: God exercising his royal power to save his people and to judge evil, as the prophets promised (Daniel 2:44; 7:13–14; Isaiah 52:7). The Jews longed for it. “At hand” means it has come near, arriving now, in the person of the King who is about to appear.

Why repent? Because when the King comes, he comes to save and to judge. To be ready for his reign, people must turn from their rebellion and submit to him. Jesus will begin his ministry with exactly the same words (4:17).

What it does not mean. Not that repentance earns entry into the kingdom. Repentance is the turning of empty hands to God; the kingdom is his gift. Nor is repentance a single moment only: the Christian life is a life of continual repentance. The first of Luther’s ninety-five theses (1517) says that when Jesus said “Repent”, he willed the entire life of believers to be one of repentance. And “kingdom of heaven” does not mean that God’s kingdom is only spiritual and future. It is God’s rule breaking into this world now, in Jesus, and it will be complete when he returns.

Where Christians differ: the kingdom. Dispensationalists distinguish the “kingdom of heaven” (an earthly, Jewish, millennial kingdom offered to Israel and postponed when Israel rejected it) from the “kingdom of God”. Most interpreters, including the Reformed tradition, hold that the two phrases mean the same thing (compare 19:23–24, where Jesus uses them interchangeably), and that the kingdom has come in Christ, grows now through the gospel, and will be consummated at his return. Verdict: one kingdom, already inaugurated and not yet consummated.

In a sentence. John announced that God’s promised reign was arriving, and called everyone to turn from sin to God to be ready for it.

On a Tuesday. Repentance is not only for the day you became a Christian. What do you need to turn from today?
verseByVerse.note: The wilderness of Judea is the dry, barren land between Jerusalem and the Dead Sea. Matthew usually says “kingdom of heaven” where the others say “kingdom of God” — the same thing.

verseByVerse.quote: For this is he who was spoken of by the prophet Isaiah when he said, "The voice of one crying in the wilderness: 'Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight.'" Now John wore a garment of camel's hair and a leather belt around his waist, and his food was locusts and wild honey.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John was the voice Isaiah had promised, preparing the way for the Lord himself. His rough clothing and wilderness food marked him out as a prophet like Elijah.

For this is he who was spoken of by the prophet Isaiah. Isaiah 40:3. Isaiah 40 begins the great section of comfort: God speaks tenderly to his people in exile, telling them their warfare is over and their sin is pardoned, and that he himself is coming to lead them home.

The voice of one crying in the wilderness. In Isaiah, a voice calls for a road to be prepared through the wilderness for God’s coming. John is that voice. He is not the main event; he is the announcer. He described himself in these words (John 1:23).

Prepare the way of the Lord; make his paths straight. In the ancient world, before a king visited a region, workers would prepare the road: filling in potholes, levelling hills, straightening curves. John’s preaching prepares the way by preparing hearts: repentance removes the obstacles. The striking thing is whom the road is for. In Isaiah, “the Lord” is the LORD, Yahweh, God himself. Matthew applies it to Jesus. John prepares the way for Jesus, and in doing so prepares the way for God. Jesus is the LORD come to his people.

Now John wore a garment of camel’s hair and a leather belt around his waist. This is almost exactly how the Old Testament describes Elijah: a hairy man, with a belt of leather about his waist (2 Kings 1:8). John dressed as a prophet, and as the Elijah promised in Malachi 4:5–6, who would come before the great day of the Lord. Jesus confirms that John was that promised Elijah (11:14; 17:12–13).

And his food was locusts and wild honey. Locusts were permitted food under the law (Leviticus 11:22) and are still eaten by poor people in the region. Wild honey came from wild bees in the rocks. It was the diet of a man living off the land: simple, independent and austere. He was not part of the comfortable establishment of Jerusalem.

What it does not mean. Not that rough clothing or a strict diet makes someone more spiritual. Jesus later contrasted John’s austerity with his own eating and drinking, and said that both were rejected (11:18–19). John’s lifestyle fitted his particular calling as a prophet of repentance. Nor does it mean that John was literally Elijah returned from heaven: he denied that (John 1:21). He came in Elijah’s spirit and power (Luke 1:17).

In a sentence. John was the herald Isaiah foretold, dressed like Elijah, preparing hearts for the coming of the Lord, who is Jesus.

On a Tuesday. Like John, every Christian is a voice, not the main event. Point people to Christ, not to yourself.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jerusalem and all Judea and all the region about the Jordan were going out to him, and they were baptized by him in the river Jordan, confessing their sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Crowds from Jerusalem, all Judea and the Jordan valley went out to John, and he baptised them in the river Jordan as they confessed their sins.

Then Jerusalem and all Judea and all the region about the Jordan were going out to him. A great movement. “All” is a natural exaggeration for very many. People walked a day or more into the wilderness. The Jewish historian Josephus also records John’s popularity.

And they were baptized by him. To baptise (baptizō) means to dip, immerse or wash. Jews used ritual washings for purification, and Gentile converts to Judaism were washed as part of their conversion. John’s baptism was startling because he called Jews to be baptised, as if they needed to start again like outsiders. Being born a Jew was not enough.

In the river Jordan. The river where Israel had crossed into the promised land under Joshua (Joshua 3). Coming through the Jordan again pictured a new entry into the land, a new beginning as God’s people.

Confessing their sins. Confession means agreeing with God about one’s sin, naming it openly. John’s baptism was a baptism of repentance (Mark 1:4; Acts 19:4). It did not take away sin by itself; it expressed repentance and pointed forward to the forgiveness the coming one would bring.

What it does not mean. Not that John’s baptism is the same as Christian baptism. Christian baptism is into the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit (28:19), and signifies union with Christ in his death and resurrection (Romans 6:3–4). Paul rebaptised disciples who had only received John’s baptism (Acts 19:1–5). Nor does confession mean that we must list every sin to a priest to be forgiven. Confession is made to God (1 John 1:9), and sometimes to those we have wronged or to fellow believers (James 5:16).

In a sentence. Crowds went out to John and were baptised in the Jordan as a sign of repentance, openly confessing their sins.

On a Tuesday. Is there sin you have not confessed to God by name? Name it today.

verseByVerse.quote: But when he saw many of the Pharisees and Sadducees coming to his baptism, he said to them, "You brood of vipers! Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come? Bear fruit in keeping with repentance."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When John saw many of the religious leaders coming to watch or to be baptised, he denounced them as a nest of snakes and demanded proof of real repentance: a changed life.

Pharisees and Sadducees. The two leading religious parties, who normally opposed each other. The Pharisees (“separated ones”) were a lay movement, devoted to strict keeping of the law and of the oral traditions that interpreted it, and widely respected by ordinary people. They believed in the resurrection and in angels. The Sadducees were the wealthy priestly aristocracy who controlled the temple, cooperated with Rome, accepted only the five books of Moses as fully authoritative, and denied the resurrection (22:23; Acts 23:8). Here both groups come together. They will unite again against Jesus (16:1).

Coming to his baptism. Possibly to inspect it, possibly to be seen taking part. Luke 7:30 says the Pharisees rejected John’s baptism. Either way, John saw no sign of true repentance.

You brood of vipers! A brood is a family of offspring; vipers are poisonous snakes. In the desert, when a fire swept through the brush, snakes would flee in front of it. John pictures these leaders as snakes slithering away from the fire of judgment, not because they hate their sin, but because they fear the flames. It may also echo the serpent in Eden (Genesis 3): they are children of the deceiver (John 8:44). Jesus uses the same words of the Pharisees (12:34; 23:33).

Who warned you to flee from the wrath to come? “The wrath to come” is God’s coming judgment on sin at the day of the Lord (Malachi 4:1; 1 Thessalonians 1:10). John is asking sarcastically: what has suddenly made you, so confident in your righteousness, think you need to escape it?

Bear fruit in keeping with repentance. Fruit is what a tree produces, the visible result of its life. Repentance is invisible, in the heart; but real repentance shows itself in a changed life. Luke records examples: share your clothing and food with the poor; tax collectors, collect no more than you are authorised; soldiers, do not extort money (Luke 3:10–14). “In keeping with” means matching, worthy of, fitting.

What it does not mean. Not that the fruit earns forgiveness. Fruit does not make a tree good; it shows that the tree is good (7:17–18). Repentance and faith receive forgiveness as a gift; good works are the evidence that the repentance was real. Nor does John’s harshness license Christians to insult people. John spoke as a prophet with a unique role, and his anger was aimed at religious leaders who were misleading others, not at seekers or ordinary sinners, whom he received.

In a sentence. John exposed religious leaders whose fear of judgment had produced no real repentance, and demanded a changed life as its proof.

On a Tuesday. What fruit in your life shows that your repentance is real? Not perfection, but a change of direction others can see.
verseByVerse.note: Pharisees were a lay movement devoted to strict keeping of the law; Sadducees were the priestly aristocracy, who denied the resurrection.

verseByVerse.quote: And do not presume to say to yourselves, "We have Abraham as our father," for I tell you, God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham. Even now the axe is laid to the root of the trees. Every tree therefore that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John warned them not to rely on being descendants of Abraham. God could make children of Abraham out of the desert stones. Judgment was imminent, like an axe already resting against the roots of a tree: every tree that does not bear good fruit will be cut down and burned.

And do not presume to say to yourselves. Do not even think it, do not comfort yourselves with it.

We have Abraham as our father. Many Jews believed that being physically descended from Abraham guaranteed a place in God’s kingdom. Some rabbis taught that Abraham sat at the gate of Gehenna (hell) to turn back any Israelite. John says: your ancestry will not save you. Jesus makes the same point (John 8:33–44), and Paul explains that the true children of Abraham are those who share Abraham’s faith (Romans 4:11–12; Galatians 3:7).

God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham. Probably a wordplay in Hebrew or Aramaic: “children” (banim) and “stones” (abanim). Pointing to the stones of the desert, John says: God does not need you. If he wishes, he can make Abraham’s children out of rocks. This anticipates the Gentiles, “dead stones”, being brought into Abraham’s family by faith (8:11).

Even now the axe is laid to the root of the trees. A woodcutter about to fell a tree first lays his axe against its base to measure the stroke. Judgment is not far off; it is about to fall. Israel was often pictured as God’s tree or vineyard (Isaiah 5:1–7; Jeremiah 11:16).

Every tree therefore that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire. A tree that produces no fruit is useless and is cut down for firewood (Luke 13:6–9). Fire is a common biblical image of God’s judgment.

What it does not mean. Not that God had rejected the Jewish people as a whole, or that being born into a believing family is worthless. Being in a godly family is a great privilege (Romans 3:1–2; 9:4–5). But privilege does not save. Each person must repent and believe. The same applies to people raised in Christian families or churches today: a Christian upbringing is a gift, not a guarantee.

In a sentence. Religious ancestry cannot save anyone; judgment is imminent, and only a life of real repentance shows that a person is ready.

On a Tuesday. Are you relying on your Christian family, your church membership or your baptism, rather than on Christ himself? Those are gifts, but they are not faith.

parallels.desc: every tree that does not bear good fruit

verseByVerse.quote: I baptize you with water for repentance, but he who is coming after me is mightier than I, whose sandals I am not worthy to carry. He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire. His winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will clear his threshing floor and gather his wheat into the barn, but the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
John contrasted his own ministry with that of the one coming after him. John washed people with water as a sign of repentance; the Coming One, far greater, would baptise with the Holy Spirit and fire, gathering his people like grain and burning the chaff in unquenchable fire.

I baptize you with water for repentance. John’s baptism was an outward sign of repentance. Water can wash the body; it cannot change the heart.

He who is coming after me is mightier than I. “The coming one” was a title for the Messiah (11:3). John, the greatest prophet (11:11), says that the Messiah is far greater than he.

Whose sandals I am not worthy to carry. Carrying or untying a master’s sandals was a task given to the lowest slave. Some Jewish teachers said that a disciple should do anything for his teacher except handle his sandals, because that was too degrading. John says he is not worthy even of that task. John, the great prophet, knew his place.

He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit. The prophets promised that in the last days God would pour out his Spirit on his people, giving them new hearts and new life (Ezekiel 36:26–27; Joel 2:28–29). The Messiah would do this. It happened at Pentecost, when the risen Jesus poured out the Spirit (Acts 1:5; 2:1–4, 33). To baptise with the Spirit is to immerse a person in the Spirit’s life: to bring them into the new covenant, regenerating, cleansing and indwelling them. Every believer receives this (1 Corinthians 12:13).

And fire. Fire in Scripture can mean purifying (Malachi 3:2–3; Isaiah 4:4) or judgment (vv. 10, 12). The context, with fire in verse 10 and verse 12, points to judgment. The Coming One brings a double baptism: the Spirit for those who repent, fire for those who do not. Some also see a purifying sense, fulfilled in the tongues of fire at Pentecost (Acts 2:3). Verdict: chiefly judgment, though the Spirit’s work also purifies; the Messiah comes both to save and to judge.

His winnowing fork is in his hand. After harvest, grain was threshed on a flat threshing floor to loosen the husks. Then a farmer used a winnowing fork, a large wooden pitchfork, to toss it into the wind. The heavy grain fell back to the floor; the light husks and straw, called chaff, blew to one side.

He will clear his threshing floor and gather his wheat into the barn. The wheat, his true people, will be gathered and kept safe.

But the chaff he will burn with unquenchable fire. The chaff was swept up and burned. “Unquenchable” means it cannot be put out: final, eternal judgment (Isaiah 66:24; Mark 9:43–48). John’s picture is sobering: the Messiah comes not only to bless but to separate.

What it does not mean. Not that the baptism with the Spirit is a second experience after conversion that only some Christians receive. Some Pentecostal traditions teach this, often with speaking in tongues as its sign. But Paul says all believers have been baptised by one Spirit into one body (1 Corinthians 12:13). Verdict: Spirit baptism happens at conversion for every believer, though believers may be filled with the Spirit again and again (Ephesians 5:18). Nor does the warning of fire mean God delights in judgment. He is patient, not wishing that any should perish (2 Peter 3:9). But the warning is real, and John speaks it because he wants people to escape.

Where Christians differ: hell. Some evangelicals hold annihilationism: that the wicked are destroyed and cease to exist, and that the fire is unquenchable but its victims are consumed. The traditional view holds that hell is conscious, eternal punishment (25:46; Revelation 14:11). Verdict: the traditional view. Jesus sets eternal punishment beside eternal life in the same sentence (25:46).

In a sentence. The Coming One, far greater than John, will pour out the Spirit on those who repent and bring fiery judgment on those who do not.

On a Tuesday. Jesus is the Saviour who gives the Spirit, and the Judge who separates wheat from chaff. Do not take the first and ignore the second.
verseByVerse.note: A winnowing fork tossed threshed grain into the wind; the heavy grain fell back, the chaff blew away and was burned.

parallels.desc: tongues as of fire at Pentecost

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan to John, to be baptized by him. John would have prevented him, saying, "I need to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then Jesus himself came from Galilee to the Jordan to be baptised by John. John tried to stop him: he was the one who needed Jesus’ baptism, not the other way round.

Then Jesus came from Galilee. From Nazareth (2:23), about seventy miles (110 kilometres) north. This is Jesus’ first appearance as an adult in Matthew. He was about thirty years old (Luke 3:23).

To the Jordan to John, to be baptized by him. He came on purpose, for this. It is a surprise: John’s baptism was a baptism of repentance, with confession of sins. Why would the sinless Son of God (1:20–21) be baptised?

John would have prevented him. The verb means he kept trying to stop him. John recognised who Jesus was. (In John’s Gospel, the Baptist says he did not know him until the Spirit descended, John 1:31–33. Perhaps John knew Jesus personally and sensed his holiness, while the sign of the Spirit confirmed that he was the Messiah.)

I need to be baptized by you, and do you come to me? John confesses his own sin and need. He has just said that the Coming One will baptise with the Spirit (v. 11); he himself needs that. Even the greatest prophet needs the Saviour.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus came to confess his own sins. Scripture is clear that he had none (2 Corinthians 5:21; Hebrews 4:15; 1 Peter 2:22). Verse 15 explains why he was baptised.

In a sentence. Jesus came to be baptised by John, and John, knowing his own sin and Jesus’ greatness, tried to refuse.

On a Tuesday. John’s humility was the right response to Jesus: “I need you.” Can you say that to him today?

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus answered him, "Let it be so now, for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness." Then he consented. And when Jesus was baptized, immediately he went up from the water, and behold, the heavens were opened to him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming to rest on him;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus told John to go ahead, because it was right for them to fulfil all righteousness. So John baptised him. As Jesus came up from the water, heaven opened, and the Spirit of God came down on him like a dove.

Let it be so now. “Now”: for the present, at this stage of God’s plan. Jesus does not deny that he is greater than John; he asks John to accept this for now.

For thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness. The key sentence, found only in Matthew. “Righteousness” in Matthew means doing what God requires, living in line with his will (5:6, 20; 6:33). “Fulfil” is Matthew’s great word: Jesus fulfils the Scriptures and the law (5:17). Why is it right for Jesus to be baptised? Several truths fit together:

1. Identification. Jesus identifies himself with sinners. He stands with them in the water of repentance, though he has no sin of his own. This is the beginning of what the cross completes: he is numbered with the transgressors (Isaiah 53:12) and takes their place.

2. Obedience. John’s baptism was God’s command for Israel at that time (21:25). Jesus, as the true Israelite, obeys every command of God, so that his righteousness would be complete. Reformed theology calls this Christ’s active obedience: he kept the whole law perfectly on our behalf, so that his righteousness could be credited to us (Romans 5:19; 2 Corinthians 5:21).

3. Commissioning. His baptism marks the start of his public work as Messiah. As priests and kings were washed and anointed for their office (Exodus 29:4–7), Jesus is washed and anointed with the Spirit.

Then he consented. John obeyed.

And when Jesus was baptized, immediately he went up from the water. Probably out of the river, after being immersed. (The phrase does not settle the debate about the mode of baptism, though it fits immersion.)

And behold, the heavens were opened to him. Heaven opening was a sign that God was about to reveal something (Ezekiel 1:1; Acts 7:56). Isaiah had prayed that God would tear open the heavens and come down (Isaiah 64:1). Now he does.

He saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and coming to rest on him. The Spirit came visibly, in a form like a dove. The dove may recall the Spirit hovering over the waters at creation (Genesis 1:2), signalling a new creation; or the dove that brought Noah an olive leaf after the flood, a sign of new beginning and peace (Genesis 8:8–12). Isaiah had promised that the Spirit of the LORD would rest on the Messiah (Isaiah 11:2; 42:1; 61:1). “Messiah” means “anointed one”: here is his anointing, not with oil, but with the Spirit. Jesus, who as God the Son always had the Spirit, is now empowered as man for his messianic work (Acts 10:38).

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus became the Son of God at his baptism. Some early heretics (called adoptionists) taught that Jesus was an ordinary man adopted as God’s Son at his baptism. But Matthew has already shown that he was conceived by the Spirit and is Immanuel, God with us (1:20–23). The baptism publicly declares and equips who he already was. Nor was the Spirit a literal dove: Matthew says “like a dove”.

In a sentence. Jesus was baptised to stand with sinners and fulfil every righteous requirement on their behalf, and he was anointed with the Spirit for his work as Messiah.

On a Tuesday. Jesus obeyed perfectly for you, including in things he did not personally need. His obedience is credited to everyone who trusts him. Rest in his righteousness, not yours.
verseByVerse.note: Only Matthew records John’s protest and Jesus’ reply.

verseByVerse.quote: and behold, a voice from heaven said, "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the Father spoke from heaven: this is my beloved Son, in whom I delight. At the start of Jesus’ ministry, Father, Son and Spirit are all revealed together.

And behold, a voice from heaven said. God the Father speaks. Jews in Jesus’ time spoke of a “daughter of the voice” (bat qol), an echo of God’s voice, since prophecy had ceased. Here is not an echo but God’s own voice.

This is my beloved Son. Echoes Psalm 2:7, where God says to his anointed King, you are my Son. It declares Jesus as the royal Messiah, the Son of David (2 Samuel 7:14). But “beloved Son” also recalls Genesis 22:2, where God told Abraham to take his son, his only son, whom he loved, Isaac, and offer him as a sacrifice. The beloved Son will be offered. And it goes deeper still: Jesus is the Son of God not merely as a title of kingship, but by nature, the eternal Son (11:27).

With whom I am well pleased. Echoes Isaiah 42:1, about the Servant of the LORD: my chosen, in whom my soul delights; I have put my Spirit upon him. The Servant in Isaiah suffers and dies for the sins of the people (Isaiah 53). In one sentence, the Father declares Jesus to be both the royal Son of Psalm 2 and the suffering Servant of Isaiah: a King who will reign by suffering. “Well pleased” means delighted, entirely approving. Before Jesus has performed a single miracle or preached a single sermon in Matthew, the Father delights in him, after thirty years of hidden obedience.

The Trinity. Here the three persons of the Trinity appear together, each distinct: the Father speaking from heaven, the Son standing in the water, the Spirit descending. One God in three persons. The church has always seen this as one of the clearest pictures of the Trinity in Scripture. The same three names appear at the end of the Gospel in the baptismal command (28:19).

For believers. Because believers are united to Christ, the Father’s love for his Son reaches them. In Christ, God says to every believer: you are my beloved child (Ephesians 1:6; 1 John 3:1). This is the ground of our assurance, not our performance.

What it does not mean. Not that there are three gods, or that one God appears in three different modes at different times (the error called modalism). Here all three persons are present at the same moment, distinct from one another, yet one God.

Textual note. Matthew has “This is my beloved Son”, spoken about Jesus; Mark and Luke have “You are my beloved Son”, spoken to him (Mark 1:11; Luke 3:22). The Gospel writers often report speech by its sense rather than word for word. Matthew’s form stresses the public declaration to the witnesses.

In a sentence. The Father declared Jesus his beloved Son and delighted Servant, as the Spirit came on him: the whole Trinity revealed at the start of his ministry.

For worship. Worship the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. And if you are in Christ, hear the Father’s delight in his Son as spoken over you too.

parallels.desc: the servant in whom God delights
the same voice at the transfiguration

3.theology:
The Trinity at the Jordan. Matthew 3:16–17 is one of the clearest Trinitarian texts in the New Testament. The Son stands in the water; the Spirit descends upon the Son; the Father speaks from heaven. Three distinct persons, one divine act. Reformed theology has always insisted that the doctrine of the Trinity is not a late addition to Christian thought but the grammar of the gospel itself — the structure of reality that makes salvation possible.

The baptism of Jesus is a Trinitarian event. The Father approves; the Spirit empowers; the Son obeys. This pattern runs through the whole New Testament: the Father sends, the Son accomplishes, the Spirit applies. The atonement is Trinitarian (the Father gave, the Son died, the Spirit regenerates); the church is Trinitarian (baptised in the name of Father, Son, and Spirit, Matt. 28:19); the Christian life is Trinitarian (praying to the Father, through the Son, in the Spirit). The Jordan reveals the shape of everything that follows.
3.examples:
Then: John the Baptist stands in a long line of prophets who prepared the way for God’s action: Moses before Joshua, Elijah before Elisha, Isaiah before the return from exile. Each was a voice, not the Word; each pointed away from himself. John is the culmination of this pattern — the last and greatest of the preparers. His greatness lay precisely in his self-effacement: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30). Every faithful preacher, teacher, and leader stands in John’s tradition: making straight the way, getting out of the way.

Now: The Father’s declaration over Jesus at the baptism — This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased — is the word every human being is searching for. We spend our lives seeking approval: from parents, employers, social media, achievement. The gospel announces that in Christ, the deepest possible approval has already been given — not because of what we have done but because of who he is and what he has done. The restless search for significance ends not in achievement but in adoption: we are accepted in the Beloved. That is the word the Father spoke at the Jordan, and it is addressed to everyone who is hidden with Christ in God (Col. 3:3).

4.title: The Tested King
4.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Jesus was led up by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil. <sup>2</sup>And after fasting forty days and forty nights, he was hungry. <sup>3</sup>And the tempter came and said to him, “If you are the Son of God, command these stones to become loaves of bread.” <sup>4</sup>But he answered, “It is written, ‘Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God.’” <sup>5</sup>Then the devil took him to the holy city and set him on the pinnacle of the temple <sup>6</sup>and said to him, “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down, for it is written, ‘He will command his angels concerning you,’ and ‘On their hands they will bear you up, lest you strike your foot against a stone.’” <sup>7</sup>Jesus said to him, “Again it is written, ‘You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.’” <sup>8</sup>Again, the devil took him to a very high mountain and showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory. <sup>9</sup>And he said to him, “All these I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me.” <sup>10</sup>Then Jesus said to him, “Be gone, Satan! For it is written, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God and him only shall you serve.’” <sup>11</sup>Then the devil left him, and behold, angels came and were ministering to him. <sup>12</sup>Now when he heard that John had been arrested, he withdrew into Galilee. <sup>13</sup>And leaving Nazareth he went and lived in Capernaum by the sea, in the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali, <sup>14</sup>so that what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled: <sup>15</sup>“The land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, the way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles — <sup>16</sup>the people dwelling in darkness have seen a great light, and for those dwelling in the region and shadow of death, on them a light has dawned.” <sup>17</sup>From that time Jesus began to preach, saying, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand.” <sup>18</sup>While walking by the Sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers, Simon (who is called Peter) and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen. <sup>19</sup>And he said to them, “Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men.” <sup>20</sup>Immediately they left their nets and followed him. <sup>21</sup>And going on from there he saw two other brothers, James the son of Zebedee and John his brother, in the boat with Zebedee their father, mending their nets, and he called them. <sup>22</sup>Immediately they left the boat and their father and followed him. <sup>23</sup>And he went throughout all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues and proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom and healing every disease and every affliction among the people. <sup>24</sup>So his fame spread throughout all Syria, and they brought him all the sick, those afflicted with various diseases and pains, those oppressed by demons, those having seizures, and paralytics, and he healed them. <sup>25</sup>And great crowds followed him from Galilee and the Decapolis, and from Jerusalem and Judea, and from beyond the Jordan.
4.overview:
Chapter 4 is the axis on which the Gospel turns. The Spirit who descended at the baptism immediately drives Jesus into the wilderness — not as abandonment but as commission. The forty days echo Israel’s forty years in the wilderness, where God’s people failed at every test. Jesus succeeds at every one, and he does it using the same weapon available to Israel and to us: the written Word of God. Three times the devil attacks; three times Jesus answers with Deuteronomy. The true Israel passes where the nation failed.

Each temptation targets a specific aspect of Jesus’ identity and mission. Turn stones to bread: use divine power for personal comfort. Throw yourself from the temple: leverage God’s promises for public spectacle. Bow to me: gain the kingdoms without the cross. Every temptation is a shortcut past suffering to glory — and Jesus refuses every one. There is no crown without the cross, no glory without the grave, no kingdom without Calvary. Satan offers the destination without the path; Jesus insists on the path.

Then the ministry begins — in Galilee of the Gentiles (Isa. 9:1), the region of mixed ethnicity and questionable reputation, the last place a respectable rabbi would choose as his base. The people dwelling in darkness have seen a great light. The light does not go to the well-lit; it goes to the dark. And the first disciples he calls are working men with nets and boats — not scribes with scrolls. The kingdom of heaven is staffed from the margins, then and now.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — The Temptation of Jesus in the Wilderness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Immediately after his baptism, the Spirit leads Jesus into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil. The forty days echo Israel's forty years in the wilderness; the three temptations echo Israel's great failures — bread, testing God, idolatry. But where Israel fell, Jesus stands. He defeats each temptation not by miraculous power but by the word of God alone, quoting Deuteronomy three times. The temptations are not trivial: they are the offer of the kingdom by a shortcut — bread without suffering, glory without the cross, dominion without death. And he overcomes not merely as our example but as our champion — the last Adam and true Israel, whose perfect obedience is reckoned to all who are his, so that we now resist temptation not to win God's favor but from within the victory he has already won for us. Two things the summary passes over. Verse 2's hunger is the ground of the first temptation — the devil does not waste his best offer on a man with full hands, and he waits for the sixth week. And verse 11 is not the end of the matter: Luke adds that the devil departed "until an opportune time" (Lk. 4:13), and Matthew shows where those times came. At Caesarea Philippi, when Peter says the suffering shall never happen, Jesus answers with the same words he used here — "Get behind me, Satan" (16:23) — because it is the same offer, the crown without the cross, arriving from a friend. And at Golgotha the passers-by shout "if you are the Son of God, come down from the cross" (27:40), which is the identical formula the devil used twice in this wilderness (vv. 3, 6). The temptation that opens the ministry is the temptation that closes it. Note also the quiet irony of the angels: the devil had proposed a scenario in which angels would catch him spectacularly before a temple crowd, and Jesus refused — so they come instead in an empty desert with nobody watching, and the verb is an imperfect (they kept ministering) of the ordinary word for waiting at table. What he would not seize, he was given.
verseByVerse.theology: The temptation of Jesus is not merely a test of personal willpower but a cosmic conflict at the hinge of redemptive history. The devil who succeeded in Eden now faces the second Adam in a wilderness, and loses. Jesus is revealed as the true Israel — obedient where the nation failed — and the true Adam — resisting the serpent where the first man did not. His weapon is the word of God alone: not angelic power, not divine fiat, but the Scripture he has internalized and believes. This models the Christian's resource in temptation: not mystical experience but the word of God believed and obeyed.
verseByVerse.examples: The devil's three temptations all contain a kernel of legitimate desire: food is not evil, protection is real, authority over the nations is Jesus's ultimate inheritance. The temptation is in the shortcut — get the good thing the wrong way, on the wrong timetable, from the wrong source. This is how temptation almost always works: it offers real goods through illegitimate means. Jesus refuses not because the ends are bad but because the path bypasses the Father's will and the cross's necessity.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jesus was led up by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil. And after fasting forty days and forty nights, he was hungry.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Straight after his baptism, the Spirit led Jesus into the desert to be tested by the devil. After forty days without food, he was hungry. Where Adam fell in a garden and Israel failed in the wilderness, Jesus, the true Son, would stand.

Then. Immediately after the Father declared him his beloved Son (3:17). The order matters: first the Father’s word of love, then the testing. Jesus faced the devil secure in the Father’s delight. And the devil’s first attack goes straight at that word: “If you are the Son of God” (v. 3).

Jesus was led up by the Spirit. The temptation was not an accident or a defeat. God the Spirit led Jesus into it, deliberately. The same Spirit who had just come upon him (3:16) now directs him. God’s purpose was to prove his Son faithful and to begin his victory over the devil.

Into the wilderness. The Judean desert, the barren land near the Jordan (see 3:1). Israel spent forty years in the wilderness after passing through the Red Sea (1 Corinthians 10:1–2). Jesus, having passed through the water of baptism, now goes into the wilderness. He relives Israel’s story (see 2:15).

To be tempted by the devil. “Tempt” (peirazō) means both to test and to tempt. From God’s side, this was a test, to prove his Son’s faithfulness, as God tested Israel in the wilderness to know what was in their heart (Deuteronomy 8:2). From the devil’s side, it was a temptation, an attempt to make him sin. “Devil” (diabolos) means slanderer, accuser. He is a real, personal, fallen angel, the enemy of God and his people (John 8:44; Revelation 12:9). He tempted the first Adam in the garden and succeeded (Genesis 3). Now he tempts the last Adam (1 Corinthians 15:45).

After fasting forty days and forty nights. Forty is a significant number in Scripture: Moses fasted forty days and nights on the mountain when he received the law (Exodus 34:28); Elijah travelled forty days and nights to Mount Horeb (1 Kings 19:8); Israel wandered forty years in the wilderness (Numbers 14:33–34). Jesus’ fast connects him with Moses, Elijah and Israel. Fasting means going without food for a spiritual purpose, to focus on God.

He was hungry. An understatement. After forty days a human body is near starvation. Jesus was truly human, with real hunger and real weakness. The devil attacked him at his weakest point.

The three temptations. The three temptations that follow correspond to three tests of Israel in the wilderness, and Jesus answers each with a verse from Deuteronomy 6–8, where Moses reminds Israel of those tests. Israel grumbled for bread, put God to the test, and worshipped idols. Jesus trusts, does not test God, and worships God alone. Where Israel failed, the true Son succeeds.

What it does not mean. Not that God tempts anyone to sin. James says that God tempts no one (James 1:13). God tested Jesus; the devil tempted him. The same event can be both: God’s purpose for good, the devil’s for evil (Genesis 50:20). Nor does it mean that being tempted is itself sinful. Jesus was tempted in every respect as we are, yet without sin (Hebrews 4:15). Temptation is the offer of sin; sin is accepting it. A believer who is fiercely tempted has not sinned by being tempted.

Where Christians differ: could Jesus have sinned? Some say Jesus was able not to sin, but could have sinned, otherwise the temptations were not real. Most of the Reformed tradition holds that Jesus was not able to sin, because he was the eternal Son of God, who cannot sin. Verdict: he could not sin, yet the temptations were entirely real. A strong army cannot be defeated, but the attack against it is still real; indeed, only one who does not give in feels the full weight of temptation to the end. Jesus knows the pressure of temptation more fully than anyone.

In a sentence. The Spirit led Jesus into the desert to be tempted, so that as the true Israel and the last Adam he would stand where they had fallen.

On a Tuesday. Temptation often comes right after a high point, and at your weakest moment. Expect it, and remember that facing temptation is not the same as sinning.
verseByVerse.note: Forty days recalls Moses on the mountain and Israel’s forty years in the wilderness.

parallels.desc: tempted as we are, yet without sin

verseByVerse.quote: And the tempter came and said to him, "If you are the Son of God, command these stones to become loaves of bread." But he answered, "It is written, 'Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The devil’s first temptation: if you are God’s Son, use your power to turn these stones into bread. Jesus answered from Scripture: people do not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from God. He would trust his Father rather than use his power for himself.

The tempter came. The devil is called “the tempter”: that is his work (1 Thessalonians 3:5).

If you are the Son of God. The grammar in Greek assumes that it is true: “Since you are the Son of God”. The devil is not doubting it; he is twisting it. The Father had just said, “This is my beloved Son” (3:17). The devil says, in effect: if you are his Son, act like one. Use your rights. Look after yourself. Why should God’s beloved Son go hungry?

Command these stones to become loaves of bread. The desert was littered with stones the size and shape of small loaves. Was making bread wrong? Jesus later fed five thousand people (14:13–21).
