The temptation was to use his divine power for his own benefit, outside his Father’s will, and to escape the path of humble dependence the Father had given him. It was a temptation to distrust: to doubt that the Father would provide, and to take matters into his own hands. Israel did the same in the wilderness, complaining that God had brought them out to starve (Exodus 16:3).

But he answered, “It is written”. Jesus answers with Scripture. “It is written” is a perfect tense in Greek: it stands written, and remains true and authoritative. Jesus, the Son of God, submits to the written word, and uses it as his weapon (Ephesians 6:17).

Man shall not live by bread alone. From Deuteronomy 8:3. Moses tells Israel that God humbled them, let them hunger, and fed them with manna in the wilderness, so that they would learn that people do not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from God’s mouth. Physical life depends on food, but true life depends on God’s word: his promises, his commands, his will. Bread keeps the body alive for a while; God’s word gives life now and for ever.

But by every word that comes from the mouth of God. Jesus would rather be hungry and obedient than full and disobedient. He trusts that the Father who led him into the wilderness will sustain him. And he did: angels came and served him (v. 11). Jesus later said that his food was to do the will of the one who sent him (John 4:34).

What it does not mean. Not that physical needs do not matter. Jesus teaches us to pray for daily bread (6:11), and he fed the hungry. The point is the order: God’s word and will come first, and we trust him for the rest (6:33). Nor does it mean that quoting Scripture is a magic formula. Jesus quoted it because he believed it and lived by it.

In a sentence. Jesus refused to use his power to satisfy his hunger outside God’s will, because true life comes from trusting and obeying God’s word.

On a Tuesday. Where are you tempted to meet a real need in a wrong way, or a hurried way, instead of trusting God? Answer the temptation with a specific word from Scripture.

parallels.desc: man does not live by bread alone

verseByVerse.quote: Then the devil took him to the holy city and set him on the pinnacle of the temple, and said to him, "If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down, for it is written, 'He will command his angels concerning you,' and 'On their hands they will bear you up, lest you strike your foot against a stone.'" Jesus said to him, "Again it is written, 'You shall not put the Lord your God to the test.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Next, the devil took Jesus to the highest point of the temple and dared him to throw himself down, quoting a psalm that promises angels would catch him. Jesus answered with Scripture again: do not put the Lord your God to the test.

Then the devil took him to the holy city. Jerusalem, called “the holy city” because the temple was there (Nehemiah 11:1; Isaiah 52:1). Whether this happened physically or in a vision, the temptation was real.

And set him on the pinnacle of the temple. The pinnacle (literally “little wing”) was probably the southeast corner of the temple courts, where the wall towered high above the Kidron Valley. The Jewish historian Josephus said that looking down from there made a person dizzy.

If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down. Again the challenge to the Father’s word (3:17). The devil suggests: prove that God loves you. Force him to show his care. Perhaps also: give the crowds in the temple a spectacular sign, so that they will accept you without the cross.

For it is written. Now the devil quotes Scripture too, imitating Jesus’ method. The devil knows the Bible and uses it.

He will command his angels concerning you. From Psalm 91:11–12. The psalm promises God’s protection to those who trust him: he will send his angels to guard you, so that you will not even strike your foot against a stone. But the devil leaves out a phrase, “to guard you in all your ways”, meaning the paths of ordinary obedience. And he twists the meaning: the psalm promises protection for those who trust God in danger, not for those who deliberately throw themselves into danger to force God’s hand. It is a promise to the humble, not a licence for the presumptuous.

Jesus said to him, “Again it is written”. Jesus does not argue about the psalm. He answers Scripture with Scripture, showing that the Bible must be interpreted by the Bible. One verse must not be set against the rest.

You shall not put the Lord your God to the test. From Deuteronomy 6:16, which refers to Massah, where Israel, thirsty in the wilderness, demanded water and asked, “Is the LORD among us or not?” (Exodus 17:1–7). To put God to the test is to demand that he prove himself on our terms, to create a crisis and dare him to act. It is not faith, but its opposite: it is refusing to trust God unless he gives a proof we have chosen.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should never ask God for help or for guidance in danger. Faith trusts God when danger comes; presumption creates the danger and demands rescue. Nor is it wrong to quote Scripture: the problem is quoting it out of context to support what we already want. The devil can quote the Bible; we must read it whole.

In a sentence. Jesus refused to force God to prove his love by a spectacular rescue, because true faith trusts God without testing him.

On a Tuesday. Are you taking foolish risks with your health, money or morals, and expecting God to rescue you? That is not faith but presumption. And when someone quotes a verse to justify sin, ask what the rest of the Bible says.
verseByVerse.note: The pinnacle was a high point of the temple complex, perhaps a corner of its outer wall. The devil quotes Scripture but cuts it short.

parallels.desc: Israel tests the LORD at Massah

verseByVerse.quote: Again, the devil took him to a very high mountain and showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory. And he said to him, "All these I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me." Then Jesus said to him, "Be gone, Satan! For it is written, 'You shall worship the Lord your God and him only shall you serve.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Finally, the devil showed Jesus all the kingdoms of the world and their splendour, and offered them all to him in exchange for one act of worship. Jesus sent him away: worship the Lord your God and serve him only.

A very high mountain. Mountains in Matthew are places of revelation: the Sermon on the Mount (5:1), the transfiguration (17:1), and the Great Commission (28:16). This mountain is a counterfeit.

Showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory. Probably a vision. Luke says it was in a moment of time (Luke 4:5). The wealth, power and splendour of every empire.

All these I will give you. The devil claims authority over the world’s kingdoms (Luke 4:6). Jesus calls him the ruler of this world (John 12:31), and John says the whole world lies in the power of the evil one (1 John 5:19). But his authority is borrowed and limited; it is not truly his to give.

If you will fall down and worship me. The real offer: the crown without the cross. Jesus had come to receive all authority in heaven and on earth (28:18), but by way of suffering and death (Philippians 2:8–11). The devil offers a shortcut: power now, without the cross, if only Jesus will bow to him. It is the temptation to gain good ends by evil means, and to gain the world by compromising worship.

Be gone, Satan! “Satan” is Hebrew for “adversary”. Jesus commands, and the devil must obey. Later Jesus uses the same words to Peter when Peter tells him he must not go to the cross (16:23). The temptation to avoid the cross came again, through a friend.

For it is written, “You shall worship the Lord your God and him only shall you serve.” From Deuteronomy 6:13, the command that follows the great confession, the LORD is one (Deuteronomy 6:4). In the wilderness Israel made a golden calf and worshipped it (Exodus 32). Jesus worships God alone. He will receive the kingdoms, but from his Father, not from the devil, and by obedience, not compromise.

The three temptations together. The first appealed to physical need, the second to spiritual pride, the third to power and ambition. John later describes the world’s temptations as the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes, and the pride of life (1 John 2:16). Eve saw that the fruit was good for food, a delight to the eyes, and desirable to make one wise (Genesis 3:6). Jesus faced the same kinds of temptation, and conquered.

What it does not mean. Not that power, wealth or influence are evil in themselves. Christ will reign over all kingdoms (Revelation 11:15). The question is how they are gained and whom they serve. Nor does Jesus’ victory mean we can conquer temptation in our own strength. We overcome in him: he was victorious for us, and we share his victory as we trust him and use the same weapon, God’s word.

In a sentence. Jesus refused the devil’s offer of power without the cross, and worshipped God alone.

On a Tuesday. Where are you tempted to take a shortcut to something good by compromising your loyalty to God: a promotion, a relationship, influence? The crown comes by the way of the cross.
verseByVerse.note: “Satan” means adversary.

parallels.desc: worship and serve the LORD alone

verseByVerse.quote: Then the devil left him, and behold, angels came and were ministering to him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Defeated, the devil left Jesus, and angels came and cared for him.

Then the devil left him. He had to: Jesus had commanded him to go (v. 10). Luke adds that he left until an opportune time (Luke 4:13). The battle would continue throughout Jesus’ ministry, and reach its climax at the cross. But this first round was won.

And behold, angels came and were ministering to him. “Ministering” (diakoneō) means serving, especially serving food (8:15). Jesus had refused to make bread for himself; now God provided for him. He had refused to call on angels to rescue him from a fall (v. 6); now angels came to serve him on God’s terms. Elijah was fed by an angel in the wilderness (1 Kings 19:5–8). The Father did what Jesus trusted him to do.

The victory. Adam, in a garden, with every tree but one available, gave in. Israel, fed with manna, grumbled and fell. Jesus, starving in a desert, stood firm. He is the true Son, the faithful Israel, the last Adam. His victory here is the beginning of his work for us. Because he resisted temptation perfectly, he is our perfect substitute and our sympathetic High Priest (Hebrews 2:18; 4:15–16).

What it does not mean. Not that believers will never feel the devil’s attacks after resisting once. The attacks return. But if we resist him, he will flee (James 4:7), and God will provide what we need.

In a sentence. When Jesus had defeated the devil, God sent angels to care for him, providing what he had trusted the Father for.

On a Tuesday. When you are tempted, run to Jesus. He has been there, he understands, and he can help you (Hebrews 2:18). And trust God to provide what you refused to grab.

For worship. Thank Christ that he stood where Adam fell, and that his victory is counted for you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–25 — The Beginning of Ministry in Galilee
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After John's arrest, Jesus withdraws to Galilee and settles in Capernaum, fulfilling Isaiah's prophecy about light dawning in the land of Zebulun and Naphtali. He begins preaching the same message as John — "Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand" — and immediately calls his first disciples: Peter, Andrew, James, and John. They leave their nets and their father without delay and follow him. Matthew concludes with a summary of Jesus's ministry: teaching in synagogues, proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom, and healing every disease and affliction, drawing crowds from all of Syria and the surrounding regions. Three details more. The word for John's arrest (v. 12) is paradidomi, to be handed over — not the ordinary word for a legal arrest, but the very verb Matthew will use of Jesus again and again (17:22; 20:18; 26:2), and of what Judas, the council and Pilate each do. The forerunner goes before him in this too. And "he withdrew" is anachoreo, a favourite of Matthew's for keeping to a timetable his enemies are not setting (2:14, 22; 12:15; 14:13; 15:21) — never presented as cowardice. Capernaum has been excavated: a fishing village of perhaps 1,500 on the Via Maris, with a customs house (Matthew's own booth was there, 9:9) and a small garrison (hence the centurion of ch. 8). He based himself among tax collectors, soldiers, fishermen and foreigners passing through. And Zebulun and Naphtali were not chosen at random by Isaiah: they were the first tribes deported, carried off by Tiglath-Pileser in 733 BC (2 Kgs. 15:29), a decade before Samaria fell. They went into the dark first — which is exactly why Isaiah 9:1 promises the light dawns there first. God begins the repair at the place that broke earliest.
verseByVerse.theology: Jesus's settlement in Galilee of the Gentiles fulfills Isaiah 9:1–2: the regions most despised in Israel — the northern territories given first to Assyrian darkness — receive the first light of the kingdom. This is the pattern of the kingdom: light to the edges, hope to the marginalized, the first shall be last and the last first. The calling of the disciples is not recruitment but sovereign summons: "Follow me" is a command, not an invitation to consider. Their immediate response models discipleship — not eventual obedience after weighing options, but the abandonment of everything for the one who calls.
verseByVerse.examples: The disciples left their nets immediately. They left their boats. James and John left their father. The commentaries note what Matthew stresses: the immediacy and totality of their response. Jesus did not give them time to consult, calculate, or negotiate terms. He called; they followed. This is the New Testament pattern of conversion — not gradual warming to the idea of Jesus but the decisive moment of abandonment and allegiance. The question the passage presses: what are your nets? What would obedience cost you to leave behind?

verseByVerse.quote: Now when he heard that John had been arrested, he withdrew into Galilee. And leaving Nazareth he went and lived in Capernaum by the sea, in the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali,
verseByVerse.commentary:
When Jesus heard that John the Baptist had been arrested, he went back to Galilee. He left Nazareth and made his home in Capernaum, a town by the Sea of Galilee in the old tribal lands of Zebulun and Naphtali.

When he heard that John had been arrested. Literally “handed over”. Herod Antipas, ruler of Galilee, had imprisoned John because John condemned him for marrying his brother’s wife (14:3–4). John’s arrest marked the end of his ministry and the start of Jesus’ public ministry in Galilee. The word “handed over” is later used of Jesus being handed over to death (17:22; 26:2). The forerunner’s fate foreshadows the Messiah’s.

He withdrew into Galilee. Not fleeing in fear, since Galilee was Herod’s territory too. Matthew uses “withdrew” several times when Jesus moves away from opposition (12:15; 14:13). Each time, God’s plan moves forward.

And leaving Nazareth. His hometown, where he had grown up (2:23). Luke tells us that Nazareth rejected him (Luke 4:16–30).

He went and lived in Capernaum by the sea. Capernaum was a prosperous fishing town on the northwest shore of the Sea of Galilee, on a major trade route, with a customs office (9:9) and a Roman garrison (8:5). It became the base of Jesus’ Galilean ministry, called his own city (9:1). Peter’s house was there (8:14). Archaeologists have found remains of its synagogue and of a house venerated from early times as Peter’s.

In the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali. Two of the twelve tribes of Israel had been given these lands in Galilee (Joshua 19). They were among the first parts of Israel to be conquered and deported by Assyria, around 732 BC (2 Kings 15:29). After that, many Gentiles settled there, and the region was considered spiritually dark and mixed.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus’ move was merely practical or accidental. Matthew immediately shows it fulfilled Scripture (vv. 14–16). God placed his Son exactly where Isaiah said the light would dawn.

In a sentence. After John’s arrest, Jesus began his ministry from Capernaum in Galilee, in the lands that had first fallen into darkness.

On a Tuesday. God often moves his servants through events they did not choose, a closed door, an arrest, a rejection, to the places where he wants them.
verseByVerse.note: Zebulun and Naphtali were tribal territories in Galilee, among the first to fall to Assyria.

verseByVerse.quote: so that what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled: "The land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, the way of the sea, beyond the Jordan, Galilee of the Gentiles —"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus’ move to Galilee fulfilled Isaiah’s prophecy about the lands of Zebulun and Naphtali, the region by the sea and across the Jordan, “Galilee of the Gentiles”.

So that what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled. Isaiah 9:1–2. The context in Isaiah is important. Isaiah 8 ends with darkness and distress as Assyria invades. Isaiah 9 begins with hope: the lands that were first humbled will be the first made glorious. And then comes the great promise: for to us a child is born, to us a son is given; and the government shall be upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called Wonderful Counsellor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, Prince of Peace (Isaiah 9:6). Matthew is saying: the child of Isaiah 9 has come, and he has come first to the very region Isaiah named.

The land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali. See verse 13.

The way of the sea. The ancient trade route that ran along the Sea of Galilee toward the Mediterranean coast and Damascus. Galilee was a crossroads of nations.

Beyond the Jordan. The region east of the Jordan river, also once part of Israel.

Galilee of the Gentiles. “Galilee of the nations”. After the Assyrian conquest, Galilee had a mixed population of Jews and Gentiles. People in Jerusalem looked down on Galileans as half-pagan and unsophisticated, with a strong accent (26:73; John 7:52). This is the place the Messiah chose to begin.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus’ ministry was mainly to Gentiles at this stage. He went first to the lost sheep of Israel (10:6; 15:24). But beginning in “Galilee of the Gentiles” was a sign of where the gospel was heading: to all nations (28:19).

In a sentence. Jesus began his ministry in despised, mixed Galilee, exactly where Isaiah promised the Messiah’s light would first shine.

On a Tuesday. God’s light often reaches first the places and people others write off. Where is the “Galilee” near you that your church overlooks?
verseByVerse.note: “Galilee of the Gentiles”: the region had a mixed population, looked down on by Judeans.

verseByVerse.quote: "the people dwelling in darkness have seen a great light, and for those dwelling in the region and shadow of death, on them a light has dawned."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Isaiah’s prophecy continues: people living in darkness have seen a great light; on those who lived in the land of the shadow of death, light has dawned. In Jesus, that light has come.

The people dwelling in darkness. Darkness in Scripture pictures ignorance of God, sin, misery and death (Ephesians 4:18; 5:8). The people of Galilee lived in political darkness (conquered and occupied), spiritual darkness (far from the temple, mixed with pagans), and the darkness of sin that covers every human life.

Have seen a great light. Light pictures God’s presence, truth, salvation and life (Psalm 27:1; John 8:12). The light is not a doctrine but a person: Jesus himself.

The region and shadow of death. Literally “the land and shadow of death”, a phrase from Psalm 23:4 (“the valley of the shadow of death”). It describes deep darkness, where death’s power looms over life.

On them a light has dawned. Like the sunrise after a long night. Zechariah had sung of the sunrise from on high visiting those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death (Luke 1:78–79). Light does not have to be earned; it simply comes, and darkness cannot stop it (John 1:5).

What it does not mean. Not that everyone who saw Jesus received the light. Many in Galilee, including Capernaum, rejected him (11:23). Light shining is not the same as eyes opened (John 3:19).

In a sentence. In Jesus, the great light Isaiah promised dawned on people living in the darkness and shadow of death.

For worship. Thank God that the light has dawned on you, in Christ, and pray for those still sitting in the shadow.

parallels.desc: “I am the light of the world”

verseByVerse.quote: From that time Jesus began to preach, saying, "Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
From then on, Jesus began to preach the same message John had preached: turn back to God, because the kingdom of heaven has come near.

From that time Jesus began. A turning point. Matthew uses this phrase twice to mark the two great sections of his Gospel: here, as Jesus begins his public ministry, and at 16:21, as he begins to tell his disciples that he must suffer and die.

To preach. To proclaim as a herald (see 3:1).

Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand. Word for word the message of John (3:2). But with a difference. John announced the coming King; Jesus is the King. In Jesus, the kingdom has arrived. His preaching, his healings and his casting out of demons are signs that God’s reign is breaking in (12:28). The message has two parts: an announcement (the kingdom is here) and a command (repent). The announcement is good news, which is why Matthew calls it the gospel of the kingdom (v. 23). Mark adds, “and believe in the gospel” (Mark 1:15). Repentance and faith are two sides of one turning: turning from sin, and turning to God in trust.

What it does not mean. Not that Jesus’ message was only moral reform: “stop sinning and be good”. It is first good news about what God is doing, and the call to repent is the response to that news. Nor does “at hand” mean that Jesus expected the end of the world within a few years and was mistaken. The kingdom came near in his person, and it continues to grow until its full arrival at his return (13:31–33).

In a sentence. Jesus began his ministry announcing that God’s kingdom had arrived in him, and calling people to turn to God.

On a Tuesday. The gospel is first news to believe, then a call to turn. Share both parts when you speak of Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: While walking by the Sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers, Simon (who is called Peter) and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen. And he said to them, "Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men." Immediately they left their nets and followed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Walking by the Sea of Galilee, Jesus saw two brothers, Simon Peter and Andrew, fishing with a net. He called them to follow him, promising to make them fishers of people, and they left their nets at once and followed him.

The Sea of Galilee. A freshwater lake about thirteen miles (21 kilometres) long and eight (13 kilometres) wide, lying about seven hundred feet (210 metres) below sea level. It was full of fish, and fishing was a major industry. Fish were salted and exported across the region.

Simon (who is called Peter). Simon was his name; Jesus later gave him the name Peter, meaning “rock” (16:18; John 1:42). He would become the leader of the Twelve.

And Andrew his brother. Andrew had been a disciple of John the Baptist, and had first met Jesus at the Jordan and brought Peter to him (John 1:35–42). So this was not their first meeting with Jesus. They already knew him; now he calls them to leave everything and follow him permanently.

Casting a net into the sea. A casting net was circular, about fifteen to twenty feet across, weighted around the edge. The fisherman threw it over shallow water so that it spread out and sank over the fish.

Follow me. Literally “Come behind me”. In Jesus’ time, students chose their rabbi and applied to study with him. Jesus reverses this: he chooses and calls his disciples (John 15:16). And he does not call them to follow a set of teachings or a law, but to follow him personally. Discipleship is attachment to a person.

And I will make you fishers of men. “Men” means people. Jesus uses their trade as a picture of their new calling. As they had caught fish, they would now gather people into God’s kingdom. Notice “I will make you”: Jesus takes responsibility for training them. They do not need to be qualified; he will make them what he calls them to be. (In Jeremiah 16:16, fishermen are sent to gather people for judgment; Jesus’ fishermen gather people for salvation.)

Immediately they left their nets and followed him. Their nets were their livelihood, their business, their security. They left them at once. Following Jesus has a cost, and it comes first.

What it does not mean. Not that every Christian must leave their job to follow Christ. Peter and Andrew were called to be apostles, a special calling. Most believers follow Christ in their ordinary work (1 Corinthians 7:17–24). But every Christian must be willing to leave anything that stands in the way of following him (10:37–39), and every Christian is called to bring others to him.

In a sentence. Jesus called fishermen to leave their nets and follow him, promising to make them gatherers of people for God’s kingdom.

On a Tuesday. What are your “nets”, the things you rely on for security? Hold them loosely enough that you could leave them if Christ asked. And ask him to make you a fisher of people where you are.
verseByVerse.note: A casting net was a round net thrown by hand into shallow water.

parallels.desc: Luke’s account of the call by the lake
Andrew and Simon first meet Jesus

verseByVerse.quote: And going on from there he saw two other brothers, James the son of Zebedee and John his brother, in the boat with Zebedee their father, mending their nets, and he called them. Immediately they left the boat and their father and followed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Further along, Jesus called two more brothers, James and John, who were mending nets in their father Zebedee’s boat. They left both the boat and their father at once and followed him.

James the son of Zebedee and John his brother. Together with Peter, they became the inner circle of the Twelve, present at the transfiguration (17:1) and in Gethsemane (26:37). Jesus nicknamed them “Sons of Thunder” (Mark 3:17). James was the first apostle to be martyred (Acts 12:2). John wrote the Gospel of John, three letters and Revelation, and lived longest.

In the boat with Zebedee their father. Zebedee ran a fishing business with hired servants (Mark 1:20), so the family was reasonably prosperous. Their mother may have been Salome, possibly the sister of Jesus’ mother Mary (27:56; John 19:25), which would make them Jesus’ cousins.

Mending their nets. Repairing torn nets after a night’s fishing. The word (katartizō) is the same word Paul uses for equipping the saints (Ephesians 4:12). Jesus would mend them for a new work.

And he called them. Jesus’ call is personal and authoritative.

Immediately they left the boat and their father and followed him. They left not only their livelihood but their family ties. In that culture, a son working in his father’s business was expected to carry it on. Leaving was a serious break. Jesus later says that loyalty to him must come before family (10:37), and that those who leave houses or family for his sake will receive a hundredfold and eternal life (19:29).

What it does not mean. Not that they abandoned their father callously: Zebedee had hired servants. And not that following Christ means despising family. Jesus commanded honour for parents (15:4–6). But when family and Christ pull in different directions, Christ comes first.

In a sentence. James and John left their boat and father at once to follow Jesus, putting his call before work and family.

On a Tuesday. Is there a family expectation that is holding you back from wholehearted obedience to Christ? Honour your family, but follow him first.

verseByVerse.quote: And he went throughout all Galilee, teaching in their synagogues and proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom and healing every disease and every affliction among the people. So his fame spread throughout all Syria, and they brought him all the sick, those afflicted with various diseases and pains, those oppressed by demons, those having seizures, and paralytics, and he healed them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus travelled throughout Galilee, teaching in the synagogues, proclaiming the good news of the kingdom, and healing every kind of disease. His fame spread far beyond Galilee, and people brought him all kinds of sick and suffering people, and he healed them.

He went throughout all Galilee. Galilee had many towns and villages; the historian Josephus counted over two hundred. Jesus’ ministry was itinerant: he travelled on foot, from town to town.

Teaching in their synagogues. A synagogue (“gathering place”) was a local Jewish meeting house for prayer, the reading and explaining of Scripture, and community life. Synagogues developed during the exile. On the Sabbath, any qualified man could be invited to read and teach (Luke 4:16–21; Acts 13:15). Jesus used the synagogues, as Paul later did.

And proclaiming the gospel of the kingdom. “Gospel” (euangelion) means good news, an announcement of victory or of a new king. The good news is that God’s kingdom has come in Jesus (v. 17).

And healing every disease and every affliction among the people. Teaching, preaching and healing: the three parts of Jesus’ ministry (repeated in 9:35). The healings were not side-shows. They were signs of the kingdom: when God’s reign arrives, sickness, demons and death are driven back. Isaiah had promised that in the days of salvation the eyes of the blind would be opened and the lame would leap (Isaiah 35:5–6). Jesus’ healings were a preview of the new creation, where there will be no more pain (Revelation 21:4).

So his fame spread throughout all Syria. Syria was the large Roman province to the north, which included Galilee and Judea administratively. The news spread among Gentiles too.

All the sick, those afflicted with various diseases and pains. Matthew lists them: the sick; those oppressed by demons; those having seizures (literally “moonstruck”, as people believed the moon caused epilepsy); and paralytics. Matthew distinguishes demon-possession from illness. Not every illness is demonic.

And he healed them. All of them. Jesus had authority over every kind of disease and every kind of evil power.

What it does not mean. Not that God always heals today when Christians pray, or that sickness shows a lack of faith. Jesus’ healings were signs of the arrival of the kingdom and confirmed his identity (11:2–5). Christians should pray for healing, and God sometimes heals (James 5:14–15). But full healing awaits the resurrection. Paul left Trophimus ill (2 Timothy 4:20), and Paul’s own thorn was not removed (2 Corinthians 12:7–9).

Where Christians differ: healing today. Some (continuationists, especially Pentecostals) hold that the gift of healing continues as it did in the apostolic church. Cessationists hold that the miraculous sign-gifts given to confirm the apostles’ message ceased with the apostles, though God still heals in answer to prayer. Verdict: cessationist, held charitably. God still heals when and as he wills, but no one today has the authority to heal at will, and healing is not promised to every believer in this life.

In a sentence. Jesus taught, announced the good news of the kingdom and healed every disease, showing that God’s reign had arrived.

On a Tuesday. Jesus cared for bodies as well as souls. Visit someone who is sick this week, and pray for them.
verseByVerse.note: Syria was the Roman province to the north.

verseByVerse.quote: And great crowds followed him from Galilee and the Decapolis, and from Jerusalem and Judea, and from beyond the Jordan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Huge crowds followed Jesus from every direction: from Galilee, the Greek cities of the Decapolis, Jerusalem and Judea, and the region across the Jordan.

Great crowds followed him. “Followed” here means physically going after him, not necessarily becoming disciples. Crowds come and go in Matthew; they welcome Jesus at his entry to Jerusalem (21:9) and call for his death a few days later (27:20–23). Not everyone who follows the crowd follows Christ.

From Galilee. The north.

And the Decapolis. Greek for “ten cities”: a league of Greek-speaking cities, mostly east of the Sea of Galilee and the Jordan, with mainly Gentile populations (Mark 5:20; 7:31).

And from Jerusalem and Judea. The south, the religious heartland.

And from beyond the Jordan. The region east of the river, called Perea.

The whole land. The list covers almost the whole territory of ancient Israel, Jewish and Gentile areas alike. Jesus is gathering a new Israel around himself. This sets the scene for the Sermon on the Mount, which he preaches to his disciples with the crowds listening (5:1; 7:28).

What it does not mean. Not that popularity proves faithfulness, or that large crowds mean God’s blessing. Jesus often withdrew from crowds, and many who followed turned back (John 6:66).

In a sentence. Crowds from every region, Jewish and Gentile, came after Jesus, a sign of the new people he was gathering.

On a Tuesday. Are you following Jesus because others are, or because you have heard his call? The crowd is not the same as discipleship.
verseByVerse.note: The Decapolis was a league of about ten Greek cities, mostly east of the Jordan.

4.theology:
Active Obedience and the Imputed Righteousness of Christ. The temptation narrative is crucial to the Reformed doctrine of imputed righteousness. Jesus does not merely die for our sins (removing the guilt of our disobedience); he also lives in perfect obedience (providing the positive righteousness that we lack). This is called his active obedience — the life of perfect faithfulness to the Father from baptism to cross.

At each point of testing in the wilderness, Jesus does what Adam failed to do in the garden and what Israel failed to do in the desert: he trusts God’s word over his own need, refuses to demand signs, and worships God alone. This perfect obedience is credited to everyone who trusts in him. We are justified not only by the forgiveness of our sins through his death but by the clothing of his righteousness through his life. The temptation narrative is the biography of our justification — the record of the obedience that is now ours by faith.
4.examples:
Then: Israel’s forty years in the wilderness is the extended backstory of Jesus’ forty days. Every test Jesus faces has a corresponding failure in Israel’s wilderness narrative: bread (the manna crisis, Exod. 16), testing God (Massah, Exod. 17), worship (the golden calf, Exod. 32). Jesus passes where Israel failed, using the very Scriptures that Israel was given at Sinai. He is the true Israel, the faithful son, the one who finally does what the nation was always called to do.

Now: Every temptation we face follows one of Satan’s three patterns: use what you have for immediate gratification (stones to bread), demand that God prove himself (test the promise), or compromise your worship for immediate reward (kingdoms without the cross). Jesus’ answers are our weapons too: It is written. The Scripture that armed the Son of God in his temptation is the same Scripture available to every believer in theirs. The difference between victory and defeat in temptation is often simply whether we know the word well enough to wield it in the moment.

5.title: The New Law from the Mountain
5.text: <sup>1</sup>Seeing the crowds, he went up on the mountain, and when he sat down, his disciples came to him. <sup>2</sup>And he opened his mouth and taught them, saying: <sup>3</sup>“Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. <sup>4</sup>“Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted. <sup>5</sup>“Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth. <sup>6</sup>“Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied. <sup>7</sup>“Blessed are the merciful, for they shall receive mercy. <sup>8</sup>“Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God. <sup>9</sup>“Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God. <sup>10</sup>“Blessed are those who are persecuted for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. <sup>11</sup>“Blessed are you when others revile you and persecute you and utter all kinds of evil against you falsely on my account. <sup>12</sup>Rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven, for so they persecuted the prophets who were before you. <sup>13</sup>“You are the salt of the earth, but if salt has lost its taste, how shall its saltiness be restored? It is no longer good for anything except to be thrown out and trampled under people’s feet. <sup>14</sup>“You are the light of the world. A city set on a hill cannot be hidden. <sup>15</sup>Nor do people light a lamp and put it under a basket, but on a stand, and it gives light to all in the house. <sup>16</sup>In the same way, let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father who is in heaven. <sup>17</sup>“Do not think that I have come to abolish the Law or the Prophets; I have not come to abolish them but to fulfill them. <sup>18</sup>For truly, I say to you, until heaven and earth pass away, not an iota, not a dot, will pass from the Law until all is accomplished. <sup>19</sup>Therefore whoever relaxes one of the least of these commandments and teaches others to do the same will be called least in the kingdom of heaven, but whoever does them and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven. <sup>20</sup>For I tell you, unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven. <sup>21</sup>“You have heard that it was said to those of old, ‘You shall not murder; and whoever murders will be liable to judgment.’ <sup>22</sup>But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment; whoever insults his brother will be liable to the council; and whoever says, ‘You fool!’ will be liable to the hell of fire. <sup>23</sup>So if you are offering your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, <sup>24</sup>leave your gift there before the altar and go. First be reconciled to your brother, and then come and offer your gift. <sup>25</sup>Come to terms quickly with your accuser while you are going with him to court, lest your accuser hand you over to the judge, and the judge to the guard, and you be put in prison. <sup>26</sup>Truly, I say to you, you will never get out until you have paid the last penny. <sup>27</sup>“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ <sup>28</sup>But I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman with lustful intent has already committed adultery with her in his heart. <sup>29</sup>If your right eye causes you to sin, tear it out and throw it away. For it is better that you lose one of your members than that your whole body be thrown into hell. <sup>30</sup>And if your right hand causes you to sin, cut it off and throw it away. For it is better that you lose one of your members than that your whole body go into hell. <sup>31</sup>“It was also said, ‘Whoever divorces his wife, let him give her a certificate of divorce.’ <sup>32</sup>But I say to you that everyone who divorces his wife, except on the ground of sexual immorality, makes her commit adultery, and whoever marries a divorced woman commits adultery. <sup>33</sup>“Again you have heard that it was said to those of old, ‘You shall not swear falsely, but shall perform to the Lord what you have sworn.’ <sup>34</sup>But I say to you, Do not take an oath at all, either by heaven, for it is the throne of God, <sup>35</sup>or by the earth, for it is his footstool, or by Jerusalem, for it is the city of the great King. <sup>36</sup>And do not take an oath by your head, for you cannot make one hair white or black. <sup>37</sup>Let what you say be simply ‘Yes’ or ‘No’; anything more than this comes from evil. <sup>38</sup>“You have heard that it was said, ‘An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth.’ <sup>39</sup>But I say to you, Do not resist the one who is evil. But if anyone slaps you on the right cheek, turn to him the other also. <sup>40</sup>And if anyone would sue you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well. <sup>41</sup>And if anyone forces you to go one mile, go with him two miles. <sup>42</sup>Give to the one who begs from you, and do not refuse the one who would borrow from you. <sup>43</sup>“You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.’ <sup>44</sup>But I say to you, Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, <sup>45</sup>so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven. For he makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust. <sup>46</sup>For if you love those who love you, what reward do you have? Do not even the tax collectors do the same? <sup>47</sup>And if you greet only your brothers, what more are you doing than others? Do not even the Gentiles do the same? <sup>48</sup>You therefore must be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect.
5.overview:
Jesus goes up on a mountain to teach — and every Jewish reader of Matthew’s Gospel would have heard the echo: Moses went up on Sinai. But this is not a repetition; it is a surpassing. Moses received the law and gave it; Jesus gives the law with his own authority: But I say to you. No prophet ever spoke like this. The prophets said “thus says the LORD”; Jesus says “I say.” He does not claim to relay a message from God; he speaks as God.

The Beatitudes are the charter of the kingdom — and they invert every human expectation of what blessed looks like. Poor in spirit, not rich in confidence. Mourning, not celebrating. Meek, not powerful. Persecuted, not applauded. The kingdom of heaven belongs to people the world dismisses. This is not a programme for self-improvement; it is a description of those who have been broken of self-sufficiency and have learned to receive everything from God’s hand. The Beatitudes describe Jesus perfectly — and they describe every person who has been conformed to his image.

The antitheses (“You have heard… but I say”) press the law deeper than the scribal tradition imagined. It is not enough not to murder; the anger that murders in the heart is already culpable. Not enough not to commit adultery; the lust that adultery in the imagination is already a violation. The law reaches inward. And this inward reach is not only a demand; it is a diagnosis. No one can meet the standard of verse 48 — “be perfect as your heavenly Father is perfect” — by their own effort. The Sermon on the Mount is the X-ray that shows us the fracture and sends us to the only Physician who can heal it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — The Beatitudes and the Call to Witness
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus goes up the mountain — deliberately evoking Sinai, where Moses received the law — and sits to teach, the posture of a Jewish rabbi. His first words are the Beatitudes: nine declarations of blessedness that systematically invert the world's value system. The poor in spirit, the mourners, the meek, the hungry — these are not character traits to develop but descriptions of those who know their need before God. The section closes with the salt and light metaphors: disciples are to be world-preserving and world-illuminating, not by withdrawal but by visible, costly presence. Two structural things govern this whole section and are set out at length in the verse-by-verse. First, "blessed" is not a wish. Makarios is a flat declaration about how things stand, not a hope that things go well — and it does not mean "happy" in the modern sense, since half the people described are mourning, starving or being driven out. It is the word the Psalter opens with (Ps. 1:1). Second, the eight are one argument, sealed at both ends. Verse 3 and verse 10 share the same six words — "theirs is the kingdom of heaven" — and the bracket is in the tense as well as the wording: v. 3 is present, vv. 4-9 are all future (shall be comforted, shall inherit, shall be satisfied, shall receive mercy, shall see God, shall be called), and v. 10 returns to the present. Present, six futures, present. And the order is not random: the first four describe a person's need (bankrupt, grieving, unassertive, starving) and the second four describe what comes out of a person met in that need (merciful, single-hearted, peacemaking, and consequently hated). Nobody arrives at the second four by trying; they are what the first four turn into. Individual notes: "poor" is ptochos, a beggar who crouches, not penes the working poor; "mourn" is pentheo, the word for grieving the dead; Moses is Scripture's own definition of meekness (Num. 12:3), which settles that it cannot mean timidity; "satisfied" is chortazo, the animal-feeding word, fed until you stop; verse 8 answers the temple question of Psalm 24:3-4 and then promises more than David dared write; and "peacemakers" is eirenopoios, a word found nowhere else in the New Testament, where the making is the point — peacekeeping arranges for a difficulty not to be mentioned, which is very often the opposite of this.
verseByVerse.theology: The Beatitudes are not a moral ladder to climb but a portrait of kingdom citizens in their native condition. They describe the same person from different angles: the one who is poor in spirit mourns their sin, is meek before God, hungers for righteousness, shows mercy, is pure in heart, makes peace, and bears persecution gladly. This is not nine different types of Christian but one Christian seen fully. Crucially, the blessings are not rewards for achieving these qualities; they are the condition of those who have already received the kingdom. Grace precedes the beatitudes; they describe those who know it. And before they are a portrait of the Christian, they are a portrait of Christ: he alone was perfectly poor in spirit, mourning over sin, meek, hungering for righteousness, merciful, pure in heart, the peacemaker, the persecuted — he kept every blessing flawlessly, and that whole beatitude-life is reckoned to all who are united to him. This is the lens that keeps the Beatitudes from crushing the believer. We do not read them to measure ourselves and despair; we read them resting in the One who fulfilled them for us and who is now, by his Spirit, slowly forming them in us. So the struggler need not flee: the very ache of falling short — the grief over sin, the hunger to be made clean — is itself the first Beatitudes already at work, the early evidence of grace rather than the proof of its absence. Here law and gospel meet: the Beatitudes show us a righteousness we cannot produce, and then point us to the Christ who both gives it freely and grows it within.
verseByVerse.examples: Salt in the ancient world was a preservative — it slowed decay. Light is simply visible; it cannot be hidden without ceasing to be light. Jesus calls his disciples both: agents of preservation in a decaying world, and bearers of visible testimony that draws glory to the Father. Neither metaphor allows for invisible, privatized Christianity. The Christian life is inherently public — not in the sense of performance (that will be condemned in ch. 6) but in the sense of witness. The question is not whether your life will be seen, but what people will see when they look.

verseByVerse.quote: Seeing the crowds, he went up on the mountain, and when he sat down, his disciples came to him. And he opened his mouth and taught them, saying:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seeing the crowds, Jesus went up the mountain, sat down as a teacher, and began to teach his disciples. This is the Sermon on the Mount: the King describing the life of his kingdom, as Moses once brought God’s law from a mountain.

The Sermon on the Mount. Matthew 5–7 is the first of five great blocks of Jesus’ teaching in Matthew (5–7; 10; 13; 18; 24–25), each ending with words like “when Jesus finished these sayings” (7:28). Some see a deliberate echo of the five books of Moses. The sermon describes what life looks like under God’s reign: the character (5:3–12), influence (5:13–16), righteousness (5:17–48), devotion (6:1–18), trust (6:19–34), relationships (7:1–12), and the call to decide (7:13–27) of those who belong to the kingdom.

Seeing the crowds. The crowds of 4:25. Jesus teaches his disciples with the crowds listening at the edge (7:28–29).

He went up on the mountain. Probably a hillside near Capernaum; tradition places it on a slope above the northern shore of the lake. Matthew’s readers would think of Moses going up Mount Sinai to receive God’s law (Exodus 19–20). But Jesus is greater than Moses. Moses received the law from God; Jesus speaks with his own authority: “But I say to you” (vv. 22, 28, 32, 34, 39, 44). The crowds were astonished that he taught as one who had authority, not as their scribes (7:29).

And when he sat down. Jewish teachers sat to teach; listeners stood or sat at their feet (Luke 4:20). Jesus takes the position of an authoritative rabbi.

His disciples came to him. “Disciple” (mathētēs) means learner, student, apprentice. The sermon is addressed first to disciples: it describes the life of those who already follow Jesus, not a way to become his follower.

He opened his mouth and taught them. A solemn Hebrew way of introducing important speech (Job 3:1; Acts 8:35).

What it does not mean. Not a set of rules by which people can earn God’s favour. The sermon begins with grace: blessed are the poor in spirit (v. 3), those who have nothing to offer. It describes the fruit of being in the kingdom, not the price of entry. Nor is it an impossible ideal meant only to show us our sin, or a code only for a future millennial kingdom, as some have taught. It does show us our sin and drive us to Christ, but it is also the real pattern for Christian living now, lived by the Spirit’s power.

Where Christians differ: who is the sermon for? Some traditional Lutherans stress that it is chiefly law, showing our inability. Some Anabaptists and pacifists take it as a literal code for Christians, ruling out oaths, military service and courts. Classic dispensationalists applied it chiefly to the future kingdom. Verdict: it is Christ’s teaching for his disciples now: it humbles us, drives us to grace, and then shapes the life of those who have received grace. Its sayings must be read as Jesus meant them, sometimes as vivid pictures, in the light of the rest of Scripture.

In a sentence. On the mountain, Jesus, greater than Moses, taught his disciples the life of God’s kingdom with his own authority.

On a Tuesday. Read Matthew 5–7 through in one sitting this week. It takes about fifteen minutes, and it is the King’s description of your life.
verseByVerse.note: Teachers sat to teach. The mountain setting recalls Moses receiving the law on Sinai.

parallels.desc: Moses goes up to God on the mountain

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first Beatitude: God’s blessing rests on those who know they are spiritually bankrupt, with nothing to offer God. The kingdom of heaven belongs to them.

The Beatitudes. Verses 3–12 are called the Beatitudes, from the Latin beatus, “blessed”. There are eight (vv. 3–10), plus an expansion of the last (vv. 11–12). They describe not eight types of Christian but eight sides of one character, found in every true disciple. The first and the eighth end with the same promise, “theirs is the kingdom of heaven”, framing the whole.

Blessed. Makarios. Not “happy” in the sense of a feeling. It is God’s verdict: truly well off, favoured by God, in an enviable position, whatever one feels. It echoes the Psalms (Psalm 1:1; 32:1). The Beatitudes turn the world’s values upside down: the world calls the confident, the cheerful and the powerful blessed; Jesus calls the poor, the mourning and the meek blessed.

The poor in spirit. Not the poor in material terms only, nor those who lack spirit or courage. In the Old Testament, “the poor” often meant the humble faithful who depended on God because they had nothing else, and were oppressed by the proud (Psalm 34:6; Isaiah 61:1; 66:2). To be poor in spirit is to recognise one’s spiritual poverty: to know that before God I am bankrupt, with no righteousness, no merit, nothing to bring. It is the opposite of spiritual pride. The tax collector who prayed “God, be merciful to me, a sinner” was poor in spirit; the Pharisee who thanked God he was not like others was not (Luke 18:9–14).

For theirs is the kingdom of heaven. The present tense: it is theirs now. The kingdom is not earned by the rich in spirit, but given to those who come with empty hands. This is grace at the very start of the sermon. The first step into the kingdom is not achievement but admission of need.

What it does not mean. Not low self-esteem or self-hatred. The poor in spirit know their poverty before God, but they also know they are richly loved and given the kingdom. Nor does it mean that material poverty is a virtue that earns heaven. Luke’s version, “Blessed are you who are poor” (Luke 6:20), speaks of the literally poor, because they often know their need of God; but the rich can be poor in spirit, and the poor can be proud.

In a sentence. God blesses with his kingdom those who know they have nothing to bring him.

On a Tuesday. Begin your prayers today not with what you have done for God, but with what you need from him.

For worship. Come to God with empty hands. That is the only way into his kingdom.
verseByVerse.note: “Blessed” means truly well off in God’s sight, not merely happy.

parallels.desc: with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s blessing rests on those who grieve, above all over sin and its ruin, in themselves and in the world. God himself will comfort them.

Those who mourn. The word (penthountes) means deep grief, the kind of mourning for the dead. It follows naturally from the first Beatitude: those who see their spiritual poverty grieve over it. The mourning includes sorrow for our own sin (Psalm 51:3–4; James 4:9), grief over the sin and suffering of the world (Psalm 119:136; Ezekiel 9:4), and the sorrows of life in a fallen world, including bereavement. Jesus himself wept (John 11:35; Luke 19:41).

For they shall be comforted. “Comforted” (paraklēthēsontai) is related to the word for the Holy Spirit, the Comforter or Helper (John 14:16). The passive voice means God is the one who comforts. Isaiah 61:1–3 promised that the Messiah would come to comfort all who mourn, giving them a garland instead of ashes and the oil of gladness instead of mourning. Jesus fulfils it. The comfort comes partly now, in forgiveness and the Spirit’s presence, and fully at the end, when God will wipe away every tear (Revelation 21:4).

The logic. The world says, “Blessed are those who laugh; avoid sorrow.” Jesus says that those who never mourn their sin will never know the comfort of forgiveness. Only those who feel the weight of sin feel the relief of grace.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should be gloomy, or that sadness is a mark of holiness. Joy is a fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22). But Christian joy is not the shallow cheerfulness that ignores sin and suffering; it is the joy of the comforted. Nor does it mean that all grief is blessed. Self-pity and bitterness are not the mourning Jesus means. Godly grief leads to repentance; worldly grief leads to death (2 Corinthians 7:10).

In a sentence. God blesses with his comfort those who grieve over sin and its ruin.

On a Tuesday. When did you last grieve over your own sin, rather than only its consequences? And who near you is mourning, and needs you to sit with them?

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s blessing rests on the meek: those who are gentle and humble before God and others, who do not grab or retaliate, but trust God to give them what is right. They will inherit the earth.

The meek. Praeis: gentle, humble, not self-assertive. In Greek it was used of a tamed horse: strength under control (see Ephesians 4:2). Moses was called very meek, more than all people on the earth (Numbers 12:3), yet he confronted Pharaoh. Jesus called himself gentle and lowly in heart (11:29), yet he overturned the tables in the temple. Meekness is not weakness. It is the strength not to insist on one’s own rights, not to take revenge, and to accept God’s dealings without bitterness.

The connection. The poor in spirit see themselves truly before God; the mourning grieve their sin; the meek, having seen themselves truly, are gentle toward others. Someone who knows how much they have been forgiven does not demand their rights harshly.

For they shall inherit the earth. Jesus quotes Psalm 37:11. Psalm 37 tells God’s people not to fret over the wicked who prosper, but to trust the LORD, wait for him, and refrain from anger; the meek shall inherit the land. In the Old Testament, the inheritance was the land of Canaan. Jesus widens it to the whole earth. The meek, who do not grab, will receive everything. The proud seize the earth for a while; the meek will inherit the new earth for ever (Romans 4:13; Revelation 21:1–7).

What it does not mean. Not that Christians must be doormats, never speaking up for truth or justice, or never defending the vulnerable. Jesus spoke strongly against hypocrisy (chapter 23). Meekness concerns personal ambition and retaliation, not indifference to evil. Nor does it mean being shy or quiet by temperament. A bold, outgoing person can be meek; a quiet person can be proud.

In a sentence. God blesses the gentle, who trust him instead of grabbing, with the inheritance of the whole renewed earth.

On a Tuesday. Where are you insisting on your rights today, in traffic, in a meeting, at home? Practise meekness: let God defend you.
verseByVerse.note: “Meek” means gentle and humble before God, not weak.

parallels.desc: the meek shall inherit the land
“I am gentle and lowly in heart”

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s blessing rests on those who long for righteousness as a starving man longs for food and a parched man for water. God will satisfy them.

Those who hunger and thirst. Not a mild wish, but desperate desire. In the ancient world, many people knew real hunger and thirst. The Psalms use the image: as a deer pants for flowing streams, so pants my soul for you, O God (Psalm 42:1; 63:1).

For righteousness. What righteousness? In Matthew, righteousness usually means doing God’s will, a life that is right before God (5:10, 20; 6:1, 33). So the hunger includes: longing to be made right with God (forgiveness and justification); longing to be holy, to do God’s will (sanctification); and longing for justice in the world, for God’s right order to prevail. The poor in spirit, who know they have no righteousness of their own, hunger for it.

For they shall be satisfied. The word (chortasthēsontai) was used of animals being fed until full (14:20). God will fill them. In part now: those who come to Christ are given his righteousness (Philippians 3:9) and are changed by his Spirit. In full at the end, when righteousness dwells in the new heavens and new earth (2 Peter 3:13). Jesus said that whoever comes to him will never hunger, and whoever believes in him will never thirst (John 6:35).

What it does not mean. Not that we earn righteousness by hungering for it. Hunger is not food; it is the sense of need that drives us to the food. Nor is it a hunger that is satisfied once and then disappears. Christians who are being satisfied go on hungering for more of God.

In a sentence. God fully satisfies those who long desperately to be right with him and to do his will.

On a Tuesday. What do you hunger for most? Your appetites show your heart. Ask God to make you hungry for righteousness, and feed that hunger on his word.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are the merciful, for they shall receive mercy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s blessing rests on the merciful: those who show compassion and forgiveness to others in their need and failure. They will receive God’s mercy.

The merciful. Mercy is compassion in action toward those in distress, and forgiveness toward those who have wronged us. It includes both pity for the suffering (the good Samaritan, Luke 10:33–37) and pardon for the guilty (18:21–35). God himself is merciful (Exodus 34:6), and his people reflect him.

The turn. The first four Beatitudes describe our relationship to God: poverty, mourning, meekness, hunger. The next four describe how that shows itself toward others: mercy, purity, peacemaking, and enduring persecution. Those who have received mercy become merciful.

For they shall receive mercy. From God, at the final judgment and now. James says that judgment is without mercy to one who has shown no mercy (James 2:13).

The logic. This is not a deal: “be merciful, and God will pay you back with mercy”. It is a description of reality. Those who know God’s mercy cannot help showing it. A person who refuses to show mercy shows that they have never truly understood the mercy they need. Jesus’ parable of the unforgiving servant makes the point: a man forgiven a vast debt who refuses to forgive a small one shows he never grasped the first (18:21–35).

What it does not mean. Not that our mercy earns God’s mercy. God’s mercy comes first (Ephesians 2:4). Nor does mercy mean ignoring wrongdoing, removing all consequences, or pretending justice does not matter. God is merciful and just (Romans 3:26), and the merciful still want justice for the oppressed.

In a sentence. Those who show mercy, because they have received it, will receive God’s mercy at the last.

On a Tuesday. To whom can you show mercy today: someone in need, or someone who has wronged you?

parallels.desc: should not you have had mercy?

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s blessing rests on the pure in heart: those whose inner life is undivided and clean, devoted to God without hidden motives. They will see God.

The pure in heart. “Pure” (katharos) means clean, unmixed, unadulterated, like refined metal or pure water. The “heart” in the Bible is the centre of the person: mind, will, desires and feelings (see Ephesians 1:18). Purity of heart means two things. Moral cleanness, especially in thought and desire (5:28). And singleness: an undivided heart, wholly devoted to God, not double-minded (James 4:8; Psalm 86:11). The Pharisees were outwardly clean but inwardly full of greed and self-indulgence (23:25–28). Jesus wants purity at the source.

Psalm 24. The psalm asks who may ascend the hill of the LORD and stand in his holy place. The answer: those who have clean hands and a pure heart (Psalm 24:3–4). Jesus says these people will see God himself.

For they shall see God. The highest blessing. No one can see God and live (Exodus 33:20). Yet the hope of God’s people has always been to see him (Job 19:26–27; Psalm 17:15). In part, believers see God now by faith in Christ, who is the image of the invisible God (John 14:9; 2 Corinthians 4:6). In full at the end: they will see his face (Revelation 22:4; 1 John 3:2). Theologians call this the beatific vision, the blessed sight of God.

How can anyone be pure in heart? No one is by nature (Jeremiah 17:9). Purity is first God’s gift: he gives a new heart (Ezekiel 36:25–26), cleanses it by faith (Acts 15:9), and through the blood of Christ (1 John 1:7). Then it is a lifelong pursuit: everyone who hopes to see him purifies himself as he is pure (1 John 3:3; Hebrews 12:14).

What it does not mean. Not sinless perfection in this life. The pure in heart still struggle with sin; what marks them is that they hate it and fight it, and that their heart is set on God. Nor is purity merely the absence of sexual sin, though it includes that. It is the whole heart turned toward God.

In a sentence. Those whose hearts are made clean and undivided toward God will see God himself.

On a Tuesday. What are you allowing into your heart through your eyes and screens? Guard your heart, for everything you do flows from it (Proverbs 4:23).

parallels.desc: he who has clean hands and a pure heart
holiness, without which no one will see the Lord
we shall see him as he is

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s blessing rests on the peacemakers: those who work to bring reconciliation, between people and God and between people and each other. They will be called sons of God.

The peacemakers. Not peace-lovers, who simply like quiet, nor peace-keepers, who avoid conflict at any price, but peace-makers, who actively work to make peace where there is hostility. “Peace” here is the Hebrew shalom: not only the absence of conflict but wholeness and right relationship (see Ephesians 1:2). Making peace includes sharing the gospel, by which people are reconciled to God (2 Corinthians 5:18–20); reconciling people in conflict; and refusing to stir up division (Proverbs 6:19; Romans 12:18).

For they shall be called sons of God. “Called” means recognised, acknowledged, by God. In Hebrew idiom, a “son of” something shares its character. God is the God of peace (Romans 15:33), who made peace through the blood of the cross (Colossians 1:20). Christ is the great peacemaker (Ephesians 2:14–17). Those who make peace show the family likeness: they act like their Father. “Sons” includes daughters; all believers are God’s children (Galatians 3:26–28).

What it does not mean. Not peace at the expense of truth. Jesus later says he did not come to bring peace but a sword (10:34): the gospel divides between those who accept and reject it. Peacemaking does not mean papering over sin or pretending that wrongs do not matter. True peace deals with the cause of conflict. Nor does it mean that we become God’s children by making peace. We are made children by grace through faith (John 1:12); peacemaking shows that we are.

In a sentence. Those who work for reconciliation show the family likeness of God, the great peacemaker, and are recognised as his children.

On a Tuesday. Is there a conflict near you, in your family, church or workplace, where you could be a peacemaker? Take one step toward reconciliation.

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are those who are persecuted for righteousness' sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s blessing rests on those who suffer for doing right. The kingdom of heaven is theirs.

Those who are persecuted. The perfect tense suggests those who have been persecuted and still bear its marks. Persecution includes physical violence, imprisonment and death, but also exclusion, mockery, loss of jobs and reputation (v. 11).

For righteousness’ sake. Because they live rightly, according to God’s will. Not suffering for their own foolishness, rudeness or wrongdoing (1 Peter 2:20; 4:15), but because their lives of mercy, purity and peacemaking expose and challenge the world. A life described by the first seven Beatitudes provokes opposition, because it rebukes the world’s values (John 15:18–20; 2 Timothy 3:12).

For theirs is the kingdom of heaven. The same promise as the first Beatitude (v. 3). The Beatitudes begin and end with the kingdom. The world may take everything from them, but it cannot take the kingdom.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should seek persecution, or interpret every criticism as persecution. Sometimes Christians are disliked because they are unpleasant. The blessing is for suffering that comes because of righteousness. Nor does it mean that suffering earns the kingdom. It is the mark of those to whom the kingdom already belongs.

In a sentence. Those who suffer because they live God’s way have the kingdom of heaven as their possession.

On a Tuesday. If you are mocked or disadvantaged for living as a Christian, you are not cursed but blessed. And pray today for believers who face prison or death for their faith.

parallels.desc: if you suffer for righteousness’ sake, you will be blessed

verseByVerse.quote: Blessed are you when others revile you and persecute you and utter all kinds of evil against you falsely on my account. Rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven, for so they persecuted the prophets who were before you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus turns from “those who” to “you”, speaking directly to his disciples. When people insult, persecute and slander you because you belong to me, rejoice: your reward in heaven is great, and you stand in the line of the prophets.

Blessed are you. The shift to “you” makes it personal. Jesus expects his disciples to face this.

When others revile you. Insult, abuse to your face.

And persecute you. Hunt, harass, pursue.

And utter all kinds of evil against you falsely. Slander behind your back. The early Christians were accused of cannibalism (because they spoke of eating Christ’s body), atheism (because they refused the gods), and hatred of the human race. “Falsely” is important: the slander is untrue.

On my account. In verse 10, “for righteousness’ sake”; here, “on my account”, for Jesus’ sake. Jesus puts himself in the place of righteousness. To suffer for him is to suffer for what is right. Only God could say this.

Rejoice and be glad. Not merely endure, but rejoice. The second word means to leap for joy. The apostles, beaten by the council, rejoiced that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name (Acts 5:41).

For your reward is great in heaven. God rewards faithfulness (see 6:1–6). The reward is not earned wages but God’s generous gift. “In heaven” means it is kept with God, safe, not yet visible (1 Peter 1:4).

For so they persecuted the prophets who were before you. The prophets were rejected, persecuted and some killed: Elijah was hunted (1 Kings 19:2), Jeremiah was beaten and imprisoned (Jeremiah 37:15), Zechariah was stoned (2 Chronicles 24:21). To be persecuted for Christ is to join the company of God’s faithful servants through history.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should enjoy pain, or pretend it does not hurt. The joy is not in the suffering itself, but in what it means and where it leads. Nor should Christians respond to slander with slander: Jesus will tell them to pray for their persecutors (v. 44).

In a sentence. Disciples who are insulted and persecuted for Jesus can rejoice, because they have a great reward in heaven and stand with the prophets.

On a Tuesday. When you are mocked for Christ, remember who stands with you: the prophets, the apostles, and the Lord himself.

parallels.desc: rejoice as you share Christ’s sufferings

verseByVerse.quote: You are the salt of the earth, but if salt has lost its taste, how shall its saltiness be restored? It is no longer good for anything except to be thrown out and trampled under people's feet. You are the light of the world. A city set on a hill cannot be hidden.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus tells his disciples what they are in the world: they are the salt of the earth and the light of the world. Like salt, they preserve and give flavour; but salt that loses its saltiness is useless.

You are. Not “you should become”, but “you are”. This is their identity. The disciples described in the Beatitudes, poor, mourning, meek and persecuted, are the very people who affect the world.

The salt of the earth. Salt had many uses in the ancient world. It preserved food from decay, especially meat and fish, in a world without refrigeration. It gave flavour. It was used in sacrifices (Leviticus 2:13). Christians in the world act like salt: holding back moral decay, and giving the world a taste of God’s goodness. The world is like meat that rots if left to itself; disciples are rubbed into it to slow the rot.

But if salt has lost its taste. Pure sodium chloride cannot lose its saltiness. But the salt of Palestine was often gathered from the Dead Sea marshes, mixed with other minerals. If damp, the salt could be washed out, leaving a white powder that looked like salt but was useless. The word for “lost its taste” (mōranthē) also means “become foolish”. Disciples who lose their distinctiveness become useless.

How shall its saltiness be restored? It cannot. It is a warning.

It is no longer good for anything except to be thrown out and trampled under people’s feet. Useless salt was thrown on paths, where people walked on it. A church that becomes just like the world will be despised by the world.

You are the light of the world. Jesus is the light of the world (John 8:12); his disciples reflect his light, as the moon reflects the sun. Israel was called to be a light to the nations (Isaiah 42:6; 49:6); now Jesus’ disciples are.

A city set on a hill cannot be hidden. Many towns in Galilee were built on hills, visible for miles, and their lamps could be seen at night. Perhaps Jesus also thought of Jerusalem, the city on Mount Zion, to which the nations would come (Isaiah 2:2–3). The church cannot be invisible.

What it does not mean. Not that Christians should withdraw from the world to keep pure. Salt must be in contact with meat to work; it does nothing in the shaker. Nor that they should become like the world to influence it: salt that becomes like the meat is useless. The call is to be in the world, but distinct from it (John 17:15–18). And it does not mean that salvation can be lost. The warning is that a disciple or church whose life no longer differs from the world shows that something is badly wrong.

In a sentence. Disciples are salt and light: preserving, flavouring and illuminating the world, as long as they remain distinct from it.

On a Tuesday. In what ways does your life at work look different from the lives of those around you? Salt is noticed by its taste.
verseByVerse.note: Salt preserved and flavoured food. Impure salt, such as that from the Dead Sea, could have its salt leached out and lose its taste.

parallels.desc: “I am the light of the world”
shine as lights in the world

verseByVerse.quote: Nor do people light a lamp and put it under a basket, but on a stand, and it gives light to all in the house. In the same way, let your light shine before others, so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father who is in heaven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
No one lights a lamp and hides it. In the same way, disciples must let their light shine, so that people see their good works and give glory, not to them, but to their Father in heaven.

Nor do people light a lamp and put it under a basket. A household lamp was a small clay bowl filled with olive oil, with a wick of flax, giving a small light. The “basket” (modios) was a grain measure holding about eight litres, which could be put over a lamp to put it out. Lighting a lamp to hide it would be absurd.

But on a stand, and it gives light to all in the house. Ordinary homes were one room; one lamp on a stand lit the whole house.

In the same way, let your light shine before others. The light is the life of the kingdom described in the Beatitudes, and visible in good works.

So that they may see your good works. “Good works” are deeds of love, mercy, honesty and justice that flow from faith (Ephesians 2:10; Titus 2:14). The world should be able to see Christianity, not just hear it.

And give glory to your Father who is in heaven. The purpose is not our glory but God’s. The disciple’s good works are like a window, not a mirror: people look through them to God. Peter says something similar: keep your conduct honourable so that they may see your good deeds and glorify God (1 Peter 2:12). “Your Father”: the first time in Matthew that Jesus calls God the disciples’ Father. It appears seventeen times in the sermon.

The tension with 6:1. Later Jesus says not to practise righteousness before others to be seen by them (6:1). Is this a contradiction? No. The difference is the motive. In 5:16, the aim is that people glorify God. In 6:1, the aim is to be praised oneself. Show your works when you are tempted to be cowardly; hide them when you are tempted to show off.

What it does not mean. Not that good works alone are enough to bring people to God. People must hear the gospel to believe (Romans 10:14–17). Good works open ears and adorn the message (Titus 2:10), but they are not a substitute for it.

In a sentence. Let your life of good works shine openly, so that people see it and glorify your Father in heaven.

On a Tuesday. Is your faith hidden at work, among neighbours, online? Do one good work today that points beyond you to God.
verseByVerse.note: A household lamp was a small clay bowl of olive oil with a wick; the “basket” was a grain measure.

parallels.desc: they may see your good deeds and glorify God

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–48 — The Law Fulfilled: A Righteousness That Exceeds
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus addresses the relationship between his teaching and the law of Moses: he has not come to abolish but to fulfill. He then gives six antitheses — "You have heard... but I say to you" — in which he does not contradict the law but penetrates to its interior logic. Murder begins in anger; adultery begins in the look; divorce fractures the covenant; oaths corrupt speech; retaliation perpetuates violence; hatred divides what love should unite. The section climaxes with the demand: "You therefore must be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect." — a standard no one reaches by effort, which is exactly why it drives us to the Christ who fulfilled the law in our place and to the Spirit who reshapes us from within.
verseByVerse.theology: The antitheses reveal that the law was always concerned with the heart, not merely the external act. Jesus does not introduce a new, stricter morality; he discloses the full depth of what God always intended. The Pharisees' righteousness was wide but shallow — it covered the surface of behavior without reaching the roots of motive and desire. The righteousness Jesus requires exceeds theirs not by adding more external rules but by going deeper into the same terrain. This is why grace must precede the Sermon on the Mount: no one can produce this righteousness by effort; it must be worked in us by the Spirit of the one who fulfilled the law perfectly. To "fulfill" the law (v. 17) is not to abolish it but to bring it to its goal: by his flawless obedience Jesus meets its every demand, in himself he embodies the types and shadows that pointed forward, and at the cross he bears its curse.
