When they aren’t sorry. You can still release your claim; the Lord did it from the cross, praying for men who hadn’t repented. What waits on their repentance isn’t your forgiveness but the restored relationship, which may never come. That is a grief, not your sin. And if you can’t yet forgive, don’t pretend to God. Tell him you are unable, and ask him to make you willing to be made willing; he has never despised that prayer. The melting of the heart is his work. A test: are you still trying to make someone pay?

parallels.desc: forgive your brother from your heart

verseByVerse.quote: And when you fast, do not look gloomy like the hypocrites, for they disfigure their faces that their fasting may be seen by others. Truly, I say to you, they have received their reward. But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face, that your fasting may not be seen by others but by your Father who is in secret. And your Father who sees in secret will reward you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Fasting is a free and fitting way for Christ’s people to seek God, to be done privately and without legalism.

Disappearing faces. The hypocrites fast dramatically, inviting admiration for their rigour, and that applause is their whole reward. There is wordplay in the Greek: they make their faces “disappear” so that they may “appear” to others as fasting. The gloomy, advertised face is an announcement of piety — what real fasting must never be.

Look normal. Anointing the head and washing the face were ordinary grooming. Jesus says: look as if you aren’t fasting, so the fast stays between you and God. The three disciplines together shape the whole person: generosity toward others, communion with God, discipline of self — practised privately before the Father whose reward outweighs all human recognition.

Should you be fasting? Jesus says “when you fast,” not “if,” assuming his disciples will. He fasted himself (4:2), and said that when the bridegroom is taken away, “then they will fast” (9:15) — in this present age. The early church fasted and prayed before sending missionaries (Acts 13:2–3) and appointing elders (Acts 14:23). Yet nowhere is fasting laid down as a law with required days; that was the Pharisees’ way, “twice a week” and on show (Luke 18:12). So fasting is a freedom, not an obligation: no one should bind your conscience to it, nor should you shrug off what your Lord assumed his people would do.

Why fast? Fasting is setting aside food, or another comfort, for a time to seek God. It intensifies prayer at weighty moments and decisions (Ezra 8:21–23); it humbles us in repentance (Joel 2:12); and it turns the body’s hunger into a cry of the heart — “Man shall not live by bread alone” (4:4) — saying, “Lord, I want you more than food.” It isn’t a hunger strike to twist God’s arm, a diet, or a badge of piety, and it adds nothing to a standing already complete in Christ. And it has a tender side: we fast because the Bridegroom is away for now, longing for the wedding feast. True fasting also loosens the bonds of injustice and shares bread with the hungry (Isaiah 58:6–7).

How? Start small — skip a meal or a day, drink water, and let each pang send you to prayer; fasting without seeking God is just dieting. Pair it with Scripture. Keep it hidden. And use wisdom with your health: if illness, pregnancy or a fragile history makes food-fasting unwise, set aside other comforts instead — screens, sweets, leisure — for God looks at the heart. A test: have you ever set something aside simply to seek God more?
verseByVerse.note: Anointing the head with oil was part of ordinary grooming. Some Pharisees fasted twice a week (Luke 18:12). A wordplay: they disfigure (aphanizousin, literally “make invisible”) their faces so that they may appear (phanōsin) to others.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–34 — Treasure, Vision, and Trust: Seeking the Kingdom First
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second half of chapter 6 addresses anxiety about material provision through three related teachings. Disciples are commanded not to store up earthly treasure (perishable, vulnerable) but heavenly treasure (imperishable, secure). The eye as the lamp of the body: a healthy eye (generous spirit) fills the whole person with light; a diseased eye (stinginess) fills it with darkness. You cannot serve both God and money. Then the great anxiety passage: do not be anxious about food or clothing, because the Father who feeds the birds and clothes the lilies knows your needs. Seek first the kingdom and his righteousness, and everything else will be added. The three enemies of treasure are not decorative: wealth took three forms and Jesus names the destroyer of each — fine cloth eaten by moth, grain and metal by the second word (which means "eating away" and covers rust, corrosion and vermin), and coin, which neither can touch, taken by the thief, whose verb means "to dig through" (mud-brick walls were tunnelled, not forced). Every exit is closed before the point is made. The eye is a Hebrew idiom, not an optical metaphor: "a good eye" meant a generous person and "an evil eye" a stingy one (Prov. 22:9; 28:22), which is why these verses sit between the treasure and the money rather than interrupting them. And mammon is an Aramaic word Jesus leaves untranslated, whose root appears to be the one behind Hebrew "faith" and our "amen" — most likely meaning that in which one puts one's trust, which makes the sentence almost self-evident. On the anxiety passage, note that the command comes three times (vv. 25, 31, 34), that the birds are not idle (they do not sow, reap or store — that is, they do not hoard against a future they cannot see), that the "lilies" are probably the wild anemones that carpet Galilee for a few weeks and are then swept up as oven fuel, and that "O you of little faith" is a word almost unique to Matthew which he uses four times, every time to disciples and never to unbelievers. The guard on anxiety is the most important thing in the section and is given in full below: this passage has been used to tell people with anxiety disorders that their illness is sin, and that is a cruelty the text does not authorise.
verseByVerse.theology: The teaching on anxiety is not a command to be carefree but to be properly ordered: anxiety is the symptom of inverted priorities — seeking the lesser things first and trusting God to manage them, rather than seeking God first and trusting him to manage everything else. The birds and lilies do not "seek" anything in the human sense; they simply exist in dependence on the Creator who provides. The disciple is not to live without thought for the future but without anxious preoccupation with it — trusting the Father's knowledge and provision while attending to the kingdom. Anxiety is fundamentally a theological problem: it reflects a practical unbelief in the Father's care.
verseByVerse.examples: "Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness" is the organizing principle of the entire Sermon on the Mount. Everything else — the beatitudes, the antitheses, the disciplines of chapter 6 — flows from this reorientation of desire. The person who is genuinely seeking God's kingdom first finds that anxiety about secondary things diminishes, not because circumstances change, but because the center of gravity of the heart has shifted. Worry is the heart occupied with what it fears it won't have; trust is the heart occupied with the One who has everything and gives freely.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth, where moth and rust destroy and where thieves break in and steal, but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys and where thieves do not break in and steal. For where your treasure is, there your heart will be also. The eye is the lamp of the body. So, if your eye is healthy, your whole body will be full of light, but if your eye is bad, your whole body will be full of darkness. If then the light in you is darkness, how great is the darkness! No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve God and money.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Our hearts follow our treasure, so we must refuse to let money rule us and invest our lives in what lasts.

Two treasuries. The contrast isn’t now versus later but secure versus doomed. Earthly treasure has three enemies, and Jesus names the destroyer of each kind of ancient wealth. Fine cloth — a wardrobe was capital, as Joseph sent his brothers home with changes of clothes (Genesis 45:22) — was eaten by moth. Grain and goods were consumed by “rust,” a word meaning eating away, covering corrosion and vermin. And coin was taken by thieves who “break in,” literally “dig through” mud-brick walls. Every form of earthly wealth has a predator. Treasure in heaven — mercy shown, obedience offered, lives invested for God — lies beyond them all. He isn’t banning savings or property but forbidding the heart that makes accumulation its great project.

The heart follows. “Where your treasure is, there your heart will be also.” We assume the heart leads and money follows; Jesus says it runs the other way: put your money somewhere and your heart moves in after it. Do you want to love God’s kingdom more? Invest in it, and your affections will follow.

The eye. This is a Hebrew idiom. A “good eye” meant a generous person, an “evil eye” a stingy one: “Whoever has a bountiful eye will be blessed, for he shares his bread with the poor” (Proverbs 22:9); “A stingy man hastens after wealth” — literally a man with an evil eye (Proverbs 28:22; cf. Deuteronomy 15:9). So these verses aren’t a change of subject. Generosity is the light; grasping is the dark. And the darkness that thinks itself light is the worst kind: the miser who calls his grip prudence can’t see his own night.

Two masters. “You cannot serve God and money.” “Serve” means to be a slave, belonging to someone; no slave had two owners. Jesus uses the Aramaic word “mammon,” wealth set up as a rival lord. God and money give opposite commands: one says hold loosely and give, the other grip tight and keep; one says trust me, and so does the other. Money is a good servant and a deadly master.

What to do. Hold your money with an open hand. Earn honestly, save and provide wisely — that is stewardship, not greed — but give generously and gladly, sending treasure ahead through care for the poor, the church’s work and the spread of the gospel. Run simple diagnostics: Where do my daydreams drift? What would rob my peace if I lost it? What could I not bear to give up? A test: what is your money serving — you, or God’s kingdom?

What it doesn’t mean. It isn’t a call to poverty, nor a sin to own a home, hold a pension or enjoy God’s gifts, for God “richly provides us with everything to enjoy” (1 Timothy 6:17). Saving for your family isn’t hoarding; planning isn’t trusting in riches. The issue is never the figure in your account but the master of your heart: a poor man can worship money as surely as a rich one, and a rich man can hold his wealth open-handed for God. Jesus is against money not in your wallet but on the throne.
verseByVerse.note: Wealth was often stored as fine clothing (eaten by moths). A “bad” eye was an idiom for stinginess. The ESV notes that “money” renders mammon, a Semitic word for money or possessions.

parallels.desc: your eye look grudgingly on your poor brother

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I tell you, do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat or what you will drink, nor about your body, what you will put on. Is not life more than food, and the body more than clothing? Look at the birds of the air: they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not of more value than they? And which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life? And why are you anxious about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin, yet I tell you, even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. But if God so clothes the grass of the field, which today is alive and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, will he not much more clothe you, O you of little faith? Therefore do not be anxious, saying, "What shall we eat?" or "What shall we drink?" or "What shall we wear?" For the Gentiles seek after all these things, and your heavenly Father knows that you need them all. But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you. Therefore do not be anxious about tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Sufficient for the day is its own trouble.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Our Father’s care frees us from anxious striving to give ourselves to his kingdom, trusting him for everything else.

Therefore. The “therefore” ties this to money: anxiety is mammon-service in another form, the heart gripped by what it dreads losing. So Jesus floods the fear with reasons. From greater to lesser: if God gave you life and a body, won’t he give food and clothes to sustain them? From creation: the birds neither sow nor store, yet your Father feeds them; the wildflowers neither toil nor spin, yet outshine Solomon (1 Kings 10:4–7) — and you are worth far more. From futility: no anxious hour ever added an hour to anyone’s life. Worry drains today without mending tomorrow.

The details. The birds aren’t idle; they work from dawn to dusk. What they don’t do is farm and store against a future they can’t see. The “lilies” were probably the wildflowers that turn Galilee’s hillsides red for a few weeks each spring, and their fate was ordinary: in a land short of timber, dried grass and flowers were fuel for a clay oven. God dressed a weed more finely than Israel’s richest king for a few weeks’ life ending as kindling. Will he forget his own child? And verse 27 can mean adding “a single hour to his span of life” or a cubit to one’s height; either way, worry has never changed a measurement.

Little faith. Jesus names the problem gently: “O you of little faith.” Matthew uses this word repeatedly (also 8:26; 14:31; 16:8), always to disciples, never unbelievers — a word for people who have faith and are frightened anyway. The difference between the believer and the pagan isn’t that the believer has no needs but that he has a Father who knows them.

Seek first. So the cure isn’t to stop needing but to re-aim the heart: “seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.” To seek first isn’t to bolt a religious slot onto a self-centred life, but to re-centre life on Christ as King: giving God the first of your time in his Word and prayer; pursuing his righteousness; letting his concerns — the lost, the church, the poor — shape your money and hours. At every fork the question shifts from “Which path is most comfortable?” to “Which most serves my King?” And it isn’t a ban on work or planning: work hard, plan wisely, then hand the result to your Father, turning fear into prayer (Philippians 4:6; 1 Peter 5:7).

A guard about anxiety. This passage has been used to tell people with anxiety disorders that their illness is sin, and the damage is real. Jesus addresses a settled orientation of the heart, a life organised around what one fears losing; he isn’t addressing a medical condition. Clinical anxiety isn’t disobedience; it arrives uninvited in people who love God and would give anything to be free of it. So “do not be anxious” isn’t a lever to pull harder; medical help is no failure of faith, any more than a splint; and a sufferer should read this passage for its reasons, not only its command. Jesus doesn’t simply forbid anxiety; he reasons patiently against it from creation and the Father’s character. That is how he treats frightened people.

Does this promise that faithful Christians will never go hungry or poor? No. Believers have starved, been imprisoned and died for Christ (Hebrews 11:35–38), and Paul knew hunger (Philippians 4:12). The promise is that the Father will not abandon his children, that he will give what he knows they need, and above all that he gives himself. It is not a guarantee of comfort or income, and it gives no support to the teaching that faith brings wealth.

One day at a time. The last verse is nearly humorous: “tomorrow will be anxious for itself” — tomorrow can manage its own worrying without help from today. And “Sufficient for the day is its own trouble” promises no small trouble; it says today has enough already. Don’t haul tomorrow’s into it. A test: what worry for tomorrow can you hand to your Father today?
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “a single hour to his span of life” can also be read “a single cubit to his stature.” Dry grass was used as fuel for clay ovens.

parallels.desc: do not be anxious about anything
cast all your anxieties on him

6.theology:
Prayer and the Fatherhood of God. The Lord’s Prayer is the fullest Trinitarian statement about prayer in the New Testament. We pray to the Father, in the name of the Son (the one who taught us to pray this way and who intercedes for us, Rom. 8:34), in the power of the Spirit (who helps us in our weakness and intercedes with groaning too deep for words, Rom. 8:26). Reformed theology has always understood prayer as Trinitarian from beginning to end: the Father hears, the Son mediates, the Spirit enables.

The address “Our Father” is the fruit of adoption — the doctrine that those who trust in Christ are received into the family of God with all the rights and privileges of sons (Gal. 4:5–6). We do not pray as strangers petitioning a distant deity; we pray as children talking to a Father who knows us, loves us, and has already given us his Son. The confidence of Christian prayer rests entirely on the prior act of God in adoption, not on the fervency or frequency of the one praying.
6.examples:
Then: The contrast between secret devotion and public performance runs through the Old Testament. Hannah prayed so quietly that Eli thought she was drunk (1 Sam. 1:13) — and God heard. Daniel opened his window toward Jerusalem and prayed three times a day without announcement, in full view of a hostile empire (Dan. 6:10). The great saints of Israel prayed to an audience of One — and their prayers are the ones that shaped history. The hypocrites who prayed on street corners are forgotten; their reward was fully paid and fully spent.

Now: The anxiety Jesus addresses in verses 25–34 is the defining emotional experience of our age. Financial anxiety, career anxiety, health anxiety, relationship anxiety — the modern world has more to worry about (in terms of information access about possible threats) than any previous generation. Jesus’ answer is not information management but kingdom orientation: seek first the kingdom, and the Father who holds all things will hold yours. This is not naive — it is the most realistic posture available to a creature who is not God. You are not in control of tomorrow; the Father is. Trust the Father.

7.title: The Narrow Gate
7.text: <sup>1</sup>“Judge not, that you be not judged. <sup>2</sup>For with the judgment you pronounce you will be judged, and with the measure you use it will be measured to you. <sup>3</sup>Why do you see the speck that is in your brother’s eye, but do not notice the log that is in your own eye? <sup>4</sup>Or how can you say to your brother, ‘Let me take the speck out of your eye,’ when there is the log in your own eye? <sup>5</sup>You hypocrite, first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother’s eye. <sup>6</sup>“Do not give dogs what is holy, and do not throw your pearls before pigs, lest they trample them underfoot and turn to attack you. <sup>7</sup>“Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. <sup>8</sup>For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened. <sup>9</sup>Or which one of you, if his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone? <sup>10</sup>Or if he asks for a fish, will give him a serpent? <sup>11</sup>If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him! <sup>12</sup>“So whatever you wish that others would do to you, do also to them, for this is the Law and the Prophets. <sup>13</sup>“Enter by the narrow gate. For the gate is wide and the way is easy that leads to destruction, and those who enter by it are many. <sup>14</sup>For the gate is narrow and the way is hard that leads to life, and those who find it are few. <sup>15</sup>“Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves. <sup>16</sup>You will recognize them by their fruits. Are grapes gathered from thornbushes, or figs from thistles? <sup>17</sup>So, every healthy tree bears good fruit, but the diseased tree bears bad fruit. <sup>18</sup>A healthy tree cannot bear bad fruit, nor can a diseased tree bear good fruit. <sup>19</sup>Every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire. <sup>20</sup>Thus you will recognize them by their fruits. <sup>21</sup>“Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven. <sup>22</sup>On that day many will say to me, ‘Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and cast out demons in your name, and do many mighty works in your name?’ <sup>23</sup>And then will I declare to them, ‘I never knew you; depart from me, you workers of lawlessness.’ <sup>24</sup>“Everyone then who hears these words of mine and does them will be like a wise man who built his house on the rock. <sup>25</sup>And the rain fell, and the floods came, and the winds blew and beat on that house, but it did not fall, because it had been founded on the rock. <sup>26</sup>And everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them will be like a foolish man who built his house on the sand. <sup>27</sup>And the rain fell, and the floods came, and the winds blew and beat against that house, and it fell, and great was the fall of it.” <sup>28</sup>And when Jesus finished these sayings, the crowds were astonished at his teaching, <sup>29</sup>for he was teaching them as one who had authority, and not as their scribes.
7.overview:
Chapter 7 concludes the Sermon on the Mount with a series of choices, each framed as a binary: the wide gate or the narrow, the false prophet or the true, the one who hears and does or the one who hears and does not. The Sermon that began with Beatitudes ends with warnings. The kingdom is real and its entrance is narrow; the alternatives are easy and lead to destruction. This is not the comfortable conclusion of a TED talk; it is the solemn close of the greatest sermon ever preached.

The famous “Judge not” (v. 1) is the most misquoted verse in the Bible. Jesus is not prohibiting all moral discernment — he commands it in verse 6 (discern who receives what is holy) and verses 15–16 (recognise false prophets by their fruit). He is prohibiting hypocritical judgment: condemning in others what you excuse in yourself. The log-and-speck image is both humorous and devastating — the person with a beam in their eye offering to perform eye surgery. Self-examination must precede fraternal correction.

The parable of the two builders is the Sermon’s climax and its challenge. Both builders hear the words of Jesus; both face the same storm. The difference is foundation: rock or sand. And the foundation is not intellectual agreement with Jesus’ teaching but doing it — the obedience that grows from genuine faith. The crowds are astonished at the end because Jesus teaches with authority, not as the scribes. He does not say “thus says the LORD”; he says “I say to you.” He is the rock on which the house is built.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–29 — Judgment, Prayer, and the Two Ways: Concluding the Sermon
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Sermon on the Mount concludes with four warnings and a call. The warning against judging hypocritically (vv. 1–6), the invitation to persistent prayer (vv. 7–12), and the double warning about the narrow gate and false prophets (vv. 13–23) all converge on the final parable of the two builders (vv. 24–27). The Sermon does not end gently: it ends with a stark choice between two gates, two trees, two confessions, two foundations — and the crowds are astonished not by the gentleness of what they heard but by the authority of the one who said it. The verse-by-verse fills in what a 29-verse summary cannot. On "judge not": the proof that it cannot mean what the world takes it to mean is inside this same chapter — v. 6 requires the hearer to identify "dogs" and "pigs", vv. 15-20 require him to identify false prophets by their fruit, and vv. 21-23 have Jesus distinguishing those who did the Father's will from those who did not. All within twenty-two verses of the command. Elsewhere he settles it in one sentence: "Do not judge by appearances, but judge with right judgment" (Jn. 7:24); and Paul asks, "Is it not those inside the church whom you are to judge?" (1 Cor. 5:12). "With the measure you use" is a rabbinic formula (measure for measure) and is an offer of a choice — a man sets the standard he will be tried by. The speck and the log are a tradesman's joke: karphos is a wood chip, dokos is a roof beam, both from the same building yard, told by a carpenter to people who had watched carpenters work. And v. 6 is a crossover (an X): it is the pigs that trample and the dogs that turn and attack. On prayer (vv. 7-11): "how much more" is the standard rabbinic argument from lesser to greater — and the premise slipped in without pause is that the audience are evil, stated as an agreed fact on the way to proving how kind God is. Bread/stone and fish/serpent are things that look alike (Galilean limestone weathers into loaf-shaped lumps; the lake held a whiskered catfish a Jew could not eat) — so the fear being answered is not malice but substitution. The golden rule (v. 12) is treated at length below. On false prophets: "sheep's clothing" may be the prophetic uniform itself (Zech. 13:4 has false prophets putting on a hairy cloak to deceive), and "ravenous" is harpax, from the verb to snatch — what defines him is that he is taking something. The fruit test cannot be run quickly, and that is not a defect: much damage has been done by men whose fruit would have been obvious in five years and who were given authority in five weeks. "I never knew you" (vv. 21-23) is likewise absent above and is given the fullest treatment in the chapter below. On the two houses: Luke supplies the detail that bites — the wise man dug deep (Lk. 6:48). In that country a dry wadi bed is the most inviting summer site there is, flat and easy to dig; digging down is slow, costly, and invisible when the house is finished. Both houses look identical. And "these words of mine" puts his own sayings where Israel's wisdom tradition put the Torah (Ps. 1:2). Note finally that this closing section is four pairs narrowing — two gates, two trees, two confessions, two foundations — and in every one the wrong option is the comfortable one and the two are hard to tell apart from outside. On the closing formula (v. 28): "when Jesus finished these sayings" occurs five times in Matthew and only five (7:28; 11:1; 13:53; 19:1; 26:1), each sealing a discourse — five books of teaching from a man who came out of Egypt, through the water, and through forty days in the wilderness. Moses gave five books from a mountain. And "astonished" is ekplesso, to be struck out of position, in the imperfect: they went on being knocked sideways.
verseByVerse.theology: The command not to judge (v. 1) is the most misquoted verse in the Sermon and one of the most misunderstood in the Bible. Jesus does not prohibit discernment (he commands it in v. 6 and vv. 15–20); he prohibits the hypocritical judgment that ignores one's own sin while scrutinizing another's. The warning about false prophets extends the theme: discernment is required, but it must begin with self-examination. The Sermon ends where it must — with the question of foundation. Hearing Jesus's words and not doing them is not neutrality; it is the choice of sand. The storm will decide what you built on.
verseByVerse.examples: The final verse — "he was teaching them as one who had authority, and not as their scribes" — is Matthew's first and defining portrait of Jesus as teacher. The scribes taught by citing authorities: "Rabbi X says..." Jesus taught by assertion: "I say to you." This is either the most arrogant teaching in human history or the teaching of the one to whom all authority belongs. Matthew does not leave the reader in the middle. The crowd was astonished. The question is what they did with the astonishment.

verseByVerse.quote: Judge not, that you be not judged. For with the judgment you pronounce you will be judged, and with the measure you use it will be measured to you. Why do you see the speck that is in your brother's eye, but do not notice the log that is in your own eye? Or how can you say to your brother, "Let me take the speck out of your eye," when there is the log in your own eye? You hypocrite, first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to take the speck out of your brother's eye. Do not give dogs what is holy, and do not throw your pearls before pigs, lest they trample them underfoot and turn to attack you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christians must judge themselves first and humbly, help others gently, and still exercise wise discernment.

What “judge not” forbids. “Judge not” has become secular culture’s favourite verse — the one command everyone still keeps. But Jesus means something precise. He isn’t banning moral evaluation or naming wrong; he does both throughout the sermon. He is banning the hypocritical tribunal of the self-righteous, who build careful cases against others while suppressing the evidence against themselves. And the warning has teeth: “with the measure you use it will be measured to you.” That is the Jewish “measure for measure”: the standard a person applies is the standard he chooses to be tried by, and he sets it himself every time he speaks about someone else (cf. Romans 2:1).

The proof in the chapter. “Judge not” can’t mean what the world takes it to mean, and the proof is in this chapter. Verse 6 requires working out who are dogs and pigs. Verses 15–20 require recognising false prophets by their fruit. Verses 21–23 have Jesus distinguishing those who did the Father’s will from those who didn’t. Whatever “judge not” forbids, it can’t forbid what Jesus requires in the next breath. He says elsewhere, “Do not judge by appearances, but judge with right judgment” (John 7:24), and Paul asks, “Is it not those inside the church whom you are to judge?” (1 Corinthians 5:12). The problem was never judging but judging badly — on appearances, by a standard the judge exempts himself from.

The log and the speck. The picture is deliberately absurd, a carpenter’s joke: the speck is a wood chip, the log a roof beam. A man with a beam sticking out of his eye leans in to extract a splinter from his brother’s. It is meant to be laughed at, and the laugh is the argument: no one would think it reasonable if they could see it from outside — and the man with the beam is the one person in the room who can’t. But notice that Jesus doesn’t say “leave the speck alone.” He says, “first take the log out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly” to help. Self-examination isn’t an excuse never to correct; it is the qualification for correcting rightly, as one patient helping another, not a spotless judge. A test: whose speck are you focused on while ignoring your own log?

Dogs and pigs. Verse 6 isn’t a stray fragment. Having warned against being too severe a judge, Jesus warns against being no judge at all. Dogs in that world were scavengers running loose round a village, and “what is holy” likely meant consecrated sacrificial meat — tossing the offering to the strays in the street. “Dogs” and “pigs” picture those who have shown settled, aggressive contempt for holy things; to keep pressing pearls on them is to watch the treasure trampled and invite attack (cf. 10:14; Proverbs 9:7–8). The saying is carefully made: the pigs trample the pearls, the dogs turn and attack.

Two ditches. So verses 1–5 and verse 6 are a matched pair, the ditches on either side of the road: don’t be censorious; don’t be naive. Deal honestly, and first, with your own sin; correct gently, as a fellow sinner; and stay wise — keep holding out Christ, but don’t mistake love for a refusal ever to discern, nor keep forcing holy things on those who only want to trample them. Neither a harsh heart nor a gullible one, but a clear and humble eye.
verseByVerse.note: Dogs and pigs were unclean animals, images of those who scorn what is holy.

parallels.desc: in passing judgment you condemn yourself

verseByVerse.quote: Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives, and the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened. Or which one of you, if his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, will give him a serpent? If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him!
verseByVerse.commentary:
We pray with bold persistence because God is a good Father who gives what is truly good, never a counterfeit.

Keep asking. “Ask… seek… knock” are present-tense commands: keep asking, keep seeking, keep knocking. Prayer here is radical dependence — an admission that what we most need lies beyond our power to produce. It fits what came before: the sermon has described a life impossible by human effort, and now Jesus shows where the strength comes from. The demands drive us to our knees, and the door is one that opens.

How much more. Why pray with such confidence? Because of who we ask. No decent father, asked for bread, slips his child a stone, or asked for fish, hands him a snake. If flawed parents give good gifts, “how much more” will the perfect Father. That is the standard Jewish argument from lesser to greater. And notice the premise Jesus slips in: “If you then, who are evil…” He says it of his own audience, as an agreed fact, on the way to a point about generosity — a bleak verdict on human nature used as an argument for how kind God is. Our boldness rests not on our worthiness or persistence as a technique, but on his goodness.

No counterfeits. The pairs aren’t random opposites but look-alikes. The limestone of that land weathers into rounded lumps very like a flat loaf — close enough that the devil had used the resemblance in the wilderness (4:3) — and the lake had a smooth, whiskered fish, unclean to eat, that looked like a snake. So the picture isn’t a father handing over something obviously cruel, but palming off a convincing fake. That is the fear beneath much unanswered prayer: not that God is malicious, but that he substitutes — that we asked for bread and got a stone close enough to look right and no use at all. Jesus says the one thing never in the parcel is a counterfeit.

What it doesn’t mean. It is no blank cheque or vending machine, no promise that whatever we crave will come if we believe hard enough or ask often enough. The promise is “good things,” and a good Father gives what is good, not always what is wanted. Sometimes the loving answer is no, or wait, or something better; the picture assumes a child might reach for a snake thinking it a fish. A prayer answered differently isn’t the Father failing but the Father fathering. We ask boldly, yet always “according to his will” (1 John 5:14). A test: do you trust God’s “no” as much as his “yes”?

Asking for the Holy Spirit. Luke records “how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him” (Luke 11:13). If believers receive the Spirit on trusting Christ (Ephesians 1:13; Romans 8:9), why ask? In its setting the promise looked ahead to Pentecost, when the disciples waited and prayed for the Spirit (Luke 24:49; Acts 1:14). For us now, we don’t ask for a Guest we lack, but for more of his work — to be filled again and again (Ephesians 5:18; Acts 4:31), for his power, comfort and help to put sin to death and bear fruit. In giving the Spirit, God gives himself, the best good thing of all.
verseByVerse.note: Flat loaves could look like stones, and some fish like snakes.

parallels.desc: every good gift is from above
if we ask according to his will

verseByVerse.quote: So whatever you wish that others would do to you, do also to them, for this is the Law and the Prophets.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love for our neighbour means actively doing for others the good we would want — the overflow of a Father’s generosity, bounded by what God has revealed is good.

Positive, not only negative. This is the Golden Rule, and notice its shape: it is positive. Something like it had been said before. Rabbi Hillel, a generation earlier, asked to sum up the law while standing on one foot, replied: what is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbour — that is the whole Torah. Confucius said much the same centuries before, as did the book of Tobit (4:15). The negative form is one of the commonest things wise men have ever said. But it tells you what to refrain from; Jesus tells you what to do. A man can keep the negative rule while sitting still and never troubling himself about anyone. Jesus makes it impossible to obey by inaction: look at your neighbour, work out what you would long for if you stood where he stands, and go and be that for him. The one rule is a fence; the other is a road. A test: what good would you want if you were in your neighbour’s place — and will you do it?

Family likeness. The “so” that opens the verse reaches back: we have a Father who gives good gifts to those who ask (vv. 7–11), and children come to resemble their fathers. The reason to treat others this way isn’t that society runs better, or that we hope for the same in return. Reciprocity is prudence; this is family likeness.

Bounded by God’s law. A common objection: tastes differ, so “do as you would be done by” lets you inflict on your neighbour what you happen to enjoy. The second half answers it: “for this is the Law and the Prophets.” What you may wish for another is bounded by everything God has revealed about what is good. The rule summarises the law; it isn’t a licence to put your appetites in its place, nor to indulge your neighbour in what Scripture forbids (cf. Romans 13:8–10; Galatians 5:14).

The whole sermon gathered. And the phrase does more. Jesus opened the body of this sermon by saying he came not to abolish “the Law or the Prophets” but to fulfil them (5:17), and he closes it here with the same words. Everything between is bracketed by that claim. Having pressed the law past every hearer’s reach, he hands them one sentence to carry down the mountain — not a lowering of the standard but the whole of it, gathered into a form someone can begin on tomorrow morning.
verseByVerse.note: Other ancient teachers put this rule negatively (“do not do what you would hate”); Jesus puts it positively.

parallels.desc: the whole law in one word

verseByVerse.quote: Enter by the narrow gate. For the gate is wide and the way is easy that leads to destruction, and those who enter by it are many. For the gate is narrow and the way is hard that leads to life, and those who find it are few.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There are only two ways, and life is found only through Christ himself, the narrow door, by coming to him on his terms.

Two ways. The sermon ends with a series of stark contrasts, and this is the first: two gates, two ways, two destinations, two crowds. The wide gate isn’t described as obviously wicked; its mark is that it asks nothing. The narrow gate and hard way are marked by difficulty — the word means pressed, constricted, a passage one must squeeze through. Jesus takes no pleasure in the many and the few, but he won’t soften the reality (cf. Deuteronomy 30:15, 19; Psalm 1:6).

The gate is Christ. Our culture prizes being broad-minded and suspects anything narrow; Jesus reverses the values. The broad gate looks free and welcoming, yet ends in destruction; the narrow gate looks cramped and costly, yet opens onto life. The narrow gate is Christ himself: “I am the door” (John 10:9); “I am the way… No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6). It is narrow because there is one way to God, and because you must come stripped — you can’t carry your self-righteousness, sins or idols through it. The hard way beyond it is the road of discipleship this sermon has described, costly and against the grain of the world.

Four misreadings. First, “hard” doesn’t mean we earn life by effort; the gate is a Person, entered by grace through faith, and the road is hard because following Christ in a fallen world costs us. Second, “narrow” isn’t the sour narrowness of the Pharisees; it describes the one way of salvation, not an unkind spirit. Third, the broad road isn’t crowded only with the obviously wicked; it is thronged with respectable, religious people, even some who cry “Lord, Lord” (vv. 21–23). You can be devout and still be drifting the easy way. Fourth, “few” is no excuse for despair or smugness; the gate stands open, “enter” is a command anyone may obey, and those who enter do so by grace alone. A test: which road are you on — the one that asks nothing now, or the one that costs you yourself?

Will only a few be saved? Jesus is describing who is on each road now, not the final count of the redeemed, which John sees as “a great multitude that no one could number” (Revelation 7:9). When someone asked Jesus directly whether only a few would be saved, he answered, “Strive to enter through the narrow door” (Luke 13:23–24). The question is not how many, but whether you.

A summons. So hear it not as a gloomy verdict but as an urgent invitation. The easy way asks nothing now and costs everything at the end; the narrow way costs you yourself now and gives life forever. And the narrow gate is never locked: the One who is the door stretched out his arms on a cross so that whoever will may come. Enter.

parallels.desc: life and death set before you
the way of the wicked will perish

verseByVerse.quote: Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep's clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves. You will recognize them by their fruits. Are grapes gathered from thornbushes, or figs from thistles? So, every healthy tree bears good fruit, but the diseased tree bears bad fruit. A healthy tree cannot bear bad fruit, nor can a diseased tree bear good fruit. Every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire. Thus you will recognize them by their fruits.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The church must watch patiently for the fruit of teaching and character, because the heart determines the life.

Sheep’s clothing. False prophets come “in sheep’s clothing” — not as obvious enemies but as members of the flock, harmless-looking and wise-sounding. The danger is that they don’t look like wolves. And it may be more precise than it sounds: a prophet in Israel was known by his garment, like Elijah’s hairy mantle, and Zechariah speaks of false prophets who “put on a hairy cloak in order to deceive” (Zechariah 13:4). The disguise may be the prophet’s uniform itself. This is an internal threat, arising within the community: “from among your own selves will arise men speaking twisted things” (Acts 20:30).

Ravenous. The word means to seize or snatch, like the wolf that “snatches” the sheep (John 10:12). What defines the false teacher isn’t only that he is mistaken but that he is taking something, and the flock is what he takes it from.

The tree and its fruit. Grapes don’t grow on thornbushes or figs on thistles; a healthy tree bears good fruit and a diseased tree bad, and neither can do otherwise. The tree determines the fruit, as the heart determines the life. No outward religious performance can squeeze good fruit from a corrupt root; in the end it shows its nature. And the fruitless tree meets the end John warned of: “cut down and thrown into the fire” (cf. 3:10).

What good and bad fruit look like. Look in three places. The teaching: good fruit is faithful to Scripture, exalts Christ and his cross, and calls people to repentance and grace; bad fruit twists the Bible, soft-pedals sin, sells a gospel of self, money or works, and draws disciples after the teacher. The character: good fruit is “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23), shown in humility, honesty, sexual purity, integrity with money and kept promises; bad fruit is pride, greed, immorality, manipulation, deceit and a trail of wounded people. The effect on others: good fruit leaves people loving Christ more and leaning harder on God; bad fruit leaves them puffed up, crushed or fleeced, with the leader exalted.

Give it time. Don’t mistake success for good fruit; crowds, eloquence, charisma and “results” can all be counterfeited, while character and faithfulness can’t. And fruit is seasonal. No one judges a tree in March; an orchard is judged in autumn, and a bad tree can look like a good one most of the year. A single failure doesn’t make a diseased tree, since true believers still stumble; watch the settled pattern of a life over time. Much damage in churches has been done by men whose fruit would have been obvious in five years and who were given authority in five weeks. The instruction isn’t “be suspicious” but “wait, and watch what grows.” A test: are you following a teacher for his gifts, or because his life and teaching bear good fruit?

parallels.desc: the axe laid to the root

verseByVerse.quote: Not everyone who says to me, "Lord, Lord," will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven. On that day many will say to me, "Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and cast out demons in your name, and do many mighty works in your name?" And then will I declare to them, "I never knew you; depart from me, you workers of lawlessness."
verseByVerse.commentary:
What saves is not religious activity or spiritual gifts but truly knowing and being known by Christ, shown in obedience.

The most startling warning. People who called Jesus “Lord, Lord,” who prophesied, cast out demons and did mighty works in his name — shut out. Not pagans or casual churchgoers, but people with a strong claim to spiritual experience and ministry success. The test is “the will of my Father” — not power, results or even orthodox profession, but the obedience that flows from a real relationship. Gifts and performance can be present where the relationship is absent.

“I never knew you.” Not “I knew you once” or “slightly,” but never. The ministry was real and the words sincere, but knowing Christ and being known by him — the embrace of saving faith — was missing all along (cf. 2 Timothy 2:19).

The Judge. And notice who is speaking. “On that day” is the day of judgment, and Jesus presides over it, sorting the human race with a word. “Depart from me, you workers of lawlessness” echoes Psalm 6:8: “Depart from me, all you workers of evil.” There the psalmist speaks to his enemies, trusting the LORD who judges. Jesus takes the words onto his own lips as the Judge. The carpenter from Nazareth stands in God’s place on the last day. He isn’t merely the teacher of the sermon; he is its Judge.

Their defence. Notice what is missing from their defence. Every word is about them: “did we not prophesy… cast out demons… do many mighty works?” — a résumé offered at the bar of God. There is no mention of mercy, the cross, or needing forgiveness. The poor in spirit come with empty hands (5:3); these men came holding up a record. They weren’t failed disciples; they were strangers who were extremely busy. And the verdict isn’t “you did too little” but “I never knew you.” So the anxious question, “Have I done enough?”, is exactly the wrong one — the question these men were asking.

For the fearful. And these men are surprised. No one in this scene was worried on the way in. So the person lying awake frightened by this verse shows the opposite of what it describes; that fear, rightly read, is a form of the poverty of spirit the sermon called blessed. The self-deceived are perfectly comfortable. (The same logic answers the other verse that troubles tender consciences, at 12:32.)

Examine, then look away. Don’t simply be reassured; this is a warning to heed. Examine yourself by what Scripture offers. John wrote a letter “that you may know that you have eternal life” (1 John 5:13), and his tests are three: do you believe Jesus is the Christ come in the flesh; do you love other Christians in practice; and is there real obedience, however stumbling? Add: when you sin, does it grieve you? Do you want Christ, or only his benefits? Then look away from yourself, because assurance never rested on the quality of your self-examination but on him: “no one will snatch them out of my hand” (John 10:28); “he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion” (Philippians 1:6). If you still can’t be sure, don’t search yourself harder. Come again today with nothing, as this sermon has taught from its first line: “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37). The one thing you must not do is assume. A test: are you resting on your record or on Christ?

parallels.desc: depart from me, all you workers of evil

verseByVerse.quote: Everyone then who hears these words of mine and does them will be like a wise man who built his house on the rock. And the rain fell, and the floods came, and the winds blew and beat on that house, but it did not fall, because it had been founded on the rock. And everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them will be like a foolish man who built his house on the sand. And the rain fell, and the floods came, and the winds blew and beat against that house, and it fell, and great was the fall of it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Only a life resting on Christ and obeying his words will stand on the day of testing.

Hearing isn’t enough. Both builders heard the same sermon, and that is the point: hearing isn’t enough. The sermon must become the foundation of a life, not merely the content of a memory.

The same storm. Both houses face the same storm; the sermon promises no shelter from suffering. Rain, floods and winds beat on wise and foolish alike; the difference is the foundation, not the weather. Obedience doesn’t insulate us from trial; it determines what survives it. And the fool isn’t idle; he too heard, chose a site and built.

The wadi. Much of that land is cut by wadis, watercourses dry most of the year. In summer a wadi bed is an inviting site: flat, level, easy to dig. A man could build quickly and cheaply and look sensible in July. Then the winter rains come off the hills and the dry bed becomes a torrent within an hour. Luke names what the wise man did: he “dug deep and laid the foundation on the rock” (Luke 6:48). Digging is slow, costly, delays the house, and when it is done nobody sees it. The foundation is never admired, and in fair weather makes no visible difference.

Underground obedience. That is the point about obedience. What this sermon has asked — dealing with anger before it becomes murder, cutting off what feeds lust, loving an enemy, giving unseen, forgiving a debt, refusing to serve money — is almost all invisible, done underground. No one applauds it. And it is the only thing that matters when the water comes. The houses look identical; Matthew doesn’t say the fool’s house was shoddy. The difference was underground and undetectable until the one day it mattered.

Sand and rock. To build on sand is to hear Jesus and not obey — to sit under good preaching and nod along, know your Bible and enjoy discussing it, attend church, be baptized and respectable, while his words never change how you live on Monday. To build on rock is to hear Jesus and do what he says, resting your life on Christ and therefore actually obeying: forgiving the one who wronged you, turning from the sin you have been quietly keeping, telling the truth when a lie would be easier, putting the kingdom first with your calendar and wallet. And the doing doesn’t earn the house; it shows the foundation is real. A faith resting on Christ will in time get up and obey him (James 1:22–25). A test: what has Jesus said in this sermon that you have heard but not yet done?

“These words of mine.” Consider the claim. Israel’s wisdom had one foundation: the blessed man’s “delight is in the law of the LORD” (Psalm 1:2). And a carpenter from Nazareth ends his sermon by putting his own sayings in that place: build on my words and you will stand. He doesn’t say his teaching agrees with the rock; he says it is the rock.

A crash. “And great was the fall of it.” No consolation follows, no summary or softening; the sermon stops with the sound of a house going down. It is the last of four pairs that have narrowed all the way: two gates, two trees, two confessions, two foundations. In each the wrong option is the comfortable one, and the two are hard to tell apart from outside — a broad road looks like freedom, a wolf like a sheep, “Lord, Lord” like faith, and a house on sand like a house.
verseByVerse.note: Wadis (dry stream beds) flood suddenly in the rainy season; a house on sand could be swept away overnight.

parallels.desc: a wall smeared with whitewash falls

verseByVerse.quote: And when Jesus finished these sayings, the crowds were astonished at his teaching, for he was teaching them as one who had authority, and not as their scribes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus speaks with God’s own authority, so his words demand not mere admiration but obedience.

A structural signal. “And when Jesus finished these sayings” — that formula occurs five times, each closing a block of teaching: here (7:28), and at 11:1, 13:53, 19:1 and 26:1, the last time with “all these sayings,” as the passion begins. Matthew has built his Gospel around five great discourses: the Sermon on the Mount (5–7), the mission charge (10), the parables (13), the teaching on the church (18), and the discourse on the end (23–25). Five books of teaching from a man who came out of Egypt (2:15), passed through water, and was tested forty days in the wilderness. Anyone raised on the Scriptures would feel it: Moses gave five books; Israel came out of Egypt, through the water, and received the law at a mountain. Matthew is arranging his Gospel to say a greater than Moses has come with a greater law.

Knocked sideways. The verb is stronger than “astonished”: knocked out of position, and it kept happening. It didn’t wear off when he stopped. No one who seriously reckons with this sermon — poverty of spirit, purity of heart, love of enemies — comes away unchanged. The only options are to be astonished into obedience or walk back to the wide gate.

Authority. What struck them wasn’t chiefly the content but the authority: “he was teaching them as one who had authority, and not as their scribes.” The scribes weren’t frauds; they were careful men whose method was to cite — this rabbi taught thus, and that one qualified it. That is how a tradition is faithfully handed on. What they had never heard was a man who cited nobody. Six times in one sermon: “You have heard that it was said… But I say to you.” He amends Moses on his own word, without a supporting authority, and ends by telling them their eternal safety depends on doing what he has said.

No modest reading. That is either breathtaking arrogance or the voice of the One to whom “all authority in heaven and on earth has been given” (28:18). There is no modest middle reading, and Matthew’s Gospel will press the choice again and again. The crowd’s astonishment is the right first response; the question is what comes next — whether astonishment becomes allegiance and hearing becomes obedience. The sermon has been preached; the builder must now choose the site. A test: do you treat Jesus’ words as advice to consider, or commands from the One with all authority?
verseByVerse.note: Scribes taught by citing earlier authorities; Jesus spoke on his own authority (“But I say to you”).

7.theology:
Hearing and Doing: Faith and Works in Reformed Theology. Matthew 7:24–27 has sometimes been read as teaching salvation by works: do the words of Jesus and be saved. Reformed theology reads it more carefully. The doing is not the foundation; the rock is. The foundation is Christ himself, received by faith. The doing is the evidence and expression of genuine faith — what James calls the faith that works (Jas. 2:17).

Calvin wrote that we are justified by faith alone, but the faith that justifies is never alone. The wise builder who hears and does is the person who has been genuinely changed by the words of Jesus — not merely intellectually persuaded but existentially transformed. The doing of the Sermon on the Mount is not the cause of salvation but its fruit; not the foundation but the superstructure. And the foundation, as Paul will make clear (1 Cor. 3:11), is Jesus Christ himself — the one whose words these are.
7.examples:
Then: The two builders have their Old Testament counterparts in the wise and foolish in Proverbs: the one who builds their house on wisdom (Prov. 9:1) and the one who builds on folly (Prov. 9:13–18). Israel’s history is the extended parable of a nation that heard God’s word at Sinai and alternately built on it (David, Hezekiah, Josiah) and ignored it (the cycle of judges, the divided monarchy, the exile). The storm that came on the sandbuilders in Israel’s history was Babylon — and Jeremiah watched the great fall of it (Jer. 7:1–15, which echoes this passage).

Now: The Sermon on the Mount ends with the most personal challenge of the entire Gospel so far: what are you building on? The storm is coming — the storms of suffering, of loss, of death — and the question that will matter then is being answered now by what you build with your ordinary days. The person who reads the Sermon and is intellectually impressed but does nothing with it is the sand builder. The person who allows its demands to drive them to the Christ who fulfils them, and who in the Spirit begins to do what the Sermon commands — that person is building on rock. The flood will reveal the foundation. Build now while the weather is good.

8.title: The King’s Authority Over All
8.text: <sup>1</sup>When he came down from the mountain, great crowds followed him. <sup>2</sup>And behold, a leper came to him and knelt before him, saying, “Lord, if you will, you can make me clean.” <sup>3</sup>And Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him, saying, “I will; be clean.” And immediately his leprosy was cleansed. <sup>4</sup>And Jesus said to him, “See that you say nothing to anyone, but go, show yourself to the priest and offer the gift that Moses commanded, for a proof to them.” <sup>5</sup>When he had entered Capernaum, a centurion came forward to him, appealing to him, <sup>6</sup>“Lord, my servant is lying paralyzed at home, suffering terribly.” <sup>7</sup>And he said to him, “I will come and heal him.” <sup>8</sup>But the centurion replied, “Lord, I am not worthy to have you come under my roof, but only say the word, and my servant will be healed. <sup>9</sup>For I too am a man under authority, with soldiers under me. And I say to one, ‘Go,’ and he goes, and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes, and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.” <sup>10</sup>When Jesus heard this, he marveled and said to those who followed him, “Truly, I tell you, with no one in Israel have I found such faith. <sup>11</sup>I tell you, many will come from east and west and recline at table with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven, <sup>12</sup>while the sons of the kingdom will be thrown into the outer darkness. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” <sup>13</sup>And to the centurion Jesus said, “Go; let it be done for you as you have believed.” And the servant was healed at that very moment. <sup>14</sup>And when Jesus entered Peter’s house, he saw his mother-in-law lying sick with a fever. <sup>15</sup>He touched her hand, and the fever left her, and she rose and began to serve him. <sup>16</sup>That evening they brought to him many who were oppressed by demons, and he cast out the spirits with a word and healed all who were sick. <sup>17</sup>This was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah: “He took our illnesses and bore our diseases.” <sup>18</sup>Now when Jesus saw a crowd around him, he gave orders to go over to the other side. <sup>19</sup>And a scribe came up and said to him, “Teacher, I will follow you wherever you go.” <sup>20</sup>And Jesus said to him, “Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.” <sup>21</sup>Another of the disciples said to him, “Lord, let me first go and bury my father.” <sup>22</sup>And Jesus said to him, “Follow me, and leave the dead to bury their own dead.” <sup>23</sup>And when he got into the boat, his disciples followed him. <sup>24</sup>And behold, there arose a great storm on the sea, so that the boat was being swamped by the waves; but he was asleep. <sup>25</sup>And they went and woke him, saying, “Save us, Lord; we are perishing.” <sup>26</sup>And he said to them, “Why are you afraid, O you of little faith?” Then he rose and rebuked the winds and the sea, and there was a great calm. <sup>27</sup>And the men marveled, saying, “What sort of man is this, that even winds and sea obey him?” <sup>28</sup>And when he came to the other side, to the country of the Gadarenes, two demon-possessed men met him, coming out of the tombs, so fierce that no one could pass that way. <sup>29</sup>And behold, they cried out, “What have you to do with us, O Son of God? Have you come here to torment us before the time?” <sup>30</sup>Now a herd of many pigs was feeding at some distance from them. <sup>31</sup>And the demons begged him, saying, “If you cast us out, send us away into the herd of pigs.” <sup>32</sup>And he said to them, “Go.” So they came out and went into the pigs, and behold, the whole herd rushed down the steep bank into the sea and drowned in the waters. <sup>33</sup>The herdsmen fled, and going into the city they told everything, especially what had happened to the demon-possessed men. <sup>34</sup>And behold, all the city came out to meet Jesus, and when they saw him, they begged him to leave their region.
8.overview:
Matthew 8 is a gallery of authority. Coming down from the mountain where he gave the law of the kingdom, the King now demonstrates the power of the kingdom. In rapid succession Jesus heals a leper with a touch, a Gentile servant with a word, a feverish woman with a hand, and a raging sea with a rebuke. The crowds ask the right question: “What sort of man is this?” Matthew intends the reader to answer: the Son of God, in whom all authority in heaven and on earth is vested.

The chapter also sounds the notes of grace toward outsiders. A leper — ritually unclean, excluded from community — is touched rather than avoided. A Roman centurion — a Gentile, an occupier — displays faith that shames Israel. Jesus announces that many from east and west will recline at the messianic banquet while presumptuous insiders face exclusion. The kingdom breaks every boundary of ethnic privilege. The centurion’s faith is the model: he grasps that Jesus’ authority is absolute, that his word accomplishes what he speaks. This is saving faith — resting wholly on the word of the King.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–17 — The Messiah Heals: Authority over Leprosy, Paralysis, and Fever
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Matthew groups ten miracles in chapters 8-9, presenting Jesus as the one Isaiah promised: "He took our illnesses and bore our diseases" (v. 17, citing Isa. 53:4). The leper, the centurion's servant, and Peter's mother-in-law are the first three — representing the ritually unclean, the Gentile, and the woman. Jesus heals all with equal authority and without discrimination. The verse-by-verse fills in what these three lines cannot. On the leper: Leviticus prescribes torn clothes, loose hair, a covered lip and a shouted "Unclean, unclean", and dwelling alone outside the camp (Lev. 13:45-46) — so this man had not been touched by anyone for as long as the disease had lasted. Note that he broke the law to approach, and that his prayer is the reverse of ours: he is certain of the power and unsure of the willingness. And Jesus did not need to touch him — the very next healing in this chapter is done at a distance, by a spoken word — so the contact was gained for its own sake. He touched him first and said "be clean" second. The command to show himself to the priest handed the priesthood a ceremony (Lev. 14: two birds, cedar, scarlet, hyssop, running water) that they had learned and almost certainly never performed — in the whole Old Testament only Miriam and Naaman were cleansed of this. On the centurion: Matthew has him speak to Jesus directly while Luke has him send Jewish elders and then friends (Lk. 7:3-8); this is the ordinary convention by which a man does what he does through agents, and Luke supplies the reason the elders would carry his message — he had built their synagogue. His "I am not worthy" is not self-disparagement but consideration: a Jew entering a Gentile house contracted defilement, and he is protecting Jesus from a cost he judges unnecessary. His sentence has stood in the liturgy for centuries. And Jesus marvels exactly twice in the Gospels — here at faith, and at Nazareth's unbelief (Mk. 6:6) — so faith in its presence and its absence is the only thing recorded as astonishing him.
verseByVerse.theology: Each healing is an enacted parable of salvation: Jesus touches what is untouchable (the leper), heals at a distance by his word alone (the centurion's servant), and raises up those laid low by sickness. The healing of disease and the forgiveness of sins are not unrelated — both are expressions of the same redemptive authority. Isaiah 53:4 locates these healings within the atonement: Jesus bore our diseases not merely by healing them but ultimately by carrying them on the cross.
verseByVerse.examples: The centurion's faith astonishes Jesus and becomes the template for Gentile inclusion: "not even in Israel have I found such faith." Faith is not a Jewish property or a product of religious background; it is the trust that recognizes authority and rests in it. The centurion understood command-and-response because he lived under authority. His insight: if Jesus commands, it is done.

verseByVerse.quote: When he came down from the mountain, great crowds followed him. And behold, a leper came to him and knelt before him, saying, "Lord, if you will, you can make me clean."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The most excluded may come to Christ, trusting both his power and his willingness to save.

The life he had lived. Leviticus sets it out: “The leprous person who has the disease shall wear torn clothes and let the hair of his head hang loose, and he shall cover his upper lip and cry out, ‘Unclean, unclean.’ … He shall live alone. His dwelling shall be outside the camp” (Leviticus 13:45–46). Torn clothes and loose hair were a mourner’s dress; he attended his own funeral daily. Later Jewish rules fixed the distance he had to keep. He hadn’t been touched — not by a wife, not by his children — for as long as the disease had lasted.

What “leprosy” was. The biblical word covers more than modern leprosy; Leviticus uses it even of mould in fabric and walls. It was a category of visible skin disease that made a person ritually unclean. That doesn’t soften the picture; it widens it. Whatever he had, it had put him outside.

He came anyway. He wasn’t permitted to approach. Every step toward the crowd broke the law he had lived under; the correct thing was to stand off and shout. He came anyway, and knelt — the word used of worship.

“If you will.” He has no doubt about Jesus’ power; what he doesn’t know is whether Jesus would want to. We usually have it the other way round: sure God is kind, unsure he will act. This man is certain of the ability and uncertain of the willingness — which is what years of being untouchable do to a person’s sense of whether anyone wants him near. And his prayer is a model: “you can” — faith in Christ’s power; “if you will” — submission to his will. A test: do you doubt Christ’s power, or his willingness to receive someone like you?
verseByVerse.note: “Leprosy” in the Bible covers a range of skin diseases. A leper had to live apart and was ritually unclean.

parallels.desc: the leper must live alone, crying “Unclean”

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him, saying, "I will; be clean." And immediately his leprosy was cleansed. And Jesus said to him, "See that you say nothing to anyone, but go, show yourself to the priest and offer the gift that Moses commanded, for a proof to them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ’s holiness isn’t defiled by our uncleanness but drives it out, and he restores outcasts to God’s people.

He didn’t have to touch him. The next healing in this chapter is done at a distance, by a word. The power didn’t need contact. Nothing was gained by touching except the touch itself. And “stretched out his hand” echoes the outstretched arm of God in Exodus. That hand crossed the distance the law had set and rested on skin nobody had willingly touched in years.

Contagion reversed. He touched first, then said, “be clean.” For a moment Jesus was in contact with an unclean man not yet healed. By the law, touching made a person unclean. Here the flow runs the other way: his holiness isn’t contaminated by the leper’s uncleanness; it expels it. That is the gospel in a gesture. “I will; be clean” — no formula, no process, simply the will of the Creator restoring what disease destroyed. A test: what in you do you think is too unclean for Christ to touch?

Say nothing. The silence wasn’t arbitrary. Mark tells us the man “went out and began to talk freely about it,” so that Jesus “could no longer openly enter a town” (Mark 1:45). A reputation as a healer would bury the preaching under crowds, and it did.

Show yourself to the priest. Jesus honours the law (5:17). Only a priest could declare a leper clean and readmit him to Israel’s worship, with the offerings Leviticus 14 prescribes: two birds, cedarwood, scarlet yarn and hyssop, washings, eight days and sacrifices. Every priest knew the ceremony and none expected to use it; in the whole Old Testament only Miriam and Naaman are recorded as cleansed. So a man walking into the temple asking for the rite of a cleansed leper was “a proof to them” — handing the priesthood a page they had never had cause to open, and making someone ask who had done this.

verseByVerse.quote: When he had entered Capernaum, a centurion came forward to him, appealing to him, "Lord, my servant is lying paralyzed at home, suffering terribly."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A powerful Gentile humbles himself for a lowly servant — showing the faith and compassion that please Christ.

A centurion. The backbone of the Roman military system: a career officer nominally commanding a hundred men, risen from the ranks. Capernaum lay in Herod Antipas’s territory, so he may have served Herod’s Roman-style army; either way, he was a Gentile soldier in a force the locals resented. Every centurion in the New Testament is presented sympathetically — a striking fact in an occupied land.

For a servant. He comes not commanding but “appealing,” and for a servant — someone of low status whose suffering moves him. The word can mean servant or boy; Luke says he was a slave the centurion highly valued (Luke 7:2). Those with power often notice only their own needs; this man uses his for the powerless. A test: how do you use whatever power you have — for yourself or for those beneath you?

Did he come himself? Matthew has the centurion speak with Jesus directly; Luke says he sent Jewish elders and then friends, and the two never meet (Luke 7:3–8). That is a difference of reporting, not a contradiction. A man is said to do what he does through his agents, as we say a king built a palace. Matthew compresses the exchange to its principals because his point is the centurion’s faith; Luke, interested in how Jews and Gentiles dealt with each other, keeps the messengers.

Why the elders came. Luke explains why Jewish elders would carry a message for an officer of the occupation: “he loves our nation, and he is the one who built us our synagogue” (Luke 7:5). The ruined synagogue at Capernaum today is later, but it seems to stand on a first-century foundation, very possibly the floor of his.
verseByVerse.note: A centurion commanded about a hundred soldiers. This one was a Gentile, probably serving Herod Antipas.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to him, "I will come and heal him." But the centurion replied, "Lord, I am not worthy to have you come under my roof, but only say the word, and my servant will be healed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
True faith rests on the power of Christ’s word alone, and humbly recognises its unworthiness before him.

Protecting Jesus. “I am not worthy to have you come under my roof.” This is more than self-abasement. A Jew who entered a Gentile house incurred ceremonial defilement — why Peter needed a vision before going to Cornelius (Acts 10:28), and why the leaders wouldn’t enter Pilate’s headquarters before Passover (John 18:28). The centurion knows it. He is saying, “Coming under my roof will cost you, and it isn’t necessary” — the courtesy of a man who has learned what his neighbours believe, offered while his servant is dying.

A question? Jesus’ words in verse 7 can also be read as a question: “Shall I come and heal him?” — raising the very issue of entering a Gentile house so the centurion can answer it. It can’t be settled, and the sense is much the same.

Only say the word. What makes this faith rather than respect is what it assumes. He doesn’t think Jesus needs to be present, see the patient or touch him. The word alone is enough — which is how Genesis says the world came to be, and what the psalm says of God: “He sent out his word and healed them” (Psalm 107:20). The church has prayed his sentence for centuries before communion: “Lord, I am not worthy… but only say the word.” And it is why we pray to the ascended Lord now: distance is nothing to his power. A test: do you trust Christ’s word even when you can’t see him act?
verseByVerse.note: A devout Jew would not normally enter a Gentile house; the centurion spares Jesus the problem.

parallels.desc: unlawful for a Jew to visit a foreigner
he sent out his word and healed them

verseByVerse.quote: For I too am a man under authority, with soldiers under me. And I say to one, "Go," and he goes, and to another, "Come," and he comes, and to my servant, "Do this," and he does it." When Jesus heard this, he marveled and said to those who followed him, "Truly, I tell you, with no one in Israel have I found such faith."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Faith sees that Christ’s word carries God’s own authority — and such faith can astonish the Son of God.

The argument from authority. The centurion reasons by analogy: because he stands under authority, his commands carry the weight of the power above him. When he says “Go,” Rome stands behind the word. So he sees that when Jesus speaks, God’s power stands behind his word. That is the core of faith: confidence not in the one asking but in the authority of the one asked.

Further than he knew. But press the analogy further than he could. He pictures Jesus like himself, a man under authority whose word carries weight because a greater power backs it. That is true insofar as the Son is sent by the Father. It isn’t the whole truth. Jesus isn’t a prophet holding God’s power on loan, as Elijah and Elisha did; he is the Son in whom “the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily” (Colossians 2:9). When Elisha raised the dead he prayed; when Jesus heals he simply speaks. The centurion had the right end of the truth and didn’t yet know how deep it went.

He marvelled. “With no one in Israel have I found such faith.” Faith isn’t a national or religious achievement; it is seeing who Jesus is, open to anyone. And the Gospels record Jesus marvelling at only two things: this Gentile’s faith, and his hometown’s unbelief — “he marveled because of their unbelief” (Mark 6:6). Not storms, demons, crowds or his own betrayal. Faith is what astonished him, in both directions. A test: which would Jesus marvel at in you — your faith or your unbelief?

verseByVerse.quote: I tell you, many will come from east and west and recline at table with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven, while the sons of the kingdom will be thrown into the outer darkness. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. And to the centurion Jesus said, "Go; let it be done for you as you have believed." And the servant was healed at that very moment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The kingdom belongs to those who believe, whatever their background, and no privilege of birth or membership secures it.

The feast. “From east and west” echoes the prophets’ gathering promises: “I will bring your offspring from the east, and from the west I will gather you” (Isaiah 43:5; cf. Psalm 107:3). And reclining at table is Isaiah’s banquet on the mountain, “a feast of rich food” where God swallows up death (Isaiah 25:6–8). The imagery is wholly Jewish. What is new is who sits at the table: the nations recline with the patriarchs, while the patriarchs’ own descendants stand outside.

Sons of the kingdom. “Weeping and gnashing of teeth” is Matthew’s recurring phrase for final loss (8:12; 13:42, 50; 22:13; 24:51; 25:30), and the first time he uses it, those in view are “the sons of the kingdom” — insiders by birth. Jesus takes the title people used of themselves with satisfaction and attaches it to the ones put out.

A guard. This verse has been misused. It doesn’t say God has finished with Israel and replaced her. Paul answered that flatly — “has God rejected his people? By no means!” (Romans 11:1) — and warned Gentile believers against arrogance (Romans 11:18–21). What Jesus dismantles isn’t Israel but presumption: the assumption that descent secures anything. John the Baptist said the same (3:9), and it is just as false when a Gentile assumes church membership secures it. The warning has been transferred, not retired. A test: are you trusting your religious background, or Christ himself?

Healed that hour. “Go; let it be done for you as you have believed.” Faith is the channel, not the source. The centurion’s faith didn’t heal his servant; Jesus’ word did. But faith received what only Jesus could give, and “at that very moment” distance collapsed before his word.
verseByVerse.note: Guests reclined at a banquet. “Weeping and gnashing of teeth” is Matthew’s recurring picture of final judgment.

parallels.desc: from the north and from the west
