Tyre and Sidon, Gentile ports and bywords for pagan pride in the prophets (Isaiah 23), would have repented in sackcloth and ashes — as Nineveh did (Jonah 3:5–6) — had they seen what these Jewish towns saw and dismissed. The pagan cities will fare better on judgment day than the privileged ones.

Would have repented. A harder question lies here. Jesus doesn’t say Tyre and Sidon might have repented, but that they would have. So the miracles that failed to move Chorazin would have moved them — and God didn’t send them there. Why not? First, what the sentence establishes: God knows not only what happens but what would have happened; he knows the road not taken as exactly as the road taken. Then be honest about what isn’t told. Scripture says God determines the times and places of people’s lives (Acts 17:26), and draws a line: “The secret things belong to the LORD our God, but the things that are revealed belong to us and to our children” (Deuteronomy 29:29). When Paul reached this wall he didn’t climb it, but asked who we are to answer back to God (Romans 9:20). Past that point, the honest answer is that we haven’t been told.

A mirror, not a riddle. And notice where Jesus aims the sentence. He isn’t lecturing on how grace is distributed among nations; he is indicting two towns that saw everything and did nothing. The comparison measures their guilt. So the question it presses isn’t why others were given less light, but what you have done with the light you were given — and the one asking the first question is often avoiding the second. A test: what have you done with all you have seen and heard of Christ?
verseByVerse.note: Chorazin and Bethsaida were towns near Capernaum at the north end of the lake. Tyre and Sidon were Gentile port cities. Sackcloth was coarse goat-hair cloth worn in mourning.

verseByVerse.quote: And you, Capernaum, will you be exalted to heaven? You will be brought down to Hades. For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Sodom, it would have remained until this day. But I tell you that it will be more tolerable on the day of judgment for the land of Sodom than for you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Living near Christ without being changed by him brings the heaviest judgment.

Babylon’s taunt. The exaltation language quotes Isaiah’s taunt against the king of Babylon: “You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend to heaven; above the stars of God I will set my throne on high’… But you are brought down to Sheol, to the far reaches of the pit” (Isaiah 14:13–15). Jesus applies it to a fishing village on the north shore — a customs post, a synagogue and a beach. The disproportion is the point. Capernaum had no imperial ambitions. What it had was Jesus living in it, and it received him as a local celebrity and went on fishing. The sentence written for Babylon fits it exactly.

Worse than Sodom. Capernaum was his ministry base, the town most saturated with his presence and works. Sodom, destroyed for its wickedness (Genesis 19:24–25), would have remained had it seen what Capernaum saw. The city that hosted the Son of God will be lower in judgment than the byword for depravity. A test: has living close to the things of Christ made you complacent rather than changed?

The ruins. Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum are all gone. Chorazin is a field of black basalt ruins; Capernaum an archaeological site with no inhabitants; Bethsaida’s location is still argued over. They weren’t destroyed in any recorded catastrophe; they simply declined and emptied.

A guard. This passage often frightens the wrong people. The condemnation is on towns that watched the works and were unmoved, “because they did not repent.” It isn’t aimed at someone who has heard much and worries whether he has responded well enough; that worry is itself a response, and Chorazin wasn’t troubled by anything.
verseByVerse.note: Hades is the realm of the dead.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time Jesus declared, "I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children; yes, Father, for such was your gracious will.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God reveals himself by sovereign grace to the humble and dependent, not to the self-sufficient, and Jesus rejoices in his Father’s choice.

The wise and understanding. The phrase comes from a judgment oracle in Isaiah against the religious establishment: “the wisdom of their wise men shall perish, and the discernment of their discerning men shall be hidden” (Isaiah 29:14), which Paul quotes to explain why the cross looks foolish (1 Corinthians 1:19). Jesus isn’t making a general remark about clever people; he applies the text in which God confounds the professionally religious to the men who decided John had a demon and Jesus was a drunkard.

Infants. The word is stronger than “little children”: infants, pre-verbal and wholly dependent, with no accomplishments. The contrast isn’t educated versus simple, but those who can do something versus those who can do nothing (cf. 1 Corinthians 1:26–29).

Not against learning. This verse has been used to bless laziness. It isn’t an attack on learning. The man praying it knew the Scriptures better than anyone, out-argued the best minds of his day, and chose Paul, the most educated man of his generation. What is condemned isn’t intelligence but self-sufficiency — and there is a form of it peculiar to the well-taught: having enough answers not to need anything. A test: does your knowledge of God make you more dependent on him, or less?

Is this election? Yes. The Father hides and reveals, and the Son reveals the Father to anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him (v. 27). Some read the “little children” as those who humble themselves and respond, so that God reveals himself in answer to their openness. The more likely reading is that the openness is itself God’s gift. Yet Jesus sets this beside two other truths: the cities that did not repent are guilty (vv. 20–24), and the invitation that follows is to everyone who labours (v. 28). God’s choosing never cancels human responsibility, and it never closes the door on anyone who comes.

He gives thanks. Jesus doesn’t lament or apologise for the hiding. He thanks the Father: “yes, Father, for such was your gracious will.” The concealment is God’s act and good pleasure, and the Son is glad. There is mercy in it too — a kingdom reachable by cleverness would be closed to almost everyone — but the passage offers thanks, not excuse.

parallels.desc: God chose what is foolish in the world

verseByVerse.quote: All things have been handed over to me by my Father, and no one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him. Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus alone, as the divine Son, can make God known, and he freely invites every weary person to come to him for rest.

A thunderbolt. Verse 27 has been called a “Johannine thunderbolt”: it reads like the fourth Gospel, dropped into Matthew — the Father handing all things to the Son, the mutual knowing, the Son alone revealing the Father (cf. John 3:35; 14:6–9). And it sits in Matthew and Luke (Luke 10:22), not in John. That undercuts the old claim that a high view of Christ is a late development found only in John.

Mutual knowledge. That the Father knows the Son perfectly is unsurprising; God knows everything. That the Son knows the Father with the same completeness, and no one else does, puts him on God’s side of the line between Creator and creature, for no creature comprehends his Maker.

Then: “Come.” The transition is the most abrupt in the Gospel. The sentence before is as high and remote as anything Jesus said — the knowledge of God exclusive, given at the Son’s discretion, the language of a locked door. The next word is “Come.” No conditions, no narrowing. Having established that he alone holds the knowledge of God, he calls anyone who is tired. The halves need each other: an invitation from someone with lesser credentials wouldn’t be worth accepting, and credentials without an invitation would leave everyone outside. The one with the only key opens the door himself and asks people in.

All who labour. Every kind of crushing burden — moral failure, religious performance, anxiety, grief — is invited. All. A test: what burden are you still carrying instead of coming to him?

parallels.desc: the Father has given all things into his hand
whoever has seen me has seen the Father

verseByVerse.quote: Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Following Christ isn’t a crushing load of religious demands but a life shared with a gentle, humble Saviour who gives rest.

A different yoke. In Jewish speech, taking a teacher’s yoke meant accepting his interpretation of the law. The Pharisees’ yoke was heavy, “burdens, hard to bear” (23:4), a yoke Peter later said “neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear” (Acts 15:10). Jesus offers his own — not the abolition of demand but a different kind, borne with him. A yoke joined two animals to pull together; his yoke is easy not because it asks little but because he bears it with us, and because it is the yoke of love: “his commandments are not burdensome” (1 John 5:3).

Rest for your souls. “You will find rest for your souls” echoes Jeremiah: “ask for the ancient paths, where the good way is; and walk in it, and find rest for your souls” (Jeremiah 6:16). Jeremiah’s generation refused that path; Jesus is the way they couldn’t find.

Gentle and lowly in heart. Don’t let the eye slide past these words. Jesus says many things about himself — the door, the vine, the bread, the light — but here alone he tells us what his heart is like. Not harsh and demanding, not exacting and disappointed, but gentle and lowly. “Gentle” is the word he blessed in the meek (5:5); “lowly” means humble, the opposite of the proud religion that had been crushing these people. It is the settled disposition of his heart, not a mood on his better days. When you come to him weary, ashamed, having failed again, you aren’t coming to a reluctant judge who tolerates you, but to the gentlest heart there is, more ready to receive you than you are to come. The old Puritans loved to dwell here, and rightly. A test: do you picture Christ’s heart toward you as he describes it, or as your fears describe it?
verseByVerse.note: A yoke joined animals to pull together; teachers spoke of the “yoke” of the law.

parallels.desc: you will find rest for your souls
a yoke our fathers could not bear

11.theology: The gentleness of Christ. “I am gentle and lowly in heart” (v. 29) is the only place in the Gospels where Jesus describes his own inner character. The word “gentle” (praus) is the same word used of Moses in Numbers 12:3 and of the meek in the Beatitudes. Christ’s gentleness is not weakness but strength under restraint: the one who has all authority in heaven and earth bends to receive the weary. Thomas Goodwin wrote that Christ’s heart is more moved by our miseries than by all his own glory. The invitation “Come to me” is the theological centre of grace: not “make yourself worthy,” not “prepare yourself,” not “clean yourself up first,” but “come.”
11.examples:
Then: John the Baptist in prison represents every believer whose faith has been tested by circumstances that did not match expectation. The answer Jesus gives is always the same: look at what the Scriptures say I would do, and look at what I am doing. Faith is anchored in the word.

Now: The invitation of 11:28–30 is the greatest recruitment speech in history. Every generation of tired, guilt-laden, performance-exhausted people is addressed. The church that does not centre its preaching on this invitation has lost the gospel. The yoke of Christ is easy not because it makes no demands but because the one who makes the demands has already borne their weight.

12.title: Lord of the Sabbath
12.text: <sup>1</sup>At that time Jesus went through the grainfields on the Sabbath. His disciples were hungry, and they began to pluck heads of grain and to eat. <sup>2</sup>But when the Pharisees saw it, they said to him, “Look, your disciples are doing what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath.” <sup>3</sup>He said to them, “Have you not read what David did when he was hungry, and those who were with him: <sup>4</sup>how he entered the house of God and ate the bread of the Presence, which it was not lawful for him to eat nor for those who were with him, but only for the priests? <sup>5</sup>Or have you not read in the Law how on the Sabbath the priests in the temple profane the Sabbath and are guiltless? <sup>6</sup>I tell you, something greater than the temple is here. <sup>7</sup>And if you had known what this means, ‘I desire mercy, and not sacrifice,’ you would not have condemned the guiltless. <sup>8</sup>For the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath.” <sup>9</sup>He went on from there and entered their synagogue. <sup>10</sup>And a man was there with a withered hand. And they asked him, “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?”— so that they might accuse him. <sup>11</sup>He said to them, “Which one of you who has a sheep, if it falls into a pit on the Sabbath, will not take hold of it and lift it out? <sup>12</sup>Of how much more value is a man than a sheep! So it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath.” <sup>13</sup>Then he said to the man, “Stretch out your hand.” And the man stretched it out, and it was restored, healthy like the other. <sup>14</sup>But the Pharisees went out and conspired against him, how to destroy him. <sup>15</sup>Jesus, aware of this, withdrew from there. And many followed him, and he healed them all <sup>16</sup>and ordered them not to make him known. <sup>17</sup>This was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah: <sup>18</sup>“Behold, my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved with whom my soul is well pleased. I will put my Spirit upon him, and he will proclaim justice to the Gentiles. <sup>19</sup>He will not quarrel or cry aloud, nor will anyone hear his voice in the streets; <sup>20</sup>a bruised reed he will not break, and a smoldering wick he will not quench, until he brings justice to victory; <sup>21</sup>and in his name the Gentiles will hope.” <sup>22</sup>Then a demon-oppressed man who was blind and mute was brought to him, and he healed him, so that the man spoke and saw. <sup>23</sup>And all the people were amazed, and said, “Can this be the Son of David?” <sup>24</sup>But when the Pharisees heard it, they said, “It is only by Beelzebul, the prince of demons, that this man casts out demons.” <sup>25</sup>Knowing their thoughts, he said to them, “Every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, and no city or house divided against itself will stand. <sup>26</sup>And if Satan casts out Satan, he is divided against himself. How then will his kingdom stand? <sup>27</sup>And if I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they will be your judges. <sup>28</sup>But if it is by the Spirit of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you. <sup>29</sup>Or how can someone enter a strong man’s house and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man? Then indeed he may plunder his house. <sup>30</sup>Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters. <sup>31</sup>Therefore I tell you, every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven people, but the blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven. <sup>32</sup>And whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven, but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come. <sup>33</sup>“Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad, for the tree is known by its fruit. <sup>34</sup>You brood of vipers! How can you speak good, when you are evil? For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. <sup>35</sup>The good person out of his good treasure brings forth good, and the evil person out of his evil treasure brings forth evil. <sup>36</sup>I tell you, on the day of judgment people will give account for every careless word they speak, <sup>37</sup>for by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.” <sup>38</sup>Then some of the scribes and Pharisees answered him, saying, “Teacher, we wish to see a sign from you.” <sup>39</sup>But he answered them, “An evil and adulterous generation seeks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah. <sup>40</sup>For just as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so will the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth. <sup>41</sup>The men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and behold, something greater than Jonah is here. <sup>42</sup>The queen of the South will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and behold, something greater than Solomon is here. <sup>43</sup>“When the unclean spirit has gone out of a person, it passes through waterless places seeking rest, but finds none. <sup>44</sup>Then it says, ‘I will return to my house from which I came.’ And when it comes, it finds the house empty, swept, and put in order. <sup>45</sup>Then it goes and brings with it seven other spirits more evil than itself, and they enter and dwell there, and the last state of that person is worse than the first. So also will it be with this evil generation.” <sup>46</sup>While he was still speaking to the people, behold, his mother and his brothers stood outside, asking to speak to him. <sup>48</sup>But he replied to the man who told him, “Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?” <sup>49</sup>And stretching out his hand toward his disciples, he said, “Here are my mother and my brothers! <sup>50</sup>For whoever does the will of my Father in heaven is my brother and sister and mother.”
12.overview:
Chapter 12 marks a decisive turning point in Matthew. The Pharisees, having sought ways to trap Jesus, now plot his destruction (v. 14). The conflict comes to a head over the Sabbath, the temple, and the identity of Jesus. Jesus makes two enormous claims: “something greater than the temple is here” (v. 6) and “the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath” (v. 8). The temple was the dwelling place of God; the Sabbath was the sign of the covenant. To claim authority over both is to claim divine identity.

The chapter also introduces the sin against the Holy Spirit — attributing the works of the Spirit to Beelzebul. This is not a sudden slip but the settled, hardened rejection of the evidence of God’s kingdom. The Pharisees have seen the blind healed, the deaf hearing, the demon-possessed set free; they call it the work of Satan. This deliberate, informed, hardened reversal of moral and spiritual categories is the sin that cannot be forgiven — not because the blood of Christ is insufficient but because the one who commits it has placed himself permanently beyond repentance.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–21 — Lord of the Sabbath and Servant of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 12 opens the extended conflict section of Matthew. The Pharisees attack Jesus twice on Sabbath observance: first for his disciples plucking grain, then for healing a man with a withered hand. Jesus defends both from Scripture and declares himself Lord of the Sabbath. The Pharisees then plot his destruction, and Matthew quotes Isaiah's first Servant Song at length, identifying Jesus as the gentle, bruised-reed-not-breaking Servant of the LORD. Note the link across the chapter break: "at that time" follows immediately on the offer of rest (11:28-29), so the man who has just promised rest is challenged about the day of rest. And Matthew alone adds that the disciples were hungry, because that is the hinge of the argument — David was hungry too. The charge was not theft (Deut. 23:25 permits plucking by hand) but Sabbath-breaking: rabbinic tradition listed thirty-nine forbidden classes of work, and reaping, threshing and winnowing are among them. The David precedent is stranger than it looks — David lied to Ahimelech, and the episode ends with Doeg reporting it and Saul slaughtering eighty-five priests (1 Sam. 22:18-19). Jesus reaches for an incident with a body count, and the parallel is exact: the anointed king not yet in his kingdom, hungry, with his men, pursued. The priestly argument: the Sabbath doubled the temple workload (two extra lambs, Num. 28:9-10), so the Sabbath has always yielded to something. And "something greater than the temple" is neuter — as are "greater than Jonah" (v. 41) and "greater than Solomon" (v. 42). Three times in one chapter, and the three are the pillars of Israel's life: the temple where God met his people, the prophet through whom he spoke, the king through whom he ruled. The trap at v. 10 is precise: rabbinic law allowed Sabbath healing only where life was in danger, and a withered hand is not — so the honest answer on their terms was "wait until sundown", and Jesus heals anyway. Note which day the murder plot is formed on: restoring a hand is a Sabbath violation; convening to arrange a killing is not. Mark records the only named anger of Jesus in the Gospels at exactly this point (Mk. 3:5). And the Servant Song is the longest OT quotation in Matthew — used, remarkably, to explain not a miracle but the absence of spectacle.
verseByVerse.theology: The Sabbath controversies reveal the Pharisees' fundamental error: they have turned a gift (the Sabbath rest) into a burden, and a sign (rest pointing to God's shalom) into a system of control. Jesus does not abolish the Sabbath; he fulfills it. He is the one in whom the true Sabbath rest is found (11:29) — the rest that the weekly day always pointed toward. The Servant Song quotation (Isa. 42:1-4) interprets his retreat from conflict not as weakness but as fulfillment: the Servant does not "quarrel or cry aloud" but pursues justice to victory through gentleness.
verseByVerse.examples: The healing of the withered hand poses the sharpest question of the controversy: "Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?" Jesus answers with an argument from worth: if you would rescue a sheep that fell in a pit on the Sabbath, how much more a person? The comparative worth of persons over animals is the premise; the compassionate action follows from it. Every Sabbath restriction that would prevent healing a human being has missed the Sabbath's point — the Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath (Mark 2:27).

verseByVerse.quote: At that time Jesus went through the grainfields on the Sabbath. His disciples were hungry, and they began to pluck heads of grain and to eat. But when the Pharisees saw it, they said to him, "Look, your disciples are doing what is not lawful to do on the Sabbath."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The One who offers true rest is immediately challenged by those who had turned God’s day of rest into a burden.

Rest, then a fight about rest. “At that time” ties this to what came just before: “Come to me… and I will give you rest” (11:28). The next thing that happens is a fight about the day of rest. The man who offered rest to the exhausted is challenged at once by men who had made the rest day into work.

They were hungry. Matthew alone adds that the disciples were hungry — the hinge of the argument, since David was hungry too. They weren’t making a point about Sabbath law; they were walking through a field and hadn’t eaten.

The charge. No one accuses them of theft; the law let a traveller pluck grain by hand from a neighbour’s field (Deuteronomy 23:25). The charge is Sabbath-breaking. Later rabbinic tradition listed thirty-nine kinds of forbidden work, including reaping, threshing and preparing food. Pulling heads of grain, rubbing them in the hands (Luke 6:1) and blowing away the chaff was, on a determined reading, harvesting (cf. Exodus 34:21). That is the accusation: harvesting, on a technicality, in a quantity that fits in two hands. A test: do you ever load others with rules God never gave?
verseByVerse.note: Picking grain by hand from a neighbour’s field was allowed; the objection was that plucking counted as harvesting, which was work on the Sabbath.

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, "Have you not read what David did when he was hungry, and those who were with him: how he entered the house of God and ate the bread of the Presence, which it was not lawful for him to eat nor for those who were with him, but only for the priests?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s law is to be read in the light of mercy and human need, and the true anointed King is now present.

“Have you not read?” Jesus asks this six times in Matthew, always of the professionally religious (12:3, 5; 19:4; 21:16, 42; 22:31), never of a crowd. The question isn’t whether they know the words but whether they understood what they read — the most withering thing a teacher can say to a scholar.

The holy bread. The bread of the Presence was twelve loaves set out each Sabbath before the LORD and afterward eaten only by the priests (Leviticus 24:5–9). David asked for it, received it, and Scripture records no judgment on him (1 Samuel 21:1–6). The principle: the law must be read in light of mercy and human need. If David could eat the holy bread, Jesus’ disciples may pluck grain. A test: does your use of God’s law make you merciful or merely strict?

A desperate day. Notice the state David was in: on the run from a king who wanted him dead, lying to the priest about being on the king’s business — and the episode ended in atrocity, when Doeg reported it and Saul had eighty-five priests of Nob killed (1 Samuel 22:18–19). Jesus chooses a desperate, compromised day in the life of the anointed king not yet come into his kingdom. And the parallel is exact: here is the anointed King not yet enthroned, hungry with his men, pursued by the authorities. If the son of Jesse could eat holy bread on such a day, the Son of David and his men may take a handful of grain.

Abiathar. Mark names Abiathar as high priest (Mark 2:26), while 1 Samuel names his father Ahimelech — a real difficulty with several proposed answers, including that Mark means “in the passage about Abiathar.” Matthew names no one, so nothing here turns on it.
verseByVerse.note: The bread of the Presence was twelve loaves set before the LORD each Sabbath and eaten by the priests.

verseByVerse.quote: Or have you not read in the Law how on the Sabbath the priests in the temple profane the Sabbath and are guiltless? I tell you, something greater than the temple is here.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Sabbath always yielded to God’s higher purposes, and now the One greater than the temple has come.

The priests’ busiest day. The Sabbath didn’t reduce the temple’s workload; it doubled it. Besides the daily offerings, two more lambs were sacrificed (Numbers 28:9–10); the holy bread was changed; and a boy born on a Sabbath was circumcised on the next, because the eighth day is the eighth day (John 7:22). On the day all Israel rested, the priests worked harder, by God’s command, and no one called it sin. So the Sabbath has always yielded to something. The question is what.

Something greater. “Something greater than the temple is here.” The Greek is neuter — not someone, but something — and Jesus says it twice more in this chapter: “something greater than Jonah” (v. 41) and “something greater than Solomon” (v. 42). Temple, prophet and king — the three pillars of Israel’s life: the place where God met his people, the voice that called them back, the throne that ruled them. He doesn’t merely say he is a better temple, prophet and king, which would already be blasphemy to them; he says something greater than all three is present — standing in a cornfield, in an argument about breakfast. The temple was where God dwelt (cf. John 2:19–21). Those arrangements are being quietly wound up in the presence of what they were for. A test: do you treat Jesus as one religious figure among others, or as greater than every religious institution?
verseByVerse.note: The priests worked hardest on the Sabbath, offering extra sacrifices.

verseByVerse.quote: And if you had known what this means, "I desire mercy, and not sacrifice," you would not have condemned the guiltless. For the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God values mercy above ritual, and Jesus is the Lord of the Sabbath and the true rest it pointed to.

Mercy before ritual. Matthew alone quotes Hosea 6:6, and twice: at Levi’s table (9:13) and here, both times about food, both times against Pharisees. Hosea wrote to a nation whose religious machinery was in good order and whose life was rotten: plenty of sacrifice, no faithfulness. God’s complaint wasn’t that they stopped worshipping but that worship had become a substitute for what it was meant to produce. That should make careful readers uncomfortable. These men weren’t lax; they were the most rigorous and scripturally literate in the land, and they failed at the point of their strength. A test: has your religious discipline crowded out mercy?

Lord of the Sabbath. As Creator (John 1:3), he has authority to interpret the day he made. But there is more. Matthew sets this beside “Come to me… and I will give you rest” (11:28). The Sabbath was never merely a day off but a signpost. God rested on the seventh day, and Israel kept the day as a weekly rehearsal of a rest still ahead — one Joshua never fully gave them; “there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God” (Hebrews 4:9). So when Jesus calls himself lord of the Sabbath, he claims to be what the day was about. The rest it promised is a Person, standing in a cornfield being rebuked for letting hungry men eat. The Pharisees guarded the signpost so fiercely they couldn’t see they were arguing with the destination.

parallels.desc: I desire steadfast love and not sacrifice

verseByVerse.quote: He went on from there and entered their synagogue. And a man was there with a withered hand. And they asked him, "Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?" — so that they might accuse him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When religion uses suffering people as props in an argument, it has lost its way — and Jesus refuses to let the day of restoration pass without restoring.

A prop. The Pharisees ask not from interest but “so that they might accuse him.” The man’s need is incidental to their agenda. When a suffering person becomes a means of scoring points, something has gone deeply wrong with the religion.

The trap. It is carefully set. The accepted rule was that danger to life overrides the Sabbath; you dig a man out of rubble and treat the wound. But where there is no danger to life, it waits. A chronic condition will still be there tomorrow. The withered hand was useless and probably ruined his living, but it wasn’t dangerous. By the standard of the day the answer was obvious: wait till sundown and heal him then. They weren’t asking whether healing is good, but whether it is urgent — and on their terms it wasn’t.

Why not wait? Jesus heals him anyway, there and then, when six hours’ delay would have cost nothing and avoided everything. Because more than the hand was being decided: whether the day God gave for restoration could be used to restore someone. Answering that on Monday would have answered nothing. A test: do you delay mercy for the sake of convenience or reputation?

“Their synagogue.” Matthew uses that possessive repeatedly (9:35; 10:17; 13:54), the language of an institution beginning to close against him.
verseByVerse.note: A “withered” hand is shrunken or paralysed. In the rabbis’ rulings, healing a condition that was not life-threatening had to wait until the Sabbath was over.

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, "Which one of you who has a sheep, if it falls into a pit on the Sabbath, will not take hold of it and lift it out? Of how much more value is a man than a sheep! So it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath."
verseByVerse.commentary:
People made in God’s image matter more than rules, and doing good honours the purpose of God’s day.

Trapped by their own practice. If you rescue your property, a sheep, on the Sabbath, how much more a person, worth far more? The practice they accept commits them to the conclusion they deny (cf. Luke 14:5). The Sabbath was given for human good; healing honours its purpose. It is not merely lawful to do good on the Sabbath; it is right.

Should Christians keep a Sabbath? Believers who love the Scriptures land in two places. Some hold that the fourth commandment stands with the other nine as moral law, and that the day has moved to the first of the week in honour of the resurrection, so the Lord’s Day is to be set apart from ordinary work for worship and rest. That is the historic Reformed and Puritan position, and it has produced some of the most joyful, well-ordered lives the church has seen. Others hold that the Sabbath belonged to the shadows that have found their substance in Christ, and that no particular day now binds the conscience, pointing to Paul: “One person esteems one day as better than another, while another esteems all days alike” (Romans 14:5–6; Colossians 2:16–17). The second fits the New Testament better and is the view taken here: Paul calls the Sabbath a shadow whose substance belongs to Christ (Colossians 2:16–17), the apostles laid no Sabbath on the Gentile churches (Acts 15:28–29), and the church gathered on the first day without calling it a Sabbath (Acts 20:7; 1 Corinthians 16:2). Even so, Paul’s chief concern is to forbid the quarrel, which should shape how firmly any of us holds an opinion here.

What both agree on. The pattern of rest is older than Sinai: God rested on the seventh day and blessed it (Genesis 2:2–3). It was given as a gift: “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath” (Mark 2:27). Gathering with God’s people is commanded whatever your view (Hebrews 10:25). And we are creatures with limits, made to stop.

Our danger. The Pharisees’ error was too much Sabbath, fenced with rules; ours is rarely that. It is a life with no boundary anywhere — work bleeding into every evening, a phone that never stops, Sunday spent catching up. So, whatever your view of the day, put a real boundary in your week and defend it: work laid down, worship unhurried, time with people who aren’t a task — not to earn anything, but because you are a creature, not a machine, and the day pointed to the Person who is your rest. And if your practice becomes a stick to measure others with, you have reproduced the Pharisees’ mistake, whichever side you are on. A test: where in your week do you actually stop and rest in Christ?

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to the man, "Stretch out your hand." And the man stretched it out, and it was restored, healthy like the other. But the Pharisees went out and conspired against him, how to destroy him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ’s command gives the power to obey it, and hearts closed to him may answer his goodness with hatred.

Stretch it out. The command seems to ask the impossible of a useless hand, but Jesus’ command creates the ability to obey. And notice what he asks: to do in public the very thing the man had likely spent his life not doing. A withered hand is kept out of sight, in the sleeve. He is told to hold it out in a synagogue with every eye on him. The healing didn’t come first; he had to extend the ruined thing before there was anything to see. A test: what shameful thing do you need to hold out to Christ rather than hide?

Restored. The hand was “restored,” put back as it was — the word the disciples use asking whether he will “restore the kingdom to Israel” (Acts 1:6), and related to Peter’s “time for restoring all the things” (Acts 3:21). A small sample of the last day happened in one man’s hand on a Sabbath morning.

The plot. Notice which day the conspiracy is formed. Healing a man on the Sabbath counts as work; going out to plan a murder apparently doesn’t (cf. John 5:16–18). Matthew doesn’t comment; he puts the two clauses in one sentence. Mark tells us what Jesus felt: “he looked around at them with anger, grieved at their hardness of heart” (Mark 3:5) — not over the plot against his life, which he bore calmly, but over their willingness to leave a crippled man crippled rather than lose an argument.

parallels.desc: seeking to kill him over the Sabbath

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus, aware of this, withdrew from there. And many followed him, and he healed them all and ordered them not to make him known.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus keeps to his Father’s timetable, avoiding a premature confrontation, yet never stops his work of mercy.

Withdrawal, not retreat. “He withdrew” is a word Matthew uses repeatedly — of Joseph taking the child to Egypt and to Galilee (2:14, 22), and of Jesus moving away from danger (4:12; 14:13; 15:21). It is never cowardice. His hour hadn’t come; the cross would happen on the Father’s schedule, not the Pharisees’.

He healed them all. He has been accused, reported and targeted for death, and he leaves the district and goes on healing everyone who comes — a considerable answer to the idea that withdrawal meant fear. What he stops isn’t the work but the publicity: he “ordered them not to make him known,” as before (9:30), to avoid inflaming false messianic hopes before the cross. A test: under pressure, do you stop doing good, or only stop seeking attention for it?

The reason Matthew gives. A hunted man has an obvious reason to keep quiet, and Matthew declines it. He doesn’t say Jesus kept quiet so they wouldn’t find him, but that it fulfilled Isaiah — and then quotes four verses about a Servant who doesn’t shout in the street.

verseByVerse.quote: This was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah: "Behold, my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved with whom my soul is well pleased. I will put my Spirit upon him, and he will proclaim justice to the Gentiles."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus is God’s chosen, Spirit-anointed Servant whose quiet ministry will bring justice to all nations.

The longest quotation. Isaiah 42:1–4, the first Servant Song, is the longest Old Testament quotation in Matthew. He usually quotes a line or two; here he stops and lets a prophet speak at length — to explain not a miracle but a decision to avoid confrontation and ask for quiet. The thing being explained is the absence of spectacle.

The baptism voice. “My beloved with whom my soul is well pleased” is almost exactly what the Father said at the Jordan (3:17), and Matthew has waited nine chapters to show where it came from. From the start, the identity announced was not only Messiah but Servant — and anyone who knew Isaiah knew the Servant Songs lead to Isaiah 53, to one despised and rejected, wounded for others’ transgressions.

Justice to the Gentiles. The one the Pharisees plot to destroy is the one the Father appointed to reach every nation. The Spirit given at his baptism is the Spirit by whom he works.

His own translation. Matthew’s wording matches neither the Hebrew nor the Greek Old Testament exactly; it seems to be his own rendering, as a Jewish writer working from the Hebrew for Greek readers. He doesn’t bend the sense. The Servant of Isaiah 42 is chosen, Spirit-anointed, quiet, gentle with the damaged, and destined for the nations — the very man Matthew has been describing, most recently walking away from an argument he could have won. A test: do you expect God’s work to come with noise and spectacle, or with the Servant’s quiet faithfulness?

parallels.desc: my chosen servant, with my Spirit upon him
the Father’s voice at the baptism

verseByVerse.quote: He will not quarrel or cry aloud, nor will anyone hear his voice in the streets; a bruised reed he will not break, and a smoldering wick he will not quench, until he brings justice to victory;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ is gentle with the weak and failing, tending them patiently toward the full restoration he will surely bring.

The Servant’s gentleness. The Pharisees quarrel, plot and accuse; the Servant doesn’t quarrel or seek confrontation for its own sake. The One who could silence his opponents by force chooses gentleness with the weak.

The reed and the wick. Picture what Isaiah chose. A reed is a hollow stalk used for a pen or a simple pipe; once cracked and bent it won’t write or play, and the ordinary thing is to snap it and throw it away. A wick with no flame left is a thread of smoke and a smell; you pinch it out. Both are things a reasonable person discards because they have stopped being useful. And the promise is that he won’t.

For the flickering. If your faith is down to a flicker; if your praying has shrunk to a sentence or two, and not good ones; if you come to church out of habit rather than hunger and feel a fraud; if you have failed at the same thing so often you have stopped making promises — this verse has your name on it. He isn’t standing over you ready to pinch. And Matthew puts it right after the Pharisees walk out to plan a murder (v. 14); the world around him was as hard as it gets, and this is how he treated the weak in the middle of it. A test: do you believe Christ is gentle with your weakness?

Toward victory. But the comfort mustn’t go soft. “Until he brings justice to victory” — the tending has a destination. He isn’t indifferent to your ruin; he is patient with it and intends to finish the repair. Gentleness isn’t the absence of purpose but its manner.

The reed he held. Read to the end of Matthew. When the soldiers mocked him as king, they put a reed in his right hand for a sceptre, then took it and struck him on the head (27:29–30). The bruised reed was handled the way bruised reeds always are — snapped, mocked, used to hit someone. He went through that so he would never do it to you.
verseByVerse.note: A bruised reed and a smouldering lamp-wick are pictures of the weak and failing, easily finished off.

parallels.desc: he will not cry aloud, nor break a bruised reed

verseByVerse.quote: and in his name the Gentiles will hope.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gentle Servant whom his own leaders plot to kill is the hope of all the nations.

The nations’ hope. Not in the Pharisees’ aggressive religion, Rome’s military power, or Israel’s ethnic privilege, but in his name the nations will hope (cf. Romans 15:12). The cross they plan won’t end his name; it will make it “the name that is above every name” (Philippians 2:9). Their murder becomes his throne. A test: is your hope placed in his name, or in something else?

Two reeds. Matthew has put two reeds a chapter apart. In 11:7 Jesus asked whether the crowd went out to see “a reed shaken by the wind” — the emblem on Herod’s coins, the man who bends with the weather. Here the Servant won’t break “a bruised reed.” The same plant, two very different things: the reed a person can become, blown about and worthless; and the reed a person can be reduced to, crushed and of no use to anyone. Jesus has no patience with the first and won’t lay a finger on the second.

The text. The Hebrew of Isaiah 42:4 reads, “the coastlands wait for his law”; Matthew follows the Greek tradition, “in his name the Gentiles will hope.” The coastlands are the Gentile lands, and waiting for his instruction is close to hoping in his name. The direction is the same: the Servant Song reaches past Israel to everyone — and Matthew places it just where Israel’s leaders begin plotting his death. The nations receive their hope in the same paragraph in which his own people decide he must die.

parallels.desc: the coastlands wait for his law
in him will the Gentiles hope

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–50 — The Unforgivable Sin, the Sign of Jonah, and True Family
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter's second half escalates the conflict. Jesus heals a blind and mute demoniac; the Pharisees attribute it to Beelzebul. Jesus dismantles the accusation with three arguments, then pronounces the solemn warning about blasphemy against the Holy Spirit. The scribes and Pharisees demand a sign; Jesus offers only the sign of Jonah. The chapter ends with a redefinition of family: those who do the will of the Father are Jesus's true mother and brothers. Four things more. The crowd's question in v. 23 expects the answer no — closer to "this can't be the Son of David, can it?" They are edging toward a confession and flinching. And the title fits this miracle exactly: Solomon, David's son, had a reputation as master of spirits, and Josephus describes a Jewish exorcist working "according to the methods of Solomon" — with a ring and a root. Jesus says "go". Luke records v. 28 with one word different — "by the finger of God" (Lk. 11:20), which is a quotation: it is what Pharaoh's magicians said when they could no longer reproduce the plagues (Exod. 8:19). The exorcisms are a new exodus, and the Pharisees are standing where the magicians stood. "come upon you" is ephthasen — arrived, overtaken; not an offer drawing near but a thing that has landed. "every careless word" is argos, literally not-working: the unemployed remark that achieved nothing and was forgotten within the hour — and the guard that "by your words you will be justified" is forensic, evidence rather than payment. Both witnesses at the judgement are Gentiles: Nineveh, capital of the empire that destroyed the northern kingdom, which had one reluctant preacher; and the queen of Sheba, who had a rumour and a long journey. Neither had Scripture, temple, covenant or promise. The returning Spirit finds the house "empty, swept, and put in order" — three approving words, and the first is fatal. It is not a passage about losing salvation; there is no indwelling in the story, which is the whole problem. And v. 50 names brother, sister and mother — but not father, because the Father is already in the sentence (cf. 23:9). Mark tells us why the family came: they thought he was out of his mind (Mk. 3:21); John notes his brothers did not believe (Jn. 7:5); and Mary is in the upper room in Acts 1:14. She did not stay outside.
verseByVerse.theology: The blasphemy against the Holy Spirit — attributing the Spirit's work to Satan — is the one sin Jesus calls unforgivable. It is not unforgivable because it exceeds God's mercy but because it closes the door through which mercy enters: it calls the Spirit of conviction a demon, and the person who has hardened to that degree has no remaining capacity to receive the grace they are calling evil. The Pharisees are approaching this condition, if they have not already reached it. The warning is pastoral, not vindictive: it is the warning of a doctor who sees a patient choosing death.
verseByVerse.examples: The sign of Jonah — three days and three nights in the earth — is the only sign Jesus offers to an evil and adulterous generation. The resurrection is the final and definitive sign, the one that vindicates all his claims. No amount of healing, no accumulation of miracles, will convince those whose hearts are already set against him; only the empty tomb is sufficient — and even that will not convince those determined not to believe (28:13-15).

verseByVerse.quote: Then a demon-oppressed man who was blind and mute was brought to him, and he healed him, so that the man spoke and saw. And all the people were amazed, and said, "Can this be the Son of David?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ frees and restores those utterly helpless, and his works press the question of who he is.

Threefold ruin. Possessed, blind and mute: he couldn’t see who had come, couldn’t ask for anything, and had no power to resist what was in him. There is no record of his faith, because there couldn’t be. Matthew says only that he was brought. Someone else carried the whole transaction — worth knowing for anyone praying for a person past asking for himself (cf. 9:32–34). A test: whom are you bringing to Christ who can’t come on their own?

A hesitant question. The crowd’s question is more hesitant in Greek, expecting “no”: “This can’t be the Son of David — can it?” They aren’t confessing but edging toward it and flinching, having seen enough to ask and not enough to want to own it. That is often how faith begins.

The right title. “Son of David” means the Messiah. And Jewish tradition remembered Solomon, David’s son, as a master over spirits; Josephus describes an exorcist named Eleazar drawing a demon from a man before Vespasian with a ring and a root, by methods credited to Solomon. A man who casts out demons with a word, without ring or incantation, is doing what the son of David was famous for. The crowd puts it together, tentatively — and the Pharisees produce their explanation within a verse.
verseByVerse.note: “Son of David” is a title for the Messiah.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the Pharisees heard it, they said, "It is only by Beelzebul, the prince of demons, that this man casts out demons." Knowing their thoughts, he said to them, "Every kingdom divided against itself is laid waste, and no city or house divided against itself will stand."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ’s enemies couldn’t deny his works, only twist their source — and their explanation collapses on itself.

They don’t deny it. The most important thing here is what the Pharisees don’t say: that it didn’t happen. A blind, mute, possessed man stands there seeing and talking, and the official response is an explanation of the mechanism. That holds throughout the Gospels. His enemies had every motive to deny his works and never did. The council later said, “this man performs many signs,” and treated it as the problem (John 11:47). The charge at his trial was blasphemy, not fraud. Even the story spread after the resurrection conceded the empty tomb and disputed only how it got that way (28:13). The question was never whether he did these things, but by whose power.

Divided houses. Jesus answers with logic, descending from kingdom to city to house — reaching toward the strong man’s house he will describe in verse 29. If the accusation were true, the devil would be dismantling his own operation, one prisoner at a time, in public, on request. No power ever ran that way. (On the name Beelzebul, “lord of the house,” see 10:25; cf. 2 Kings 1:2.)

Knowing their thoughts. They had spoken, but he answers what lay beneath their words — another quiet claim to divine knowledge, which Matthew records without pausing. A test: when Christ’s work is undeniable, do you look for reasons not to believe it?
verseByVerse.note: Beelzebul is a name for Satan, probably related to Baal-zebub, the god of Ekron.

verseByVerse.quote: And if Satan casts out Satan, he is divided against himself. How then will his kingdom stand? And if I cast out demons by Beelzebul, by whom do your sons cast them out? Therefore they will be your judges.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Pharisees’ charge was inconsistent and manufactured, exposing a hostility that had nothing to do with evidence.

Real exorcists. Jewish exorcism was a real and respected practice. Josephus describes it as an ancient national skill. Acts records seven sons of a Jewish high priest named Sceva attempting it at Ephesus, badly (Acts 19:13–16). So “by whom do your sons cast them out?” points to practitioners the Pharisees knew, possibly in their own circle.

The trap closes. If exorcism as such is satanic, their own people stand condemned. If it isn’t, their explanation of his exorcisms was invented for the occasion — “therefore they will be your judges.” The same act was attributed differently according not to evidence but to prior hostility. A test: do you judge the same thing differently depending on who does it?

No borrowed power. And there was a difference they couldn’t account for. Every exorcist worked with apparatus — names, rings, roots, formulas, the invocation of a higher authority. Jesus says “Go,” and it is over. A man with borrowed authority must name his source; a man who never names one is either a fraud, and the demons wouldn’t leave, or he isn’t borrowing. They grasped that he wasn’t borrowing. Their only remaining move was to name the wrong owner.
verseByVerse.note: Other Jewish exorcists were active at the time; “your sons” probably means Jewish exorcists of their own circle.

verseByVerse.quote: But if it is by the Spirit of God that I cast out demons, then the kingdom of God has come upon you. Or how can someone enter a strong man's house and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man? Then indeed he may plunder his house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ has come as the stronger one, binding Satan and setting his captives free, and every deliverance shows that God’s kingdom has arrived.

The finger of God. Where Matthew has “by the Spirit of God,” Luke has “by the finger of God” (Luke 11:20) — a quotation. In Egypt, when Pharaoh’s magicians, who had matched Moses until then, couldn’t produce the gnats, they told their king, “This is the finger of God” (Exodus 8:19). That is the sentence in which the professional opposition conceded. So the exorcisms are a new exodus — a stronger power arriving in enemy territory and taking prisoners out — and the Pharisees stand where Pharaoh’s magicians stood, watching what they can’t do or explain, and choosing the other answer.

The strong man. The picture is a burglary. No one walks into an occupied house and carries out the furniture while the owner stands there. The goods come out only after he is on the floor. So every demon that leaves is evidence that someone has already been dealt with in the next room. Isaiah raised it as impossible: “Can the prey be taken from the mighty, or the captives of a tyrant be rescued? For thus says the LORD: ‘Even the captives of the mighty shall be taken, and the prey of the tyrant be rescued’” (Isaiah 49:24–25).

Come upon you. “Has come upon you” means arrived, overtaken — got there before expected. The kingdom hasn’t merely drawn near; it has landed on them, and those it has overtaken are explaining it away. A test: have you recognised that God’s kingdom has come in Christ, or are you explaining it away?

Is Satan bound now? In this sense, yes: Christ has bound the strong man so that he can no longer hold the nations and his captives against the gospel (Luke 10:18; Colossians 2:15; Hebrews 2:14). Satan is still active and dangerous (1 Peter 5:8), but restrained. Many amillennial readers see the same binding in Revelation 20:1–3; premillennial readers take that passage as a future binding during a thousand-year reign. The first is the more likely, and it fits what Jesus says here.

parallels.desc: the prey taken from the mighty
he disarmed the rulers and authorities

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters. Therefore I tell you, every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven people, but the blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
There is no neutral ground toward Christ, God’s forgiveness is wide enough for every sin, and the one exception is the settled rejection of the Spirit’s witness.

No neutral ground. Neutrality toward Jesus is opposition; in the harvest, those who don’t gather scatter. Elsewhere he says, “the one who is not against us is for us” (Mark 9:40). Both are true because they answer different questions. Here he speaks of a person’s own standing before Christ: there is no middle ground, and indifference is a verdict. There he spoke of an outsider casting out demons in his name, whom the disciples wanted to stop: the rule for judging others’ work is the opposite. Be strict with your own allegiance and generous about someone else’s. Most of our trouble comes from reversing those. A test: are you gathering with Christ, or merely standing near him?

Every sin. Don’t let the warning swallow the promise. The sentence contains the widest offer in the Gospel and its single exception, in that order: “every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven people.” Weigh “every,” and the company Jesus kept: a tax collector made an apostle, a sinful woman defended (Luke 7:36–50), a thief promised paradise (Luke 23:43). And blasphemy is speech against God himself. The man who wrote these words had collaborated with an occupying power; the man who carried them across the empire called himself formerly “a blasphemer, persecutor, and insolent opponent” who “received mercy” (1 Timothy 1:13). Whatever you carry — the thing never said aloud, the words said about God in a hospital corridor at the worst hour, years spent arguing against him — this verse was drafted wide enough on purpose.

The exception. The exorcisms are the Spirit’s work; calling them demonic, knowingly and with a hardened heart, is the one sin that shuts the door — not by a limit in God’s mercy but by a self-exclusion from the only channel of grace. The next verses explain why the person who fears he has committed it hasn’t.

verseByVerse.quote: And whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man will be forgiven, but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come. Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad, for the tree is known by its fruit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The unforgivable sin is the hardened, settled rejection of the Spirit’s plain witness to Christ — and anyone who fears having committed it shows by that fear that he hasn’t.

Against the Son, against the Spirit. Speaking against the Son of Man is forgivable; Peter denied him and was restored. Speaking against the Spirit is the deliberate attributing of the Spirit’s visible work of liberation to Satan — the hardening of the heart against his testimony, which the Pharisees are doing in this very scene. And the tree and its fruit restate 7:16–20: their slander reveals the root.

For the frightened. No verse has frightened tender souls more. If you fear you have committed the unforgivable sin, that very fear is the surest proof you haven’t. This sin is a settled, defiant, clear-eyed hatred of the light — a heart that looks at God’s work, calls it the devil’s, and feels no grief. Someone who commits it has no desire for Christ and no fear of offending him. A trembling conscience, a longing to be right with God, a dread of having sinned against him — these are the Spirit’s own work, and the Spirit doesn’t grieve over a heart he has abandoned. Come to Christ: “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37). A test: do you want Christ? Then this sin isn’t yours.

Can this sin still be committed? Some think it was possible only for those who saw Christ’s own miracles and called them Satan’s. Others think it recurs wherever someone knowingly and finally rejects the Spirit’s witness to Christ (cf. Hebrews 10:26–29). The second is the more likely. Either way, the person who fears he has committed it shows by that fear that he has not; the hardened heart does not grieve.

“In the age to come.” Some have read “either in this age or in the age to come” to mean certain sins can be forgiven after death, a seed of the doctrine of purgatory. But it is a Hebrew way of saying “never, in all the ages.” Its force is total finality, not postponed pardon. Scripture knows one place of forgiveness: here, in this life, at the cross (Hebrews 9:27).

verseByVerse.quote: You brood of vipers! How can you speak good, when you are evil? For out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. The good person out of his good treasure brings forth good, and the evil person out of his evil treasure brings forth evil.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Our words reveal what fills our hearts, and only a heart changed by grace can produce good.

Vipers. “Brood of vipers” appears three times in Matthew: John the Baptist at the Jordan (3:7), Jesus here, and Jesus in the temple at the climax of the woes (23:33) — always at the same people. The first man to say it was beheaded and the second crucified. A nest of small poisonous snakes, hard to see and deadly; and in a chapter about what comes out of the mouth, the viper’s mouth is the whole problem.

A leak. “Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks” — the overflow, what spills when a container is full. So speech isn’t primarily a decision but a leak. What comes out under pressure isn’t what a person chose to say but what there was too much of to keep in. Anyone can control his words while thinking about them; no one controls what he says when startled, tired or contradicted in public. That is when the level shows (cf. 15:18). A test: what came out of your mouth the last time you were under pressure?

Not despair. This doesn’t say the treasury can’t change; the New Testament is about hearts given new contents. It says the mouth reports the current stock honestly. So the right response to hearing something ugly come out of yourself isn’t merely to resolve to say less, but to ask what has been going in.

Not for us to copy. Jesus forbade calling a brother a fool (5:22). Here he speaks as prophet and judge to hardened teachers who had just blasphemed the Spirit. His disciples aren’t licensed to copy the words as personal abuse (James 3:9–10; Titus 3:2), though false teaching must sometimes be named sharply (Galatians 1:9; Titus 1:13).

parallels.desc: what comes out of the mouth

verseByVerse.quote: I tell you, on the day of judgment people will give account for every careless word they speak, for by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Our ordinary speech matters to God because it reveals the true state of our hearts, which only grace can change.

Idle words. The word translated “careless” means idle, not working — used of labourers standing unemployed in the marketplace (20:3, 6) and of those who “learn to be idlers, going about from house to house” (1 Timothy 5:13). So the words in view aren’t mainly the wicked ones, which any conscience flags, but the throwaway ones: the comment that cost nothing, meant nothing, and was forgotten within the hour by everyone except the person it was about.

The setting. That sounds intolerable until you remember the setting: an argument in which men have just called the Holy Spirit a demon. It isn’t general anxiety about small talk but the conclusion of a paragraph about the mouth revealing the heart: nothing is exempt from disclosure, not even what we discount ourselves (cf. James 3:2–12; Proverbs 18:21). A test: what do your casual words reveal about your heart?

Evidence, not payment. “By your words you will be justified” can’t mean speech earns acquittal; the man who said it would soon die to secure acquittal on entirely different grounds. The language is legal. In court, evidence doesn’t create a fact; it establishes one. Words are exhibits, not payment; they show what was in the treasury, and the treasury is what grace changes. So the verse is terrifying to someone who thinks his words are trivial, and not to someone whose heart has new contents and whose tongue keeps embarrassing him. Those are different situations, and the sentence distinguishes them.

parallels.desc: death and life are in the power of the tongue

verseByVerse.quote: Then some of the scribes and Pharisees answered him, saying, "Teacher, we wish to see a sign from you." But he answered them, "An evil and adulterous generation seeks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of the prophet Jonah."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who have decided not to believe will always demand more proof, but God gives the one decisive sign: Christ’s death and resurrection.

“Teacher.” In Matthew, disciples call Jesus “Lord,” while outsiders call him “Teacher” (see 8:19). The address is the assessment: these men have come to test a religious lecturer.

After the sign. The request is astonishing in its timing. They have just watched a blind, mute, possessed man walk away seeing, speaking and free. That was the sign. What they want isn’t evidence but a demonstration on demand, on their terms — what the devil proposed in the wilderness and Jesus refused (4:5–7). No evidence would be enough; the request is cover for continued rejection (cf. 1 Corinthians 1:22). A test: are you demanding that God prove himself on your terms before you trust him?

Adulterous. The word isn’t casual abuse. In the prophets, Israel’s covenant with God is a marriage, so unfaithfulness is adultery; Hosea was told to marry a faithless woman so the nation could see itself. To call a generation adulterous is to say it isn’t a stranger to God but a spouse who has gone elsewhere. That is why the demand for a sign is so galling: a wife doesn’t ask her husband to prove his identity.
verseByVerse.note: “Adulterous” is the prophets’ word for Israel’s unfaithfulness to God.

verseByVerse.quote: For just as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so will the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth. The men of Nineveh will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for they repented at the preaching of Jonah, and behold, something greater than Jonah is here.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ’s death and resurrection is the decisive sign, and those who hear it and don’t repent are more guilty than pagans who repented at far less.

The sign of Jonah. The sign is the resurrection, the one that makes all others unnecessary. And Jesus is greater than Jonah: Jonah was swallowed unwillingly; Jesus lays down his life freely. Jonah preached reluctantly to a foreign city; Jesus to his own people. The Ninevites repented at Jonah’s preaching (Jonah 3:5); this generation hears something greater and stays unmoved.

Three days and three nights. How is Friday afternoon to Sunday morning “three days and three nights”? By Jewish reckoning any part of a day counted as a whole day and night. Esther calls a fast for “three days, night or day,” (Esther 4:16), and then acts “on the third day” (Esther 5:1); the same idiom appears in 1 Samuel 30:12–13 and 2 Chronicles 10:5, 12. Some propose a Wednesday crucifixion to make seventy-two hours, but the Gospels’ “on the third day” fits ordinary Jewish counting.

The heart of the earth. Not “in the grave” but “in the heart of the earth,” answering Jonah’s own prayer from the fish: “out of the belly of Sheol I cried, and you heard my voice… The waters closed in over me to take my life; the deep surrounded me… I went down to the land whose bars closed upon me forever” (Jonah 2:2–6). That is the language of a man describing his own death from underneath. So the sign is the whole of it: going down into the place no one returns from, and being brought up — so that Gentiles could be preached to. And the irony: Jonah went into the deep running from the commission to preach to pagans; Jesus goes into the earth to fulfil it.

Was Jonah a real person? Many critics treat the book as a parable. But Jesus sets Jonah beside his own death and resurrection and says the men of Nineveh will stand up at the judgment (cf. Luke 11:30). That makes best sense if the events happened, and the more likely reading is that Jesus believed they did. A test: has the sign of Christ’s resurrection led you to repent?
verseByVerse.note: “Three days and three nights” was a way of counting any part of a day as a day. Nineveh was the capital of Assyria.

parallels.desc: three days and three nights in the fish

verseByVerse.quote: The queen of the South will rise up at the judgment with this generation and condemn it, for she came from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon, and behold, something greater than Solomon is here. When the unclean spirit has gone out of a person, it passes through waterless places seeking rest, but finds none.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Pagans who sought God’s wisdom with less will condemn those who had Christ himself and turned away.

Two Gentile witnesses. Jesus names two figures who will rise to condemn this generation: the men of Nineveh and the queen of the South. Both Gentiles. Nineveh was the capital of Assyria, the empire that destroyed northern Israel, the cruellest power in Israel’s memory, whose kings boasted of flaying their enemies. The queen came from Sheba in south Arabia, a pagan monarch on a trade mission (1 Kings 10:1–13). Neither had the Scriptures, temple, covenant or promises. Nineveh had one reluctant preacher with a single sentence of warning; Sheba had a rumour of a wise king and a long journey. Both responded. And they will stand as witnesses against people who had everything, watched him heal a blind mute, and called it Beelzebul.

Not Israel’s finest. Jonah ran away and sulked; Solomon ended badly. They weren’t Israel’s finest, simply the two who reached the Gentiles. Against them: “something greater than Jonah… something greater than Solomon is here” — the same construction as “greater than the temple” (v. 6). Temple, prophet, king, all named in one chapter, and the same word used of what has arrived to surpass them. A test: are you seeking Christ’s wisdom with the earnestness of a pagan queen who travelled across the world for less?

The wandering spirit. Then the parable begins: an unclean spirit, gone out of a person, wanders seeking rest and finds none — leading into the warning of the next verses.
verseByVerse.note: The queen of the South is the queen of Sheba, in south-west Arabia.

parallels.desc: the queen of Sheba visits Solomon

verseByVerse.quote: Then it says, "I will return to my house from which I came." And when it comes, it finds the house empty, swept, and put in order. Then it goes and brings with it seven other spirits more evil than itself, and they enter and dwell there, and the last state of that person is worse than the first. So also will it be with this evil generation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Moral reformation without Christ himself filling the life leaves a person more exposed than before.

Empty, swept, in order. The three words are all approving. Nothing is dirty; someone has been at work: cleaned out, swept, the furniture arranged. On inspection it would pass. And the first word is the fatal one: empty. The house isn’t reoccupied. That is what a reformation that goes no further than removal leaves: the habit given up, the company dropped, the language cleaned — and nothing moved in.

Not about losing salvation. This isn’t about a Christian losing his salvation. There is no indwelling in the story; that is the whole problem. A house with an occupant isn’t vacant, and the New Testament’s word for a believer is that God has taken up residence. The parable describes moral improvement without new birth — what looks most like progress and is most vulnerable, because it produces a clean space with no defender (cf. 2 Peter 2:20–22).

This generation. Jesus applies it outright: “So also will it be with this evil generation.” They had a genuine national awakening — crowds at the Jordan confessing sins and being baptized. The house was swept. Then the One who was to fill it arrived, and they said he had a demon. Within forty years the temple was rubble and the nation scattered; the last state was worse than the first.

For anyone who had a clear-out. An emptied life isn’t a safe one. It is vacant, and the previous tenant knows the address. A test: has your life merely been cleaned up, or has Christ moved in?

parallels.desc: the last state worse than the first

verseByVerse.quote: While he was still speaking to the people, behold, his mother and his brothers stood outside, asking to speak to him. Someone told him, "Your mother and your brothers are standing outside, seeking to speak to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even Jesus’ own family, who had come to take him home, had yet to understand who he was.

Why they came. Mark tells us: “his family… went out to seize him, for they were saying, ‘He is out of his mind’” (Mark 3:21). They hadn’t come to visit but to take him home, believing he had lost his reason. John adds, “not even his brothers believed in him” (John 7:5). Yet one of them, James, later led the church in Jerusalem and opened his letter by calling himself “a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ” (James 1:1). It took a resurrection. A test: are you praying patiently for family members who don’t yet believe?

Verse 47. The messenger’s report is missing from several early manuscripts, and many Bibles footnote it. It is very likely original, lost by an easy copying slip since verses 46 and 47 end almost alike. Nothing turns on it.

Who were his brothers? Matthew names four brothers — James, Joseph, Simon and Judas — and mentions sisters (13:55–56). Christians have read this in three ways. The oldest Eastern view takes them as Joseph’s children by an earlier marriage. The Western Catholic view, from Jerome on, takes them as cousins. The Protestant view takes them as later children of Joseph and Mary, pointing to Matthew’s wording that Joseph “knew her not until she had given birth” (1:25), and Luke’s “firstborn.” The plain reading favours the third, and it is followed here. But the virgin birth, which all three affirm, is untouched by the question, and it would be a poor use of a chapter about family to be uncharitable about it.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts insert verse 47: “Someone told him, ‘Your mother and your brothers are standing outside, asking to speak to you.’”

verseByVerse.quote: But he replied to the man who told him, "Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?" And stretching out his hand toward his disciples, he said, "Here are my mother and my brothers!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ’s true family is made up of those who follow him, a bond deeper than blood.

The gesture. “Stretching out his hand” is the same verb as verse 13, where the man held out his withered hand. The chapter has two outstretched hands: a ruined one held out on command and restored, and this one held over a circle of ordinary men to say, here is my family. The church isn’t a club but a family, with all the obligations, closeness and mutual responsibility that family implies. A test: do you treat your fellow believers as family?

Hard to hear. Be honest about how hard this is. His mother is outside. She had carried him, been told by an angel who he was, watched shepherds come, and kept these things in her heart. She stands in the street, unable to get in, and he doesn’t go out. It is a public preference exercised at his mother’s expense, when she had come to take him away for his own good. He wasn’t dishonouring her — he provided for her from the cross (John 19:26–27).

She came in. And see where she ends up: in the upper room after the ascension, among those devoting themselves to prayer with the apostles (Acts 1:14). She didn’t stay outside. The circle he pointed to that day was the one she joined — not as his mother, never in doubt, but through the door he described, open to her on the same terms as everyone else. He wasn’t disowning her; he was telling her, in the room’s hearing, that the relationship she would need wasn’t the one she already had.

verseByVerse.quote: For whoever does the will of my Father in heaven is my brother and sister and mother.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone who follows Christ in obedience belongs to God’s family, with one Father in heaven and all others as brothers and sisters under him.

Doing the Father’s will. The mark of his family is “doing the will of my Father,” the same standard as for entering the kingdom (7:21). It isn’t works-righteousness but a description of those being shaped by the Father’s will, learning from Jesus (11:29) and taking up their cross (10:38). And “sister” is added — women named explicitly in his family, in a culture that often excluded them from religious community.

No father named. Count the relations: brother, sister, mother. He doesn’t say father. That can’t be accidental, because the missing word is already in the sentence: “the will of my Father in heaven.” There is a Father, and the place is taken. He says it outright later: “call no man your father on earth, for you have one Father, who is in heaven” (23:9). So this new family isn’t an association of like-minded people but a household — siblings, a mother’s place, one Father, and everyone at the same level under him.

A fact, not a feeling. That is why the obligations are what they are. Christians aren’t asked to be fond of each other, which can’t be arranged; they are told what they are: people with the same Father. That is a fact about the arrangement, not a description of feeling (cf. John 15:14).

Badly, together. He said this with his mother outside and his brothers convinced he was mad. It cost him to define the family this way, and the church has lived under that definition ever since — held together not by temperament, nation or blood but by one Father and a will everyone in the room was learning to do badly. The men he stretched his hand over would all desert him before long, and not one was struck off the list. A test: do you believe you belong to this family even when you obey badly?

parallels.desc: you are my friends if you do what I command

12.theology: Christ as the fulfilment of the Sabbath. The Sabbath controversy of chapter 12 points to one of the great themes of biblical theology: Jesus as the antitype of every Old Testament type. The Sabbath rest of creation (Gen 2) and covenant (Exod 20) pointed forward to the final rest that God’s people would enjoy in the new creation. Hebrews 4 draws this line explicitly: the rest that Joshua could not give, the rest that the weekly Sabbath symbolised, is found in Christ. When Jesus says “the Son of Man is lord of the Sabbath,” he is claiming to be both the giver and the substance of that rest. The Lord’s Day, the day of resurrection, is a weekly proclamation that the rest has arrived in Christ and will be consummated at his return.
12.examples:
Then: The Pharisees’ religion had become a burden rather than a delight. Rules multiplied around the Sabbath until the day of rest was a day of anxiety. Jesus exposed the inversion: when religious observance crushes the people it was meant to bless, something has gone terribly wrong.

Now: The temptation of every religious tradition is to mistake the form for the substance, the sign for the thing signified. The Sabbath becomes a test case: are we worshipping the living God who gives rest, or performing compliance with a schedule? The Lord’s Day is meant to be a foretaste of heaven, a weekly resurrection celebration, not a legal obligation. Christ is Lord of it — and he gives it as a gift.

13.title: The Kingdom in Parables
13.text: <sup>1</sup>That same day Jesus went out of the house and sat beside the sea. <sup>2</sup>And great crowds gathered about him, so that he got into a boat and sat down. And the whole crowd stood on the beach. <sup>3</sup>And he told them many things in parables, saying: “A sower went out to sow. <sup>4</sup>And as he sowed, some seeds fell along the path, and the birds came and devoured them. <sup>5</sup>Other seeds fell on rocky ground, where they did not have much soil, and immediately they sprang up, since they had no depth of soil, <sup>6</sup>but when the sun rose they were scorched.
