And since they had no root, they withered away. <sup>7</sup>Other seeds fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up and choked them. <sup>8</sup>Other seeds fell on good soil and produced grain, some a hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty. <sup>9</sup>He who has ears, let him hear.” <sup>10</sup>Then the disciples came and said to him, “Why do you speak to them in parables?” <sup>11</sup>And he answered them, “To you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it has not been given. <sup>12</sup>For to the one who has, more will be given, and he will have an abundance, but from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away. <sup>13</sup>This is why I speak to them in parables, because seeing they do not see, and hearing they do not hear, nor do they understand. <sup>14</sup>Indeed, in their case the prophecy of Isaiah is fulfilled that says: ”’“You will indeed hear but never understand, and you will indeed see but never perceive.” <sup>15</sup>For this people’s heart has grown dull, and with their ears they can barely hear, and their eyes they have closed, lest they should see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn, and I would heal them.’ <sup>16</sup>But blessed are your eyes, for they see, and your ears, for they hear. <sup>17</sup>For truly, I say to you, many prophets and righteous people longed to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it. <sup>18</sup>“Hear then the parable of the sower: <sup>19</sup>When anyone hears the word of the kingdom and does not understand it, the evil one comes and snatches away what has been sown in his heart. This is what was sown along the path. <sup>20</sup>As for what was sown on rocky ground, this is the one who hears the word and immediately receives it with joy, <sup>21</sup>yet he has no root in himself, but endures for a while, and when tribulation or persecution arises on account of the word, immediately he falls away. <sup>22</sup>As for what was sown among thorns, this is the one who hears the word, but the cares of the world and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word, and it proves unfruitful. <sup>23</sup>As for what was sown on good soil, this is the one who hears the word and understands it. He indeed bears fruit and yields, in one case a hundredfold, in another sixty, and in another thirty.” <sup>24</sup>He put another parable before them, saying, “The kingdom of heaven may be compared to a man who sowed good seed in his field, <sup>25</sup>but while his men were sleeping, his enemy came and sowed weeds among the wheat and went away. <sup>26</sup>So when the plants came up and bore grain, then the weeds appeared also. <sup>27</sup>And the servants of the master of the house came and said to him, ‘Master, did you not sow good seed in your field? How then does it have weeds?’ <sup>28</sup>He said to them, ‘An enemy has done this.’ So the servants said to him, ‘Then do you want us to go and gather them?’ <sup>29</sup>But he said, ‘No, lest in gathering the weeds you root up the wheat along with them. <sup>30</sup>Let both grow together until the harvest, and at harvest time I will tell the reapers, “Gather the weeds first and bind them in bundles to be burned, but gather the wheat into my barn.”’” <sup>31</sup>He put another parable before them, saying, “The kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard seed that a man took and sowed in his field. <sup>32</sup>It is the smallest of all seeds, but when it has grown it is larger than all the garden plants and becomes a tree, so that the birds of the air come and make nests in its branches.” <sup>33</sup>He told them another parable. “The kingdom of heaven is like leaven that a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, till it was all leavened.” <sup>34</sup>All these things Jesus said to the crowds in parables; indeed, he said nothing to them without a parable. <sup>35</sup>This was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet: “I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter what has been hidden since the foundation of the world.” <sup>36</sup>Then he left the crowds and went into the house. And his disciples came to him, saying, “Explain to us the parable of the weeds of the field.” <sup>37</sup>He answered, “The one who sows the good seed is the Son of Man. <sup>38</sup>The field is the world, and the good seed is the sons of the kingdom. The weeds are the sons of the evil one, <sup>39</sup>and the enemy who sowed them is the devil. The harvest is the end of the age, and the reapers are angels. <sup>40</sup>Just as the weeds are gathered and burned with fire, so will it be at the end of the age. <sup>41</sup>The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather out of his kingdom all causes of sin and all law-breakers, <sup>42</sup>and throw them into the fiery furnace. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. <sup>43</sup>Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father. He who has ears, let him hear. <sup>44</sup>“The kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden in a field, which a man found and covered up. Then in his joy he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field. <sup>45</sup>“Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a merchant in search of fine pearls, <sup>46</sup>who, on finding one pearl of great value, went and sold all that he had and bought it. <sup>47</sup>“Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a net that was thrown into the sea and gathered fish of every kind. <sup>48</sup>When it was full, men drew it ashore and sat down and sorted the good into containers but threw away the bad. <sup>49</sup>So it will be at the end of the age. The angels will come out and separate the evil from the righteous <sup>50</sup>and throw them into the fiery furnace. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. <sup>51</sup>“Have you understood all these things?” They said to him, “Yes.” <sup>52</sup>And he said to them, “Therefore every scribe who has been trained for the kingdom of heaven is like a master of a house, who brings out of his treasure what is new and what is old.” <sup>53</sup>And when Jesus had finished these parables, he went away from there, <sup>54</sup>and coming to his hometown he taught them in their synagogue, so that they were astonished, and said, “Where did this man get this wisdom and these mighty works? <sup>55</sup>Is not this the carpenter’s son? Is not his mother called Mary? And are not his brothers James and Joseph and Simon and Judas? <sup>56</sup>And are not all his sisters with us? Where then did this man get all these things?” <sup>57</sup>And they took offense at him. But Jesus said to them, “A prophet is not without honor except in his hometown and in his own household.” <sup>58</sup>And he did not do many mighty works there, because of their unbelief.
13.overview:
Chapter 13 is the third great discourse of Matthew — a collection of seven parables about the kingdom of heaven. Jesus shifts to parables at a moment of escalating opposition (chapters 11–12), and explains to his disciples that parables reveal to the insiders and conceal from the hardened outsiders. This is not capricious; it is the judicial hardening of those who have repeatedly refused the light (v. 15, quoting Isa 6:9–10).

The parables themselves paint a picture of a kingdom that is present but not yet consummate, growing but not yet glorious, mixed but not yet purified. The mustard seed and leaven speak of unexpected, hidden growth from small beginnings. The wheat and tares speak of a kingdom growing alongside counterfeit until the final harvest. The treasure and pearl speak of the surpassing value of the kingdom that makes all sacrifice worthwhile. Together they answer the perennial question: why is the kingdom not more obvious? Because this is the age of seed-sowing, not harvest. The harvest is coming.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–23 — The Parable of the Sower and the Mystery of the Kingdom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus goes to the seashore and teaches in parables for the first time in Matthew. The parable of the sower describes four kinds of reception of the kingdom's word — the path, the rocky ground, the thorns, and the good soil. When the disciples ask why he teaches in parables, Jesus answers that parables reveal the kingdom to those with ears to hear and conceal it from those whose hearts are hardened. He then interprets the parable of the sower in detail. What the summary cannot hold. First-century sowing came before ploughing, not after: a man broadcast seed across the whole field as it stood and then turned the soil to cover it. So the sower is not careless — the path, the rock shelf and the thorn roots are all ground he is about to plough, and the parable is about ground rather than about a fool with a bag. "rocky ground" is not soil with stones in it but a shelf of limestone a few inches down, extremely common in Galilee — and thin soil over rock warms faster, which is exactly why that seed comes up first. The fastest green in the field is growing over the shallowest ground. The yields are the point and are usually skimmed: a normal harvest returned seven to tenfold, so thirty is triple a good year and a hundredfold is what Genesis records of Isaac as a Mark of extraordinary blessing (Gen. 26:12). One patch of good ground repays the whole sowing many times over — the parable is not pessimistic arithmetic. On the hardening, Matthew and Mark genuinely differ: Matthew has "because (hoti) seeing they do not see"; Mark has "so that (hina)... lest they should turn and be forgiven" (Mk. 4:12). Consequence and purpose. Both are in the Isaiah passage both writers quote — "their eyes they have closed" is active and theirs, and "lest they should turn, and I would heal them" is purpose and God's. Anybody who resolves that has dropped one half. Isaiah 6:9-10 is quoted in all four Gospels and in Acts; it is the settled apostolic explanation for Israel's unbelief. And "grown dull" is epachynthe, thickened — the language of a callus, which is formed by repetition rather than by one injury.
verseByVerse.theology: The parable of the sower is really a parable of soils — the sower and the seed are constant; the variable is the heart that receives the word. The four soils are not four types of people as if fixed in their category, but four ways the same heart can receive or resist the word. The parable is both diagnostic (what kind of soil am I?) and eschatological (the harvest will reveal what was real). The interpretation makes explicit that the word of the kingdom is the seed and the devil, persecution, worldly care, and the deceitfulness of riches are the enemies of fruitfulness.
verseByVerse.examples: The mystery of the kingdom — given to the disciples, hidden from others — is not arbitrary divine caprice but the consistent pattern of revelation-and-response: those who have ears to hear receive more; those who have closed their ears lose even what they have. The disciple's responsibility is to cultivate the good soil of an open, honest, persevering heart — "hear the word and understand it" (v. 23) — so that the seed which is sown can bear its appointed fruit.

verseByVerse.quote: That same day Jesus went out of the house and sat beside the sea. And great crowds gathered about him, so that he got into a boat and sat down. And the whole crowd stood on the beach.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus brings his word to a mixed crowd, and what follows is about how different hearts receive it.

From the house to the shore. “That same day Jesus went out of the house” — the house of 12:46–50, where his family stood outside and he named his disciples his true family. Matthew places a scene about who truly belongs to him right before a discourse about who truly receives his word. In that crowd are all four soils of the parable to come.

A floating pulpit. The shore near Capernaum has a small bay where the ground rises from the water in a curve, and a voice from a boat a few yards out carries remarkably far up the slope. A man on the beach is heard by the front rows; a man in a boat with water before him and a natural amphitheatre behind can be heard by thousands. He had no building, so he used the shape of the ground.

He sat. Twice in two verses. A teacher stood to read Scripture and sat to expound it, as Jesus did at Nazareth (Luke 4:20) and on the mountain (5:1). The crowd stands; the teacher sits. A test: when Jesus speaks in his word, do you listen as one under his authority?
verseByVerse.note: Teachers sat to teach; the boat let the crowd on the shore hear him.

verseByVerse.quote: And he told them many things in parables, saying: "A sower went out to sow. And as he sowed, some seeds fell along the path, and the birds came and devoured them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s word is sown generously, but a heart hardened like a trodden path doesn’t receive it, and the evil one snatches it away.

Not a careless sower. People ask why this sower wastes so much seed on path, rock and thorns. In Palestine sowing often came before ploughing: a man broadcast seed over the whole field as it stood — stubble, path and all — then turned the soil to cover it. So what looks careless was ordinary practice: he was sowing ground he was about to plough. The path was a right of way across the field; the thorns had been cut back but their roots remained. It isn’t a story about a fool with a bag of seed; it is a story about ground. And it pictures the gospel: sown broadly, generously, without calculation.

The path. On every other soil the seed at least goes in. Here it lies on top, on ground packed hard by feet; the birds don’t even have to dig. Jesus names them: “the evil one comes and snatches away what has been sown in his heart” (v. 19) — the violent verb used of a wolf seizing a sheep. And there is no struggle in the picture, no gradual erosion: the word arrives, doesn’t go in, and is gone before the man gets home. A heart packed down by busyness, distraction and long resistance lets the word lie on the surface long enough to be taken. A test: does God’s word go into you, or does it lie on the surface and disappear?
verseByVerse.note: Seed was scattered by hand, and some fell on the hard footpaths between fields.

verseByVerse.quote: Other seeds fell on rocky ground, where they did not have much soil, and immediately they sprang up, since they had no depth of soil, but when the sun rose they were scorched. And since they had no root, they withered away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Quick, enthusiastic response without depth can look impressive, but it doesn’t survive the heat of trial.

Rock beneath. “Rocky ground” isn’t soil with stones in it but a shelf of limestone a few inches below the surface — very common in Galilee. Thin soil over rock warms faster, because the stone holds the sun’s heat, so the seed germinates ahead of everything else. “Immediately they sprang up” — not enthusiasm but heat. The fastest green in the field grows over the shallowest ground.

No root. Then the roots hit the rock, can’t go through, and spread sideways in a few inches, leaving a lot of leaf on almost no anchorage or reserve. It looks better than its neighbours for a few weeks. Then the hot east wind off the desert arrives and dries everything; deep roots survive, shallow ones die quickly.

The most impressive plant. Don’t soften the picture. It doesn’t describe someone never affected, but the most impressive-looking plant in the field. Whatever this hearer had was visible and ahead of everyone else’s, and what made it grow so fast is what killed it. A test: is your faith rooted deeply enough to stand when following Christ becomes costly?
verseByVerse.note: Much of Galilee has limestone bedrock just under a thin layer of soil.

verseByVerse.quote: Other seeds fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up and choked them. Other seeds fell on good soil and produced grain, some a hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty. He who has ears, let him hear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Though much of the word seems lost, the fruit from receptive hearts far outweighs the losses, so we must hear rightly.

Thorns. The third soil receives the seed, but thorns are already there; they grow up with the grain and slowly starve it of light. It doesn’t die suddenly; it is choked.

The harvest. The numbers are the point. A normal harvest returned perhaps several times what was sown; tenfold was a good year. So thirtyfold is three times a good year, sixtyfold six, and a hundredfold a harvest few had ever seen. Genesis records one: “Isaac sowed in that land and reaped in the same year a hundredfold. The LORD blessed him” (Genesis 26:12). Read quickly, the parable sounds discouraging — three failures and one success. Read with the yields in place, it isn’t: one patch of good soil at a hundredfold repays the whole sowing many times over, losses included. The sower doesn’t come home at a loss; he comes home with more than he can carry.

Good soil varies. “Some a hundredfold, some sixty, some thirty.” Even among genuine hearers the return varies, and no reason is given. What isn’t offered is any kind of good soil that produces nothing. A test: what fruit is the word producing in your life?

Ears to hear. “He who has ears, let him hear.” Having described four ways of hearing, Jesus tells the crowd to be the fourth — a strange command if hearing were merely a matter of sound arriving. The words are in every ear; what happens next isn’t a matter of volume.
verseByVerse.note: A hundredfold would be an extraordinary harvest.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the disciples came and said to him, "Why do you speak to them in parables?" And he answered them, "To you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it has not been given. For to the one who has, more will be given, and he will have an abundance, but from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Understanding God’s kingdom is a gift of grace, and those who receive and use it are given more.

Good soil asks. The disciples’ question is itself a mark of good soil. They come to Jesus for explanation rather than assuming they understood or giving up. They weren’t quicker than others — they had to ask twice in this chapter — but they came with their questions and stayed when the crowd went home. A test: when you don’t understand Scripture, do you bring your questions to the Lord?

Mysteries. “The secrets of the kingdom” translates “mysteries.” In Greek religion a mystery was something withheld from outsiders, disclosed only to paying initiates. That isn’t the meaning here. Its background is Daniel: a thing genuinely hidden, beyond Babylon’s wise men, which God revealed (Daniel 2:28–30). A biblical mystery isn’t a puzzle to solve but a secret that has been told. The disciples haven’t joined a club; they have been let in on something — which will be shouted from the housetops (10:27).

Given. “To you it has been given” — not achieved or earned. What separated them from the crowd wasn’t capacity but a gift, and the sentence says so of both halves.

More given, or taken. “To the one who has, more will be given… from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away” (cf. 25:29). It sounds like harsh economics, but it describes how spiritual understanding works. Someone who uses what he understands finds it opening out; someone who doesn’t finds it closing. Nothing was confiscated; it went unused, and it went. There is no stable middle.
verseByVerse.note: A “secret” (mystery) in the New Testament is something once hidden and now revealed by God.

parallels.desc: to everyone who has will more be given

verseByVerse.quote: This is why I speak to them in parables, because seeing they do not see, and hearing they do not hear, nor do they understand. Indeed, in their case the prophecy of Isaiah is fulfilled that says: "You will indeed hear but never understand, and you will indeed see but never perceive."
verseByVerse.commentary:
People who close their hearts to God’s word come under his judgment of hardening, and both their choice and God’s purpose are real.

Because, or in order that? A reader with Mark open finds a difference. Matthew writes: “This is why I speak to them in parables, because seeing they do not see” — the parables respond to a condition already present. Mark records: “so that they may indeed see but not perceive… lest they should turn and be forgiven” (Mark 4:12) — the parables given with a purpose. One reads as consequence, the other as intention. Both writers then quote the same passage of Isaiah, which contains both. These are two true angles on one reality, and Scripture refuses to collapse them. Matthew gives the human side: they had already stopped their ears. Mark gives the divine side: God isn’t a bystander, and judicial hardening is genuinely his act. Anyone who resolves the tension does so by dropping half, and the New Testament never does.

Isaiah’s commission. Isaiah 6:9–10 was spoken at Isaiah’s commissioning: his preaching would harden the already hard. It is among the most quoted Old Testament passages in the New — here, in Mark and Luke, in John (12:39–40) and in Acts (28:26–27). It became the apostles’ settled explanation for why Israel’s Messiah was so widely refused: not an accident or a failure of communication, but what a prophet was told on the day he was sent.

Not hiding from the open. The parables aren’t designed to hide truth from open hearts. Those who want to understand seek explanation, as the disciples did; those who don’t receive a story they can enjoy without being confronted. A test: do you come to God’s word wanting to understand and obey, or only to be entertained?

verseByVerse.quote: "For this people's heart has grown dull, and with their ears they can barely hear, and their eyes they have closed, lest they should see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn, and I would heal them." But blessed are your eyes, for they see, and your ears, for they hear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hearts grow hardened through repeated refusal, and those who truly see Christ are blessed by God’s grace.

A callus. “This people’s heart has grown dull” — literally thickened, like tissue coarsening into a callus. Something once sensitive has been overlaid until it no longer feels. And a callus isn’t formed by one injury but by repetition, the same friction in the same place over a long time. No one in the crowd decided one morning to stop understanding. They heard and set it aside, again and again, until setting it aside became a skill. A test: is there a truth you have heard so often and set aside so long that it no longer touches you?

“Lest they turn.” The clause that troubles every serious reader: “lest they should… turn, and I would heal them.” It sounds as though God withholds sight in case someone is healed by accident, and it mustn’t be softened by pretending it says something milder. Two things hold it in place. First, the order: before “lest” comes “their eyes they have closed” — active and theirs. God’s hardening isn’t the first move; it ratifies a shutting already done. Second, what Scripture does with it: Paul takes up Israel’s hardening and asks, “did they stumble in order that they might fall? By no means!” (Romans 11:11). The hardening is real, judicial, and not final.

Blessed eyes. Then the abrupt turn: “But blessed are your eyes, for they see.” After all that, the disciples are told they are the happy ones — a blessing on eyes that see, echoing “they shall see God” (5:8). Their sight is God’s gift (v. 11), but it is real, and it is the only blessedness available in the presence of the kingdom.

parallels.desc: make the heart of this people dull

verseByVerse.quote: For truly, I say to you, many prophets and righteous people longed to see what you see, and did not see it, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it. Hear then the parable of the sower:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Believers now enjoy what the whole Old Testament longed for, and such privilege calls for careful listening.

What the prophets searched for. Peter, who was there, later wrote what this meant: “Concerning this salvation, the prophets who prophesied about the grace that was to be yours searched and inquired carefully, inquiring what person or time the Spirit of Christ in them was indicating when he predicted the sufferings of Christ and the subsequent glories. It was revealed to them that they were serving not themselves but you… things into which angels long to look” (1 Peter 1:10–12). The prophets didn’t fully understand their own words; they wrote them, then searched what they had written. They were told they wouldn’t see it. And the angels still bend down to look — the word used of the disciple stooping to look into the empty tomb.

On the beach. Isaiah wrote of a child born with the government on his shoulder, and died. Micah named the village and never saw it. David wrote of pierced hands long before crucifixion, without knowing what he described (Psalm 22:16). Abraham “rejoiced that he would see my day” (John 8:56). They worked in the dark, on material they couldn’t fully read, for an audience not yet born. And a group of fishermen and a tax collector sit in a boat’s shadow hearing the man himself explain a story about seed, with the chance to ask a follow-up question.

Hear, then. The weight of privilege is enormous, and the right response isn’t complacency but attentive hearing — so Jesus says, “Hear then the parable of the sower.” A test: do you value your Bible and the gospel as the prophets would have?

verseByVerse.quote: When anyone hears the word of the kingdom and does not understand it, the evil one comes and snatches away what has been sown in his heart. This is what was sown along the path. As for what was sown on rocky ground, this is the one who hears the word and immediately receives it with joy,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mere hearing, or even joyful response, doesn’t prove that the word has taken root.

Understand. One word holds this chapter together: “understand.” It appears at verses 13, 14, 15, here at 19, at 23 for the good soil, and at 51, where Jesus asks, “Have you understood all these things?” It isn’t about intelligence; its root sense is putting things together. The path-hearer’s problem isn’t that the word was too hard, but that nothing connected; the seed sat on top of a life it never joined, and was gone.

Joy that fails. The rocky-ground hearer “hears the word and immediately receives it with joy.” Joy — not grudging assent, but the visible, delighted response everyone in ministry is glad to see and inclined to count. And it marks the soil that fails. Joy is a fruit of the Spirit, and the good soil isn’t joyless. But the passage removes joy from the list of reliable indicators, because the one soil credited with immediate joy won’t be there in a year. That is a hard word for any ministry that measures by response: the path shows nothing, the rock shows everything, and the only soil identified with certainty is the one still standing at harvest. A test: is your faith resting on how you felt at the start, or bearing lasting fruit?

Were the rocky and thorny hearers ever truly saved? Some Christians read them as real believers who later fall away. The more likely reading is that they show a profession that was never new birth: no root, no fruit, and they did not last (cf. 1 John 2:19; John 8:31). The response was real as far as it went, but it was not the work of the Spirit that endures. That is why the parable is a warning and not a threat to those who have truly come to Christ: the mark of the good soil is fruit and endurance.

verseByVerse.quote: yet he has no root in himself, but endures for a while, and when tribulation or persecution arises on account of the word, immediately he falls away. As for what was sown among thorns, this is the one who hears the word, but the cares of the world and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word, and it proves unfruitful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Shallow faith is exposed by trouble, and divided faith is slowly smothered by worry and wealth.

Tripped. “No root in himself” — the shallowness is inward; persecution reveals what was already lacking. And “falls away” is the trap word, as in “blessed is the one who is not offended by me” (11:6). He doesn’t resign after weighing the evidence; he is tripped, brought down suddenly by something he didn’t see coming — which is how persecution feels to someone who didn’t expect the Christian life to cost anything.

The deceitfulness of riches. The word means a deliberate deception, a con. Money isn’t called evil here, but a liar — making a specific promise and not keeping it: security, that when there is enough, the anxiety will stop. And the thorns include its opposite: “the cares of the world and the deceitfulness of riches” — the worry of not having enough and the illusion of having it. They look like different problems, but they choke the same plant; they are the same preoccupation from either end (cf. 1 Timothy 6:9–10; Luke 12:16–21).

Quietly unfruitful. Nothing in this soil is dramatic. The seed germinates, roots and grows. There is no snatching or scorching. It simply produces nothing over a long time while staying green: “it proves unfruitful.” The word isn’t rejected; it is crowded into irrelevance — the slow spiritual death of the busy, comfortable Christian. A test: what has the word produced in your life over the last five years, and what is crowding it?

verseByVerse.quote: As for what was sown on good soil, this is the one who hears the word and understands it. He indeed bears fruit and yields, in one case a hundredfold, in another sixty, and in another thirty."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The genuine hearer receives God’s word into the heart and bears lasting fruit — and God can change the hardest ground into good soil.

Understanding that bears fruit. The good soil “hears the word and understands it” — not only grasping the meaning but receiving it into the heart as truth, the understanding that changes the one who understands. Fruit is the evidence. And yields vary; God doesn’t demand identical output but genuine fruit from changed hearts (cf. John 15:5).

Which soil am I? The parable isn’t a scheme for classifying others; it ended, “He who has ears, let him hear.” The honest question is which soil I am, with concrete tests. The path: is there any real hearing, or does it slide off? Ask when Scripture last changed a decision you had already made. The rocky ground: is your faith attached mainly to feeling, and does it fold when following costs something? Recall the last time obedience was expensive, and what happened. The thorny ground — which most readers of a commentary should worry about — isn’t rejection but crowding: the word squeezed into a smaller corner by things that aren’t even sinful. Look at where your mind goes when unoccupied, and at your calendar and bank statement, a fairly ruthless account of what you care about.

Is the soil fixed? If it were, anyone who recognised himself among the thorns would have been handed a life sentence. It isn’t. Real soil can’t change itself; people aren’t real soil. Hosea says, “break up your fallow ground, for it is the time to seek the LORD” (Hosea 10:12), and Jeremiah, “Break up your fallow ground, and sow not among thorns” (Jeremiah 4:3) — God commanding the very change the picture might seem to rule out. And beneath the command is the promise: “I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh” (Ezekiel 36:26). That is what no field can do for itself and what God undertakes to do.

The remedy. If you recognised yourself in the first three, that is the beginning of the remedy, not a verdict. If the ground is hard, ask him to break it, and put yourself where the word is faithfully preached. If the trouble is shallowness, grow roots — they grow in the dark, from knowing Scripture well enough to stand when feelings go, and from being known by people who won’t let you drift. If thorns, name them and cut them one by one; no one ever drifted out of thorns. A test: what will you do this week to make your heart good soil?

Keep sowing. And for anyone who sows and sees little: three soils out of four came to nothing, and the harvest was still thirty, sixty, a hundredfold. The sower isn’t told to stop scattering or to blame himself for the path and rocks. Keep sowing.

parallels.desc: whoever abides in me bears much fruit

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–58 — Six More Parables: The Kingdom's Hidden Growth and Coming Judgment
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Six parables follow the sower: the wheat and weeds (growing together until harvest), the mustard seed (tiny beginning, great growth), the leaven (invisible transformation of the whole), the hidden treasure and pearl of great price (discovering and selling everything for the kingdom), and the dragnet (mixed catch sorted at the end). Jesus then returns to Nazareth, where his neighbors take offense at him. More to notice. The weed has a name: zizania is bearded darnel, and three facts make the parable bite. It is indistinguishable from wheat until the ear forms — Jewish tradition treated it as degenerate wheat. It is poisonous, regularly fungus-infected, and the Latin temulentum means drunken because that is how a person looks who has eaten the bread. And sowing it in an enemy's field was a crime under Roman law, which means it happened often enough to legislate for. The master's refusal to weed is agriculturally exact — darnel roots interlace with wheat roots. This was the text at the centre of the donatist controversy, and Augustine answered the rigorists from it; but note the guard runs both ways, since "let both grow together" is not a ban on church discipline (18:15-17). Discipline addresses conduct and is reversible; what is forbidden is sorting by identity, which requires seeing the ear before it has formed. On the mustard seed objection — orchid seed is smaller — three answers: it was a proverb for the very small, the comparison is among seeds a farmer actually sowed ("in his field"), and this is ordinary descriptive speech, as when we say the sun rises. And the image of a great tree with birds nesting is imperial — Nebuchadnezzar's dream tree (Dan. 4:12), Ezekiel's Assyria and his cedar (Ezek. 17:23; 31:6). Jesus attaches empire-language to a garden herb. The chapter is bracketed by a door: he goes out of the house to the crowds (v. 1) and back into the house for the explanations (v. 36). "the field is the world" — not the church, and Jesus defines it explicitly. The two kinds are described by parentage, not performance, which is why sorting by inspection cannot work. The reapers are angels, and the harvest is the end of the age — the sorting is removed from human hands and from the growing season in one sentence. Note also that the weeds are gathered out of his kingdom (v. 41), so the kingdom in its present form contains what will have to be removed; and "causes of sin" is skandala, the trap-word running through 11:6, 13:21 and 13:57. The dragnet is a sagene, not a cast-net — it sweeps everything, and Levitical law (Lev. 11:9-12) meant a Jewish crew sorted catch into permitted and forbidden every working day. And v. 52's scribe trained for the kingdom is very probably Matthew's self-portrait: the evangelist who quotes the Old Testament some sixty times, structures his book in five discourses, and alone records this saying.
verseByVerse.theology: The parables of growth — mustard seed and leaven — correct the disciples' expectation that the kingdom would arrive with obvious power and immediate separation of righteous from wicked. The kingdom begins invisibly, grows slowly, works from within, and will only be sorted at the harvest. The "already-not-yet" structure of the kingdom is the key: it is genuinely present now (the treasure is in the field; the leaven is in the dough) but not yet fully revealed (the harvest is coming). Patience and trust in the hidden growth are the kingdom virtues these parables require.
verseByVerse.examples: The two treasure parables (hidden treasure, pearl) express the supreme value of the kingdom: it is worth selling everything to obtain. The joy of the man who finds the treasure is the joy of someone who has found what makes every other thing trivially small by comparison. This is the experience of genuine conversion — not reluctant sacrifice but joyful exchange, because the thing found is worth infinitely more than everything surrendered. The kingdom is not burdensome; it is the treasure that makes all other burdens light.

verseByVerse.quote: He put another parable before them, saying, "The kingdom of heaven may be compared to a man who sowed good seed in his field, but while his men were sleeping, his enemy came and sowed weeds among the wheat and went away."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s field contains false believers alongside true ones because of the devil’s deliberate work, not because of any fault in God’s sowing.

A real question. This parable answers what serious believers ask: why are there false believers among the true, and why doesn’t God sort them now? The answer: an enemy planted them; the sorting is coming; but not yet (cf. Mark 4:26–29).

Darnel. The weeds are almost certainly darnel, a grass that infests grain fields and looks virtually identical to wheat through early growth — same seedlings, leaves and height — until the heads form and show it bears no good grain. By then the roots are intertwined. And darnel is usually infected with a fungus that makes it poisonous, causing dizziness and sickness, even death, in those who eat bread made with it. Farmers regarded it not as a nuisance but as a danger. The parable uses both properties: false disciples look like the genuine early on, and they aren’t harmless.

While they slept. “While his men were sleeping” isn’t an accusation; it is simply night. The parable doesn’t fault the household for not guarding a field, and it isn’t a lesson about vigilance. It places the sabotage where sabotage happens: unobserved, when no one could reasonably be watching, leaving no trace for months. And the timing is shrewd — after sowing, before germination, the one window when the crime is both possible and invisible. He knows the calendar; that makes him an enemy, not a vandal.

In the middle. He sowed weeds “among the wheat” — not at the edges but through the middle, so the two would come up interleaved and no line could be drawn between them. He arranged it so that removing the bad would cost the good. A test: are you surprised that the church contains false believers, or ready to trust the Lord who will sort them?
verseByVerse.note: The weeds are probably darnel, a poisonous grass that looks like wheat until the heads form.

verseByVerse.quote: So when the plants came up and bore grain, then the weeds appeared also. And the servants of the master of the house came and said to him, "Master, did you not sow good seed in your field? How then does it have weeds?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
False faith often looks like true faith until fruit appears, and God isn’t the author of the evil found among his people.

Visible at the grain. The weeds became visible only when the grain formed. Early on, darnel and wheat look identical; only when the ears come does the difference show — wheat bears heavy golden grain and bows over; darnel bears small dark seed and stands upright. Jewish tradition even thought darnel a degenerate wheat, so close was the likeness. That is the church’s reality: false profession resembles genuine faith early; the difference appears with growth and fruit over time.

A known crime. Sowing darnel in another’s field was known sabotage; Roman law had a specific provision against it, which means it happened often enough to legislate for. Everyone listening would have known of a case. So the servants’ question isn’t abstract. They have found a field they thought clean full of something that looks like food and isn’t, in quantities they can’t estimate, too late to act before harvest.

An enemy. “Master, did you not sow good seed?” is the question of every troubled pastor and puzzled believer. The answer, “An enemy has done this,” is a diagnosis, not a full explanation: it says who, not why, and the parable never returns to it. But it locates responsibility: God’s field has been invaded, not corrupted by his sowing. A test: do you blame God for the evil that the enemy has sown?

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, "An enemy has done this." So the servants said to him, "Then do you want us to go and gather them?" But he said, "No, lest in gathering the weeds you root up the wheat along with them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God forbids his people to attempt the final separation of true and false believers, which belongs to him alone.

Interlaced roots. The master’s reasoning is agriculturally exact. Darnel roots interlace with wheat roots; in a field where they have stood together for weeks, pulling one lifts the other. The servants don’t argue. So the refusal isn’t sentimentality about weeds but a judgment about what would be destroyed in removing them.

The Donatists. This parable stood at the centre of the Donatist controversy in North Africa. After persecution, a rigorist party held that the church must be visibly pure — that clergy who had lapsed were no longer clergy, and a mixed church was no church. Augustine answered from this passage: the field contains both, the servants aren’t the reapers, and the demand for a pure church before the harvest is a demand God has refused. That instinct recurs and is always sincere, rising from love of holiness, and it always produces the same result: the sharper the sieve, the more wheat goes out with the darnel.

Not against discipline. The guard runs the other way too. “Let both grow together” doesn’t forbid church discipline. Jesus soon lays out a procedure for confronting sin in the congregation that can end in exclusion (18:15–17), and Paul applies it. The difference is between two operations. Discipline addresses conduct, is corrective, aims at restoration, and can be reversed. What the master forbids is sorting people by identity — deciding who is finally wheat and who darnel — because that requires seeing the ear before it forms: “do not pronounce judgment before the time” (1 Corinthians 4:5). A test: are you trying to judge others’ final state, rather than humbly correcting conduct and leaving the rest to God?

parallels.desc: do not pronounce judgment before the time

verseByVerse.quote: Let both grow together until the harvest, and at harvest time I will tell the reapers, "Gather the weeds first and bind them in bundles to be burned, but gather the wheat into my barn." He put another parable before them, saying, "The kingdom of heaven is like a grain of mustard seed that a man took and sowed in his field."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judgment is certain though delayed, and God’s kingdom, though small in its beginnings, will grow to fill the earth.

Delayed, not cancelled. The harvest verdict is certain and final: weeds gathered first and burned, wheat safely into the barn (cf. 3:12). Judgment isn’t avoided, only delayed. The patience of the growing season isn’t laxity toward evil but wisdom about timing.

The smallest seed? An objection: the mustard seed isn’t the smallest seed in the world; orchid seed is finer. But “smallest of all seeds” was a proverb; the rabbis used mustard seed as their standard of the very small. The comparison is within the category the sentence supplies — what “a man took and sowed in his field.” Among seeds a Galilean farmer handled, mustard was the smallest. And this is ordinary speech, as we say “the sun rises” without asserting astronomy.

Small beginnings. The contrast is between beginning and end. The kingdom’s origin was astonishingly small — a band of Galileans around a travelling teacher — and its destiny is to shelter the nations. Its smallness at the start isn’t weakness but hidden power. A test: do you despise the small, unimpressive beginnings of God’s work?

parallels.desc: the wheat gathered, the chaff burned

verseByVerse.quote: "It is the smallest of all seeds, but when it has grown it is larger than all the garden plants and becomes a tree, so that the birds of the air come and make nests in its branches." He told them another parable. "The kingdom of heaven is like leaven that a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, till it was all leavened."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s kingdom grows from tiny, hidden beginnings into something vast and all-pervading.

A garden herb as an empire. Black mustard grows fast and can reach eight or ten feet in a season, enough for birds to perch in. And the picture of a great tree with birds nesting in its branches is imperial: Nebuchadnezzar’s tree with “the birds of the heavens” in its branches (Daniel 4:12); Ezekiel’s cedar that God plants on Israel’s mountain, under which “every kind of bird” will nest (Ezekiel 17:23; 31:6). That is the language of empires, and Jesus attaches it to a garden herb. His hearers expected the cedar — the kingdom arriving with obvious magnificence. He gives them mustard: small enough to be overlooked, fast enough to be underestimated, and ending with the nations sheltering in it.

Are the birds evil? Some note that birds stand for the evil one earlier in the chapter (vv. 4, 19), and read these birds as a corrupted church. But the image here comes from Ezekiel and Daniel, where birds nesting in a great tree picture nations sheltering in a kingdom (Ezekiel 17:23; Daniel 4:12). The same image can mean different things in two different parables, and the good sense is the more likely here.

Leaven. Leaven works from within, invisibly, until the whole batch rises. The kingdom doesn’t transform the world by outward force — the constant temptation of political religion — but by the Spirit’s hidden work in hearts, gradually permeating everything. And three measures is a huge batch, what Sarah baked for her guests (Genesis 18:6). A test: are you trusting the quiet work of God’s word and Spirit, or looking for power and spectacle?

Isn’t leaven always evil? Everywhere else leaven pictures corruption. Israel swept it out before Passover (Exodus 12:15); Paul warns that “a little leaven leavens the whole lump,” speaking of tolerated sin (1 Corinthians 5:6–8); and Jesus will say, “beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees” (16:6). Some conclude this parable warns of corruption spreading through the church. It is an honest reading, but it doesn’t fit the sentence: “the kingdom of heaven is like leaven,” exactly as it is like a mustard seed, both describing growth from small to total. The better answer is that leaven pictures how something spreads, not a verdict on what spreads. A small hidden agent working through a large mass is morally neutral; sin does it, and so does the kingdom. A parable borrows an everyday thing for one point.
verseByVerse.note: Mustard seed was proverbially tiny; the plant can grow taller than a man. Three measures of flour is a very large batch — about what Sarah baked for her three guests.

parallels.desc: birds nest in the cedar’s branches

verseByVerse.quote: All these things Jesus said to the crowds in parables; indeed, he said nothing to them without a parable. This was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet: "I will open my mouth in parables; I will utter what has been hidden since the foundation of the world."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Through Christ’s parables God reveals purposes he planned before creation, to those with ears to hear.

Psalm 78. The text Matthew quotes opens one of the longest psalms, Asaph retelling Israel’s history from the Exodus to David, failures included: “I will open my mouth in a parable; I will utter dark sayings from of old, things that we have heard and known, that our fathers have told us” (Psalm 78:2–3). Its purpose: “that the next generation might know them… so that they should set their hope in God and not forget the works of God” (Psalm 78:6–7). So the text explaining parabolic teaching is itself parabolic teaching — a long story told to children so they wouldn’t repeat their fathers’ failures. The method is older than the Gospel, always aimed at the next generation. Matthew calls Asaph “the prophet”; Chronicles calls him a seer (2 Chronicles 29:30).

Nothing without a parable. “He said nothing to them without a parable.” Mark says the same and adds the other half: “privately to his own disciples he explained everything” (Mark 4:34). This chapter is built that way. At verse 1 Jesus goes out of the house to the crowd; at verse 36 he leaves the crowds and goes into the house for the explanation. Out to the parables, back for the meaning; the chapter is bracketed by a door.

Hidden since the foundation. What is disclosed on that beach isn’t new information about God’s plans but old — older than Israel or Abraham, in place before creation, and kept. A test: do you treat Christ’s teaching as one opinion among many, or as God’s eternal purpose now revealed?
verseByVerse.note: The psalm’s author, Asaph, is called a seer in Chronicles; Matthew calls him “the prophet.”

parallels.desc: I will open my mouth in a parable

verseByVerse.quote: Then he left the crowds and went into the house. And his disciples came to him, saying, "Explain to us the parable of the weeds of the field." He answered, "The one who sows the good seed is the Son of Man."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who come to Christ with their questions receive understanding, and the whole field and harvest belong to him.

Through the door. Verse 1: he went out of the house to the crowds. Verse 36: he left the crowds and went into the house with the disciples. Everything the crowd hears is a story; everything the disciples get is the meaning, through the same door opened twice. That is what he told them: “To you it has been given to know the secrets of the kingdom” (v. 11). Matthew has built the chapter to enact it.

They asked. “Explain to us the parable of the weeds.” They didn’t understand it either. The twelve weren’t insiders who followed everything; they were as lost as anyone and simply asked. The difference between the fourth soil and the others isn’t comprehension but what someone does when he hasn’t understood. A test: when you don’t understand, do you give up or ask the Lord?

The Son of Man sows. “The one who sows the good seed is the Son of Man” — the figure of Daniel 7, given everlasting dominion. The ordinary man with a bag of seed in a Galilean field turns out to be Daniel’s Son of Man, and he will reappear sending the angels to reap (v. 41). The same one plants and harvests; nothing in the field belongs to anyone else.

Can the weeds ever become wheat? The parable describes how things stand at the harvest, not a fixed caste in the growing season. Sons of the evil one are brought out of that condition by new birth (Colossians 1:13; John 1:12–13), and that is why the gospel is preached to all. Some object that the image makes conversion impossible, but the parable is about the end of the age, not the beginning of a life.

verseByVerse.quote: the field is the world, and the good seed is the sons of the kingdom. The weeds are the sons of the evil one, and the enemy who sowed them is the devil. The harvest is the end of the age, and the reapers are angels.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Good and evil people grow together in the world until the end, and only God, through his angels, will separate them.

The field is the world. Not the church. Jesus says it outright; it is the element he defines most explicitly. Read as a picture of the church, the parable becomes an argument for tolerating anything in the congregation, which collides with chapter 18 and with Paul, who tells a church to remove an unrepentant man. Read as Jesus defines it, it pictures the whole human community, with two kinds of people growing side by side, indistinguishable to the eye, until the end.

Parentage, not performance. “The sons of the kingdom… the sons of the evil one” — Semitic idiom: a “son of” something belongs to it and bears its character. The distinction isn’t that one group behaves well and the other badly, but that they have different origins. That explains why sorting can’t be done by inspection: parentage is invisible, and wheat and darnel look alike precisely because appearance isn’t what is being sorted.

Not now, not us. “The harvest is the end of the age” — not now, not in any purge or council; no zeal can bring the date forward. “The reapers are angels” — not us, not the servants who volunteered in verse 28 (cf. Joel 3:13; Revelation 14:14–16). The parable takes the sorting out of the growing season and out of human hands, and leaves the church a different job meanwhile: to sow, grow and bear fruit. A test: are you busy trying to sort others, or faithfully bearing fruit yourself?

parallels.desc: put in the sickle, for the harvest is ripe

verseByVerse.quote: Just as the weeds are gathered and burned with fire, so will it be at the end of the age. The Son of Man will send his angels, and they will gather out of his kingdom all causes of sin and all law-breakers,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ himself will purify his kingdom at the end, removing everything that causes others to stumble.

Out of his kingdom. “They will gather out of his kingdom all causes of sin.” Not out of the world — out of the kingdom. In its present form the kingdom contains things that must be removed. It isn’t yet the pure part. The field is the world, the kingdom is being planted across it, good and bad grow inside the cultivated area, and the harvest is a clearing within the King’s own territory. It is presently mixed and finally purified.

Stumbling blocks. “Causes of sin” is the trap word again — the message to John (“not offended by me,” 11:6), the rocky-ground hearer who “falls away” (13:21). So what is gathered out first is what tripped people up: not only wicked people in themselves, but whatever in the field brought others down (cf. Zephaniah 1:3). Someone in that judgment is there partly because of what he did to another’s faith. A test: is anything in your life causing someone else to stumble?

His angels. “The Son of Man will send his angels” (cf. 24:31). Throughout the Old Testament angels belong to God, his host and messengers. Here they are the Son of Man’s, sent at his order to execute his judgment in his kingdom. No first-century Jew would have missed that possessive.

parallels.desc: I will sweep away the stumbling blocks
he will send out his angels

verseByVerse.quote: and throw them into the fiery furnace. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father. He who has ears, let him hear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The end holds terrible judgment for the wicked and glorious radiance for God’s children.

The furnace. “The fiery furnace,” the image of Daniel 3:6, with “weeping and gnashing of teeth” (cf. 8:12) — Jesus doesn’t soften the end.

Shine like the sun. The promise quotes Daniel: “those who are wise shall shine like the brightness of the sky above; and those who turn many to righteousness, like the stars forever and ever” (Daniel 12:3). It follows the clearest statement of resurrection in the Old Testament: “many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt” (Daniel 12:2). Jesus places the wheat where Daniel placed the wise — and sharpens it. Daniel says like the sky and the stars; Jesus says “like the sun.” Stars are many and distant; the sun is what you can’t look at directly. It is how his own face shone on the mountain of transfiguration (17:2). What happened to him there is promised to them. The final state isn’t merely the absence of suffering but radiance.

Their Father’s kingdom. Throughout the explanation the kingdom has been the Son of Man’s; in the last clause it is the Father’s, and those shining in it are his children. A test: do you long for that day, and live in its light now?

Ears to hear. “He who has ears, let him hear” closes the explanation as it closed the parable (v. 9) — once for the crowd on the beach, once for the twelve in the house. Being on the inside of the door doesn’t exempt anyone from the call to hear rightly.

parallels.desc: the wise shall shine like the brightness of the sky

verseByVerse.quote: The kingdom of heaven is like treasure hidden in a field, which a man found and covered up. Then in his joy he goes and sells all that he has and buys that field. Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a merchant in search of fine pearls,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The kingdom of God is worth more than everything we have, and those who see its worth give all for it gladly.

Joy. Everything turns on “in his joy he goes.” He doesn’t reluctantly surrender his possessions; he gladly exchanges them for something worth incomparably more. That is conversion at its truest: not the grim duty of giving up good things for God, but the delighted exchange of lesser goods for the supreme good (cf. Philippians 3:7–8; Proverbs 3:13–15). The kingdom found makes everything else look small — not worthless, but small. A test: does following Christ feel to you like a grim cost, or a joyful bargain?

Wasn’t he dishonest? He finds treasure in someone else’s field, covers it, says nothing, and buys the field — like spotting oil under a farm and buying it cheap. Is Jesus commending sharp practice? A parable makes one point, and its details are scenery, not moral instruction. Jesus tells stories about a dishonest manager, an unjust judge and a thief in the night, and commends none; he takes one feature of each. Here the feature is joy. And the man’s conduct was probably less questionable than it sounds: with no banks and frequent invasions, valuables were often buried, and law generally attached what was buried in a field to the field. The honest route to the treasure ran through buying the field. He could have pocketed it; instead he paid for the ground.

Who is the man who sells everything? Most read him as the believer, who gives up all for the kingdom because he has seen its worth. Others read him as Christ, who gave all to buy his people (Ephesians 5:25). The first is the more likely, since the next parable makes the same point about a merchant. But the believer buys nothing that earns grace (Isaiah 55:1); the “price” is the glad surrender of everything else. That surrender is real, though it does not always mean literally selling everything (19:21).
verseByVerse.note: With no banks, people commonly buried valuables in the ground. Pearls were among the most prized luxuries of the ancient world.

parallels.desc: counting everything as loss for Christ

verseByVerse.quote: who, on finding one pearl of great value, went and sold all that he had and bought it. Again, the kingdom of heaven is like a net that was thrown into the sea and gathered fish of every kind,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whether found by surprise or after long searching, Christ’s kingdom is worth everything, and the gospel net gathers all kinds until the final sorting.

Two ways in. The two treasure parables are a pair with one deliberate difference. The man in the field wasn’t looking; he was working someone else’s land and his spade struck something. The merchant was looking; finding fine pearls was his trade, and he had trained his eye for years. Both sell everything. So the pair covers two ways people come: some ambushed in an ordinary working day, others searching for years who finally find. The parables refuse to make either the rule. A test: has Christ become your pearl of great value?

Traded up. In neither parable is the selling a hard thing bravely done. Someone who exchanges everything for something worth vastly more hasn’t sacrificed; he has traded up, and knows it. Whether following Christ feels like a cost paid or a bargain struck says more about how we value him than any statement of belief.

The dragnet. The net is a dragnet — a long weighted net drawn between boats or hauled to shore, sweeping everything in its path. A cast-net is aimed; a dragnet isn’t. It takes what is in the water, and the sorting is done later on the sand. So the gospel gathers broadly, and the church shouldn’t be surprised that it contains both kinds.
verseByVerse.note: A dragnet was drawn between boats or to shore, catching everything in its path.

verseByVerse.quote: When it was full, men drew it ashore and sat down and sorted the good into containers but threw away the bad. So it will be at the end of the age. The angels will come out and separate the evil from the righteous
verseByVerse.commentary:
God will make a final, complete separation, and it is his work, not ours.

Sorting on the sand. The Sea of Galilee holds many species, and the law allowed only fish with fins and scales to be eaten (Leviticus 11:9–12); catfish and eels were unclean. A Jewish fisherman hauling a dragnet ashore sorted his catch into permitted and forbidden. So this was the ordinary end of a working day for men in the audience: the net on the sand, the crew sitting beside it, going through the pile by hand.

Good and rotten. The good fish are “fine,” sound; the bad are “rotten,” the word used of a bad tree that can’t bear good fruit (7:17–18). Not disappointing fish, but fish that have gone off.

Said twice. This is the second time the chapter ends a parable this way. The wheat and weeds ended with separation and burning; the net ends the same. Two pictures — field and lake, farming and fishing — reaching the same conclusion (cf. 25:31–33). Matthew gives the warning twice, in the two trades his readers worked in, so no one could file it as agricultural imagery and move on. And in both, the sorting is done by angels at the end, not by the workers who brought the catch in. A test: are you ready for the day of separation?
verseByVerse.note: Fish without fins and scales were unclean under the law and could not be sold as food.

verseByVerse.quote: and throw them into the fiery furnace. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Have you understood all these things?" They said to him, "Yes."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus calls his followers to account for their hearing, and even partial understanding, honestly offered, is received and deepened.

The last question. “Have you understood all these things?” — the word that has run through the chapter (vv. 13, 14, 15, 19, 23), now its last occurrence, put as a direct question. The chapter has been about the difference between hearing and understanding, and it ends by asking the twelve which side of the line they are on. They answer with one word: “Yes.”

What their yes was worth. Be honest. Soon Peter will be told, “Get behind me, Satan!” for objecting to the cross. They will argue about who is greatest, fail to cast out a demon “because of your little faith,” and still ask at the supper where he is going; by the end of that night, every one will have fled. So their yes wasn’t false, but it wasn’t adequate. They had grasped the outline and almost nothing of what it would cost.

Received and deepened. That is mercy for anyone who has said yes to God and later discovered how little he knew he was agreeing to. Jesus doesn’t correct them. He accepts the answer and adds one more parable, as though to say: good — and there is much more in the store. A test: is your “yes” to Christ growing deeper as you learn what it means?

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to them, "Therefore every scribe who has been trained for the kingdom of heaven is like a master of a house who brings out of his treasure what is new and what is old." And when Jesus had finished these parables, he went away from there,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ’s disciples are to read the whole Bible together, Old and New, each shedding light on the other.

Old and new. The scribe trained for the kingdom is the disciple who reads all of Scripture in the light of the kingdom. The old (the Law and the Prophets) and the new (the teaching of Jesus) come from the same house. The Old Testament isn’t replaced by the New but fulfilled in it (5:17), and the New can’t be understood without the Old.

Matthew’s self-portrait. This is very probably Matthew’s self-portrait. Consider the author: a man who quotes the Old Testament more than any other evangelist, structures his Gospel in five discourses echoing Moses’ five books, repeatedly says “this was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet,” alone records this saying — and lists himself as “Matthew the tax collector” (10:3). A man who kept records for a living, knew the Scriptures well enough to weave them through every chapter, and was called from a customs booth. If anyone is a scribe trained for the kingdom bringing out things old and new, it is the author of this sentence.

The storeroom. The word means the place where treasure is kept; the householder goes to the store and fetches. And notice the order: “what is new and what is old.” New first — this scribe has something recent to set beside the old, and leads with it. But he doesn’t discard the old. He hasn’t replaced his library; something has been added that makes the rest legible. The mustard seed, darnel and dragnet mean what they mean because Daniel, Ezekiel and Asaph stand behind them. Bring out both. A test: do you read the Old Testament as Christ’s own book?

The third seal. “When Jesus had finished these parables” is the third of Matthew’s five closing formulas (7:28; 11:1; 13:53; 19:1; 26:1).

parallels.desc: not to abolish but to fulfil

verseByVerse.quote: and coming to his hometown he taught them in their synagogue, so that they were astonished, and said, "Where did this man get this wisdom and these mighty works? Is not this the carpenter's son? Is not his mother called Mary? And are not his brothers James and Joseph and Simon and Judas?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Familiarity with Jesus can blind people to who he really is.

The right question. “Where did this man get this wisdom and these mighty works?” is the right question. Their astonishment is genuine; they can’t explain him by his background. But instead of reaching upward — “he must be from God” — they reach back into the ordinary: “we know this family.” The familiarity that should have been their greatest privilege becomes their stumbling block (cf. John 6:42). They reduce him to what they already know instead of letting what they see revise it. A test: has familiarity with Jesus made you stop wondering at him?

The carpenter. “The carpenter’s son” — a general word for a builder or craftsman in wood or stone.

His brothers. The names — James, Joseph, Simon and Judas, and his sisters — most naturally mean his actual younger siblings, born to Joseph and Mary after him. (The other views and the reasons for this one are set out at 12:46–47.) And there is gospel gold here. These brothers didn’t believe in him during his ministry — “not even his brothers believed in him” (John 7:5) — yet after the resurrection they are in the upper room praying (Acts 1:14), and James and Jude wrote letters now in our New Testament, James becoming a pillar of the Jerusalem church. What turns a sceptical younger brother into a man who calls his own brother “the Lord”? Only an empty tomb. The conversion of Jesus’ brothers is a quiet, powerful evidence that he rose.
verseByVerse.note: “Carpenter” is a general word for a builder or craftsman in wood or stone.

parallels.desc: “Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph?”

verseByVerse.quote: And are not all his sisters with us? Where then did this man get all these things?" And they took offense at him. But Jesus said to them, "A prophet is not without honor except in his hometown and in his own household."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those closest to Christ may reject him because he seems too ordinary.

Correct facts, wrong conclusion. Their questions aren’t stupid or hostile at first. “Is not this the carpenter’s son? Is not his mother called Mary? … are not all his sisters with us?” Every fact is accurate; no one in Nazareth is mistaken about anything. Then they repeat their opening question — “Where then did this man get all these things?” — this time as objection, not enquiry. That is the tragedy in a paragraph. They asked where it came from, assembled a complete and correct account of what they knew about him, found it didn’t explain what they were seeing, and concluded the problem was with him. The evidence raised a question their information couldn’t answer. The right response was to widen their information; they narrowed the evidence instead. A test: when Jesus doesn’t fit what you know, do you let him correct you, or dismiss him?

Tripped. “They took offense at him” — the chapter’s trap word again (11:6; 13:21, 41). They didn’t argue him down; they tripped over him, over the very thing that should have made him easiest to believe: they had known him all his life. “He came to his own, and his own people did not receive him” (John 1:11).

Nothing mysterious. “His sisters are with us” — still living there, presumably married locally; their neighbours could point to their houses. Nothing about this family was mysterious, and that was the difficulty. “A prophet is not without honor except in his hometown,” he says, as John also records (John 4:44).

parallels.desc: his own people did not receive him

verseByVerse.quote: And he did not do many mighty works there, because of their unbelief.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Unbelief that has already decided against Christ shuts itself off from his blessing — though this is never a formula blaming the suffering for unanswered prayer.

Not a formula. This verse must be handled carefully, because read carelessly it becomes a cruelty: miracles run on faith, so if God hasn’t acted for you, your faith was too thin. Some have been told exactly that at a hospital bed. It isn’t what the verse means. He “did not do many mighty works there” — and Mark says “he laid his hands on a few sick people and healed them” (Mark 6:5). Even there, some were healed. So it isn’t a mechanism in which a quantity of faith buys a quantity of power. Elsewhere he heals a paralysed man on his friends’ faith (9:2), raises the dead, who contribute nothing, and restores people who don’t yet know who he is. Faith is the open hand, never the currency.

What unbelief prevented. What Nazareth’s unbelief prevented was simpler and sadder. They didn’t bring their sick to him, because they had already decided who he was: the carpenter’s boy whose family lived down the road. You can’t receive what you have decided not to come for. If you have prayed and not received, this passage isn’t an accusation against you (see 8:16–17); Paul, whose faith was equal to anything, asked three times and kept his thorn.

The real warning. But take the warning that is genuinely here, aimed at the kind of person who reads commentaries. Those who got least from Jesus were those nearest him longest. They weren’t hostile; they were familiar. They had him filed. A lifetime of church can do the same: sermons heard before, passages you already know, the quiet assumption that there is nothing here you haven’t met. Nazareth is what happens when knowing about him has replaced knowing him. A test: has familiarity made you stop coming to Jesus expecting anything?

13.theology: The hiddenness and growth of the kingdom. The parables of Matthew 13 develop a theology of the kingdom that runs against both triumphalism and despair. Against triumphalism: the kingdom grows secretly, like leaven, not by worldly power or coercion. Against despair: the smallest seed becomes the largest tree; the handful of leavened dough leavens the whole batch. The kingdom’s smallness is not its failure but its method. Reformed theology has always insisted that the church advances through the ordinary means of grace — word, sacrament, prayer — not through political power or cultural dominance. The harvest will be glorious; the sowing is patient.
13.examples:
Then: The disciples were living through the mustard-seed phase of the kingdom. From their vantage point, a small band of Galileans following a rabbi who was being plotted against by the religious establishment, the kingdom’s glory was not obvious. Jesus tells them: do not judge the end by the beginning.

Now: Every era of church history has felt like the mustard-seed phase. Persecution, secularisation, nominalism — all seem to contradict the kingdom’s advance. The parables of Matthew 13 are the antidote to both despair and triumphalism. The Sower keeps sowing. The leaven keeps working. The net keeps gathering. The harvest belongs to the Lord.

14.title: Bread in the Wilderness
14.text: <sup>1</sup>At that time Herod the tetrarch heard about the fame of Jesus, <sup>2</sup>and he said to his servants, “This is John the Baptist. He has been raised from the dead; that is why these miraculous powers are at work in him.” <sup>3</sup>For Herod had seized John and bound him and put him in prison for the sake of Herodias, his brother Philip’s wife, <sup>4</sup>because John had been saying to him, “It is not lawful for you to have her.” <sup>5</sup>And though he wanted to put him to death, he feared the people, because they held him to be a prophet. <sup>6</sup>But when Herod’s birthday came, the daughter of Herodias danced before the company and pleased Herod, <sup>7</sup>so that he promised with an oath to give her whatever she might ask. <sup>8</sup>Prompted by her mother, she said, “Give me the head of John the Baptist here on a platter.” <sup>9</sup>And the king was sorry, but because of his oaths and his guests he commanded it to be given. <sup>10</sup>He sent and had John beheaded in the prison, <sup>11</sup>and his head was brought on a platter and given to the girl, and she brought it to her mother. <sup>12</sup>And his disciples came and took the body and buried it, and they went and told Jesus. <sup>13</sup>Now when Jesus heard this, he withdrew from there in a boat to a desolate place by himself. But when the crowds heard it, they followed him on foot from the towns. <sup>14</sup>When he went ashore he saw a great crowd, and he had compassion on them and healed their sick. <sup>15</sup>Now when it was evening, the disciples came to him and said, “This is a desolate place, and the day is now over; send the crowds away to go into the villages and buy food for themselves.” <sup>16</sup>But Jesus said, “They need not go away; you give them something to eat.” <sup>17</sup>They said to him, “We have only five loaves here and two fish.” <sup>18</sup>And he said, “Bring them here to me.” <sup>19</sup>Then he ordered the crowds to sit down on the grass, and taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and said a blessing. Then he broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds. <sup>20</sup>And they all ate and were satisfied. And they took up twelve baskets full of the broken pieces left over. <sup>21</sup>And those who ate were about five thousand men, besides women and children. <sup>22</sup>Immediately he made the disciples get into the boat and go before him to the other side, while he dismissed the crowds. <sup>23</sup>And after he had dismissed the crowds, he went up on the mountain by himself to pray. When evening came, he was there alone, <sup>24</sup>but the boat by this time was a long way from the land, beaten by the waves, for the wind was against them. <sup>25</sup>And in the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking on the sea. <sup>26</sup>But when the disciples saw him walking on the sea, they were terrified, and said, “It is a ghost!” and they cried out in fear. <sup>27</sup>But immediately Jesus spoke to them, saying, “Take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid.” <sup>28</sup>And Peter answered him, “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the water.” <sup>29</sup>He said, “Come.” So Peter got out of the boat and walked on the water and came to Jesus. <sup>30</sup>But when he saw the wind, he was afraid, and beginning to sink he cried out, “Lord, save me.” <sup>31</sup>Jesus immediately reached out his hand and took hold of him, saying to him, “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?” <sup>32</sup>And when they got into the boat, the wind ceased. <sup>33</sup>And those in the boat worshiped him, saying, “Truly you are the Son of God.” <sup>34</sup>And when they had crossed over, they came to land at Gennesaret. <sup>35</sup>And when the men of that place recognized him, they sent around to all that region and brought to him all who were sick <sup>36</sup>and implored him that they might only touch the fringe of his garment. And as many as touched it were made well.
14.overview:
Chapter 14 moves from Herod’s banquet of death (John’s head on a platter) to Jesus’ banquet of life (five thousand fed in the wilderness). The contrast is deliberate. Herod’s table is supplied by cruelty, vanity, and the murder of a prophet. Jesus’ table is supplied by compassion, prayer, and the creative power of the Creator multiplying what is surrendered to him. John’s death is the herald’s fate; Jesus will face his own; but the meals he gives point beyond death to the resurrection feast.

The feeding of the five thousand is the only miracle recorded in all four Gospels (besides the resurrection). Matthew frames it with Exodus typology: a desolate place (wilderness), manna-like provision, the Shepherd feeding his people. Jesus looks up to heaven, blesses, breaks, and gives — the same fourfold action he will perform at the Last Supper. Every Lord’s Supper echoes this meal. The chapter closes with Peter walking on water — and sinking. The disciples worship: “Truly you are the Son of God.”

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–21 — The Death of John and the Feeding of the Five Thousand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Herod Antipas hears of Jesus and fears John has risen from the dead. Matthew then narrates the death of John the Baptist — arrested for condemning Herod's marriage to his brother's wife, beheaded to fulfill a rash oath at a banquet. Jesus withdraws on hearing the news, but the crowds follow him. He heals them and then feeds five thousand men from five loaves and two fish. The feeding is the great Eucharistic sign, anticipating the Last Supper and the heavenly banquet. What the summary cannot hold. Herod is a tetrarch, not a king — Herod the Great's realm was quartered at his death and this son got Galilee and Perea. He wanted the higher title, went to Rome to ask for it, and was exiled for his trouble. He came to power soon after the nativity and was still in power at the crucifixion, and Luke has Pilate send Jesus to him during the trial (Lk. 23:12). His explanation is theologically bizarre: nobody in Judaism expected an individual to be raised in the middle of history, so "this is John, he has been raised" is not a belief he is reaching for — he has invented it on the spot, and said it to his servants, the people who had watched the platter come in. On the geography, Josephus names the prison: Machaerus, a fortress-palace east of the Dead Sea with luxurious apartments above and cells below — so the banquet and the dungeon were in the same building. He also names the girl: Salome.
