And Matthew calls her a korasion, the diminutive, the same word used of Jairus's twelve-year-old (9:24-25) — a child, put up to it, who goes out to ask her mother what to say. The oath is a quotation: Mark gives it in full, "up to half my kingdom" (6:23), which is what Ahasuerus says to Esther three times, at her banquets (Est. 5:3, 6; 7:2). A drunken king, a rash promise, a woman with a prepared request, a man's life in the balance — and every element inverts. Esther's request saved a people from a murderer; this one murders a prophet. Note too that Herod and the chief priests are restrained by the same calculation, in almost identical words: both fear the crowd "because they held him to be a prophet" (14:5; 21:46). And verse 12 is the quietest sentence in the chapter — John's disciples walked into a royal fortress to ask for the body, buried what there was, and then went to the one man who had told them who John was. Matthew records no reply. The next thing Jesus does is withdraw; the next thing after that is to feed five thousand men, besides women and children. On the day he heard.
verseByVerse.theology: John's death is the dark center of the chapter: the fate of the forerunner anticipates the fate of the one he announced. Herod's fear that Jesus is John raised from the dead is simultaneously wrong (Jesus is not John) and prophetically ironic (the resurrection John could not achieve, Jesus will). The feeding of the five thousand is the messianic act par excellence: the shepherd-king who provides bread for his people in the wilderness, echoing the manna of the Exodus. Jesus takes, blesses, breaks, and gives — the fourfold action of the Last Supper.
verseByVerse.examples: The disciples' protest — "we have only five loaves here and two fish" — is the protest of faith that has not yet learned what it is living with. They are calculating from what they have; Jesus acts from who he is. "Bring them here to me" is the word for every situation where human resources fall desperately short of human need. The miracle occurs not in the disciples' hands but in his: he takes, blesses, breaks, gives — and twelve baskets remain. Twelve: one for each tribe of Israel, one for each disciple. The abundance of the kingdom always exceeds the need.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time Herod the tetrarch heard about the fame of Jesus, and he said to his servants, "This is John the Baptist. He has been raised from the dead; that is why these miraculous powers are at work in him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A guilty conscience can’t silence the memory of wrongdoing, but dread without repentance changes nothing.

The tetrarch. Herod Antipas got a quarter of his father Herod the Great’s kingdom — Galilee and Perea — with the rank of tetrarch, not king. He wanted the higher title badly, later went to Rome to ask for it, and was exiled to Gaul instead. He ruled the district where Jesus grew up for nearly all of Jesus’ life, and at the trial Pilate sent Jesus to him, and the two became friends that day (Luke 23:12).

A guilty invention. His explanation is theologically bizarre. Jews didn’t expect one person to be raised in the middle of history; resurrection belonged to the last day. Herod invents it on the spot. That is what a guilty conscience does: he isn’t reasoning from evidence; he is being haunted. And he says it to his servants — those who had been in the palace, who had seen the platter come in. Guilt confirms that John was innocent and Herod’s deed murder. It should have been the beginning of repentance; it remained only dread. A test: is there a guilt you carry as dread rather than bringing it to God in repentance?

He wanted to see him. Luke adds: “he sought to see him” (Luke 9:9). He got his wish at the end, and when he finally had Jesus before him he asked for a show and got silence.
verseByVerse.note: Herod the tetrarch is Herod Antipas, son of Herod the Great, who ruled Galilee and Perea. A tetrarch was a ruler of part of a divided kingdom.

verseByVerse.quote: For Herod had seized John and bound him and put him in prison for the sake of Herodias, his brother Philip's wife, because John had been saying to him, "It is not lawful for you to have her."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Faithful witness speaks God’s truth to the powerful, whatever it costs.

Truth to power. “It is not lawful for you to have her.” Herodias was Herod’s niece, who had left his half-brother to marry him — a union the law forbade (Leviticus 18:16; 20:21). John didn’t soften it for safety or politics. He said it to the ruler’s face and paid with his freedom and then his life. That is the prophet’s calling: to speak God’s word to the powerful as to the powerless. John’s imprisonment wasn’t mismanagement; it was the expected fate of a faithful prophet in a world that prefers comfortable lies. A test: is there a truth you are keeping quiet because speaking it would cost you?

Which Philip? Critics note that Josephus names Herodias’s first husband as Herod, another son of Herod the Great, and says Philip the tetrarch married her daughter Salome — so the Gospels, it is said, muddled the family. They haven’t; the tangle is Herod’s own. Herod the Great had many wives and sons and named a remarkable number of them Herod; more than one was called Philip, and Josephus himself gives some of them two names. A son known formally as Herod and familiarly as Philip is quite possible, and Matthew’s readers, close to the events, would have needed the second name to tell the brothers apart — as this Gospel’s author is called Matthew (9:9) and Levi (Mark 2:14). It doesn’t touch the point: whichever brother she left, the marriage was unlawful, and John said so and died for it. But where the Gospels can be checked against an independent historian, they hold up; an apparent collision, patiently examined, usually turns out to be a detail we were missing.
verseByVerse.note: Herodias had been married to Antipas’s half-brother; the law forbade marrying a brother’s wife while he lived.

parallels.desc: the nakedness of your brother’s wife

verseByVerse.quote: And though he wanted to put him to death, he feared the people, because they held him to be a prophet. But when Herod's birthday came, the daughter of Herodias danced before the company and pleased Herod,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Power without principle is governed by fear of opinion and appetite, not conscience.

The feast and the cell. Josephus says John was held at Machaerus, a fortress-palace east of the Dead Sea in the bleakest country in the region — a place a ruler could entertain in and hold prisoners under at once. So the birthday feast and the cell were in the same building; the music could be heard from the dungeon.

A girl. Josephus names her Salome, Herodias’s daughter by her first marriage; she was probably in her teens. The scene is often painted as seduction by a grown woman, but the text doesn’t say that. Matthew calls her a “girl,” the word used of Jairus’s daughter (9:24–25). She is a child put up to it, who goes to ask her mother what to say.

Ruled by a headcount. Herod wanted John dead and didn’t dare, “because he feared the people, because they held him to be a prophet.” Later the chief priests will hesitate to seize Jesus for the same reason: “they feared the crowds, because they held him to be a prophet” (21:46). The ruler and the temple establishment are governed by the same calculation, neither restrained by conscience. What restrains them is a headcount, and in both cases it only postpones matters. A test: are your choices governed by conscience or by what others will think?
verseByVerse.note: The historian Josephus names Herodias’s daughter Salome.

verseByVerse.quote: so that he promised with an oath to give her whatever she might ask. Prompted by her mother, she said, "Give me the head of John the Baptist here on a platter."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sin works through a chain of vanity, rash promises and malice, and the preacher of repentance is murdered by the very sins he named.

Esther reversed. Mark gives the oath in full: “Whatever you ask me, I will give you, up to half of my kingdom” (Mark 6:23). That echoes King Ahasuerus to Esther at her banquets: “What is your request? Even to the half of my kingdom, it shall be fulfilled” (Esther 5:6; 7:2). A king at a feast, a rash and enormous promise, a woman with a prepared request, and a life hanging on it. Then everything inverts. Esther used her request to save a people from a murderer; this one is used to murder a prophet. Esther risked her life going in unbidden; this girl is sent in. In Esther the villain hangs on his own gallows; here the villain gets what she wants. The Persian court behaved better than the Jewish one.

The mother. Herodias is the real agent. “Prompted by her mother” — pushed forward, instructed. Mark says the girl went out and asked, “For what should I ask?”, and hurried back with the answer, adding “at once” (Mark 6:24–25). Herodias had wanted this for months and been blocked (Mark 6:19). She doesn’t appear at the feast or speak; she arranged the conditions, waited, and used her daughter as the instrument. A test: is there a grudge you are nursing until the right moment comes?

Here. The request has one word of pure cruelty: “here.” Not “have him executed,” but here, on a dish, now, while the guests are still at table — designed to make retreat impossible and turn murder into the evening’s entertainment.

parallels.desc: up to half of my kingdom

verseByVerse.quote: And the king was sorry, but because of his oaths and his guests he commanded it to be given. He sent and had John beheaded in the prison,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Knowing what is right and doing wrong anyway to protect our reputation is sin at its most human.

He was sorry. Matthew records the sorrow, which makes the surrender worse. Mark goes further: Herod used to send for John and “heard him gladly,” though “greatly perplexed” (Mark 6:20). He didn’t hate the prophet; he was fascinated by him and protected him from his wife. And he killed him anyway, for two reasons.

Oaths and guests. His oaths: a rash promise to a dancing girl that no court would have held him to and any decent man would break. He kept it because breaking it would cost him. And his guests — the real reason. The room was full of nobles, commanders and the leading men of Galilee (Mark 6:21), whose opinion was his standing. So a man who privately admired John had him beheaded before dessert because of what a roomful of officials would think. Nothing requires Herod to have wanted it, which is what makes it so recognisable. He didn’t lose an argument with his conscience; he valued the opinion of the people in the room above the life of a man in the cellar, and it took about a minute. A test: whose opinion in the room could make you go against your conscience?

“The king.” In verse 1 Matthew called him “the tetrarch,” the accurate title. Here he is “the king,” the courtesy his vanity enjoyed. And there is a bitter providence in the word. Josephus tells us that Herodias later pressed him to sail to Rome and ask for the royal title; instead he was accused, stripped of his tetrarchy, and exiled to Gaul. The woman for whom he broke God’s law and shed a prophet’s blood steered him to ruin. Sin keeps its promises backwards: he grasped for a crown and lost what he had. “Whoever loves his life loses it” (John 12:25).
verseByVerse.note: Antipas was only a tetrarch, but was popularly called king.

verseByVerse.quote: and his head was brought on a platter and given to the girl, and she brought it to her mother. And his disciples came and took the body and buried it, and they went and told Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In grief and loss, the right place to go is to Jesus.

No comment. Matthew narrates the platter without comment, because no comment is adequate.

They came. “His disciples came and took the body and buried it.” That took courage: followers of a man executed for criticising the ruler, walking into a royal fortress to ask for the corpse — as Joseph of Arimathea would “take courage” at another execution (Mark 15:43). They took the body, not the head, which had gone to Herodias. They buried what there was.

They told Jesus. Then, having done the last thing that could be done, they went to the one man who had told them who John was. They had been something like rivals: these were the disciples who complained that Jesus’ followers didn’t fast (9:14) and who carried John’s question from prison (11:2–3). John had settled it himself: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30). And when their teacher was dead, they knew where to go. A test: when grief comes, do you take it to Jesus?

His silence. Matthew records no reply. The next verse says Jesus withdrew by boat to a desolate place by himself. For the man who called John the greatest born of women, his kinsman who had baptized him, that is more eloquent than any sentence. And then the crowds followed, and he healed them and fed them all — on the day he heard.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Jesus heard this, he withdrew from there in a boat to a desolate place by himself. But when the crowds heard it, they followed him on foot from the towns. When he went ashore he saw a great crowd, and he had compassion on them and healed their sick.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus truly grieved and sought solitude, yet his compassion kept giving — and he also teaches us to take the rest we need.

He grieved. Told that his cousin and forerunner had been beheaded to amuse a dinner party, the Son of God went away by himself. That settles a question that troubles sincere Christians: is sorrow a failure of faith? It isn’t. It is what love does when it loses something, and here the only sinless person does it. If you have been made to feel your grief is unspiritual, or that you should be over it by now, this verse is your answer.

He withdrew. He withdrew deliberately, and more than once in this chapter. Solitude wasn’t an indulgence when nothing else pressed; it was a necessity he arranged. Anyone who thinks stepping back from demands is weakness should notice who is doing it. You aren’t more robust than he was.

Interrupted. And he didn’t get it. The crowds walked round the lake and were waiting when the boat came in. Instead of solitude he found thousands wanting things from him — and he didn’t send them away. “He had compassion on them,” the word for being moved in one’s inmost being (cf. 9:36; Numbers 27:17). The grieving healer still healed.

Not a theology of burnout. This is where the passage gets misused, as though the ideal Christian never rests and always serves. Read on. After the feeding, he sends the disciples off, dismisses the crowds, and goes up the mountain alone to pray (v. 23). He got his solitude; it came later that night, but it came, and he took it. The pattern isn’t the abolition of rest but its postponement, once, under particular pressure — and then actually taking it.

For the weary. For anyone in a season of relentless demand — the parent of small children, someone nursing a dying relative, the pastor, the carer who can’t see the end — take it together. Grief needs room and is allowed. Withdrawal must be planned, because it never happens by accident. Interruptions will come, and compassion rather than resentment is possible only for someone not treating exhaustion as permanent policy. And what is taken from you now must be taken back later, as he did. Notice where the day’s resources came from: he fed thousands from a boy’s lunch, and the place he went for supply was a mountain alone with his Father. A test: where in your week do you go to be alone with the Father?
verseByVerse.note: Luke places the feeding near Bethsaida, at the north end of the lake.

parallels.desc: not as sheep without a shepherd

verseByVerse.quote: Now when it was evening, the disciples came to him and said, "This is a desolate place, and the day is now over; send the crowds away to go into the villages and buy food for themselves." But Jesus said, "They need not go away; you give them something to eat."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus calls his people not to send needs away but to bring them to him and serve.

You give them. The pronoun is emphatic: “you yourselves, give them something to eat.” He isn’t making a suggestion; he is putting the crowd’s dinner on their account. And John tells us why: “He said this to test him, for he himself knew what he would do” (John 6:6). The impossibility was deliberate.

A sensible plan. Their proposal was reasonable, and should be said so. It is late, there is nothing here; send them off to the villages before dark to buy their own. No one would be harmed. It is the responsible, administratively sound answer, with one defect: it gets the crowd off their hands.

Dispersal or provision. “They need not go away.” The disciples’ solution was dispersal; his was provision. That difference has divided Christian ministry ever since, because sending people somewhere else to be dealt with is always available and always looks sensible. A test: whose need are you tempted to send elsewhere, rather than bring to Jesus?

On the worst day. And remember the day. This is the same day John’s disciples brought the news. He had gone away to be alone; the crowd found him; he healed their sick; and now, at evening, the twelve want him to send them away, and he won’t.

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him, "We have only five loaves here and two fish." And he said, "Bring them here to me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
What we have is never enough in itself, but placed in Christ’s hands it is all that is needed.

A child’s lunch. John adds what Matthew omits: Andrew found them — “There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish, but what are they for so many?” (John 6:9). Barley loaves, the poor man’s bread; and “fish” is a diminutive, small fish, pickled or dried, eaten as a relish. So what was brought was a child’s packed lunch against a crowd of perhaps fifteen thousand.

“Bring them here to me.” He doesn’t ask for more, or tell them to find more or take a collection. He asks for the ridiculous thing they had already measured and dismissed. The miracle doesn’t happen in the disciples’ hands but in his; but bringing what seems useless is the first step.

The missing term. We do the disciples’ arithmetic instinctively: measure the need, measure the resource, conclude the gap is unbridgeable, and look for a way to reduce the need. That calculation is usually correct, and it is why so much is never attempted. The passage adds the term the arithmetic leaves out. The five loaves were genuinely inadequate, and genuinely all that was required, because the multiplying didn’t happen in the boy’s basket. The instruction isn’t to pretend the loaves are enough, but to hand them over anyway. A test: what small, inadequate thing do you need to put in Christ’s hands?
verseByVerse.note: John adds that the loaves were barley loaves, the bread of the poor.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he ordered the crowds to sit down on the grass, and taking the five loaves and the two fish, he looked up to heaven and said a blessing. Then he broke the loaves and gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds. And they all ate and were satisfied. And they took up twelve baskets full of the broken pieces left over.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ is the true bread from heaven who abundantly satisfies, and he gives his gifts through his disciples.

Took, blessed, broke, gave. Matthew’s readers would recognise the four verbs at once. He will record them in the same order at the Last Supper: “Jesus took bread, and after blessing it broke it and gave it to the disciples” (26:26). And Luke records them at Emmaus: “he took the bread and blessed and broke it and gave it to them. And their eyes were opened” (Luke 24:30–31). A hillside, an upper room, an inn — the same four movements, and the third time they were enough to identify him without a word.

Through the disciples. “He gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds.” He could have distributed it himself. Instead twelve men who had just said it was impossible spent an hour walking the hillside handing out food that kept coming from their own hands. They learned that the supply ran through them, not from them. A test: are you willing to be a channel of Christ’s provision to others?

Bread in the wilderness. Green grass recalls the shepherd’s pastures (Psalm 23). And notice where the meal happens: a desolate place, bread from heaven’s hand to a hungry crowd, more left over than they began with. Israel ate such a meal under Moses, gathered each morning in the wilderness (Exodus 16), and Elisha fed a hundred men with some left over (2 Kings 4:42–44). Jesus does openly what the manna only sketched, and the next morning he said, “I am the bread of life” (John 6:35). The manna stopped after forty years, and everyone who ate it died. This bread doesn’t run out, and neither do those who feed on it.

Not a picnic. Some suggest the crowd simply shared food they had hidden. But they were in a desolate place, the disciples had only five loaves and two fish, twelve baskets were left over, and the crowd wanted to make Jesus king because of what they had seen (John 6:14–15). That is a response to a sign, not a picnic.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus says the blessing as the head of a Jewish household did at a meal.

parallels.desc: Elisha feeds a hundred men with some left over
he took bread, blessed and broke it

verseByVerse.quote: And those who ate were about five thousand men, besides women and children.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ provided abundantly for a whole city’s worth of people, and every one was fed.

Correcting the count. Mark, Luke and John also give five thousand men. Matthew alone adds “besides women and children.” Read carelessly it sounds dismissive; it is the opposite. The others leave the impression five thousand were fed; Matthew tells us the real number was considerably higher and the reported figure had left people out. He is correcting an undercount, not making one.

A city. So perhaps ten to fifteen thousand — not a large meeting but a city. Capernaum held perhaps a thousand or two; Herod’s new capital Tiberias perhaps several thousand. More people sat on that hillside than lived in any town on the lake, assembled without notice, on foot, with no food, because they heard where he had gone.

All fed. And every one ate — “they all ate and were satisfied” (v. 20), filled to the point of stopping. Then twelve baskets were gathered from the leftovers. The surplus at the end was larger than the supply at the start. He didn’t stretch five loaves across fifteen thousand; he produced a meal for a city and had more left than he began with. A test: do you trust Christ’s provision to be more than enough?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–36 — Walking on Water and Healings at Gennesaret
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Immediately after the feeding, Jesus sends the disciples ahead by boat and goes up the mountain alone to pray. In the early morning hours the disciples are struggling against the wind; Jesus walks to them on the sea. Peter walks on the water toward Jesus, sinks when he doubts, is rescued, and worship breaks out in the boat. They land at Gennesaret, and Jesus heals all who touch the fringe of his garment. Four things more. "he made the disciples get into the boat" is anankazo, to compel — the word for forcing someone to do what they do not want. They did not want to go, and John supplies the reason: the crowd was about to seize him and make him king (Jn. 6:15). Thousands of people on a Galilean hillside who have just watched dinner appear out of nothing is a political event, and the country had seen risings before. He got the twelve off the beach before it could form. The boat is "beaten" by the waves — basanizomenon, a word for torture, used of the demons begging not to be tormented (8:29). And "the fourth watch" is Roman reckoning, three to six in the morning: they had been rowing since evening, roughly nine hours, and had covered three or four miles of a lake they could normally cross in two (Jn. 6:19). Note that they were exactly where he had sent them — this was not a wrong turning, and Mark says he saw them from the mountain (6:48). Mark preserves one clause Matthew omits and it is the strangest in the account: "he meant to pass by them" (6:48). Read flatly that is baffling; but passing by is technical Old Testament language for a theophany — what God does for Moses in the cleft of the rock (Exod. 33:19-22) and for Elijah at Horeb (1 Kgs. 19:11). The intention was to be seen. He does not ask for ability; he asks to be commanded, having just watched a word do this to five loaves. The record stands that one man got out of a boat in a gale in the dark and walked on a lake, and Matthew reports it in a single sentence. Finally, "the fringe of his garment" is the kraspedon, the tzitzit commanded in Numbers 15:38-39 — and the Hebrew for the corner of a garment, kanaph, also means wing. Malachi's last page promises that "the sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings" (Mal. 4:2). They were reaching for the corners of the robe of the one Malachi described, and finding that it was there.
verseByVerse.theology: Jesus walking on the water is another creation-sovereignty miracle: the same one who stilled the storm (8:26) now walks on it. In the Old Testament, God alone treads on the waves of the sea (Job 9:8; Ps. 77:19). Jesus is doing what God does. Peter's walking on the water is the only time anyone but his Master is recorded doing this, and it happens not by Peter's power but by Jesus's command: "Come." The sinking and rescue express the pattern of every disciple's faith: bold initial response, fear when looking at the circumstances, cry for help, rescue by the one who is always within reach.
verseByVerse.examples: The disciples' worship in the boat — "Truly you are the Son of God" — is the first time in Matthew that the disciples make this full confession. The storm-stilling produced "What sort of man is this?" (8:27); the water-walking produces "Truly you are the Son of God." The miracles are cumulative revelation. Each display of his authority over creation moves the disciples closer to the full confession that Peter will make at Caesarea Philippi (16:16). Faith grows through the accumulation of evidence seen with open eyes.

verseByVerse.quote: Immediately he made the disciples get into the boat and go before him to the other side, while he dismissed the crowds. And after he had dismissed the crowds, he went up on the mountain by himself to pray. When evening came, he was there alone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus refused a crown offered on the world’s terms, and after giving himself to others he renewed his strength in prayer with his Father.

Compelled. “He made the disciples get into the boat” — the word means compelled, the word Paul used of forcing people to blaspheme (Acts 26:11). They didn’t want to go, and he overrode them. John gives the reason: “Perceiving then that they were about to come and take him by force to make him king, Jesus withdrew again to the mountain by himself” (John 6:15). Fifteen thousand on a Galilean hillside, having watched a man produce dinner from nothing, was a political event — the raw material of a rising, with twelve eager lieutenants. He got the disciples off the beach before the crowd could reach them. He wouldn’t be made king by acclamation; his crown would be of thorns. A test: are you tempted to follow a Christ who gives you what you want, rather than the Christ of the cross?

Alone at last. “When evening came, he was there alone.” Think what that day held: news of John’s beheading, an attempted escape followed by thousands, the sick healed, a city fed, a movement to crown him broken up, his friends sent away over the water. And then, at last, he got what he had set out for that morning — and used it to pray. After the largest public success of his ministry, on the day he heard of his kinsman’s murder, he went to his Father.
verseByVerse.note: John says the crowd wanted to make him king by force.

verseByVerse.quote: but the boat by this time was a long way from the land, beaten by the waves, for the wind was against them. And in the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking on the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Obedient disciples may face long, hard struggle, but Christ sees them and comes to them as only God can.

Tormented. The boat is “beaten by the waves” — a word for torture, used of the demons begging not to be tormented (8:29) and of the servant “suffering terribly” (8:6). Matthew applies an interrogator’s word to a boat.

All night. The fourth watch, by Roman reckoning, was three to six in the morning. They had set out at evening — perhaps nine hours of rowing into a headwind in the dark, on a lake they knew, going nowhere. Mark says they were “making headway painfully” (Mark 6:48), and John that they had gone three or four miles (John 6:19), about halfway across.

Where he sent them. And they were exactly where he had sent them. This wasn’t a storm sailed into by poor judgment. He put them in that boat over their objection and pointed them at the far shore. The wind blew against men on the very errand he had compelled. That should be held against the comfortable idea that difficulty means a wrong turn. And Mark says he saw them (Mark 6:48) — from a mountain, in the dark, miles offshore, its own kind of statement. A test: when you are struggling in obedience, do you believe Christ sees you?

Walking on the sea. “He came to them, walking on the sea.” Job says God “alone stretched out the heavens and trampled the waves of the sea” (Job 9:8; cf. Psalm 77:19). Jesus does what Job said only God does.

Did he really walk on water? Others have suggested that Jesus walked along the shore or on a sandbar. But the boat was a long way from the land (v. 24), Peter also walked and sank (v. 30), and the disciples worshipped (v. 33). Nothing in the account can be explained away.
verseByVerse.note: The fourth watch of the night ran from about 3 to 6 a.m.

parallels.desc: who alone trampled the waves of the sea
your way was through the sea

verseByVerse.quote: But when the disciples saw him walking on the sea, they were terrified, and said, "It is a ghost!" and they cried out in fear. But immediately Jesus spoke to them, saying, "Take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ reveals himself to his frightened people as the LORD himself, and his first gift in the storm is his voice.

Passing by. Mark adds a strange clause: “He meant to pass by them” (Mark 6:48). As ordinary narrative it is baffling — a man walking past a boat in distress. But “passing by” is the language of God revealing himself. God told Moses, “I will make all my goodness pass before you… while my glory passes by I will put you in a cleft of the rock” (Exodus 33:19–22); at Horeb, “behold, the LORD passed by” (1 Kings 19:11). It isn’t indifference but theophany — God making himself seen by going past. He came out on the water so they would look up and see who was walking on it.

A ghost. They looked, and concluded it was a ghost, and “cried out in fear.” Men who had spent the night fighting a hopeless sea were more frightened by the sight of him than by the wind.

“It is I.” Then three short sentences: “Take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid.” The middle one is “I am” — the name God gave Moses at the bush (Exodus 3:14), and the words that will draw stones in John’s Gospel. In English it identifies him; in Greek it is also the Name. And “do not be afraid” is what God says when he appears to people undone by the encounter (Genesis 15:1; Isaiah 41:10; cf. Isaiah 43:1–2). He doesn’t begin by stopping the wind, which blows for the next four verses. What comes first is a voice across black water saying who it is. A test: in your storm, are you listening for his voice?
verseByVerse.note: “It is I” can also be heard as the divine name, “I am.”

parallels.desc: when you pass through the waters

verseByVerse.quote: And Peter answered him, "Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the water." He said, "Come." So Peter got out of the boat and walked on the water and came to Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Faith acts on Christ’s word, and his command gives the power to obey it.

Since it is you. Peter’s condition isn’t doubt. The Greek construction assumes it is true — closer to “since it is you.” He has heard the voice and believed it.

A command. What he asks for is a command: “command me to come to you on the water.” That is the careful part of a reckless request. He doesn’t ask for the ability or announce he will try. He asks Jesus to order him, because he has grasped that this man’s word makes things possible — as he had just seen with five loaves. One word comes back: “Come.” A test: do you step out only on Christ’s word, or on your own ideas of adventure?

He walked on water. “So Peter got out of the boat and walked on the water and came to Jesus.” Not far or for long, and it ends badly enough that the failure is what everyone remembers. But one man got out of a boat in a gale in the dark and walked on a lake, and Matthew reports it in one sentence without comment. Peter is usually the cautionary tale here, but the other eleven are still in the boat, and nothing is said about them. And notice the direction: he “came to Jesus.” Not walking about, demonstrating anything, or heading for shore, but toward the one who called him — the only reason the water was ever going to be crossed.
verseByVerse.note: Only Matthew records Peter walking on the water.

verseByVerse.quote: But when he saw the wind, he was afraid, and beginning to sink he cried out, "Lord, save me." Jesus immediately reached out his hand and took hold of him, saying to him, "O you of little faith, why did you doubt?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When we take our eyes off Christ we falter, but he rescues those who cry to him, and his rebuke comes from one already holding us up.

Who sinks. This is the passage for anyone who stepped out at Christ’s word and went under — the ministry that didn’t flourish, the move that went wrong, the costly obedience that has so far produced only water round the ankles. Notice who sinks. Peter is the only man besides his Master ever to walk on water, and the only man in the boat who failed at it. The other eleven had a dry night and no story. This humiliation is available only to those who attempted something; some safety is really just refusal.

What went wrong. It wasn’t getting out; Jesus had said “Come.” Nor the wind; it was already blowing when he climbed over the side. What changed was where he looked: “when he saw the wind, he was afraid.” He sank when the storm became more real to him than the word that sent him into it. Sinking doesn’t prove the step was presumption; before concluding that, check where your eyes have been. A test: what is more real to you right now — the wind or Christ’s word?

The prayer. “Lord, save me” — three words from a man with a mouthful of water, no time to make it respectable (cf. Psalm 69:1–2). It was enough. Don’t wait till you can compose something better; you will drown politely. Cry out in the shape the panic actually takes.

The order. “Jesus immediately reached out his hand and took hold of him” — and only then, “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?” The rebuke is real, but spoken by someone whose grip is already on him, above the water (cf. Psalm 18:16). Hear it in that tone: not contempt from the shore but the question of a man holding you up.

A guard. This passage has launched much foolishness. Peter didn’t leap; he asked — “if it is you, command me” — and didn’t move until Jesus said “Come.” Wanting an adventure isn’t being sent, and the desire to do something dramatic for God isn’t itself a call. Test the word first, as he did; then get out of the boat, and keep your eyes where they belong.

parallels.desc: save me, O God, for the waters have come up to my neck
he drew me out of many waters

verseByVerse.quote: And when they got into the boat, the wind ceased. And those in the boat worshiped him, saying, "Truly, you are the Son of God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus’ mere presence brings peace, and his saving power leads his people to worship him as God’s Son.

Without a word. In chapter 8, on this lake, he “rebuked the winds and the sea, and there was a great calm” (8:26). Here he says nothing. “When they got into the boat, the wind ceased.” He steps over the side and it stops; hours of headwind end without a word spoken to it.

From question to confession. After the earlier storm they asked, “What sort of man is this, that even winds and sea obey him?” (8:27) — a question. Now: “Truly you are the Son of God” — a statement, with “truly,” offered as worship, the word for falling prostrate. Two storms, two responses: they have moved from asking what he is to telling him who he is, on their faces, in a wet boat, at dawn. A test: has Christ’s rescue in your life led you to worship him?

Before Caesarea Philippi. Peter’s confession at Caesarea Philippi (16:16) is usually called the turning point, rightly, since Jesus receives it formally and builds on it. But the words are first said here, by the whole crew — and their ground isn’t an insight into his identity but a night of terror and rescue. The theology at Caesarea Philippi came from a conversation; this came from the water. Men who thought they would drown, and watched one of their number sink and be caught by Jesus’ hand, were the first in this Gospel to get the sentence right.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they had crossed over, they came to land at Gennesaret. And when the men of that place recognized him, they sent around to all that region and brought to him all who were sick
verseByVerse.commentary:
Faith responds to Christ’s presence by bringing every need to him.

Gennesaret. A crescent of land on the north-west shore, a few miles long and famous for its fertility. Josephus describes walnuts, palms, figs and olives growing side by side, which normally need different climates, and fruit available most of the year. It was the most productive and densely settled ground on the lake, and the boat came ashore in the middle of it.

They sent runners. “When the men of that place recognized him, they sent around to all that region.” Messengers went out; villages were told; and what came back was “all who were sick,” carried on mats along the paths of the plain to a beach. A test: whom do you know who needs to be brought to Jesus?

Nazareth and Gennesaret. Nazareth asked, “Where then did this man get all these things?” and took offence, and he did few mighty works there “because of their unbelief” (13:58). Gennesaret asked nothing; it sent runners. The difference wasn’t information — Nazareth had more, thirty years of it — but what each did in the first hour after learning he was there.
verseByVerse.note: Gennesaret was a fertile plain on the north-west shore of the lake.

verseByVerse.quote: and implored him that they might only touch the fringe of his garment. And as many as touched it were made well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even the smallest reaching faith finds Christ’s full healing power, and none who come are turned away.

The tassel. The “fringe” is the tassel God commanded every Israelite to wear on the corners of his outer garment, with a blue cord — “a tassel for you to look at and remember all the commandments of the LORD” (Numbers 15:38–39). So Jesus wore them, keeping the law like any observant Jew, and the sick reached for a tassel on the corner of his cloak, as the bleeding woman had (9:20).

Healing in his wings. The Hebrew word for the corner of a garment also means “wing.” Ruth asked Boaz to spread his wing over her (Ruth 3:9), and God spread his over Israel (Ezekiel 16:8). And the Old Testament’s last page promises: “for you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings” (Malachi 4:2). Whether or not the crowds knew it, they were reaching for the corners of the robe of the One Malachi said would rise with healing in them — and finding it there.

As many as touched. “As many as touched it were made well.” Not most, nor only those in the right frame of mind or who understood the prophecy — every one, including the last in line and those who got there by being carried. Faith that only reaches, without full understanding, is still met by his full mercy. A test: what holds you back from reaching out to Christ?
verseByVerse.note: The fringe was the tassel the law required on the corners of a garment.

parallels.desc: the woman who touched the fringe

14.theology: Christ as the true bread from heaven. John 6 makes explicit what Matthew implies: the feeding of the five thousand points to Christ as the bread of life. He is the antitype of the manna — not merely a physical provision for the body but the living bread who gives eternal life to all who feed on him by faith. The Lord’s Supper is the sacramental extension of this meal: in it, we receive not merely bread and wine but Christ himself, the bread of heaven, by faith. The wilderness feeding thus stands at the intersection of Exodus typology, Eucharistic anticipation, and kingdom eschatology: we are fed by Christ in the wilderness of this age until the great feast of the new creation.
14.examples:
Then: Five loaves and two fish were laughably inadequate for five thousand people. The disciples knew it. Jesus knew it. He asked for them anyway. What he asks for is never the measure of what he can do with it.

Now: Every pastor, teacher, parent, and missionary knows the feeling of inadequate resources — not enough time, energy, money, or skill. Matthew 14 is not a promise that resources will always multiply visibly, but it is a call to bring what we have to Jesus and trust him with the rest. The twelve baskets of leftovers are the testimony: what is given to Christ is never wasted, and rarely runs out.

15.title: What Defiles a Person
15.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Pharisees and scribes came to Jesus from Jerusalem and said, <sup>2</sup>“Why do your disciples break the tradition of the elders? For they do not wash their hands when they eat.” <sup>3</sup>He answered them, “And why do you break the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition? <sup>4</sup>For God commanded, ‘Honor your father and your mother,’ and, ‘Whoever reviles father or mother must surely die.’ <sup>5</sup>But you say, ‘If anyone tells his father or his mother, “What you would have gained from me is given to God,” <sup>6</sup>he need not honor his father.’ So for the sake of your tradition you have made void the word of God. <sup>7</sup>You hypocrites! Well did Isaiah prophesy of you, when he said: <sup>8</sup>“‘This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me; <sup>9</sup>in vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men.’” <sup>10</sup>And he called the people to him and said to them, “Hear and understand: <sup>11</sup>it is not what goes into the mouth that defiles a person, but what comes out of the mouth; this defiles a person.” <sup>12</sup>Then the disciples came and said to him, “Do you know that the Pharisees were offended when they heard this saying?” <sup>13</sup>He answered, “Every plant that my heavenly Father has not planted will be rooted up. <sup>14</sup>Let them alone; they are blind guides. And if the blind lead the blind, both will fall into a pit.” <sup>15</sup>But Peter said to him, “Explain the parable to us.” <sup>16</sup>And he said, “Are you also still without understanding? <sup>17</sup>Do you not see that whatever goes into the mouth passes into the stomach and is expelled? <sup>18</sup>But what comes out of the mouth proceeds from the heart, and this defiles a person. <sup>19</sup>For out of the heart come evil thoughts, murder, adultery, sexual immorality, theft, false witness, slander. <sup>20</sup>These are what defile a person. But to eat with unwashed hands does not defile anyone.” <sup>21</sup>And Jesus went away from there and withdrew to the district of Tyre and Sidon. <sup>22</sup>And behold, a Canaanite woman from that region came out and was crying, “Have mercy on me, O Lord, Son of David; my daughter is severely oppressed by a demon.” <sup>23</sup>But he did not answer her a word. And his disciples came and begged him, saying, “Send her away, for she is crying out after us.” <sup>24</sup>He answered, “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.” <sup>25</sup>But she came and knelt before him, saying, “Lord, help me.” <sup>26</sup>And he answered, “It is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.” <sup>27</sup>She said, “Yes, Lord, yet even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table.” <sup>28</sup>Then Jesus answered her, “O woman, great is your faith! Let it be done for you as you desire.” And her daughter was healed instantly. <sup>29</sup>Jesus went on from there and walked beside the Sea of Galilee. And he went up on the mountain and sat down there. <sup>30</sup>And great crowds came to him, bringing with them the lame, the blind, the crippled, the mute, and many others, and they put them at his feet, and he healed them, <sup>31</sup>so that the crowd wondered, when they saw the mute speaking, the crippled healthy, the lame walking, and the blind seeing. And they glorified the God of Israel. <sup>32</sup>Then Jesus called his disciples to him and said, “I have compassion on the crowd because they have been with me now three days and have nothing to eat. And I am unwilling to send them away hungry, lest they faint on the way.” <sup>33</sup>And the disciples said to him, “Where are we to get enough bread in such a desolate place to feed so great a crowd?” <sup>34</sup>And Jesus said to them, “How many loaves do you have?” They said, “Seven, and a few small fish.” <sup>35</sup>And directing the crowd to sit down on the ground, <sup>36</sup>he took the seven loaves and the fish, and having given thanks he broke them and gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds. <sup>37</sup>And they all ate and were satisfied. And they took up seven baskets full of the broken pieces left over. <sup>38</sup>Those who ate were four thousand men, besides women and children. <sup>39</sup>And after sending away the crowds, he got into the boat and went to the region of Magadan.
15.overview:
Chapter 15 confronts the deepest corruption in religion: the substitution of human tradition for the word of God. The Pharisees have constructed an elaborate system of ritual purity — washings, dietary rules, oral traditions — that they treat as divinely binding. Jesus cuts through it all with a single theological move: defilement is not external but internal. The heart is the problem. No ceremony can cleanse it; only the blood of the covenant can reach it.

Then, in a jarring turn, Jesus goes to Gentile territory and encounters a Canaanite woman whose persistence in faith stands in shaming contrast to the Pharisees' hypocrisy. She is the wrong ethnicity, the wrong gender, the wrong religion — and Jesus commends her as having “great faith.” She is the second Gentile in Matthew to receive this commendation (after the centurion in chapter 8). The kingdom breaks every ethnic and ritual boundary. The chapter closes with a second feeding miracle — four thousand this time, in Gentile territory — extending the bread of the messianic banquet to the nations.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — What Defiles a Person: Tradition and the Heart
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Pharisees from Jerusalem confront Jesus about his disciples eating without washing hands. Jesus counters by exposing how their tradition nullifies the command to honor parents, then teaches the crowd that defilement comes from within, not without. He explains privately to the disciples: it is what comes out of the heart that defiles a person — evil thoughts, murder, adultery, all the rest. What the summary cannot hold. The handwashing was not about dirt. It is netilat yadayim, a ritual pouring in prescribed quantity and order to remove ceremonial uncleanness — a man with filthy hands who performed it was clean, and a man who had scrubbed and not performed it was not. And the Torah requires it of priests, before the altar, on pain of death (Exod. 30:19-21); the tradition had extended priestly purity to everybody at every meal. The impulse is not contemptible — if Israel is a kingdom of priests, why not treat the table like the altar? — but it had become the thing a delegation walked ninety miles from Jerusalem to complain about. Watch the structure of the reply: they ask why his disciples break the tradition; he asks why they break the commandment for the sake of their tradition. Same verb, nouns exchanged, and it puts them on trial in one sentence. Note also that he says "your tradition" twice, where they had said "the tradition of the elders" — a phrase that gives it distance and belongs to nobody. And the two texts he cites are the fifth commandment and its capital sanction (Exod. 21:17), so nobody can claim a small matter is being inflated. "hypocrite" is the Greek theatre word for the masked actor — and the mask was not a disguise but a device for projecting a character to people too far off to see a face. Matthew uses it thirteen times, more than the rest of the New Testament together. On the quotation, Matthew follows the Greek of Isaiah 29:13, which sharpens the Hebrew rather than altering it. "in vain" is maten — not wrongly, not insincerely: useless, which is a colder verdict than hypocrisy about men who fasted twice a week and tithed their herb garden. And note what he does at v. 10: he stops answering the delegation, calls the crowd, and gives the answer to them directly.
verseByVerse.theology: The controversy exposes the Pharisees' deepest error: they have allowed their oral tradition to override the written word of God. The corban rule (declaring assets dedicated to God, thereby relieving oneself of the duty to support parents) is the example Jesus uses — a legal fiction that honored the letter of piety while violating the command to honor father and mother. Isaiah's word stands: "This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me." External religion without heart-transformation is hypocrisy by definition.
verseByVerse.examples: The list of defiling things in verses 19-20 is a heart-audit: from the inside come evil thoughts, murder, adultery, sexual immorality, theft, false witness, slander. These are not random vices; they map onto the second table of the Decalogue. Jesus is saying: the law you claim to keep is being broken from the inside out. Clean hands matter less than clean hearts — and clean hearts are precisely what the Pharisees have not addressed.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Pharisees and scribes came to Jesus from Jerusalem and said, "Why do your disciples break the tradition of the elders? For they do not wash their hands when they eat."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Human religious rules, however well meant, must never be confused with God’s commands.

A rite, not hygiene. This washing wasn’t about dirt. It was a ritual pouring of water over the hands, in a set amount and order, to remove ceremonial uncleanness. A man with filthy hands who had done it was clean; one who had scrubbed them without it wasn’t. No one accuses the disciples of eating with dirty hands, but of eating without a rite.

A rule for priests. The law required priests to wash hands and feet before approaching the altar, on pain of death (Exodus 30:19–21). That was the whole biblical requirement, for men on duty in the sanctuary. The tradition had extended priestly purity to everyone, at every meal. The impulse wasn’t contemptible: if Israel is “a kingdom of priests” (Exodus 19:6), why not treat the table like the altar? It was a serious idea seriously held — and it had become the thing they came from Jerusalem to complain about (cf. Luke 11:38).

A delegation. They came “from Jerusalem” — around ninety miles on foot, several days’ walk. No one makes that journey to raise a question about hand-washing. The centre had sent a deputation north, and its opening charge was that his men ate wrongly. A test: are you treating a human custom as if it were God’s command?
verseByVerse.note: The “tradition of the elders” was the body of oral rules built around the law. The washing was a ritual of purity, not hygiene.

parallels.desc: the Pharisee astonished that Jesus did not wash

verseByVerse.quote: He answered them, "And why do you break the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition? For God commanded, 'Honor your father and your mother,' and, 'Whoever reviles father or mother must surely die.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
When human tradition overrides God’s plain command, the tradition must give way.

The charge reversed. They ask: why do your disciples break the tradition? He answers: why do you break the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition? The same verb thrown back, the nouns exchanged. It isn’t a change of subject or evasion; it is the same charge at a higher level, putting them on trial in one sentence.

Chosen texts. He cites the fifth commandment, “Honor your father and your mother” (Exodus 20:12) — “the first commandment with a promise” (Ephesians 6:2) — and its sanction, “Whoever reviles father or mother must surely die” (v. 4, citing Exodus 21:17), a capital statute. He doesn’t pick a minor rule; he goes to the Ten Commandments and the death penalty behind it, so no one can say a small matter is being inflated.

“Your tradition.” They called it “the tradition of the elders,” a phrase with weight and distance, as though it belonged to no one in particular. He calls it theirs. Whatever its pedigree, the men before him enforce it and will answer for it. A test: which of your convictions came from Scripture, and which from tradition?

Does that death penalty still apply? Jesus cites it to show how seriously God takes the fifth commandment, and how guilty the Pharisees were in evading it. The civil penalty belonged to Israel’s law as a nation; the moral duty to honour parents still stands for Christians (Ephesians 6:1–3).

verseByVerse.quote: But you say, "If anyone tells his father or his mother, 'What you would have gained from me is given to God,' he need not honor his father." So for the sake of your tradition you have made void the word of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Using religious activity to excuse a plain moral duty is a way of cancelling God’s word.

Corban. Mark gives the formula its Aramaic name, “Corban,” given to God. A person could declare his assets dedicated to the temple and so claim that supporting his parents from them was impossible, even if no donation ever happened. It was a legal fiction that put institutional religion above family duty. “For the sake of your tradition you have made void the word of God” — the gravest charge: the tradition hadn’t supplemented the command but abolished it in practice.

The manoeuvre lives on. Name the manoeuvre, because it long outlived the practice. A man owed his parents support. He couldn’t simply refuse; everyone would call it wrong. So he found a religious way of being unavailable: the money was dedicated, his hands tied by piety, the duty not neglected but outranked. It survives wherever religious activity excuses moral duty: I am too committed at church to visit my mother; I give generously, so my brother’s situation is someone else’s problem; I am busy with the Lord’s work, which is why my children see so little of me. Each is true on its face, and each is Corban. The tell: the thing done for God happens to be exactly what lets you off something costly, unglamorous and plainly commanded (cf. 1 Timothy 5:4, 8).

The test. The test isn’t whether the religious activity is good; dedicating property to God was honourable. It is what it is being used to avoid. Is there a duty you are dodging, and is your reason a spiritual one? Jesus doesn’t call this a lapse or imbalance; he calls it making void the word of God, said to the most devout men of their generation, who would have been genuinely shocked.
verseByVerse.note: Mark gives the formula its Aramaic name, Corban — “given to God.” Property declared dedicated could no longer be used to support one’s parents.

verseByVerse.quote: You hypocrites! Well did Isaiah prophesy of you, when he said: "This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me;"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God isn’t honoured by outward religion when the heart is far from him.

Actors. “Hypocrite” was a theatre word, the actor speaking from behind a mask — no moral charge, simply a job. In the Greek theatre the mask projected a character to a crowd too far away to see a face. So the accusation isn’t only that they lie about themselves, but that what people see is a constructed exterior designed to be read from a distance, while behind it is a man whose own face is doing something else. Matthew uses the word more than the rest of the New Testament together, almost always of these men. A test: does your outward religion match what is happening in your heart?

Isaiah’s Jerusalem. Isaiah 29 was addressed to Jerusalem, in a chapter about a people who couldn’t read a sealed book. Its complaint wasn’t that they had abandoned religion but that they were performing it accurately and had gone somewhere else while doing it. Matthew follows the Greek version, which sharpens what the Hebrew implies; nothing is invented, the emphasis moves. Seven centuries later a deputation from that same city walked north to complain about hand-washing and got read its own mail.

Does this condemn all church tradition? No. Paul told believers to hold to the traditions he had taught (2 Thessalonians 2:15), and creeds and orders of worship can serve the church well. Traditions become wrong when they are bound on the conscience as if they were God’s commands, or when they override what God has plainly commanded. The Roman Catholic and Orthodox churches give tradition authority alongside Scripture; Reformed churches hold that Scripture alone is the final rule, and that tradition must always answer to it.

parallels.desc: this people draw near with their mouth

verseByVerse.quote: "in vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men." And he called the people to him and said to them, "Hear and understand:"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Worship built on human commands treated as divine is useless, and Christ gives his truth directly to ordinary people.

In vain. “In vain” means to no purpose, useless — a colder verdict than hypocrisy. These men prayed at set hours, fasted twice a week, tithed their herbs and kept a purity code stricter than the law required. The verdict isn’t that it was inadequate but that it accomplished nothing.

How it happens. “Teaching as doctrines the commandments of men.” No one threw Scripture out; they revered and memorised it. What went wrong was that human material was promoted into the same category (cf. Colossians 2:20–22). Once a tradition is taught as doctrine, it acquires the authority of what it was built to protect, and can then overrule it — as verses 5–6 showed with the fifth commandment. The danger isn’t irreverence but reverence attached to the wrong object, by people who can no longer tell which convictions came from God. A test: could you tell which of your religious rules come from God and which from people?

To the crowd. “He called the people to him.” He stops answering the Jerusalem delegation and speaks to the crowd. Ordinary people, told all their lives that these men understood, are made witnesses and then given the answer directly. “Hear and understand” — the call of chapter 13, now to the crowd rather than the experts.

verseByVerse.quote: it is not what goes into the mouth that defiles a person, but what comes out of the mouth; this defiles a person." Then the disciples came and said to him, "Do you know that the Pharisees were offended when they heard this saying?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Defilement is a matter of the heart, not of food, and Christ’s words began the end of the ceremonial food laws.

Inward, not outward. This would have sounded revolutionary to ears trained to think of defilement as ritual and dietary. The Pharisees’ whole theology of defilement looked outward, when the real problem is inward. Told that they were offended, Jesus doesn’t apologise; he presses further.

All foods clean. Mark, telling the same scene, adds: “Thus he declared all foods clean” (Mark 7:19). That isn’t small: the saying carried an implication reaching to the dietary laws. The accounts don’t conflict. Jesus states the principle; Mark supplies the conclusion it was bound to force. And the conclusion wasn’t obvious even then. Had Peter grasped that afternoon that all foods were clean, he wouldn’t have needed a sheet let down from heaven three times, years later, before he would eat with Gentiles — and he argued with the voice even then (Acts 10:9–16; 10:14–15). The church needed years, a vision, a council and many letters to work it through (cf. Romans 14:14).

Seed and fruit. So the difference between Matthew and Mark is the difference between a seed and its fruit. Matthew, writing for Jewish readers, records what Jesus said; Mark, for Gentiles among whom the question had become urgent, says where it led. The ceremonial laws weren’t abolished by being broken; they were fulfilled by the arrival of what they pointed to. A test: are you more concerned about outward religious correctness than about what comes from your heart?

verseByVerse.quote: He answered, "Every plant that my heavenly Father has not planted will be rooted up. Let them alone; they are blind guides. And if the blind lead the blind, both will fall into a pit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
False teaching that isn’t from God will not stand, and it ruins both teachers and those who follow them.

Not planted by the Father. The Pharisaic tradition, however old and elaborate, wasn’t of divine origin and won’t stand. God’s people are “the branch of my planting” (Isaiah 60:21); what he didn’t plant will be uprooted.

Let them alone. A startling instruction. Told the Pharisees were offended (v. 12), Jesus doesn’t explain, try again, or tell the disciples to smooth things over. “Leave them.” It must be held carefully: it isn’t a licence to give up on people. The man saying it wept over Jerusalem, kept preaching to these men until his last week, and prayed for those nailing him to a cross. But there comes a point when further argument isn’t owed — when someone has seen enough, decided and hardened, and the loving thing is not to keep supplying material. Paul says the same after real effort: “after warning him once and then twice, have nothing more to do with him” (Titus 3:10). It is a permission, not a command, and it concerns religious leaders, not the lost. A test: are you wearing yourself out arguing with someone who has already decided against the truth?

Blind guides. The two words don’t go together. A guide is hired because he can see the road; this one can’t, hasn’t said so, and is taking money for it. Matthew will make it a refrain (23:16, 24). And the result is put without cruelty: “both will fall into a pit.” The tragedy of false teaching is that the teacher is rarely the only casualty, and in this picture he isn’t even the one who most deserves to be in the hole.

verseByVerse.quote: But Peter said to him, "Explain the parable to us." And he said, "Are you also still without understanding?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even close followers are slow to grasp Christ’s teaching, and he keeps patiently teaching them.

Still. The word is chapter 13’s: “without understanding,” the negative of the verb that ran through the parables, ending with “Have you understood all these things?” — “Yes” (13:51). That was two chapters ago. Now the same men are told they are “still” without understanding. Their yes was honest and thin, and this is the first place Matthew shows it tested.

Also. “Are you also…?” For a moment the inner circle is placed in the same column as the crowd and the Pharisees. That is a mercy to record. These men weren’t spiritual naturals; they were slow, asked for basic things to be explained twice, and Peter is the one asking here. Jesus doesn’t pretend otherwise, and he explains anyway. A test: are you willing to admit what you don’t yet understand and ask him?

Not a parable. It wasn’t a parable; verse 11 is a plain statement with no story or hidden image. Peter files it as a riddle because it can’t mean what it seems to. Raised on food laws God himself gave, he hears something that sounds as though it dismantles them, so he assumes a second level. He is wrong about the form and right about the size: Mark adds, “Thus he declared all foods clean” (Mark 7:19).

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not see that whatever goes into the mouth passes into the stomach and is expelled? But what comes out of the mouth proceeds from the heart, and this defiles a person.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Our moral problem is in the heart, the centre of who we are, and only a changed heart can produce changed lives.

Matthew’s restraint. Mark records the same argument and adds his conclusion: “(Thus he declared all foods clean.)” (Mark 7:18–19). Matthew records the argument and leaves the conclusion out. Mark wrote for Gentiles, for whom the matter was settled and welcome. Matthew wrote for Jewish Christians, for whom the food laws were their grandmothers’ whole practice and the most painful issue in the early church — the one that divided Peter and Paul at Antioch (Galatians 2:11–14). He gives them Jesus’ words and lets them draw it out.

The route traced. The physiology is deliberately blunt: into the stomach and expelled. The argument requires the route to be traced — in at the mouth, through the gut, out — and at no point does food pass through the heart. Whatever a food is, it never touches the place where defilement happens.

The heart. In Scripture the heart isn’t the seat of emotion as opposed to the head; it is the whole inner control room — thinking, willing, deciding, loving. “Keep your heart with all vigilance, for from it flow the springs of life” (Proverbs 4:23). So “out of the heart” means out of the place a person actually operates from, and the mouth is where that becomes audible (cf. 12:34). A test: what do your words reveal about the state of your heart?
verseByVerse.note: Mark adds, “Thus he declared all foods clean.”

parallels.desc: out of the abundance of the heart

verseByVerse.quote: For out of the heart come evil thoughts, murder, adultery, sexual immorality, theft, false witness, slander. These are what defile a person. But to eat with unwashed hands does not defile anyone.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The human heart is the source of sin, and only God’s gift of a new heart can make us clean.

The heart’s list. The list maps onto the second half of the Ten Commandments: evil thoughts (the root), murder, adultery and immorality, theft, false witness, slander. The commandments are broken first in the heart, then in action (cf. Galatians 5:19–21). The Pharisees policed the outside while the inside went unexamined. Clean hands with a dirty heart: defiled. Unwashed hands with a changed heart: not defiled.

The hardest question. But that leaves the hardest question in the chapter: if the trouble is my heart, and my heart is what does the wanting, how will it ever change? Jeremiah gives the bleakest diagnosis: “The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it?” (Jeremiah 17:9). That is what older theologians meant by total depravity, often misheard. It doesn’t mean every person is as wicked as possible; it means no part of us — mind, will, affections — is untouched, so there is no clean corner to start the repairs from.

A transplant. So the cure can’t be a better tradition, a stricter rule or a firmer resolution. It must be a replacement, as God promised: “And I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you. And I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh” (Ezekiel 36:26). That isn’t reform but transplant — the Spirit’s work, purchased at the cross this Gospel walks toward. Jesus isn’t telling you to try harder at the impossible. He is showing where the disease is, so you will stop treating your hands and bring him your heart, which he came to make new. A test: have you asked Christ for a new heart, or only tried to clean up the outside?

parallels.desc: the heart is deceitful above all things

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–39 — The Canaanite Woman and the Feeding of the Four Thousand
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus withdraws to the region of Tyre and Sidon, where a Canaanite woman cries out for her demon-oppressed daughter. After testing her faith through apparent reluctance, he heals the daughter and commends her great faith. Jesus then returns to Galilee, heals many on a mountain, and feeds four thousand people from seven loaves and a few fish. More to notice. This is the one time in his ministry that Jesus goes into Phoenicia — he had already crossed to the Gentile east bank at 8:28 and will go north to pagan Caesarea Philippi at 16:13, but Tyre and Sidon are foreign soil. Tyre and Sidon are Phoenician cities outside Israel, outside Herod's jurisdiction — and in the Old Testament they are bywords, with Ezekiel devoting three chapters to Tyre's fall and Jezebel a Sidonian princess. That is the address he withdraws to after Jerusalem sends a deputation about hand washing. And Matthew's word for her is deliberately archaic: Mark calls her a Syrophoenician, the ordinary current term; Matthew calls her a Canaanite — the Old Testament name for the nations Israel was to drive out, rarely heard in his day. He has reached back for maximum freight, and then has her say "Son of David". On the dogs, Greek has two words: kyon is the street scavenger and the word used when "dogs" is an insult (7:6; Phil. 3:2), and Jesus does not use it. He uses kynarion, the diminutive — the animal that lives in the house, belongs there, and is fed there. The saying is about order, not worth. But the shock should not be dissolved: he ignored her, the disciples asked him to send her away, and he answered her kneeling with a proverb about dogs. What resolves it is the outcome rather than the vocabulary. Her reply begins "yes, LORD" — she agrees, disputes nothing, and adds only "for even", staying inside his picture and finding that it contains her. And Jesus commends faith of this order in only two people: this woman (great is your faith) and the centurion (with no one in Israel have I found such faith, 8:10) — both Gentiles, both asking for somebody else, and neither present when the healing happens. The crowd at vv. 29-31 is Gentile, and Matthew signals it by how they worship: they glorified "the God of Israel", which is what an outsider says. Which explains the second feeding — and the two are not one story twice. The basket words differ consistently: kophinos at the five thousand (a small stiff wicker basket a Jew carried his own food in) and spyris at the four thousand (a hamper big enough to hold a man — the one Paul was lowered down the Damascus wall in, Acts 9:25). Jesus himself distinguishes the two events at 16:9-10.
verseByVerse.theology: The Canaanite woman episode is one of the most theologically dense in Matthew. Jesus's apparent reluctance — "I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel" and the difficult "dogs" saying — is best understood as testing her faith rather than expressing genuine exclusion. Her response — "Yes, Lord, yet even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their masters' table" — is the model of faith that does not demand, does not argue, does not claim rights, but presses through apparent rejection on the strength of the Savior's character. Jesus pronounces her faith "great" — the only time this word is used of any individual's faith in the Synoptics.
verseByVerse.examples: The second feeding (four thousand) parallels the first (five thousand) but occurs in Gentile territory — the region of the Decapolis. Where the first feeding fed a Jewish crowd (twelve baskets, echoing the twelve tribes), the second feeds a largely Gentile crowd (seven baskets, echoing the seven Gentile nations of Canaan). The Messiah who first came to the lost sheep of Israel is already extending his table to the nations.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus went away from there and withdrew to the district of Tyre and Sidon. And behold, a Canaanite woman from that region came out and was crying, "Have mercy on me, O Lord, Son of David; my daughter is severely oppressed by a demon."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A woman from the most despised background recognises Israel’s Messiah and brings her need to him.

Foreign soil. Tyre and Sidon were Phoenician cities on the Mediterranean coast, outside Israel and outside Herod’s rule — the furthest Jesus goes into foreign soil in the Gospels. He had crossed to the Gentile east bank before (8:28), but this is beyond the land of promise. And in the Old Testament these cities are bywords: Ezekiel devotes chapters to Tyre’s fall, Isaiah, Joel and Amos pronounce against them, and Jezebel, who brought Baal into Israel, was a Sidonian princess. Yet nearby, Elijah had once been fed by a widow of Zarephath (1 Kings 17:8–16). That is where Jesus withdraws after a Jerusalem deputation complains about hand-washing.

A Canaanite. Mark calls her “a Syrophoenician by birth” (Mark 7:26), the ordinary description. Matthew calls her a “Canaanite,” the Old Testament name of the nations Israel was told to drive out — the people of Jericho and Ai. It is like calling someone a Philistine today. Matthew reaches back centuries for a word with maximum weight, so that we feel the full distance between this woman and the covenant before she speaks.

“Son of David.” And then she says, “Son of David” — a Canaanite using Israel’s messianic title correctly in Gentile country, while back in Galilee the scribes who owned the title argued about washed hands. Her prayer begins with who he is, not with any claim of her own; she names him and states her need. That is always where prayer starts. A test: do you come to Christ on the strength of who he is, or of who you think you are?
verseByVerse.note: Tyre and Sidon were Gentile cities on the coast north of Galilee. Mark calls her a Syrophoenician; Matthew uses the old name Canaanite, Israel’s ancient enemies.

parallels.desc: Elijah and the widow of Zarephath, near Sidon

verseByVerse.quote: But he did not answer her a word. And his disciples came and begged him, saying, "Send her away, for she is crying out after us." He answered, "I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Silence from God isn’t always refusal; it may be drawing out a deeper faith.

Silence. “He did not answer her a word.” Her position is harder than the disciples’ in the storm (8:24–26) or Jairus’s on the road (9:18–26) — not sleep or delay, but nothing at all, and then what sounds like a closed door. The disciples want her gone because she keeps crying after them.

What she does. Watch what she does, the most instructive thing in the chapter. She doesn’t withdraw offended, which most of us would call self-respect, or argue that the arrangement is unfair. She takes the very words that seem to shut her out and finds the opening inside them. And she never rests her case on herself — no protest that she deserves better, no account of how long she has waited. Her whole argument is about what he is like: that enough falls from his table to heal her daughter.

Did Jesus come only for the Jews? His earthly ministry was directed to Israel, as he told the Twelve (10:5–6), because God’s promises came first to them (Romans 1:16; 15:8–9). The mission to all nations came after the resurrection (28:19). Yet even here he blesses a Gentile woman, a foretaste of the gathering of other sheep (John 10:16).

For those praying into silence. If you are praying into silence, copy her — not louder, not a better case for your deserving, but persistence fastened to his character rather than your merit. The silence was never a refusal; it was the last thing standing between her and a sentence she would never otherwise have heard, and a daughter healed that hour. He wasn’t withholding from her; he was drawing out something she didn’t know was there. A test: will you keep praying when heaven is silent?

parallels.desc: the lost sheep of the house of Israel
a servant to the circumcised, that the Gentiles might glorify God

verseByVerse.quote: But she came and knelt before him, saying, "Lord, help me." And he answered, "It is not right to take the children's bread and throw it to the dogs."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus tests faith by stating God’s order — Israel first — not to shut her out but to draw out her trust.

“Lord, help me.” The briefest, most urgent prayer, stripped of argument. And “she came and knelt” — the word for worship: a Canaanite woman on her knees in Phoenicia, doing what the Pharisees of Jerusalem had never done.

Little dogs. Greek has two words. One is the dog of the streets and rubbish heaps — a scavenger, the word used as an insult, as in “do not give dogs what is holy” (7:6) and “Look out for the dogs” (Philippians 3:2). Jesus doesn’t use it. He uses the diminutive, the little dog of the house. The picture changes completely: not a pack outside the gate, but a family at a meal with an animal under the table. The dog belongs there and is fed there. What is said isn’t “you are vermin” but “the children eat first” — a statement about order, not worth. She hears that at once, which is why her reply works.

Don’t dissolve the difficulty. But don’t dissolve it entirely. He ignored her; the disciples wanted her sent away; he said his commission didn’t extend to her; and when she knelt, he answered with a proverb about dogs. No amount of word study makes that gentle, and readers who feel the shock read correctly. What resolves it isn’t the vocabulary but the outcome: within two verses he calls her faith great, grants her request without qualification, and heals the girl at a distance that hour. Whatever he was doing, it wasn’t refusing her. He was drawing out the finest reply anyone gives him in the Gospel. A test: can you trust Christ when his ways with you seem hard?
verseByVerse.note: “Dogs” was a common Jewish insult for Gentiles; here the picture is of household dogs under the table.

verseByVerse.quote: She said, "Yes, Lord, yet even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their masters' table." Then Jesus answered her, "O woman, great is your faith! Let it be done for you as you desire." And her daughter was healed instantly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Great faith accepts God’s terms and trusts that even the overflow of his grace is enough.

“Yes, Lord.” She agrees. That is the foundation of her argument: she doesn’t dispute the order, call it unfair, point to her daughter’s suffering or appeal to her decency. She says yes, and adds: “for even.” “Yes, Lord — for even the dogs eat the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table.” She takes the picture he offered, stays inside it, and finds that it contains her.
