If the household is as he says, there is a floor under the table, things fall onto it, and the animal that lives there eats them. Nothing need be taken from the children or rearranged. She asks for what drops — and the crumbs of the Messiah’s blessing are enough to heal her daughter.

Winning by agreeing. Twice in this Gospel someone argues with Jesus and wins, and both are Gentiles. Neither wins by disputing him. The centurion accepted that he was unworthy to have Jesus under his roof (8:8); this woman accepts that she isn’t a child of the house. Both press through on what they have grasped about him, not about themselves.

Great faith. “O woman, great is your faith!” The two people whose faith Jesus singles out for such praise are both Gentiles: this woman and the centurion, of whom he said, “with no one in Israel have I found such faith” (8:10). Both asked for someone else, a child or a servant; neither saw the healing happen. He went north to Phoenicia to find the second. A test: is your faith resting on Christ’s goodness, or on your own worthiness?

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus went on from there and walked beside the Sea of Galilee. And he went up on the mountain and sat down there. And great crowds came to him, bringing with them the lame, the blind, the crippled, the mute, and many others, and they put them at his feet, and he healed them,
verseByVerse.commentary:
In Christ the promised age of restoration has come, reaching even beyond Israel.

Isaiah fulfilled. The list echoes Isaiah: “Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf unstopped; then shall the lame man leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute sing for joy” (Isaiah 35:5–6). Jesus quoted that to John in prison as evidence the age had begun (11:5). Here Matthew reports it happening in bulk on a hillside. And Mark places it in the Decapolis (Mark 7:31), the Gentile region east of the lake. Isaiah 35 is about the redeemed coming home to Zion; it is happening on the other side of the lake.

The mountain. “He went up on the mountain and sat down” — the same pairing as at the start of the Sermon on the Mount (5:1). On that mountain he taught; on this one he heals, and Matthew records no word.

At his feet. “They put them at his feet” — not “brought them to him” but set them down, people who couldn’t stand, carried some distance and laid on the ground before a seated man. No preaching or dialogue is recorded, no faith examined, no one questioned. They were put down at his feet and picked up again whole. A test: whom can you carry to Jesus’ feet in prayer?
verseByVerse.note: Mark places this in the Decapolis, the Gentile region east of the lake.

parallels.desc: the lame leap and the mute sing

verseByVerse.quote: so that the crowd wondered, when they saw the mute speaking, the crippled healthy, the lame walking, and the blind seeing. And they glorified the God of Israel. Then Jesus called his disciples to him and said, "I have compassion on the crowd because they have been with me now three days and have nothing to eat. And I am unwilling to send them away hungry, lest they faint on the way."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ’s compassion reaches Gentiles too, and cares for ordinary bodily needs.

The God of Israel. “They glorified the God of Israel.” The qualifier is the kind an outsider adds, distinguishing this God from those he grew up with. So the people on this mountain were largely Gentiles, signalled by how they worship — the nations praising Abraham’s God as they see his Messiah at work.

Compassion. The word is physical, from the inward organs: not pity at a distance but the churning a person feels at something he can’t bear. The Gospels use it almost only of Jesus — for the shepherdless crowds (9:36), the sick at the first feeding (14:14), two blind men (20:34), and here.

Three days. The reason is specific: “they have been with me now three days and have nothing to eat.” Not an afternoon’s crowd; people camped three days on a hillside in Gentile country, their food gone, some from far away (Mark 8:3). And the concern isn’t dressed up as spiritual: “lest they faint on the way.” He is thinking of people collapsing on the walk home. After three days of healing and teaching, his last concern before they disperse is whether they will get home without falling over. A test: do you care about others’ practical needs as Christ does?
verseByVerse.note: “The God of Israel” may suggest a largely Gentile crowd.

verseByVerse.quote: And the disciples said to him, "Where are we to get enough bread in such a desolate place to feed so great a crowd?" And Jesus said to them, "How many loaves do you have?" They said, "Seven, and a few small fish."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Our slowness to remember God’s past provision is exposed, yet Christ patiently begins again with what we have.

The same men. “Where are we to get enough bread…?” These are the same twelve who, not long before, each carried a basket of leftovers from a hillside where five loaves fed a crowd of similar size — and they ask as though it never happened. Some have found this so implausible that they argue the two feedings are one story told twice. Jesus settles it: “Do you not remember the five loaves for the five thousand, and how many baskets you gathered? Or the seven loaves for the four thousand, and how many baskets you gathered?” (16:9–10). He treats them as two events and rebukes the disciples for learning from neither. The implausibility is real, and it lies in the men, not the record (cf. Moses, Numbers 11:21–22).

An honest record. That is a quiet argument for the Gospels’ honesty. A writer inventing a movement’s founding generation doesn’t make them look like this. Matthew was one of the twelve; he describes his own forgetfulness and puts his name to the book.

What is in the bag. And the answer is the same question as at the first feeding: “How many loaves do you have?” (Mark 6:38). The rebuke comes later (16:8–11); now he simply asks what is in the bag. Seven loaves and a few fish — more than last time for a smaller crowd. They have improved slightly on the arithmetic and not at all on the conclusion. We believe after the miracle and doubt before the next; each new need feels as if there had been no previous provision. A test: what has God already provided that you have forgotten in your present worry?

parallels.desc: Moses asks how so many can be fed

verseByVerse.quote: And directing the crowd to sit down on the ground, he took the seven loaves and the fish, and having given thanks he broke them and gave them to the disciples, and the disciples gave them to the crowds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ is the source of every provision, and his people distribute what they receive from him.

The same four movements. He took, gave thanks, broke and gave — again anticipating the Last Supper. The word for giving thanks gives us “Eucharist”; it and the word for blessing in chapter 14 are interchangeable in this formula, and both appear in accounts of the Supper. The disciples are again servants at the table; the men who asked where bread could come from spent the next hour handing it out. We distribute what we have received; the source is always the One who took, gave thanks, broke and gave. A test: are you passing on to others what you have received from Christ?

Not a duplicate. The two feedings differ in a way decisive in Greek. At the five thousand, twelve baskets were gathered — the small, stiff wicker basket a Jew carried his own food in when travelling (Roman satirists mocked Jews for it). Here, seven baskets — the large hamper, big enough to hold a man, the kind Paul was let down the Damascus wall in (Acts 9:25). The two words are used consistently every time each feeding is mentioned, in Matthew, Mark and Jesus’ own recollection (16:9–10). That isn’t how a duplicated story behaves.

Twelve and seven. Twelve may recall Israel’s tribes; seven may suggest completeness, or the seven nations of Canaan (Deuteronomy 7:1), or the seven later appointed to serve Greek-speaking widows (Acts 6:3). Twelve baskets on the Jewish shore; seven on the Gentile one.

verseByVerse.quote: And they all ate and were satisfied. And they took up seven baskets full of the broken pieces left over. Those who ate were four thousand men, besides women and children.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ is bread enough for Jew and Gentile alike, and his provision overflows.

Two feedings, two peoples. The differences run throughout: five thousand on the Jewish shore, four thousand in the Gentile Decapolis; five loaves, seven; twelve small baskets, seven hampers; a crowd there for an evening, one there three days. Even the disciples’ forgetfulness isn’t the seam of a clumsy editor but the very thing the text exposes: the slowness of the human heart to carry yesterday’s grace into today’s need, which Jesus will rebuke (16:8). Two feedings, two peoples, one Lord who is bread enough for both.

Besides women and children. Matthew adds the same words as at the first feeding (14:21), spelling out what the round number leaves out. The count was of men; the actual crowd was likely eight or ten thousand, so the two feedings were closer in size than the numbers suggest.

The leftovers. Seven hampers of surplus, after everyone had eaten their fill, from seven loaves — the supply at the end exceeding the supply at the start, in a desolate place, among foreigners. No one recorded what happened to it. Presumably someone ate the leftovers on the road home — which, in a story about a man who didn’t want people fainting on the way, is likely the point of gathering them. A test: do you trust that Christ’s provision for you will be more than enough?
verseByVerse.note: The word for these baskets is different from the one used at the feeding of the five thousand, and could mean a large hamper.

parallels.desc: Paul let down in such a basket

verseByVerse.quote: And after sending away the crowds, he got into the boat and went to the region of Magadan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ’s compassion crosses every boundary, and those with little often receive him more readily than those with much.

Magadan. Matthew has Magadan; Mark has Dalmanutha (Mark 8:10); some manuscripts of Matthew read Magdala. None can be identified with certainty. The likeliest account is ordinary: a stretch of western shoreline known by more than one landmark. Magdala, Mary Magdalene’s home town, sat on that shore, and a small harbour there has been excavated. Matthew’s geography isn’t usually vague; this is one obscure landing place.

The end of an arc. He left Jewish territory at verse 21 and hasn’t been back. In between: a Canaanite woman commended for great faith, a mountain of Gentile sick healed, a crowd praising the God of Israel as outsiders do, and thousands fed. The boundary the Pharisees guarded so carefully is already being crossed by a Messiah whose compassion has no ethnic limit; the commission of chapter 28 is the conclusion of what these chapters have shown.

Side by side. And the first thing that happens on the other side is that Pharisees and Sadducees come and ask him for a sign (16:1). Matthew puts the two paragraphs side by side without comment. Gentiles who had nothing glorified the God of Israel on a hillside; the men who had everything met the boat and asked for evidence. A test: are you receiving Christ gladly, or still demanding proof?
verseByVerse.note: The location of Magadan is uncertain; Mark names it Dalmanutha.

15.theology: Total depravity and the need for regeneration. Matthew 15:18–19 is one of the clearest statements of the doctrine of the heart’s corruption in the Gospels. The evil that defiles comes not from outside but from within — from the heart that Jeremiah described as “deceitful above all things” (Jer 17:9). Reformed theology insists that this corruption is total in extent (reaching every faculty) though not infinite in degree (common grace restrains it). The implication is that the solution must be equally radical: not education, not ceremony, not moral effort, but the new heart promised in Ezekiel 36:26 — “I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh.” That is the work of regeneration by the Spirit, purchased by the cross of Christ.
15.examples:
Then: The Pharisees’ tradition had become a way of performing piety while avoiding its cost. The Corban ruling let a man appear devout while dishonoring his parents. Religion had become a loophole system. Jesus shut it down.

Now: Every generation finds ways to honour God with the lips while protecting the heart from real submission. Theological correctness without personal holiness, church attendance without costly love, tithing without generosity of spirit — all are versions of the Pharisaic trap. The Canaanite woman is the antidote: no credentials, no performance, just desperate faith in the mercy of Christ. That is always enough.

16.title: Who Do You Say I Am?
16.text: <sup>1</sup>And the Pharisees and Sadducees came, and to test him they asked him to show them a sign from heaven. <sup>2</sup>He answered them, “When it is evening, you say, ‘It will be fair weather, for the sky is red.’ <sup>3</sup>And in the morning, ‘It will be stormy today, for the sky is red and threatening.’ You know how to interpret the appearance of the sky, but you cannot interpret the signs of the times. <sup>4</sup>An evil and adulterous generation seeks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah.” So he left them and departed. <sup>5</sup>When the disciples reached the other side, they had forgotten to bring any bread. <sup>6</sup>Jesus said to them, “Watch and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees.” <sup>7</sup>And they began discussing it among themselves, saying, “We brought no bread.” <sup>8</sup>But Jesus, aware of this, said, “O you of little faith, why are you discussing among yourselves the fact that you have no bread? <sup>9</sup>Do you not yet perceive? Do you not remember the five loaves for the five thousand, and how many baskets you gathered? <sup>10</sup>Or the seven loaves for the four thousand, and how many baskets you gathered? <sup>11</sup>How is it that you fail to understand that I did not speak about bread? Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees.” <sup>12</sup>Then they understood that he did not tell them to beware of the leaven of bread, but of the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees. <sup>13</sup>Now when Jesus came into the district of Caesarea Philippi, he asked his disciples, “Who do people say that the Son of Man is?” <sup>14</sup>And they said, “Some say John the Baptist, others say Elijah, and others Jeremiah or one of the prophets.” <sup>15</sup>He said to them, “But who do you say that I am?” <sup>16</sup>Simon Peter replied, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” <sup>17</sup>And Jesus answered him, “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah! For flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven. <sup>18</sup>And I tell you, you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. <sup>19</sup>I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven.” <sup>20</sup>Then he strictly charged the disciples to tell no one that he was the Christ. <sup>21</sup>From that time Jesus began to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things from the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised. <sup>22</sup>And Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him, saying, “Far be it from you, Lord! This shall never happen to you.” <sup>23</sup>But he turned and said to Peter, “Get behind me, Satan! You are a hindrance to me. For you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of man.” <sup>24</sup>Then Jesus told his disciples, “If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me. <sup>25</sup>For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will find it. <sup>26</sup>For what will it profit a man if he gains the whole world and forfeits his soul? Or what shall a man give in return for his soul? <sup>27</sup>For the Son of Man is going to come with his angels in the glory of his Father, and then he will repay each person according to what he has done. <sup>28</sup>Truly, I say to you, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom.”
16.overview:
Chapter 16 is the turning point of Matthew’s Gospel. Peter’s confession — “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” — is the summit of the disciples’ journey of recognition. Jesus affirms it as divinely revealed, not humanly deduced, and builds the future of his church on this confession. But he immediately turns to the cross: the Christ, the Son of the living God, must go to Jerusalem and die. Peter, who has just made the highest confession of faith in the Gospel, immediately becomes “Satan” — a stumbling block — by refusing the necessity of the cross.

The pairing is deliberate and profound. You cannot confess Jesus as Christ without receiving the cross. Caesarea Philippi was a pagan city at the foot of Mount Hermon, a centre of Roman imperial cult and pagan worship. Here, at the edge of empire and paganism, Jesus declares that he will build his church — and the gates of hell will not prevail. The church is built on the confession, and on Peter only as the first man to make it; and it advances not by cultural power but by the cruciform mission of a cruciform King.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — The Sign of Jonah, Peter's Confession, and the Keys of the Kingdom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Pharisees and Sadducees demand a sign from heaven. Jesus refuses, offering only the sign of Jonah, and warns the disciples about the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees. At Caesarea Philippi he asks the disciples who they say he is, and Peter confesses: "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God." Jesus pronounces a blessing on Peter, declares he will build his church on this rock, and gives him the keys of the kingdom. Then, having accepted the confession, he forbids them to repeat it (v. 20): the title is true, but it is sealed until the cross can say what kind of Christ he is.
verseByVerse.theology: Peter's confession is the christological climax of the first half of Matthew's Gospel. The question Jesus asks — "But who do you say that I am?" — is addressed to the disciples after they have lived with him through chapters 4-15. Peter's answer is the only possible answer for those who have truly seen: "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God." Jesus responds with the foundational promise of the church's existence: "I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it." The church does not build itself; it is built by Christ on the confession of who he is. The first half of the section is a study in reading. Men who can forecast weather cannot read the moment they are standing in (vv. 1-4), and the only sign they will get is a grave and an empty tomb. The leaven warning that follows (vv. 5-12) names the two ways a faith is brought under human management: the Pharisees added to God's word until their tradition outranked it, the Sadducees subtracted from it until nothing supernatural was left, and verse 12 calls the two of them one teaching. And the section closes on a deliberate silence (v. 20). The confession is true and the definition in the hearers' heads is false, so the title goes under guard until Jerusalem explains it — and the ban is lifted only when the risen Christ commands the nations to be told (28:19).
verseByVerse.examples: "Who do you say that I am?" is the question every person must answer. The crowds reach for the biggest names they have — John the Baptist, Elijah, Jeremiah — and every one of them belongs to the past and is a forerunner, a signpost rather than a destination. Peter offers the only category that fits the evidence: Messiah, Son of the living God. The confession is the door through which everything else follows — the keys of the kingdom, the binding and loosing, the promise that the church will stand against the gates of hell. The church is not a human institution that may or may not endure; it is Christ's building, constructed on the indestructible foundation of the confession that he is Lord. Two practical edges run through the same section. The leaven warning is spoken to the Twelve about themselves, with no opponent present — it is not a licence to hunt heresy in other people but a question about which way your own faith drifts when nobody is checking: toward a list of things you are careful about, or toward a quiet removal of everything in the Bible that would be awkward to say out loud at work. And the silence of verse 20 is a warning to anyone impatient for results: it is entirely possible to get a man to say the right sentence about Jesus by leaving out what it costs. Our Lord had that option, with a crowd ready to take it, and chose silence instead.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Pharisees and Sadducees came, and to test him they asked him to show them a sign from heaven. He answered them, "When it is evening, you say, 'It will be fair weather, for the sky is red.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who demand a sign from God after rejecting the signs he has given show not an open mind but a closed heart.

A strange alliance. Pharisees and Sadducees, theological opponents, unite to test him with a demand for a sign “from heaven” — something unmistakably divine. The healings, feedings and exorcisms they had already dismissed as possibly demonic (12:24). Jesus begins with the weather: you read the sky and forecast accurately. The ability to read signs exists; what is missing is willingness to apply it to what is unfolding before them.

The brackets in your Bible. The ESV brackets the weather saying, from “When it is evening” to “the signs of the times” in verse 3, noting that some manuscripts omit it. Two of the oldest and best copies, Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, lack it, as do several early translations, and Jerome noted that many copies he knew lacked it; many later manuscripts have it. The likeliest explanation is that Luke records almost the same saying (Luke 12:54–56), and a copyist who knew it from Luke filled what looked like a gap in Matthew — as Luke 19:10 found its way into some copies of Matthew 18:11. Others argue that copyists in Egypt, where a red morning sky doesn’t forecast storms, dropped a line that made no sense there. We can’t be certain, which is why your Bible uses brackets rather than deleting or printing the words plainly.

Little at stake. Everything carrying weight stands in undisputed text: they came to test him, demanded a sign from heaven, and were told none would be given but the sign of Jonah. Matthew gave the same refusal at 12:38–39, and the rebuke about reading the sky is secure in Luke. The bracket marks a question about a copyist, not a doubt about the Lord’s words. A test: are you asking God for more proof while ignoring what he has already shown you?

parallels.desc: reading the sky but not the times

verseByVerse.quote: "And in the morning, 'It will be stormy today, for the sky is red and threatening.' You know how to interpret the appearance of the sky, but you cannot interpret the signs of the times. An evil and adulterous generation seeks for a sign, but no sign will be given to it except the sign of Jonah." So he left them and departed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The decisive sign God gives is Christ’s death and resurrection, and those who demand more evidence while refusing the evidence given are left to their unbelief.

The signs of the times. The events of Jesus’ ministry — the healings, teaching, crowds and opposition — are signs of the messianic age, readable by those with discernment. Men who can read the weather can’t read the moment they are living in.

Adulterous. “An evil and adulterous generation.” Adultery is an odd charge against men who asked for evidence, but it isn’t about their morals; it is about their marriage. The prophets described God’s covenant with Israel as a marriage, and turning to other gods as a wife’s unfaithfulness. These men were married to God and stood before his Son asking him to prove himself, the way a wife asks for one more piece of evidence from a husband she has already decided to leave.

The sign of Jonah. Matthew has told us what it is: “as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so will the Son of Man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth” (12:40). They asked for a sign from heaven, above the argument; they are promised a sign from underneath — a grave, and an empty tomb, which can’t be watched from a safe distance. And Nineveh repented at a preacher who gave no sign; those Ninevites will stand at the judgment beside men given every sign who wanted one more (12:41).

For the frightened asker. Most of us have said, in a hospital corridor or at two in the morning, “Lord, if this is really you, show me something.” Is that under this rebuke? Almost certainly not. Scripture isn’t against asking. Gideon asked twice and was answered without reproach (Judges 6:36–40). Ahaz was told to ask, refused out of false piety, and was given a sign anyway (Isaiah 7:10–14). John the Baptist asked from prison, “Are you the one who is to come?” and received evidence and then public praise (11:2–11). The difference is never the asking but what it is for. These men weren’t gathering evidence; they were auditioning a candidate they had resolved to reject. The frightened believer wants the evidence to work. A test: are you asking God for help, or setting terms he must meet?

He left them. “So he left them and departed.” He doesn’t argue or perform; he walks away from men still waiting to be impressed. To be contradicted by Christ is a mercy — Peter is about to receive a hard contradiction and be kept. To be left by him is something else. They got what they asked for, an end to the conversation, and that was the punishment.

verseByVerse.quote: When the disciples reached the other side, they had forgotten to bring any bread. Jesus said to them, "Watch and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees."
verseByVerse.commentary:
False teaching works quietly and pervasively like leaven, so Christ’s followers must keep watching their own hearts against both adding to God’s word and taking away from it.

Leaven. Leaven wasn’t bought in a packet; it was a lump of last week’s dough, gone sour, kept back and worked into the new batch. A small piece leavened a whole baking (cf. 1 Corinthians 5:6–8). Nothing about it is visible or fast. The dough doesn’t decide to change; it is changed from inside by something folded in before anyone was watching, and by the time you can taste it, there is no separating it out. That is the force of the warning, and why the verb is “watch” — a standing habit, not a single inspection.

Two teachings. Verse 12 says the leaven is teaching. The Pharisees added: they built a fence of tradition around the law, and the fence came to outrank the law — as at 15:6, where Jesus said, “for the sake of your tradition you have made void the word of God.” The Sadducees subtracted: they held only the five books of Moses, denied the resurrection, angels and spirits (Acts 23:8; cf. 22:23), ran the temple, and had made peace with Rome. What is left after that subtraction is a religion with nothing supernatural in it, competently administered and politically safe.

One leaven. And verse 12 speaks of “the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees” — one teaching covering two parties who agreed on almost nothing. That is the diagnosis: adding to God’s word and subtracting from it arrive at the same place, a faith brought under human management. Either way you get a religion no larger than the men running it — exactly the size that can demand a sign from heaven and refuse the one given.

Which way do you drift? Both are still in production. Which way does your faith drift when no one is checking — toward a list of things you are careful about, which you could keep whether or not God were alive; or toward a quiet, respectable removal of everything in the Bible that would be embarrassing to say at work? A test: be honest about which way you lean.

A guard. This isn’t a commission to go hunting for heresy in others. He says it to the Twelve, about themselves, with no Pharisee in sight. Leaven isn’t what you detect in someone else’s loaf; it is what is already working in yours. And the men who were warned still misheard him.
verseByVerse.note: Leaven (yeast) works invisibly through the whole lump; it often pictures a corrupting influence.

parallels.desc: a little leaven leavens the whole lump

verseByVerse.quote: And they began discussing it among themselves, saying, "We brought no bread." But Jesus, aware of this, said, "O you of little faith, why are you discussing among yourselves the fact that you have no bread?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
A mind preoccupied with worry hears everything as a comment on its fears, but Christ gently rebukes the little faith of his own people without casting them off.

Leaven heard as bread. He said “leaven,” and they heard “bread.” They weren’t disputing with him; they simply weren’t listening, because their heads were full of an empty bag, and someone with an empty bag hears every subject as a comment on his bag. Whatever he had said that morning would have come out sounding like lunch.

A test to run. Think of the last sermon you heard or chapter you read, and ask what it had become by the time you reached the car. Someone worried about money hears a sermon on God’s sovereignty and comes out thinking about his mortgage; someone lonely hears a sermon on the church and comes out counting who didn’t speak to her. That isn’t wickedness; it is what a preoccupied mind does — and why the Twelve could be warned about false teaching and come away discussing catering. A test: what are you worried about that keeps you from hearing God’s word?

Little faith. “O you of little faith” — nearly Matthew’s own word, used of anxiety about clothing (6:30), the storm (8:26), Peter on the water (14:31), here, and the mustard seed (17:20). It is always spoken to disciples, never to Pharisees — a family word for people already inside.

The mercy in it. He doesn’t say “you of no faith” or “unbelievers.” He weighed what they had, found it small, said so, and kept them in the boat, took them north, and within days called one of them blessed and took three up a mountain. Little faith isn’t a verdict of exclusion; it is a diagnosis by a physician with no intention of discharging the patient. And the cure he offers isn’t “try harder” but a question about the past. The opposite of little faith in this scene isn’t great faith; it is memory.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not yet perceive? Do you not remember the five loaves for the five thousand, and how many baskets you gathered? Or the seven loaves for the four thousand, and how many baskets you gathered?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Remembering specifically what God has already done is the antidote to present anxiety — though our poor memory doesn’t end Christ’s commitment to us.

Count. He makes them remember precisely, not with a general feeling of gratitude: five loaves, five thousand, how many baskets; seven loaves, four thousand, how many baskets. Matthew even kept the two different kinds of basket — twelve small ones, seven large hampers (14:20; 15:37). Those men had carried them; the arithmetic went through their own arms. He isn’t saying “remember I am generous”; he is saying “count.” The God who has acted is the God who acts now: “He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” (Romans 8:32).

Try it. Name three specific things you were genuinely afraid of five years ago — the ones that woke you — and say what became of each. Most Christians can’t. Not because God did nothing, but because we carry the fears forward and leave the answers behind on the road. The bag we keep holds tomorrow’s worry; last year’s rescue is set down and not picked up again. That is why a written page — dated, specific, what was asked and what happened — is worth more to a frightened person at three in the morning than a shelf of resolutions. A test: what has God done for you that you need to write down and remember?

Not a technique. But remembering isn’t a technique that makes anxiety vanish; it didn’t for the Twelve. They would fail again, and every one would run. Someone who remembers faithfully and is still afraid stands where the apostles stood. And see what their Lord does with memory as poor as theirs: he puts the question, gets no good answer, then walks them north, asks who he is, and calls the one who answers rightly blessed. He rebuked their memory; he didn’t revise his plans for them.

verseByVerse.quote: How is it that you fail to understand that I did not speak about bread? Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees." Then they understood that he did not tell them to beware of the leaven of bread, but of the teaching of the Pharisees and Sadducees.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The difference between those Christ leaves and those he keeps isn’t intelligence but teachability, and he patiently repeats himself until his disciples understand.

He repeated himself. He gives the warning in verse 6; they mishear; he asks four questions; then he gives the same warning again in almost the same words — and only then, “they understood.” He wasn’t too grand to repeat himself.

Who can be told. Set this beside the men he left on the shore. Both groups failed to read what was before them: the Pharisees demanded evidence with the evidence in hand; the disciples had watched two crowds fed and still counted loaves. Measured by results, the score is level. The difference is one thing: one group could still be told. So verse 4 ends with him leaving, and verse 12 with them understanding. He walked away from the closed mind and stayed in the boat with the slow one. Partial understanding open to more is far better than confident misunderstanding closed to correction.

The question. So the question isn’t whether you understand your Bible well. It is what happened the last time someone showed you that you had a passage wrong — a preacher, a book, a friend who loved you enough to risk it. Not whether you turned out right, but whether you could be told. A Christian often wrong and always teachable is in the boat; one usually right and never correctable is on the shore. A test: when were you last corrected, and how did you respond?

Patience. “Then they understood” cost him a whole conversation, four questions and a repetition, and he paid without complaint. It is the patience that will keep these men through a denial, a scattering and a locked room, and it should make a slow learner love him rather than despair of himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Jesus came into the district of Caesarea Philippi, he asked his disciples, "Who do people say that the Son of Man is?" And they said, "Some say John the Baptist, others say Elijah, and others Jeremiah or one of the prophets."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Even the highest human estimates of Jesus — great prophet, great teacher — fall far short of who he is and leave the admirer untouched.

Far from the centre. Caesarea Philippi lay at the far north, near the Jordan’s headwaters, a Gentile city with a shrine to Pan — about as far from Jerusalem as Jesus ever took his disciples. There he asks the question that will determine everything that follows.

Jeremiah. Matthew alone reports the guess “Jeremiah.” Of all names, why that one? Jeremiah stood in the temple and told the worshippers that the house they trusted would be pulled down; was called a traitor and dropped into a cistern; wept over a city that wouldn’t listen; and announced a new covenant written on hearts. Someone had watched Jesus and reached for the rejected prophet of a doomed temple and a coming covenant — the shrewdest of the guesses, and nearer the mark than he knew.

All from the past. Every answer belongs to the past. John had just been beheaded (14:10; cf. 14:1–2); Elijah was taken up centuries before; Jeremiah had been dead six hundred years. To account for a living man, the crowd went to the graveyard; no ordinary category was large enough.

Signposts. And every answer makes Jesus a signpost, not the destination: the forerunner, the herald before the day of the LORD (Malachi 4:5), a prophet pointing forward — a great man on the road to someone greater. The compliments still do that: a fine moral teacher, a good man ahead of his time, a revolutionary, one of history’s great spiritual figures. Each is warm and respectful, and each leaves the speaker with nothing to do on Monday. A signpost asks nothing; you admire it and drive on.

Admiring, and missing him. So don’t sneer at the crowd. Their answers were reverent and generous, the highest compliment their vocabulary allowed. That is the uncomfortable part: you can hold Christ in the highest regard your categories permit, speak of him warmly, and miss him altogether, politely, the whole time. A test: is Jesus to you a great figure to admire, or the Lord who claims your life?
verseByVerse.note: Caesarea Philippi was a Gentile city at the foot of Mount Hermon, north of the Sea of Galilee, with a shrine to the god Pan.

parallels.desc: Herod thinks he is John raised

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, "But who do you say that I am?" Simon Peter replied, "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God, and each person must confess him personally, not merely repeat what others say.

You. The pronoun is emphatic and placed first: “But you — who do you say that I am?” He has let them report public opinion and then sweeps it aside. He isn’t asking what the villages say, but what these men, who have eaten with him, watched him and been rebuked by him, will say for themselves.

The confession. “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” The Christ — the anointed, the Messiah Israel awaited; and the Son of the living God — not merely a son in the general sense, as Israel was God’s son, but the Son, in a unique relationship. Peter confesses both his office and his nature.

Had Peter not already said something like this? Andrew told him, “We have found the Messiah” (John 1:41), and Peter later confessed Jesus as “the Holy One of God” (John 6:69). Those were real but partial; the disciples’ idea of the Messiah was still shaped by hopes of a political deliverer, as Peter’s rebuke in verse 22 shows. What is new here is the full content, the Son of the living God, given by the Father after all they had seen.

Your answer. Turn the question on yourself, because church life can be conducted for decades without ever answering it. Someone can attend for forty years, recite a creed and sing every hymn, holding it all as information received rather than something he has ever said. If the question were put to you with nothing to recite — no creed, no hymn, no borrowed phrasing — what would you say? Not what is true; what you would say. And this isn’t a demand for eloquence or feeling. Peter’s answer is one short sentence. Nor is it a demand that your life already match it; this same man will be called Satan before the conversation ends and will deny him within a year. The question is only whether it is yours. A test: have you ever said to Christ, in your own words, who he is to you?

The living God. The phrase is the old covenant name for the God not made of wood — David’s “the armies of the living God” (1 Samuel 17:26), and a contrast with the shrines nearby. And it appears once more in Matthew. At the trial the high priest says, “I adjure you by the living God, tell us if you are the Christ, the Son of God” (26:63) — almost Peter’s words. Peter says them and is called blessed; Jesus agrees to them and is condemned. The sentence that opens heaven to a fisherman sends the Son of God to the cross, and he knew that when he asked (cf. John 11:27).

parallels.desc: “you are the Holy One of God”

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus answered him, "Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah! For flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven. And I tell you, you are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Knowing who Jesus is comes by the Father’s revelation, and on the apostolic confession of Christ he builds his church, which death itself can never overcome.

Revealed. “Flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven.” True knowledge of Jesus is always given, never achieved. A test: do you thank God that you know Christ, or think you worked it out yourself?

The setting. At Caesarea Philippi a cave sanctuary to Pan was cut into the cliff, with a spring surging from it and disappearing underground; some ancient writers treated such openings as gates to the underworld. Here, before what the ancient world might call the gates of Hades, Jesus announces his church and says those gates won’t prevail. Matthew doesn’t point it out, but the setting may be significant.

Who is the rock? No verse divides Christians more sharply. Rome reads it simply: the rock is Peter himself, Jesus builds his church on him, and the authority given here passes down through an unbroken line of successors, the bishops of Rome; this is the chief New Testament pillar of the papacy. And the Roman case is stronger than a slogan. Peter is named first in the list of apostles (10:2), more often than all the others together; three times Jesus speaks to him alone in unique terms — here, the name and the keys; in the upper room, prayed for so that he may strengthen his brothers (Luke 22:31–32); and after the resurrection, charged three times to feed the sheep (John 21:15–17). And a foundation is permanent; if Christ founded a visible church on a man, the office would outlive him, as offices do in Scripture, from Moses to Joshua and from Judas to Matthias (Acts 1:20).

The answer. Older Protestants often pressed the Greek: “Peter” (a stone) and “rock” (bedrock), as though Jesus distinguished the man from his confession. That argument is weaker than it looks, since in Aramaic both words are one, Kepha. Honesty admits Peter himself is most likely the rock — as the first to confess Christ, the leading stone in the foundation “of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone” (Ephesians 2:20). That foundation is laid once, not handed on as an office. Three things answer the Roman case. First, the one apostolic vacancy the New Testament fills is filled on a condition that closes the category: the replacement had to have been with them from John’s baptism and be a witness of the resurrection (Acts 1:21–22). When James is killed (Acts 12:2), no one replaces him. Second, a permanent foundation stays laid; it isn’t laid again each generation. If it required living successors, we would need successors to the prophets too. The apostles still hold the church up, in what they wrote. Third, what Peter is singled out for are firsts — first to confess, first to preach at Pentecost, first into Samaria and into a Gentile house — and there is no office in being the one who went first. And the text guards against the papal leap: the same keys go to the whole body of disciples two chapters later (18:18); James sums up the Jerusalem council (Acts 15); Paul withstands Peter to his face (Galatians 2:11); and five verses on, this rock is called “Satan.” The honour is real grace, the honour of a forgiven confessor, not the founding of a throne (cf. John 1:42; 1 Peter 2:4–6).

The gates of Hades. Matthew’s word isn’t Gehenna, the place of judgment (5:22; 10:28; 23:33), but Hades, the realm of the dead; “the gates of Sheol” was a Hebrew way of speaking of death’s power (Isaiah 38:10; Job 38:17). So the promise is more exact than the slogan: death will not hold this church down — because it won’t hold him, who will soon say he is going to Jerusalem to be killed and raised. And this is the first time “church” appears in the New Testament, on Jesus’ own lips; it occurs only here and at 18:17 in the Gospels. It means the called-out assembly, the word the Greek Old Testament uses for Israel gathered before God at the mountain (Deuteronomy 4:10). He isn’t founding a society; he is claiming a very old one and building it on himself.

Not your congregation’s guarantee. This promise is about the church, not about your church. Congregations close; denominations grow proud and cold and are buried. The seven churches of Revelation received letters from the risen Christ, and none survives; Ephesus’s lampstand was removed as warned (Revelation 2:5). If you have watched your fellowship shrink to nothing and wondered whether this verse failed, it didn’t. What is guaranteed is that Christ will never be without a church, that he is building it, and that the last enemy will never shut the doors.
verseByVerse.note: Bar-Jonah means “son of Jonah.” Peter means “rock.” The ESV notes that “hell” here renders Hades, the realm of the dead; its gates stand for the power of death. A play on words: “Peter” (Petros) and “rock” (petra) are closely related Greek words.

parallels.desc: built on the foundation of the apostles

verseByVerse.quote: I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven." Then he strictly charged the disciples to tell no one that he was the Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ gives his church the keys to open and shut the kingdom by declaring the gospel and exercising discipline, and he guards his messiahship until the cross can define it.

Isaiah’s key. The background is Isaiah 22. Shebna, steward over King Hezekiah’s household, is caught carving himself a grand tomb, and God installs another man: “I will place on his shoulder the key of the house of David. He shall open, and none shall shut; and he shall shut, and none shall open” (Isaiah 22:22). The key was a large wooden thing carried on the shoulder, the badge of office. The steward isn’t the king; he runs the king’s house and decides who is brought into the king’s presence. And the risen Christ takes that sentence for himself: “the holy one, the true one, who has the key of David, who opens and no one will shut” (Revelation 3:7). The key is his; he gives a servant the use of it, not the house.

The Roman case at its strongest. Isaiah 22 is about a post, not just a man: Shebna removed, Eliakim installed, the stewardship continuing while the king’s house stands. If the Son of David reached for that text, he instituted a stewardship, which is refilled when its holder dies. Add that “you” here is singular, to one man, with the new name, and the Roman reading isn’t perverse; it may be what a first-century Jew would most naturally hear.

The answer. First, Isaiah’s oracle doesn’t end there. Three verses later: “the peg that was fastened in a secure place will give way, and it will be cut down and fall, and the load that was on it will be cut off” (Isaiah 22:25) — a strange charter for an office that can’t fail, and matched four verses later here when the keyholder is called Satan. Second, watch Peter use the keys: at Pentecost three thousand Jews come in (Acts 2); at Samaria the despised neighbours are let in (Acts 8:14–17); in a Gentile house the door to the nations opens (Acts 10). Three doors, each opened once and never needing to be opened again. By Acts 15 James gives the ruling, and Peter then disappears from Luke’s story — not the career of a permanent office but of a doorkeeper who has finished with the doors. Third, the authority doesn’t stay in one pair of hands: the same binding and loosing is given to a congregation (18:18), and after the resurrection forgiving and retaining is given to the gathered disciples (John 20:23).

Heaven’s decision. The Greek is unusual: roughly, “shall have been bound in heaven.” Some argue it means the church announces heaven’s decisions rather than heaven ratifying the church’s; others say the idiom won’t bear that weight. The grammar alone can’t settle it, but the New Testament does: the apostles never invent terms of admission. Peter at Pentecost doesn’t decide who may be saved; he tells a crowd what God has done and what they must do. The key doesn’t make the door; it opens the one the King built.

On an ordinary Sunday. When a church hears someone confess Christ, baptizes him and receives him to the Lord’s Table, it isn’t offering an opinion; it does on earth what Christ authorised. When, after long patience, a church must tell an unrepentant member that his life and profession no longer agree (18:15–17), that isn’t a committee being unkind but the same key turned the other way. So belonging to a real congregation isn’t optional: the keys were given to a church, not to individuals with Bibles and strong opinions. And the keys are terrible in the wrong hands, as when forgiveness was sold at a church door in the Reformers’ day. Abuse doesn’t abolish them; it makes their right use urgent. A test: are you a committed member of a church under its care and discipline?

Tell no one. He has just blessed Peter for saying it, and forbids them to tell anyone. Because the word was true and the meaning in the hearers’ heads false. “Christ” in Galilean mouths meant a son of David with an army to drive out Rome; say it in a village and you start a rising. So the title is sealed until the cross defines it — and in the very next verse he begins to tell them plainly that he must be killed. At the trial he answers openly under oath (26:63–64), when the word could no longer be misheard, and after the resurrection the charge is reversed: “Go therefore and make disciples of all nations” (28:19). There is a warning here: it is possible to get someone to say the right sentence about Jesus by leaving out what it costs, and count it a conversion. Our Lord had that option, with a crowd ready, and chose silence.
verseByVerse.note: Keys give authority to open and shut. “Bind” and “loose” were used of forbidding and permitting.

parallels.desc: the key of the house of David
the same authority given to all the disciples

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–28 — The First Passion Prediction and the Call to Cross-Bearing
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: From the moment of Peter's confession, Jesus begins to teach that he must go to Jerusalem, suffer, be killed, and rise on the third day. Peter rebukes him; Jesus rebukes Peter with the sharpest words in the Gospel: "Get behind me, Satan!" He then calls the crowd and disciples to cross-bearing: whoever loses his life for his sake will find it. The section ends with a warning about the coming of the Son of Man in his Father's glory. Between the two he asks what a man could possibly hand over in exchange for his soul (v. 26), and he closes by promising that some standing there will not taste death before they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom (v. 28) — a promise kept six days later on the mountain, as one of the men who heard it says himself (2 Pet 1:16-18).
verseByVerse.theology: The first passion prediction marks the watershed of Matthew's Gospel: the confession at Caesarea Philippi is the turning point from which Jesus now sets his face toward Jerusalem. The cross is not an unexpected tragedy but the appointed path. Peter's rebuttal — "Far be it from you, Lord! This shall never happen to you" — is the most natural human response and the most spiritually dangerous: it substitutes human preferences for divine purpose. "You are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of men" is the diagnosis of every theology that wants a cross-free Christianity. The section then puts a price on the choice. Verse 26 is a market question — what sum would buy back a soul? — and it is left unanswered until 20:28, where the Son of Man gives his own life as the ransom no man could pay. Verse 27 supplies the frame: he will repay each person according to what he has done. That is not a scoreboard, for Matthew twice rules one out — the impressive workers of 7:21-23 are turned away because they were never known, and the sheep of 25:31-46 cannot remember their own good deeds. Works are the evidence of a righteousness received, never the ground of it.
verseByVerse.examples: The cross-bearing saying moves from Jesus's cross to the disciple's: "If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me." The disciple's cross is not their personal hardships and inconveniences; it is the public cost of standing with a man under sentence, and the losing of a life organised around self-interest in order to find one organised around Christ. The paradox of verse 25 — finding life through losing it — is the gospel in miniature: the life surrendered to Jesus is the life truly found. Verse 26 makes the same point as a transaction. Ask a man what he would take for his car and he names a figure; ask what he would take for his son and he refuses the category outright. There is one thing in his possession that no market will quote, and it is himself. And verse 28 shows how this Master treats frightened followers: the cross-bearing call is issued on a Monday, so to speak, and by the following week three of them have been taken up a mountain and shown what the road ends in. The order of those two events is the mercy in them, and it is set out at vv. 23-24.

verseByVerse.quote: From that time Jesus began to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things from the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised. And Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him, saying, "Far be it from you, Lord! This shall never happen to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ must suffer, die and rise according to God’s plan, and even sincere love that tries to keep him from the cross is opposing God.

From that time. The same phrase opened his public ministry (4:17); now it opens his teaching on the passion. “He must go” — the necessity of God’s plan. Suffer, be killed, be raised: the resurrection is part of the first announcement, not an afterthought (cf. 17:22–23; 20:17–19).

Peter’s rebuke. Peter takes him aside and “began to rebuke him” — the verb Jesus uses against demons (17:18) and the storm (8:26). The man who just confessed the Son of the living God tries to redirect the living God from his stated purpose.

Ninety seconds. Hold the conversation together. In verse 16 Peter says the most exalted sentence any human has said in this Gospel, and Jesus says the Father taught him. In verse 23 the same man is called Satan — same afternoon, same mouth, no interval for gradual decline. Revelation received doesn’t immunise you against the next hour. The highest and lowest moments aren’t separated by decades in most people; they come in the same week, even the same conversation. If your walk with God has genuine heights followed by embarrassing collapses, you aren’t a special case. You are Peter, and Peter is normal.

Love as the danger. And notice where the collapse came from. Peter isn’t being wicked but protective: “Far be it from you, Lord! This shall never happen to you” is affection, what you say to someone you love who has just said he will die. That is what makes it dangerous. The worst advice most of us receive comes from people who love us and can’t bear to see us suffer, and the worst we give ourselves is usually dressed as care. Satan didn’t need an enemy for this errand; a devoted friend did it sincerely, within a minute of a God-given confession. A test: is someone’s loving concern — or your own — steering you away from obedience?

Not dismissed. Jesus rebukes Peter as hard as anyone in the Gospels, and doesn’t dismiss him. Six days later Peter is one of the three on the mountain. He will deny his Lord with oaths and be restored by a charcoal fire. Full severity and unbroken commitment together. Don’t read your worst moment as your verdict.

verseByVerse.quote: But he turned and said to Peter, "Get behind me, Satan! You are a hindrance to me. For you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of man." Then Jesus told his disciples, "If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Opposing the cross sets our minds on human things rather than God’s, and following Jesus means disowning our self-rule and accepting death to self behind him.

“Get behind me, Satan!” Peter isn’t possessed; he is voicing Satan’s agenda, the agenda of the wilderness: the kingdom without the cross (cf. 4:10). “You are a hindrance to me” — a stumbling stone. The man to be the rock is for a moment the stone in the Saviour’s path. And “not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of man” names it: human thinking about how a Messiah should win.

Deny himself. It doesn’t mean self-hatred or doing without for its own sake. Matthew uses the word for Peter’s denial in the courtyard: “I do not know the man” (26:72, 74). To deny is to disown, to refuse to be identified with someone. So to deny yourself is to do to your own claims what Peter did to Jesus — to hear the demands of your comfort, reputation and being in the right, and say, “I do not know him.” Not to despise yourself, but to stop automatically taking your own side.

Take up his cross. The phrase has been flattened to mean any chronic trouble — a difficult relative, a job you dislike. Hear it as the men on that road did. A man carrying a crossbeam through a town wasn’t carrying a burden; he was walking to his execution, in public, and everyone knew he wasn’t coming back. A cross isn’t a weight you carry; it is a death you have agreed to (cf. 10:38).

Your cross. So your illness isn’t your cross, nor your difficult marriage, bad back, awkward colleague or ageing parents. Those are afflictions, and God is deeply present in them. Your cross is the specific cost of following Jesus — what you wouldn’t bear if you weren’t his: the promotion refused because the figures would have to be wrong, the relationship ended, the truth told when silence would be cheaper, the money given that you had other plans for, the reputation quietly lost. Calling an ordinary hardship a cross lets us feel discipleship is costing us when it may be costing nothing. Luke adds the word that sets its shape: “daily” (Luke 9:23) — not one dramatic renunciation, but a small repeated decision mostly unseen. A test: what is following Christ actually costing you right now?

Behind him. Deny, take up, follow — and the following is behind him, on a road he walks first. He asks nothing he declined to do himself. And in mercy, six days later he takes three of them up a mountain to see the glory beyond the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: For whoever would save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for my sake will find it. For what will it profit a man if he gains the whole world and forfeits his soul? Or what shall a man give in return for his soul?
verseByVerse.commentary:
The self we clutch we lose, the self we give for Christ we gain, and our soul is beyond all price — so great that only Christ’s own life could ransom it.

One word. “Life” in verse 25 and “soul” in verse 26 are the same Greek word, used four times in three sentences; English changes the word and hides the logic. He isn’t moving from earthly life to a separate point about souls. It is one argument: the self you clutch, you lose; the self you hand over, you get back; the self can’t be bought at any price; and there isn’t a second one for another attempt. You have one self, and every day you are spending it on something.

A guard. This is sometimes used to bully decent people. Nothing here forbids ambition; Scripture tells us to work well and provide for our households. And three words keep it from praising sacrifice in general: “for my sake.” People lose their lives for a country, a company, a cause or a reputation, and lose them altogether. What turns loss into finding isn’t the size of the sacrifice but the Person it is made for. Self-denial isn’t the point of Christianity; he is.

Name the price. “What shall a man give in return for his soul?” The word means the price handed over in an exchange. He invites a bid: name the figure. The terrible thing isn’t that the price is high but that there is none. Everything else converts — house to money, money to time, time to comfort. One possession has no market quote: yourself (cf. Psalm 49:7–8). Ask someone what he would take for his car, and he names a figure; his house, perhaps after a pause; his son, and the question stops being a question — he refuses the category and is offended it was raised. That is what a soul is, and many who would be outraged by the second question have been answering the first about themselves for years, at rates they would be ashamed to write down. A test: what are you trading your soul for, a little at a time?

The answer given. The question is asked and not answered, and four chapters later Matthew supplies the only answer: “the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (20:28) — the same word for life, and “ransom,” the price paid to buy a person out. He knew the arithmetic when he asked: no one had anything worth a single soul, and everyone had already sold his own cheaply. Knowing it, he walked to Jerusalem and paid the price with his own life. The One who warned us not to sell ourselves for the world bought us when we already had.

parallels.desc: the ransom of a life is costly

verseByVerse.quote: For the Son of Man is going to come with his angels in the glory of his Father, and then he will repay each person according to what he has done. Truly, I say to you, there are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Son of Man who goes to the cross will come in glory to judge everyone by what they have done, and some of his disciples were about to glimpse that glory before they died.

The judgment. “He will repay each person according to what he has done” — the promise of Psalm 62:12, and judgment by works, on Jesus’ lips, beside the cross. The New Testament teaches it everywhere, Matthew most insistently: those turned away in 7:21–23, the account for every careless word (12:36–37), the sheep and goats separated by what was and wasn’t done (25:31–46). The resolution isn’t softening the words but asking what a court is for. Two questions are asked at any trial: on what ground is this person received, and what was he actually like? Righteousness is received, never earned; that is settled at the cross. But received righteousness always shows, and faith is invisible. God doesn’t hold an invisible judgment; the deeds are its visible form, produced in evidence as handwriting shows whose hand it was.

Not an audit. Matthew rules out a scoreboard twice. In 7:21–23 those rejected aren’t rejected for a low total; their works are impressive, and the verdict is “I never knew you.” In 25:31–46 the righteous are astonished at their own record: “when did we see you hungry?” On a scoreboard no one is surprised by his score. It isn’t an audit but a recognition.

For the tender conscience. Don’t turn this into a lash. He says it to men who couldn’t follow a warning about bread that morning, one just called Satan and soon to deny him. He tells them of the judgment to steady them, as the reason they can afford to lose their lives: nothing spent on him will be mislaid. Someone who examines his deeds and finds them thin hasn’t thereby discovered he is lost. The question that day isn’t how much was done but whose he was — and deeds are how that shows. A test: whose are you?

Was Jesus mistaken? “Some standing here… will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom” is often cited as a failed prediction of his return. What did Jesus mean by the Son of Man coming in his kingdom? Christians have read it in several ways: of the transfiguration that follows; of the resurrection, ascension and Pentecost, when Christ was enthroned; of the judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70; or of the final return. The transfiguration is the most likely, since all three Gospels place it immediately after this saying. And it fits the language of Daniel 7 (Daniel 7:13–14), where the Son of Man comes to the Ancient of Days to be crowned, because the transfiguration was a preview of the glory the Son would receive at his resurrection and ascension, when “all authority in heaven and on earth” was given to him (28:18). (The similar sayings at 10:23 and 24:34 are taken up there.)

Why “not taste death”? If he meant an event six days away, why speak of some not dying first? The emphasis falls on “some”: he has just spoken of his coming to judge, and now distinguishes — that day isn’t what you are about to see, but a few of you will see something of it. All three Gospels place the transfiguration in the following week. And one of the men standing there tells us what he saw. Defending the promise of Christ’s coming late in life, Peter appeals to that mountain: “we did not follow cleverly devised myths when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of his majesty… we ourselves heard this very voice borne from heaven, for we were with him on the holy mountain” (2 Peter 1:16–18). The man who heard the promise cites its fulfilment. And into the bleakest hour of their training — told their Master would die and they must carry a cross — he drops a promise: some of you will see who I really am. He shows them the far side of the cross first.

parallels.desc: you will render to a man according to his work

16.theology: The church and the confession. Matthew is the only Gospel that records Jesus using the word “church” (ekklesia — the called-out assembly), and it appears on his lips in only two passages: here, and again in the discipline of 18:17. His promise is breathtaking in its confidence: he will build it, not we; and it will endure against all opposition. The church’s indestructibility rests not on its institutional strength or cultural influence but on the identity of its Lord and the truth of its confession. When the church loses the confession — that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of the living God — it loses the rock on which it stands. The Reformation was at its heart a recovery of this confession: Christ alone, known through Scripture alone, received through faith alone, to the glory of God alone.
16.examples:
Then: Caesarea Philippi was the last place you would expect the church to be founded — a pagan city, politically dangerous territory, far from Jerusalem’s religious centre. Jesus chose it deliberately. The church is born at the margins, in hostile territory, by a divine confession that overturns every human calculation.

Now: The question “Who do you say that I am?” is not a theological quiz but an existential confrontation. Every person who hears the gospel must answer it. Correct doctrine about Jesus (acknowledging him as a great teacher, a moral exemplar, a historical figure) falls short of Peter’s confession. Jesus demands a verdict — not about what others say, but about what you say. The church is built on those who answer as Peter answered, by the same Spirit who revealed it to him.

17.title: The Transfiguration
17.text: <sup>1</sup>And after six days Jesus took with him Peter and James, and John his brother, and led them up a high mountain by themselves. <sup>2</sup>And he was transfigured before them, and his face shone like the sun, and his clothes became white as light. <sup>3</sup>And behold, there appeared to them Moses and Elijah, talking with him. <sup>4</sup>And Peter said to Jesus, “Lord, it is good that we are here. If you wish, I will make three tents here, one for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah.” <sup>5</sup>He was still speaking when, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them, and a voice from the cloud said, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased; listen to him.” <sup>6</sup>When the disciples heard this, they fell on their faces and were terrified. <sup>7</sup>But Jesus came and touched them, saying, “Rise, and have no fear.” <sup>8</sup>And when they lifted up their eyes, they saw no one but Jesus only. <sup>9</sup>And as they were coming down the mountain, Jesus commanded them, “Tell no one the vision, until the Son of Man is raised from the dead.” <sup>10</sup>And the disciples asked him, “Then why do the scribes say that first Elijah must come?” <sup>11</sup>He answered, “Elijah does come, and he will restore all things. <sup>12</sup>But I tell you that Elijah has already come, and they did not recognize him, but did to him whatever they pleased. So also the Son of Man will certainly suffer at their hands.” <sup>13</sup>Then the disciples understood that he was speaking to them of John the Baptist. <sup>14</sup>And when they came to the crowd, a man came up to him and, kneeling before him, <sup>15</sup>said, “Lord, have mercy on my son, for he has seizures and he suffers terribly. For often he falls into the fire, and often into the water. <sup>16</sup>And I brought him to your disciples, and they could not heal him.” <sup>17</sup>And Jesus answered, “O faithless and twisted generation, how long am I to be with you? How long am I to bear with you? Bring him here to me.” <sup>18</sup>And Jesus rebuked the demon, and it came out of him, and the boy was healed instantly. <sup>19</sup>Then the disciples came to Jesus privately and said, “Why could we not cast it out?” <sup>20</sup>He said to them, “Because of your little faith. For truly, I say to you, if you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Move from here to there,’ and it will move, and nothing will be impossible for you.” <sup>22</sup>As they were gathering in Galilee, Jesus said to them, “The Son of Man is about to be delivered into the hands of men, <sup>23</sup>and they will kill him, and he will be raised on the third day.” And they were greatly distressed. <sup>24</sup>When they came to Capernaum, the collectors of the two-drachma tax went up to Peter and said, “Does your teacher not pay the tax?” <sup>25</sup>He said, “Yes.” And when he came into the house, Jesus spoke to him first, saying, “What do you think, Simon? From whom do kings of the earth take toll or tax? From their sons or from others?” <sup>26</sup>And when he said, “From others,” Jesus said to him, “Then the sons are free. <sup>27</sup>However, not to give offense to them, go to the sea and cast a hook and take the first fish that comes up, and when you open its mouth you will find a shekel. Take that and give it to them for me and for yourself.”
17.overview:
The Transfiguration is a window into eternity opened for three disciples on a mountain. For a moment the veil of Jesus’ humanity is drawn back and the uncreated glory of the Son shines through: his face blazes like the sun, his garments become white as light. Moses and Elijah appear — the Law and the Prophets — converging on the one they pointed to, discussing the “exodus” he was about to accomplish in Jerusalem (Luke 9:31). The Father speaks from the cloud — the shekinah glory — as he did at the baptism: “This is my beloved Son; listen to him.”

The Transfiguration is the answer to Peter’s confusion in chapter 16. Peter could not accept a suffering Messiah. The mountain shows him why the cross is not a defeat: the one who will be crucified is the radiant Son of God, whose glory is momentarily unveiled. The cross does not contradict his glory; it is the appointed path through which his glory reaches the world. The disciples descend the mountain and immediately confront a demon-possessed boy they could not heal — from glory to weakness, from the height to the valley of need, which is always where the church must work.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Six days after Peter's confession, Jesus takes Peter, James, and John up a high mountain. He is transfigured before them — his face shining like the sun, his clothes white as light. Moses and Elijah appear and speak with him. A cloud overshadows them and the Father's voice speaks: "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased; listen to him." The disciples fall on their faces; Jesus touches them and they see no one but Jesus alone. Coming down, he forbids them to speak of the vision until he is raised from the dead, and answers their question about Elijah: Elijah has already come, in John the Baptist, and was not recognised but treated however his enemies pleased — and so also, he says, the Son of Man will suffer at their hands.
verseByVerse.theology: The Transfiguration is the mountain-top confirmation of Peter's confession: the Son of God whose glory was hidden in flesh is momentarily unveiled. Moses (the law) and Elijah (the prophets) appear alongside Jesus — the whole of the Old Testament represented — and then disappear. Jesus alone remains. The command "listen to him" supersedes Sinai and Carmel: not the law through Moses, not the prophetic word through Elijah, but the Son himself who is their fulfillment. The disciples' prostration and their rising at Jesus's touch enact the pattern of every encounter with the holy: undone by the presence, restored by the touch of grace. There is a quiet fitness in which two men were chosen to stand there. Moses and Elijah are the two men in the Old Testament who met God on Horeb, and each was given something less than an unveiled sight of his glory: Moses was hidden in a cleft of the rock and shown only the back of the glory as it passed (Exod 33:18-23), and Elijah wrapped his face in his cloak at the mouth of the cave and would not look (1 Kings 19:9-13). Now the two of them stand on a mountain with the glory in front of them, unveiled and in the open, holding a conversation with it. What neither prophet was permitted to see, both of them at last see in the face of a Galilean carpenter. And the descent (vv. 9-13) attaches the vision to the cross: the silence is to hold until the resurrection, and the Elijah question is answered by pointing at a man already dead. John came in Elijah's spirit and power and was killed on a whim; the pattern of the forerunner is the pattern of the King.
verseByVerse.examples: The descent from the mountain with the charge to silence (until the resurrection) and the discussion about Elijah frames the Transfiguration within the larger passion narrative. The glory on the mountain will be followed immediately by the failure to heal the epileptic boy in the valley — the constant movement between mountain-top and valley-floor, between the unveiled glory and the demanding need. The disciples are not left on the mountain; they descend with Jesus to where the need is. Two practical edges run through the descent itself. The first is the order to say nothing (v. 9): three men walk down to nine colleagues who were not invited and are about to have the worst day of their ministry, and they are to keep the greatest experience of their lives to themselves. Not everything God gives is given for circulation; some of it is given to be carried. The second is the plain warning of vv. 12-13. God's own forerunner, the greatest man born of women, was beheaded because a king did not want to look foolish in front of his dinner guests, and God did not prevent it. Faithfulness does not purchase a comfortable outcome. What it secures is a place in a pattern that runs through the Son himself and out the far side on the third day.

verseByVerse.quote: And after six days Jesus took with him Peter and James, and John his brother, and led them up a high mountain by themselves. And he was transfigured before them, and his face shone like the sun, and his clothes became white as light.
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the mountain the hidden glory of the Son broke through for a moment, so that men about to follow him to a cross would know who they were following.

Six days. “After six days” ties this to the confession and the first passion prediction of chapter 16, and to the promise that some standing there would see the Son of Man in his kingdom before they died (16:28). That promise is kept within the week. Luke says “about eight days” (Luke 9:28): the ordinary Jewish way of counting included the first and last days, so it is one interval counted two ways.

Which mountain? Matthew says only “a high mountain.” Tradition settled on Tabor, but Tabor is low and had a settlement on its summit; Hermon, towering over Caesarea Philippi where they had just been, is the likelier candidate. We don’t know, and Matthew didn’t think it worth recording — a hint about where he wants our eyes to go.

Nothing added, something unveiled. “He was transfigured” — changed in form. But nothing was added to Jesus on that mountain; something stopped being hidden. Moses came down from Sinai with a shining face, but that light was borrowed, reflected from a glory not his own, and it faded behind a veil (Exodus 34:29–35). Here nothing is reflected. The light isn’t falling on Jesus; it is coming out of him. And “his face shone like the sun” echoes his own promise that at the end “the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (13:43). What awaits the end of the world stood on a hillside in the middle of it.

The thirty years. If this was in him all along, it was in him at Nazareth. For about thirty years that face was an ordinary face in an ordinary village; men haggled with him over a yoke and later said, “Is not this the carpenter’s son?” (13:55). The wonder isn’t only that he shone for an hour. It is the years he didn’t — glory held back, day after day, by a choice he kept making for our sake (Philippians 2:6–7).

For the follower. He had just told these men to carry a cross behind him. Before the road to Jerusalem, he lets them look at who it is they are following. He doesn’t explain the glory; he shows it. A test: when following Christ costs you, do you remember who he is?
verseByVerse.note: The mountain is unnamed; tradition says Tabor, but Hermon, near Caesarea Philippi, is also suggested.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, there appeared to them Moses and Elijah, talking with him. And Peter said to Jesus, "Lord, it is good that we are here. If you wish, I will make three tents here, one for you and one for Moses and one for Elijah."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Law and the Prophets meet Jesus on the mountain to speak of his cross, and the glory is given not to be kept but to carry us down into ordinary obedience.

Moses and Elijah. The two great figures of the old covenant, the Law and the Prophets, stand with him. Luke tells us what they spoke of: “his departure, which he was about to accomplish at Jerusalem” (Luke 9:31). The whole Old Testament is in conversation with the cross. The glory isn’t an alternative to it; it is a conversation about it.

How did they know them? The text doesn’t say; recognising them was part of what God showed.
