verseByVerse.quote: So his fellow servant fell down and pleaded with him, "Have patience with me, and I will pay you." He refused and went and put him in prison until he should pay the debt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Refusing to forgive doesn’t deny the reality of the wrong done to us; it forgets the far greater mercy we have received and builds ourselves a prison.

The same words. The fellow servant falls down and pleads in almost the first servant’s own words: “Have patience with me, and I will pay you.” And this debt really was payable. The first servant refuses and puts him in prison, where he could never earn it — unforgiveness is irrational as well as cruel.

“What was done to me wasn’t a hundred denarii.” A deeply wounded reader may object fairly: it wasn’t a borrowed tool or a sharp word; it was years, a childhood, a betrayal that reorganised a life. Does the parable call that small? No. The hundred denarii is measured not against your suffering but against ten thousand talents, a sum the story has made unpayable. The point isn’t that your wound is small but that God’s mercy to you is vast beyond calculation, and no human debt against you exceeds it. That is a claim about the forgiveness you have received, not a verdict on the harm you have suffered.

He takes it seriously. The same discourse began with the millstone for those who harm a little one (v. 6). The Jesus who tells you to stop counting is the Jesus who said that. He takes what was done to you more seriously than you do, and he still won’t let it own you.

A self-built prison. Look at the first servant’s day. Released from a debt no lifetime could clear, he spends the afternoon with his hands round someone’s throat over a sum he could have written off. He walks out free and builds himself a prison. Unforgiveness keeps the offender living rent-free in your life and hands him a second victory. Christ doesn’t ask you to say the wrong was nothing. He asks you to stop carrying the man who did it. (On what forgiving does and doesn’t require, see on 6:14–15.) A test: whom are you still carrying?

verseByVerse.quote: When his fellow servants saw what had taken place, they were greatly distressed, and they went and reported to their master all that had taken place. Then his master summoned him and said to him, "You wicked servant! I forgave you all that debt because you pleaded with me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When we see cruelty among the forgiven, we should grieve and take it to those with authority to act, and we should remember that God forgave us simply because we asked.

The bystanders. We read expecting to be the man forgiven a fortune, or on a bad day the man being choked. But most Christians, most of the time, are the third group: those who saw it and had to decide what to do about something that wasn’t their business.

Greatly distressed. Matthew uses the very words he used of the disciples told their Lord would be killed: “they were greatly distressed” (17:23). What broke the disciples at the news of the cross breaks these men at the sight of cruelty between two of the forgiven. It is meant to be the same grief.

Upward, not sideways. They didn’t just discuss it among themselves, form a party, or confront the man themselves — they weren’t the injured party. They went to the one with standing and authority to act and told him everything. Verse 15 still stands: if someone sins against you, go to him first, alone. But when a wrong is done to someone else and the pattern is plain, the route is upward, not sideways. The difference between reporting and gossiping is the difference between the one you take it to and the many you tell it to.

The charge and the ground. “You wicked servant!” The king doesn’t say “you are still in debt” or reopen the ledger. The charge isn’t arrears but character. Then he names the ground of the pardon: “I forgave you all that debt because you pleaded with me.” Not because he deserved it or promised well. He asked, and that was enough. A test: when you see a believer mistreated, do you gossip about it or take it to those who can help?

verseByVerse.quote: "And should not you have had mercy on your fellow servant, as I had mercy on you?" And in anger his master delivered him to the jailers, until he should pay all his debt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Mercy received obliges mercy given, and an unforgiving heart shows that God’s forgiveness was never truly taken in — a warning meant to shake the complacent, not crush the struggling.

The question. “Should not you have had mercy on your fellow servant, as I had mercy on you?” It answers itself. The obligation to show mercy comes from the mercy received (Ephesians 4:32).

Purgatory? “Until he should pay all his debt” has been cited, with 5:26, for purgatory — a punishment after death that ends when the debt is paid (see on 5:25–26). But here the debt is ten thousand talents, which the parable has made sure could never be paid. The “until” isn’t a sentence with an end date; it is a door that doesn’t open.

Can forgiveness be taken back? The forgiveness was given and then withdrawn. Does a Christian who won’t forgive lose his salvation? Three things. First, a parable makes a point; it isn’t a system. Matthew likens the Lord’s return to a burglar (24:43) and uses leaven both for the Pharisees’ teaching (16:6) and for the kingdom (13:33). Second, the New Testament’s weight falls the other way: an unforgiving heart is evidence, not cause. The parable itself shows it — the man never understood he had been released; he left thinking he had an extension. You can’t lose what you never truly took. Third, don’t defuse the verse. Jesus told this to frighten, and the next sentence says so. Assurance and complacency aren’t the same, and this is aimed at complacency.

For the one struggling to forgive. Someone badly hurt, who can’t yet forgive and knows it, may read verse 34 as his own sentence. Look at the man in the story. He isn’t lying awake wrestling with a wound or trying and failing. Within the hour of being released from an unpayable debt, he has his hands round a colleague’s throat over three months’ wages and jails a man who begged him. This parable is about contempt, not difficulty. If you want to forgive and can’t yet get there, you aren’t in this parable; you are back at verse 22, where seventy-seven is room to keep coming back. The question is which way you are facing.

In anger. The king’s feelings are named twice: pity at a man who can’t pay, and anger at a man who won’t forgive. What finally provokes him isn’t the ten thousand talents but the hundred denarii. A test: is there a hundred denarii you are still demanding?

parallels.desc: as God in Christ forgave you
as the Lord has forgiven you

verseByVerse.quote: So also my heavenly Father will do to every one of you, if you do not forgive your brother from your heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Only forgiveness from the heart reflects the mercy God has shown us, and the truly great in the kingdom are those who forgive because they know what they were forgiven — at the cost of Christ’s blood.

What it rules out. “From your heart” rules out forgiveness announced and then followed by a relationship that is polite, correct and noticeably colder. It rules out keeping the file open in case it is needed later — the grievance not pressed but carefully preserved. And it questions “I have forgiven him but I will never forget,” which is sometimes an honest description of memory and sometimes a way of keeping the debt on the books.

What it doesn’t require. It doesn’t require a feeling; the servant’s failure wasn’t a shortage of warmth. It doesn’t require amnesia. It doesn’t require that trust be restored or that anyone put himself back within reach of harm (see on vv. 21–22). And it doesn’t require that it all be finished today. Forgiveness from the heart is a decision about what you will do with a debt, made once and renewed every time the memory comes back with the bill — which is why the number was seventy-seven and not one.

The frame. The chapter opens with “Who is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven?” and ends with forgiving a brother from the heart. Between stand a child in the middle, a millstone, a severed hand, a shepherd on the hills, three stages of correction, two or three in a front room, and a king with two debtors. Jesus never returns to the word “greatest.” He doesn’t need to. The answer is the one who forgives, because he has grasped what he was forgiven. They asked for a league table and were handed a mirror.

What the parable couldn’t show. The king cancelled ten thousand talents at no cost to himself but a line in a ledger. God’s forgiveness of our debt wasn’t arranged that way. The one telling this story was soon to set out for Jerusalem, and what it cost to cancel “the record of debt that stood against us” was not ink (Colossians 2:14). That is why the man who understands it can’t go out and choke anyone. A test: does your forgiveness of others look like the forgiveness you have received?

parallels.desc: if you do not forgive others

18.theology: Forgiveness and the gospel. Matthew 18:21–35 is among the most searching passages in the Gospels on the nature of Christian forgiveness. The parable does not ground forgiveness in the worthiness of the offender or the severity of the offence but in the prior, overwhelming forgiveness of God. This is the gospel logic of ethics: we forgive because we have been forgiven a debt we could never pay. The Reformers called this the indicative grounding the imperative — what God has done for us in Christ is the foundation and motive for what we are to do for one another. Forgiveness is not optional for the Christian; it is the evidence that the gospel has actually taken root in the heart.
18.examples:
Then: The disciples’ argument about greatness was entirely natural — they had left everything and wanted to know what the return on their investment would be. Jesus placed a child in their midst and dismantled their entire framework. The kingdom does not run on the world’s economy of status and reward.

Now: Church conflict is the great test of whether the gospel has penetrated the heart. It is easy to believe in forgiveness in the abstract; it is hard to forgive the specific person who sinned against you specifically. The unforgiving servant stands as a warning: the one who has truly received grace cannot hoard it. The debt we have been forgiven is always larger than the debt we are asked to forgive.

19.title: Marriage, Children, and the Rich Young Man
19.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when Jesus had finished these sayings, he went away from Galilee and entered the region of Judea beyond the Jordan. <sup>2</sup>And large crowds followed him, and he healed them there. <sup>3</sup>And Pharisees came up to him and tested him by asking, “Is it lawful to divorce one’s wife for any cause?” <sup>4</sup>He answered, “Have you not read that he who created them from the beginning made them male and female, <sup>5</sup>and said, ‘Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh’? <sup>6</sup>So they are no longer two but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate.” <sup>7</sup>They said to him, “Why then did Moses command one to give a certificate of divorce and to send her away?” <sup>8</sup>He said to them, “Because of your hardness of heart Moses allowed you to divorce your wives, but from the beginning it was not so. <sup>9</sup>And I say to you: whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another, commits adultery.” <sup>10</sup>The disciples said to him, “If such is the case of a man with his wife, it is better not to marry.” <sup>11</sup>But he said to them, “Not everyone can receive this saying, but only those to whom it is given. <sup>12</sup>For there are eunuchs who have been so from birth, and there are eunuchs who have been made eunuchs by men, and there are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. Let the one who is able to receive this receive it.” <sup>13</sup>Then children were brought to him that he might lay his hands on them and pray. The disciples rebuked the people, <sup>14</sup>but Jesus said, “Let the little children come to me and do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of heaven.” <sup>15</sup>And he laid his hands on them and went away. <sup>16</sup>And behold, a man came up to him, saying, “Teacher, what good deed must I do to have eternal life?” <sup>17</sup>And he said to him, “Why do you ask me about what is good? There is only one who is good. If you would enter life, keep the commandments.” <sup>18</sup>He said to him, “Which ones?” And Jesus said, “You shall not murder, You shall not commit adultery, You shall not steal, You shall not bear false witness, <sup>19</sup>Honor your father and mother, and, You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” <sup>20</sup>The young man said to him, “All these I have kept. What do I still lack?” <sup>21</sup>Jesus said to him, “If you would be perfect, go, sell what you possess and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.” <sup>22</sup>When the young man heard this he went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions. <sup>23</sup>And Jesus said to his disciples, “Truly, I say to you, only with difficulty will a rich person enter the kingdom of heaven. <sup>24</sup>Again I tell you, it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God.” <sup>25</sup>When the disciples heard this, they were greatly astonished, saying, “Who then can be saved?” <sup>26</sup>But Jesus looked at them and said, “With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.” <sup>27</sup>Then Peter said in reply, “See, we have left everything and followed you. What then will we have?” <sup>28</sup>Jesus said to them, “Truly, I say to you, in the new world, when the Son of Man will sit on his glorious throne, you who have followed me will also sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. <sup>29</sup>And everyone who has left houses or brothers or sisters or father or mother or children or lands, for my name’s sake, will receive a hundredfold and will inherit eternal life. <sup>30</sup>But many who are first will be last, and the last first.
19.overview:
Chapter 19 moves through three encounters that together form a sustained meditation on what it means to enter the kingdom. Marriage (vv. 1–12) is grounded in creation: the one-flesh union is God’s design, not a human arrangement, and cannot be dissolved at will. Children (vv. 13–15) are welcomed against the disciples’ protests: the kingdom belongs to those who come with empty hands. The rich young man (vv. 16–30) turns away sorrowful: he has great possessions, and they have him.

The three encounters build to the chapter’s most important theological statement: “With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible.” Salvation is not a human achievement; it is a divine act. The disciples’ astonished question — “Who then can be saved?” — is the right question, and Jesus’ answer is the heart of the gospel: not the most religiously qualified, not the wealthiest, not even the morally most impressive, but those in whom God himself works the miracle of new birth.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus leaves Galilee for Judea, healing crowds. The Pharisees test him with the divorce question: is it lawful to divorce for any cause? Jesus answers by returning to creation — one man, one woman, one flesh — and distinguishes Moses' concession from God's original design. The disciples are troubled; Jesus adds teaching on celibacy. Children are brought to Jesus; the disciples rebuke those who bring them; Jesus rebukes the disciples and pronounces the kingdom belongs to such as these. At the centre of the exchange stands the one exception he names — sexual immorality (v. 9) — and the section closes with him laying his hands on the children and going away (v. 15), the last thing he does in that place.
verseByVerse.theology: The divorce question was a live controversy in first-century Judaism between the school of Shammai (divorce only for sexual immorality) and the school of Hillel (divorce for any cause, including burning the food). Jesus does not take sides in the rabbinic debate; he goes behind Moses to creation. The "hardness of heart" that occasioned the Mosaic permission (Deut. 24:1) was always a concession to human sin, not God's design. Jesus restores the original standard: what God has joined, let not man separate. Verse 9 adds the one exception Jesus names, and it is not the whole of Scripture's teaching: Paul supplies a second ground, when an unbelieving spouse deserts (1 Cor 7:15), and the Reformed churches have long held these two and no others. But the exception is a fence, not a loophole — its purpose is to guard the one-flesh covenant against the hardness of heart that treats it lightly. That must be said in both directions. Nothing here requires anyone to remain in a house where they are being harmed: separation for safety is nowhere forbidden (1 Cor 7:11), a spouse who makes a home unsurvivable has deserted it in substance whoever physically leaves, and the previous chapter has already said what Christ thinks of the man who damages one of these little ones (18:6). See the verse-by-verse on vv. 9-10.
verseByVerse.examples: The episode with the children immediately follows the marriage and divorce discussion — the connection is not incidental. The children whom the disciples dismiss as unimportant are the very ones who most perfectly embody the kingdom: they have no legal standing, no social status, no achievement to present. "Of such is the kingdom of heaven" — the kingdom belongs to those who receive it as a child receives a gift, with open hands and no pretense of deserving. Verse 15 is easily read past and should not be. Straight after the disciples had turned these families away, the last recorded act of Jesus in that district is that he laid hands on their children while the parents who had been told off stood watching. The people who received the blessing are the ones who declined to be embarrassed out of the queue. But the verse is not a guarantee that every child of a believing home will come to faith, and a parent grieving over a grown son who wants none of it must not read it as a verdict on their parenting.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Jesus had finished these sayings, he went away from Galilee and entered the region of Judea beyond the Jordan. And large crowds followed him, and he healed them there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus sets his face toward Jerusalem and the cross, and he speaks God’s truth about marriage fearlessly, in the very territory where John died for saying it.

The turn to Jerusalem. “When Jesus had finished these sayings” is Matthew’s signal at the end of each of his five great blocks of teaching (7:28; 11:1; 13:53; here; 26:1). The Galilean teaching is finished; from here the road leads to Jerusalem. The healing goes on unchanged: “large crowds followed him, and he healed them there.” Nine words, and behind them hundreds of lives changed on an ordinary afternoon, none of them written down. Most of what Jesus did isn’t in the book, and what is in the book is enough (John 21:25).

The map. “Judea beyond the Jordan” is Perea, ruled by Herod Antipas. Antipas had imprisoned John the Baptist in Perea and beheaded him for saying, “It is not lawful for you to have her” (14:4) — a public verdict on Herod’s marriage. So when Pharisees meet Jesus here and ask whether it is lawful to divorce a wife, it isn’t an innocent enquiry. Matthew says they came “to test him.” They were inviting him to repeat, in Herod’s own district, the offence that cost the last preacher his head.

No hedging. Jesus doesn’t lower his voice, leave the district, or give an answer with room to wriggle. What follows is the strongest teaching on marriage in the Gospels, spoken within reach of the man who killed John. A test: is there a truth you soften because saying it plainly would cost you?
verseByVerse.note: “Judea beyond the Jordan” is Perea, the land east of the river, ruled by Herod Antipas.

verseByVerse.quote: And Pharisees came up to him and tested him by asking, "Is it lawful to divorce one's wife for any cause?" He answered, "Have you not read that he who created them from the beginning made them male and female,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus answers a question about the way out of marriage by pointing back to what marriage is: God’s creation of male and female for one another.

“For any cause.” This was a technical phrase. Deuteronomy 24:1 let a man divorce his wife if he found “some indecency” in her. The school of Shammai limited that to sexual sin. The school of Hillel read it to allow divorce for any matter at all, and the Mishnah records how far that went: a spoiled dish, or, Rabbi Aqiba added, finding another woman more attractive. Hillel’s view was the popular one, the one many men in that crowd had lived by. To answer as Jesus does was to tell a great many respectable men that what they had done was adultery.

The entrance, not the exit. They asked about the exit; he answered about the entrance. They wanted the conditions for ending a marriage; he told them what a marriage is. Every argument about how far a thing may be pushed is settled by going back to what it was for.

“Have you not read?” These were professional readers of Scripture, and Jesus asks them this several times (12:3, 5; 21:16, 42; 22:31). It never means they didn’t know the text. It means they knew it perfectly and had arranged their lives so it didn’t govern them. A man can know his Bible thoroughly and use his knowledge mainly to find out how much room he has.

Male and female. Jesus grounds marriage in creation, not culture: “he who created them from the beginning made them male and female,” he says, taking up Genesis 1:27. Marriage is one man and one woman. That excludes same-sex marriage, and it excludes polygamy, which the Old Testament records but never commends.

The question behind the question. When you find yourself asking how far you may go — how much you may keep, how long you may stay angry, what exactly counts as a lie — the question has already told you something. Nobody asks where the boundary is unless he is standing near it. A test: are you asking how close you can get to sin, or what God made you for?
verseByVerse.note: Rabbis debated the grounds for divorce: some allowed it for almost any cause, others only for sexual immorality.

parallels.desc: male and female he created them

verseByVerse.quote: "and said, 'Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh'? So they are no longer two but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, let not man separate."
verseByVerse.commentary:
In marriage God himself joins a man and a woman into one flesh, so no human hand should tear apart what he has made one.

One flesh. It doesn’t mean the couple are close or well suited. It means what was two has become one, so they can no longer be separated, only torn. A partnership can be dissolved and both partners walk away whole. Cutting one flesh in two produces two halves, and they bleed for years. Anyone who has been through divorce, or watched a friend go through it, knows this, and has often been told they should be over it by now.

God joins. “Joined together” is the word for yoking — two animals under one beam, pulling the same load. And the subject is God. That settles a quiet question: is a marriage begun without God a real marriage? Two unbelievers before a registrar with no prayer said are, on this sentence, joined by God. He does the yoking whether or not he was invited to the wedding.

“Let not man separate.” This isn’t only addressed to the couple. It reaches the judge who grants divorce lightly, the friend who has spent months saying she deserves better, the parent who never accepted the marriage, the colleague who makes the affair easy. There are usually more hands on a broken marriage than the couple’s.

Leave, then hold fast. Genesis puts leaving first: “a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife” (Genesis 2:24). Much trouble in early marriage is a leaving problem: a husband who still runs decisions past his mother, a wife whose father is still the final court of appeal, a couple whose holidays are still arranged by someone else. You can’t glue something that is still attached to where it was fixed before. A test: have you truly left, so that you can hold fast?

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him, "Why then did Moses command one to give a certificate of divorce and to send her away?" He said to them, "Because of your hardness of heart Moses allowed you to divorce your wives, but from the beginning it was not so."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s law made allowance for hardened hearts, but what the law permits never lowers what God made marriage to be.

Commanded or allowed? They said Moses “command[ed]” a certificate of divorce; Jesus says he “allowed” it. That is the argument over. They had taken a permission and promoted it to a duty, which is what a hard heart always does with a concession: tolerated becomes normal, normal becomes expected, and soon the concession is quoted as though it were the command.

What Deuteronomy actually says. Deuteronomy 24:1–4 is one long sentence. Divorce appears only in the conditions — if he divorces her, and she marries another, and the second husband divorces her or dies. The command comes in verse 4: the first husband may not take her back. Moses wasn’t legislating divorce but regulating a remarriage. The Pharisees had built a licence out of a subordinate clause. And the certificate itself protected the woman: without it, a discarded wife couldn’t prove she was free and could be accused of adultery if she remarried. They had turned her shield into his sword.

Your hardness. Jesus doesn’t say “their” hardness, as though of a generation long dead, but “your,” to the men in front of him. Hardness of heart isn’t weakness or confusion but a heart gone stiff. The concession was made because men were like that, and are.

Should a nation have divorce laws? If divorce law is a concession to sin, is it wrong for a country to have any? No; Jesus doesn’t abolish the provision he has just put in its place. God legislates for the world as it is without lowering what he made it for. But that the law permits a thing settles nothing about whether you should do it. You can be fully within your legal rights and standing exactly where Jesus locates the hard heart. A test: are you using what is legal as a reason not to ask what is right?

verseByVerse.quote: And I say to you: whoever divorces his wife, except for sexual immorality, and marries another, commits adultery." The disciples said to him, "If such is the case of a man with his wife, it is better not to marry."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Marriage is binding for life, and divorce and remarriage are allowed only where the marriage has already been broken by sexual immorality or desertion — yet grace meets the broken and the church must protect the endangered.

The exception. “Except for sexual immorality” — adultery and sexual sin of the same gravity. Such sin breaks the covenant and frees the innocent party. Apart from that, divorce and remarriage is adultery. The disciples’ reaction, “it is better not to marry,” shows how high Jesus has set the bar: marriage carries the permanence of God’s own covenants.

Why don’t Mark and Luke have the exception? Mark and Luke record none: “Whoever divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery” (Mark 10:11; cf. Luke 16:18). Some say Matthew softened his Lord. But people state rules plainly without repeating every known qualification. Mark and Luke give the principle in its blunt force; Matthew, writing for Jewish readers for whom the Shammai–Hillel debate was a daily argument, records the qualification Jesus made because his readers would ask. Neither denies what the other says.

When may a divorced person remarry? Some hold that remarriage is never allowed while a former spouse lives. Their reasons are serious: Mark and Luke have no exception; Paul says “a married woman is bound by law to her husband while he lives” (Romans 7:2); and many in the early church held it. Others read the exception only of unfaithfulness during betrothal. The historic Reformed reading is the more likely: Jesus’ exception is a real exception, and Paul adds a second ground — when an unbelieving spouse leaves, “the brother or sister is not enslaved” (1 Corinthians 7:15). So, with the Westminster Confession, adultery and wilful desertion are the two grounds on which the innocent party is free to remarry. The exception permits divorce; it doesn’t command it. Where there is repentance, reconciliation is the better way.

Must an abused wife stay? No, and vagueness here has cost real people dearly. First, separation for safety is nowhere forbidden. Paul speaks of a wife who has separated and tells her to “remain unmarried or else be reconciled” (1 Corinthians 7:11), attaching no shame to the separating. Getting out of reach of a dangerous man isn’t a step toward divorce; it is a step toward staying alive, and often the first thing that has ever cost him anything, and so made repentance possible. Second, protecting the children is obedience; the Lord who forbids easy divorce warned of the millstone for those who harm little ones (18:6). Third, a husband who makes a home unsurvivable has deserted the marriage as truly as one who packs a bag; he has only arranged for his wife to do the walking. Older Reformed pastors judged desertion by its substance, not by who left the house. Such a case should be taken to the church’s elders, not settled alone (18:15–20). A church that sends a woman home to try harder, or weighs a man’s standing against what she has described, has been careless with a life. And abuse is a crime to report to the authorities (Romans 13:4).

What if I divorced wrongly, or before I was a Christian? The guilty party who repents is called to remain single or be reconciled (1 Corinthians 7:11), though Reformed churches differ on remarriage in that case. Those already remarried shouldn’t break up the second marriage; it is a real marriage. The call is to repent of how it began and live faithfully in it. “Commits adultery” describes how the second marriage began, not a sin repeated every day it continues.

Grace for the broken. None of this is a loophole to be worked; it is a fence around something holy. And to anyone whose marriage has broken — by your sin, another’s, or both — there is no sin here that the blood of Christ doesn’t cover. The gospel meets us not in the marriage we should have had but in the life we actually have. Christ’s whole aim in this passage is to make marriage the one place on earth where a person is safe for life; a reading that shuts someone inside cruelty has turned his fence into a cage. A test: are you guarding your marriage as something God himself has joined?

verseByVerse.quote: But he said to them, "Not everyone can receive this saying, but only those to whom it is given. For there are eunuchs who have been so from birth, and there are eunuchs who have been made eunuchs by men, and there are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. Let the one who is able to receive this, receive it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Singleness for the kingdom is a real calling from God, not a waiting room for life to begin, and the church must be family to those who live it.

Three kinds. Some are unable to marry from birth; some were made so by others, through circumstances outside their control and in the ancient world often by cruelty; and some give up marriage “for the sake of the kingdom of heaven.” Jesus names all three together and honours the calling in all three. Its dignity isn’t reserved for volunteers.

What the third kind means. It is figurative: those who renounce marriage for the kingdom, not those who mutilate themselves. Nor does it require ministers to be unmarried; Peter had a wife (8:14; 1 Corinthians 9:5), and Paul expects overseers to be husbands (1 Timothy 3:2). The “eunuchs… from birth” are those born unable to marry; the text is about that incapacity, not sexual orientation.

The “gift” of singleness? Many single Christians didn’t choose this and would exchange it tomorrow: the woman who hoped to marry and is now fifty, the widower, the divorced believer who won’t remarry, the believer whose convictions about sexuality close marriage to him. Told it is a gift, they may feel asked to be grateful for a loss. But in the New Testament a gift is grace given for a purpose, not a pleasure guaranteed. Paul’s thorn was no delight, and what he was promised was “My grace is sufficient for you” (2 Corinthians 12:9). So what is promised isn’t that you will like it, but that there is grace enough, that it is a real vocation, and that it isn’t a lesser life. The most fully human person who ever lived was single, and so was the apostle who wrote most of the New Testament (1 Corinthians 7:32–35).

What the church owes. Later in this chapter Jesus promises those who have left family for his sake a hundredfold (v. 29) — Mark spells out “brothers and sisters and mothers and children” now (Mark 10:30). That is a debt the church must pay. A congregation that preaches marriage constantly and has no place at its tables for the unmarried has left half its members outside its Lord’s promise. If you carry singleness as a grief, say so to God and to someone who won’t rush you; Scripture never calls such sorrow unbelief. A test: who in your church needs a seat at your table?
verseByVerse.note: A eunuch was a man unable to marry or father children. Some, like Paul, remained single to serve the kingdom.

parallels.desc: a name better than sons and daughters

verseByVerse.quote: Then children were brought to him that he might lay his hands on them and pray. The disciples rebuked the people, but Jesus said, "Let the little children come to me and do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus welcomes little children and rebukes those who treat them as a distraction, for the kingdom belongs to such as these.

Don’t hinder them. Parents bring children for prayer, and the disciples rebuke them; children aren’t worth the Master’s time. Jesus says, “Let the little children come to me and do not hinder them, for to such belongs the kingdom of heaven.” The only people rebuked in this story are those who thought children an interruption to the real work. A church that treats its little ones as something to manage until they are old enough to matter has been told, by name, to stop.

Do infants who die go to heaven? This verse doesn’t say children are innocent; Jesus has just said we must become like them, not that they are sinless (18:3). But it shows his welcome, and Scripture gives grieving parents real hope. David said of his dead infant, “I shall go to him” (2 Samuel 12:23), and the Reformed confessions teach that elect infants dying in infancy are saved by Christ through the Spirit, who works when and where he pleases. Many Christians are confident that the Judge of all the earth will do right by every child who dies before it can believe. No verse says so in plain words, but we have the character of the God who said, “Let the little children come to me.”

Should infants be baptized? Those who say yes point to this scene — Luke says they were babies (Luke 18:15) — and set it beside the covenant sign given to Abraham’s children (Genesis 17:7), “the promise is for you and for your children” (Acts 2:39), and the household baptisms in Acts. Those who say no answer that Jesus blesses these children; he doesn’t baptize them, and every baptism the New Testament describes follows a profession of faith. That point lands. This passage doesn’t settle the question, and the wider covenant case for infant baptism is less convincing than the plain New Testament pattern of baptism after faith. So we hold to believer’s baptism, while welcoming our children warmly as Christ did. A test: do the children in your church know they are wanted?

verseByVerse.quote: And he laid his hands on them and went away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ personally blesses the children brought to him, so parents should keep bringing their children to him without being embarrassed out of it.

The sequence. The disciples had just been turning these families away. Jesus’ last act before leaving the district was to lay his hands on their children, one by one — not something done in a moment — while parents who had been told off by the inner circle watched.

Who brought them. Somebody thought it worth the walk in the heat with small children on the chance of getting near. When the men closest to Jesus told them they were wasting his time, they didn’t take the children home. Those who received the blessing were the ones who wouldn’t be embarrassed out of the queue.

Bring them. For parents and grandparents the instruction is simple and not sentimental. Put them where Christ is, week after week, when it is inconvenient, when they are difficult, when they say they would rather not. Pray with your hand on them, aloud, using their names. And don’t be argued out of it by anyone who implies the serious work of the church is elsewhere; that argument was made once in this passage by better men, and it was publicly overruled.

Not a guarantee. This isn’t a promise that every child of a believing home will come to faith. Scripture is honest about godly parents whose children went their own way. A parent grieving over a grown son who wants nothing to do with Christ shouldn’t read these verses as a verdict on their parenting or a promise that failed. What is here is Christ’s disposition toward children — warm, unhurried, personal — and that hasn’t changed for a man of forty who was once carried to him. Keep praying.

And went away. He blessed them and left for Jerusalem. Matthew doesn’t tell us what became of one of those children. The blessing wasn’t a promise of a smooth life; it was a real thing done by real hands on a man’s way to the cross. A test: are you bringing the children in your life to Christ in prayer?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–30 — The Rich Young Man and the Great Reversal
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A young man asks what good deed will earn eternal life. Jesus directs him to the commandments; he claims to have kept them all. Jesus says: sell your possessions, give to the poor, and follow me. The man goes away sorrowful, for he has great wealth. Jesus says it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom. The disciples are astonished. Jesus promises rewards for those who have left everything to follow him, and closes with the great reversal: the first shall be last and the last first. Two exchanges inside the section carry more weight than their length. Jesus meets the opening question with one of his own — why do you ask me about what is good, when there is only one who is good (v. 17)? And after the camel and the needle, Peter asks what the Twelve, who did leave everything, will have for it (v. 27); the promise of thrones and a hundredfold is his answer, and verse 30 is the warning attached to it.
verseByVerse.theology: The rich young man's failure reveals the nature of the commandment he thought he kept: "love your neighbor as yourself" (v. 19) was the final commandment in Jesus's list, and the sell-everything command is the test of whether it is actually operative. One cannot love one's neighbor as oneself while sitting on wealth that could address their need. The commandment was kept in its visible form (no theft, no fraud) but not in its spirit (genuine love that costs something). Jesus's diagnosis is precise: the man's wealth is not neutral; it is the specific obstacle between him and eternal life. Verse 17 is regularly produced as proof that Jesus denied being God — he pointed away from himself, so he cannot have thought himself divine. But he does not say I am not good. He asks a question, and the question is a door: you have called goodness a deed you can perform and me a teacher who knows the trick, and there is only One who is good, so think again about what you are asking and whom you are asking. The rest of the Gospel will not let the denial stand — this is the man who forgives sins as only God can (9:2-6), who says the Lord of the Sabbath is standing here (12:8), and who claims all authority in heaven and on earth (28:18).
verseByVerse.examples: The disciples' astonishment at the camel-and-needle saying reflects their assumption that wealth is a sign of divine blessing — the standard view. Jesus upends the assumption: wealth is a spiritual obstacle, not an advantage. The camel through the needle's eye is not a metaphor for difficulty but for impossibility — making the way of salvation clear. "With God all things are possible" is the only resolution: the rich man cannot save himself; only God can accomplish the transformation that makes a rich man enter the kingdom. Guard that promise, since it has been lifted off the page and attached to whatever a reader happens to want. The word this has an antecedent, and the antecedent is the salvation of a rich man; it is not a general assurance that anything is obtainable with enough belief. And Matthew has left the proof at the far end of his book. When the crucifixion is over, a man comes to Pilate for the body — and Matthew alone tells us he was rich, plousios, the same word used here of the man who cannot get in (27:57). The needle did not widen and the camel did not shrink. God did the thing he said only God could do.

verseByVerse.quote: And behold, a man came up to him, saying, "Teacher, what good deed must I do to have eternal life?" And he said to him, "Why do you ask me about what is good? There is only one who is good. If you would enter life, keep the commandments."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eternal life isn’t earned by a good deed, because only God is good, and the law shows us how far short we fall.

A transaction. “What good deed must I do to have eternal life?” He treats eternal life as something to secure by an action. Jesus answers, “Why do you ask me about what is good? There is only one who is good.” Goodness isn’t a deed in your hand; it belongs to God. And this man has come, without knowing it, to the one place where God’s goodness stands in human flesh.

Did Jesus deny he was God? This is often quoted that way. But Jesus doesn’t say “I am not good.” He asks a question that is a door: you talk of goodness as a trick a teacher can tell you; only One is good, so think about what you are asking and whom. The rest of the Gospel won’t let a denial stand: he forgives sins as only God can (9:2–6), calls himself Lord of the Sabbath (12:8), receives worship without refusing it (14:33), and claims all authority in heaven and on earth (28:18). Mark and Luke have “Why do you call me good?” (Mark 10:18); Matthew gives the exchange in a compressed form, as he often does, but the point is the same.

Salvation by works? “If you would enter life, keep the commandments.” Does that teach salvation by works? No. Perfect obedience would bring life, but no sinner can offer it: “by works of the law no human being will be justified in his sight” (Romans 3:20; cf. Galatians 3:10–12). Jesus uses the law to expose this man’s need, which is why he will say that salvation is impossible with man but possible with God (v. 26). A test: are you still hoping your good deeds will be enough?
verseByVerse.note: Mark and Luke record the question as “Good Teacher.” Luke calls him a ruler.

verseByVerse.quote: He said to him, "Which ones?" And Jesus said, "You shall not murder, You shall not commit adultery, You shall not steal, You shall not bear false witness, Honor your father and mother, and, You shall love your neighbor as yourself."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A religion of ticking off prohibitions can feel complete, but God’s law demands love from the heart — and Jesus exposes what this man had put in God’s place.

“Which ones?” The question gives him away. He has turned the law into a syllabus and wants to know what is on the exam, so he can tick it off and know where he stands. It is the most common way to hold a religion, comfortable because a list can be finished.

What Jesus leaves out. He recites commandments about our neighbour — murder, adultery, theft, false witness, honouring parents — and stops. He omits “You shall not covet,” and he doesn’t touch the commandments about God at all: no other gods, no idols. Those omissions are exactly this man’s problem. He has another god and is holding it with both hands. Jesus gives a list with the man’s own sin carefully removed, lets him say he has kept them all, and then asks for the one thing the missing commandments were about — as Nathan let David pass sentence before saying, “You are the man” (2 Samuel 12:7).

What he adds. He ends with a command not in the Ten Commandments: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Leviticus 19:18), which he will call the second great commandment (22:39). Every other item on the list can be kept by sitting still; a man asleep keeps five of them. This one can’t be kept by not doing something, and it has no upper limit.

Your own list. Asked what you got wrong last week, you would likely name things you did — a lost temper, a sharp reply, a lie. Few would name the person they didn’t visit, the money they didn’t give, the conversation they avoided because it would cost an evening. A conscience built only of prohibitions can be satisfied by half past ten in the morning. A test: what good have you left undone?

In his defence. “All these I have kept” may not have been a lie by the standard he had been given. That is what makes him frightening: not a hypocrite caught out, but a decent, careful, religious man who had done all he understood he was asked, knew something was still missing, and had the honesty to say so to the one person who could tell him what.
verseByVerse.note: Jesus lists the commandments about one’s neighbour and adds Leviticus 19:18.

parallels.desc: the second table of the Ten Commandments

verseByVerse.quote: The young man said to him, "All these I have kept. What do I still lack?" Jesus said to him, "If you would be perfect, go, sell what you possess and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ puts his finger on the one thing that holds our heart in place of him, and asks for it so that our hands are free to follow him.

“What do I still lack?” His honest question is the most hopeful thing about him. Jesus answers with no rule about percentages, but a command aimed at this man’s particular obstacle: “sell what you possess and give to the poor… and come, follow me.” It isn’t a universal command; Zacchaeus gave half (Luke 19:8), and believers in Jerusalem still owned property (Acts 5:4). It is the precise identification of what stood between this man and the kingdom.

Is there a higher class of Christian? Some have taught that “If you would be perfect” describes a higher grade of disciple, bound by vows of poverty and celibacy. No. “Perfect” means complete, wholehearted devotion, the word of 5:48. The call is to every disciple; what it costs differs from person to person.

What is mine? So the question isn’t how much is enough but what is mine. And the man already knew; nobody asks what he still lacks unless something has been nagging at him. Most of us, sitting still a minute, can name what we would least like Christ to ask for. It isn’t always money: a relationship pulling you away, a career that has become the point of your life, your reputation, plans for your children, an addiction you manage rather than end, a grudge you have decided to keep, the fear of what people would say. The tell is the flinch. And the test isn’t “would I be willing in principle” — principle costs nothing — but what happens when the thing is named and asked for.

Not confiscation. Read the whole sentence: sell, give, “and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.” He isn’t impoverishing the man but prising his fingers off something small so his hands are free for something enormous.

If you can’t let go. Six verses later, when the disciples ask who can be saved, Jesus doesn’t say “those strong enough to let go,” but “With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible” (v. 26). If you have found your one thing and can’t open your hand, you haven’t failed the test; you have arrived where the gospel starts. Bring that inability to him. A test: what would you least like Christ to ask of you?

verseByVerse.quote: When the young man heard this he went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions. And Jesus said to his disciples, "Truly, I say to you, only with difficulty will a rich person enter the kingdom of heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Being moved is not the same as obeying, and wealth endangers the soul by quietly removing our felt need of God.

The one who said no. Jesus personally invites him: “come, follow me,” the words that emptied a fishing boat and a tax booth. He is the one man in Matthew who receives that call and declines. Fishermen left nets; a tax collector left a table with money on it; this man went home. Matthew never tells us his name.

Sorrowful. He went away sorrowful, which means he knew Jesus was right. He felt everything a man ought to feel, and did nothing. Grief isn’t repentance. A person can be moved almost to tears on Sunday, know the sermon describes his own life, and have changed nothing by Wednesday — then mistake being moved for the change. The most dangerous heart here isn’t the hard one but the softened one that goes home anyway.

Can a rich person be saved? By world standards most readers of English commentaries are rich. Jesus doesn’t say a rich man can’t be saved, but “only with difficulty,” and then that with God all things are possible. Scripture is full of wealthy believers: Abraham, Job, the women who supported Jesus out of their means (Luke 8:3). This is a warning about a specific danger, not a sentence.

The danger named. Money isn’t evil; it quietly removes the daily experience of dependence. A man who can solve most problems by paying for them will, over twenty years, stop asking anyone for anything, and never notice, because every decision was sensible. He didn’t rebel against God; he just stopped needing him for anything specific, and faith with nothing specific in it goes thin without ever being renounced (1 Timothy 6:17).

A ten-second test. When did you last pray about something money couldn’t also fix? For many comfortable people, the honest answer is health and the people they love. That is why illness and bereavement are so often where God is finally met: they are the rooms in a wealthy life where a cheque does nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: Again I tell you, it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God." When the disciples heard this, they were greatly astonished, saying, "Who then can be saved?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Salvation is humanly impossible for anyone, and only when we stop believing some people obviously qualify can we hear that with God all things are possible.

A camel and a needle. It is impossible on purpose: the largest animal in the land through the smallest opening anyone knew. Two softenings have been tried. One is a gate in Jerusalem called “the Eye of the Needle,” a much later legend with no ancient support. The other is a handful of late manuscripts that read “rope” for “camel,” one letter different in Greek — a copyist’s improvement. Both pull the same way, to make the sentence survivable. The rabbis had their own version, an elephant through a needle’s eye, for the plainly impossible. Everyone knew it was a joke about impossibility, and nobody laughed.

“Who then can be saved?” The disciples believed, on what looked like a plain reading of Deuteronomy 28, that prosperity showed God’s favour. And this rich man was also young, morally serious, careful about the commandments, and humble enough to ask a travelling rabbi what he lacked. He was the strongest candidate they had ever seen. So their question isn’t which of the wealthy can be saved, but who at all. They had just watched the front-runner walk away.

No one obviously qualifies. Most of us keep a private category of people who obviously qualify — the missionary, the pastor’s wife, the old woman who has prayed for forty years. While that category exists, salvation stays plausible and someone else’s problem. Jesus abolishes the category; not one name survives. That isn’t cruelty but clearing the ground. Nobody hears that with God all things are possible until he has stopped believing that with men some things are. Their astonishment is the first right reaction anyone has had in this chapter. A test: is there anyone you think deserves salvation — including yourself?
verseByVerse.note: The camel was the largest animal in the land; the picture is deliberate exaggeration. The idea of a gate called “the Eye of the Needle” is a much later invention.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus looked at them and said, "With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible." Then Peter said in reply, "See, we have left everything and followed you. What then will we have?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
What no person can do — unfasten a heart from its idols and bring it into the kingdom — God does, and he is not indifferent to what his followers give up for him.

He looked at them. Matthew records that Jesus looked at them before he answered. A dozen frightened men were held in his gaze for a moment before they heard the sentence that would settle them.

The staircase removed. The chapter has been about what a man must do: keep the commandments, which ones, sell, come. Now: “With man this is impossible.” The young man asked what good deed he must do, and the final answer is that there is no deed. He asked the right person and went home six verses before the answer came.

What “all things” means. This sentence has been printed on posters and attached to whatever the reader hopes for. But “this” is the salvation of a rich man. It isn’t a promise that anything you want is obtainable if you believe hard enough; it is the promise that the one thing truly impossible — unfastening a heart welded to its possessions — is what God does. It echoes the question to Sarah: “Is anything too hard for the LORD?” (Genesis 18:14). There the impossibility was biological, and the answer was a baby.

A rich disciple. Matthew has left the proof at the end of his book. After the crucifixion, “there came a rich man from Arimathea, named Joseph, who also was a disciple of Jesus” (27:57). Mark calls him a respected member of the council, Luke good and righteous; only Matthew says he was rich, using the word of this passage. The needle didn’t widen and the camel didn’t shrink; God did what only God can do.

“What then will we have?” Peter’s question is honest and slightly grubby, and Jesus doesn’t rebuke it; he answers it at length. Christianity isn’t indifferent to reward. A piety that claims to want nothing isn’t more spiritual than Peter, only less truthful; Jesus himself told them to lay up treasure in heaven (6:19–21). The trouble isn’t the wanting but the word “we.” Peter has just watched another man fail and has begun to compare. A test: do you serve Christ looking to him for reward, or looking sideways at others?

parallels.desc: is anything too hard for the LORD?

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus said to them, "Truly, I say to you, in the new world, when the Son of Man will sit on his glorious throne, you who have followed me will also sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. And everyone who has left houses or brothers or sisters or father or mother or children or lands, for my name's sake, will receive a hundredfold and will inherit eternal life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who give up anything for Christ will receive far more — a renewed world and, even now, a family a hundred times larger in his church.

The new world. The word means rebirth or regeneration, used elsewhere of a person (Titus 3:5). What happens to a Christian is going to happen to the world: the renewal of all things at Christ’s return (Revelation 21:5). And “judging” the tribes recalls Israel’s judges, who ruled and rescued rather than merely passed sentence; the promise is nearer to governing than condemning.

Who are the twelve tribes, and when? Premillennial readers take this of ethnic Israel in a future earthly kingdom. The more likely reading is that it describes the renewal of all things at Christ’s return, and that the twelve tribes stand for the whole people of God, as the new Jerusalem has twelve gates named for the tribes and twelve foundations named for the apostles (Revelation 21:12–14).

Judas in the room. “You who have followed me will also sit on twelve thrones” is said to twelve men, one of whom would sell him. Jesus addresses the apostles as a body; Acts shows the empty seat filled by another (Acts 1:20–26). But don’t hurry past it: it is possible to stand inside the circle to whom the promise is made, hear it addressed to you, and not be in it.

A hundredfold of what? This verse has been used to promise that God repays giving a hundred times in cash. Read what is surrendered — houses, brothers, sisters, father, mother, children, lands — and what is received: the same things. It isn’t a hundred houses for one, but a family a hundred times larger for one lost, which is what the church is when it works properly. Mark spells it out: “houses and brothers and sisters and mothers and children and lands, with persecutions” (Mark 10:30).

Someone is paying this cost. The convert from Islam whose family holds a funeral for him while he is alive. The young woman whose marriage, inheritance and place at the table are gone the day she is baptized. For them this verse is the promise they staked everything on. And the only place on earth it can be handed over is a congregation. This doesn’t license neglecting family; Jesus condemned that (15:3–6), and Paul says it denies the faith (1 Timothy 5:8). It describes the cost when loyalty to Christ and to family collide. A test: is anyone receiving their hundredfold through you?
verseByVerse.note: “The new world” is the renewal of all things at Christ’s return.

parallels.desc: I am making all things new

verseByVerse.quote: But many who are first will be last, and the last first.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the kingdom God decides the order, so neither long service nor late arrival fixes anyone’s place, and those just promised thrones must beware pride most of all.

Many, not all. He doesn’t say all who are first will be last. A mechanical inversion would only be the same league table upside down, and people enjoy that rather too much — as anyone knows who has met the Christian quietly proud of having nothing to be proud of. It is a warning, not a formula.

Where it falls. This doesn’t follow the rich man’s departure but Peter’s “What then will we have?” and the enormous answer: thrones, a hundredfold, eternal life. The men most in danger of finishing last are the men just promised they will be first. He hands them the throne and immediately warns them what being handed a throne does to a man.

A hinge. Chapter 20 opens with the labourers in the vineyard and ends with this saying reversed: “So the last will be first, and the first last” (20:16). Between the brackets stands a story of men who worked all day and couldn’t be glad at the wage given to those who worked an hour.

For the long-serving. It lands on the veteran more than the newcomer: the man of thirty years who can’t rejoice when a six-month convert is given what he assumed would come to him; the unwritten seniority no church admits to and every member could recite; the faithful couple who say no one knows what this church has cost them — who are telling the truth and are in more danger for it. God doesn’t forget long service (v. 29). It just doesn’t establish a place in the queue.

For the latecomer. The one who came late, wasted the years others were building, and is privately certain he belongs at the back is the one this was spoken to encourage. He isn’t told his lateness doesn’t matter; he is told who decides the order. A test: are you counting your years of service, or rejoicing in God’s grace to others?

parallels.desc: the same saying ends the next parable

19.theology: Monergism and the impossibility of self-salvation. Matthew 19:26 is the clearest statement in this Gospel of the Reformed doctrine of monergism: God alone works the miracle of salvation; unaided human will cannot accomplish it. The rich young man is not an extreme case; he represents every human being before the grace of God. His idolatry is more visible than most, but every person has a god that competes with Christ. The new birth — God’s sovereign act of grace that overcomes the resistance of the sinful will — is what makes it possible for anyone to sell all, follow Christ, and inherit eternal life. This is the good news hidden inside the severe word: with God, even this is possible.
19.examples:
Then: The rich young man came running (Mark 10:17) — he was eager, sincere, morally serious. He went away sorrowful. Sincerity and moral seriousness are not sufficient for salvation. Only the miracle of grace is sufficient.

Now: Every generation has its version of the young man’s idol — wealth, reputation, career, family, comfort, security. Jesus’ question to every person is the same: what is the one thing you are not willing to surrender? That is the idol that must go. The command is not an obstacle to grace; it is the exposure of where grace needs to go.

20.title: First and Last
20.text: <sup>1</sup>“For the kingdom of heaven is like a master of a house who went out early in the morning to hire laborers for his vineyard. <sup>2</sup>After agreeing with the laborers for a denarius a day, he sent them into his vineyard. <sup>3</sup>And going out about the third hour he saw others standing idle in the marketplace, <sup>4</sup>and to them he said, ‘You go into the vineyard too, and whatever is right I will give you.’ <sup>5</sup>So they went. Going out again about the sixth hour and the ninth hour, he did the same. <sup>6</sup>And about the eleventh hour he went out and found others standing. And he said to them, ‘Why do you stand here idle all day?’ <sup>7</sup>They said to him, ‘Because no one has hired us.’ He said to them, ‘You go into the vineyard too.’ <sup>8</sup>And when evening came, the owner of the vineyard said to his foreman, ‘Call the laborers and pay them their wages, beginning with the last, up to the first.’ <sup>9</sup>And when those hired about the eleventh hour came, each of them received a denarius. <sup>10</sup>Now when those hired first came, they thought they would receive more, but each of them also received a denarius. <sup>11</sup>And on receiving it they grumbled at the master of the house, <sup>12</sup>saying, ‘These last worked only one hour, and you have made them equal to us who have borne the burden of the day and the scorching heat.’ <sup>13</sup>But he replied to one of them, ‘Friend, I am doing you no wrong. Did you not agree with me for a denarius? <sup>14</sup>Take what belongs to you and go. I choose to give to this last worker as I give to you. <sup>15</sup>Am I not allowed to do what I choose with what belongs to me? Or do you begrudge my generosity?’ <sup>16</sup>So the last will be first, and the first last.” <sup>17</sup>And as Jesus was going up to Jerusalem, he took the twelve disciples aside, and on the way he said to them, <sup>18</sup>“See, we are going up to Jerusalem. And the Son of Man will be delivered over to the chief priests and scribes, and they will condemn him to death <sup>19</sup>and deliver him over to the Gentiles to be mocked and flogged and crucified, and he will be raised on the third day.” <sup>20</sup>Then the mother of the sons of Zebedee came up to him with her sons, and kneeling before him she asked him for something. <sup>21</sup>And he said to her, “What do you want?” She said to him, “Say that these two sons of mine are to sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your kingdom.” <sup>22</sup>Jesus answered, “You do not know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I am to drink?” They said to him, “We are able.” <sup>23</sup>He said to them, “You will drink my cup, but to sit at my right hand and at my left is not mine to grant, but it is for those for whom it has been prepared by my Father.” <sup>24</sup>And when the ten heard it, they were indignant at the two brothers. <sup>25</sup>But Jesus called them to him and said, “You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. <sup>26</sup>It shall not be so among you. But whoever would be great among you must be your servant, <sup>27</sup>and whoever would be first among you must be your slave, <sup>28</sup>even as the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” <sup>29</sup>And as they went out of Jericho, a great crowd followed him. <sup>30</sup>And behold, there were two blind men sitting by the roadside, and when they heard that Jesus was passing by, they cried out, “Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David!” <sup>31</sup>The crowd rebuked them, telling them to be silent, but they cried out all the more, “Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David!” <sup>32</sup>And stopping, Jesus called them and said, “What do you want me to do for you?” <sup>33</sup>They said to him, “Lord, let our eyes be opened.” <sup>34</sup>And Jesus in pity touched their eyes, and immediately they recovered their sight and followed him.
20.overview:
Chapter 20 is structured around the inversion of worldly values. The parable of the workers in the vineyard opens with the same reversal that closed chapter 19: “the last will be first, and the first last.” Those hired at the eleventh hour receive the same wage as those who worked all day. The vineyard owner’s generosity is not unfair to the all-day workers (he pays exactly what was agreed) but it offends their sense of merit-based distribution. The parable is not about labour economics but about grace: God owes nothing to anyone; every denarius of salvation is sheer mercy.

The third passion prediction follows (vv. 17–19), and immediately James and John’s mother requests the seats of honour. Jesus responds with the kingdom’s law of greatness: the leader is the servant, the first is the slave. He grounds it in his own mission: “the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” This is the only place in Matthew where Jesus explicitly calls his death a ransom. The chapter closes with two blind men healed on the Jericho road — men who call him “Son of David” and, having received their sight, follow him on the road to Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — The Parable of the Laborers in the Vineyard
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The parable of the workers hired at different hours — dawn, nine, noon, three, and five — all receiving the same denarius wage at day's end. Those hired first complain; the owner insists he has done them no wrong and is free to be generous with his own resources. "So the last will be first, and the first last." The parable illustrates the preceding reversal saying and the nature of God's grace: it is not a reward calculated by duration of service but a gift determined by sovereign generosity. Two mechanics inside the story carry it. Only the dawn workers negotiate a figure; everyone hired later goes into the vineyard on the owner's character alone, with no number (vv. 3-4, 7). And the owner instructs that the last be paid first (v. 8) — he could have paid in the obvious order and bought the dawn men's contentment for nothing, and instead he arranges for them to watch.
verseByVerse.theology: The parable's offense is intentional: the all-day workers' complaint is understandable by any standard of fairness. They worked more; they should receive more. The owner's response demolishes the complaint: he paid exactly what was agreed; his generosity to others does not diminish what they received. The problem is not injustice but envy — "is your eye evil because I am good?" The evil eye (stinginess, grudging spirit) cannot tolerate grace extended to others. The parable indicts the spirit of religious entitlement that calculates reward rather than receiving grace. Two further things the parable does deliberately. It sets the wage by need rather than by output: a denarius was a day's keep for a household, and an hour's honest pay would have sent the last man home with enough for nobody. There is only one wage in the story because there is only one thing God has to give, and eternal life does not come in grades. And the men who grumble are the only men on the estate with a figure in their heads — a man holding a contract can be disappointed, while a man trusting a person cannot, since the promise was kept. Note too that the eleventh-hour men are not blamed for their idleness: because no one has hired us (v. 7) stands without qualification.
verseByVerse.examples: The owner of the vineyard represents God, whose generosity is not constrained by human calculations of desert. Those hired last — with no track record, no extended service, no obvious claim — receive the same gift as those who bore the burden and heat of the day. This is the gospel: the deathbed convert and the lifelong believer receive the same eternal life, because eternal life is not a wage proportional to service but a gift given by the one who owns the vineyard. The men left standing have a name in every congregation: the long-term unemployed, the believer converted at sixty who does the arithmetic and concludes he has nothing to bring, the chronically ill Christian who cannot do the things his church visibly counts. And notice the direction of travel in every scene — not one labourer in the parable finds his own way to the vineyard. Each is there because the owner came down to the market and found him standing.

verseByVerse.quote: "For the kingdom of heaven is like a master of a house who went out early in the morning to hire laborers for his vineyard. After agreeing with the laborers for a denarius a day, he sent them into his vineyard.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The kingdom is like a master who goes out himself, again and again, to bring workers into his vineyard — a parable about the character of God before it is about the workers.

The marketplace at dawn. A day labourer owned nothing but his hands. He came to the square before dawn and stood where he could be seen; if he was hired, his family ate that night, and if not, they didn’t. The law assumed that knife-edge: a hired man must be paid before sunset, “for he is poor and counts on it” (Deuteronomy 24:15). That is why everyone in this parable is paid at evening, and why standing unhired at five in the afternoon isn’t an inconvenience but a disaster with a family attached.

An ordinary bargain. The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage. Nothing generous has happened yet. The master pays the going rate, agrees it openly, and sends them in. The story begins as ordinary business, which is why the ending lands so hard.

He went out. This man has a foreman (v. 8), yet he walks down to the market himself at dawn, then at nine, noon, three, and five in the afternoon, when barely an hour of light is left and no sane employer is hiring. Five times in one day the owner comes out to the square where the unwanted men stand. Every scene turns on a man going out again.

The vineyard. Israel had been God’s vineyard since Isaiah’s song (Isaiah 5:1–7). So the grumblers to come aren’t outsiders resenting the church; they are inside the vineyard and have worked in it since dawn.

Is a deathbed conversion real? Yes. The thief on the cross received all of salvation in his last hours (Luke 23:43), and the eleventh-hour workers receive the same wage. But nothing here licenses delay. The late workers went the moment they were called, and “now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6:2).

Like a person. Jesus doesn’t say the kingdom is like a wage system but “like a master of a house.” Every question of fairness will be answered not with a principle but with a man. A test: when you think of God’s kingdom, do you think first of rules, or of him?
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that a denarius was a day’s wage for a labourer. The working day ran from sunrise to sunset.

parallels.desc: do not hold back a hired worker’s wages overnight

verseByVerse.quote: And going out about the third hour he saw others standing idle in the marketplace, and to them he said, "You go into the vineyard too, and whatever is right I will give you." So they went.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who follow Christ go on his word and character, not on terms, and a heart that deals with God by contract will end up bitter when he is generous to others.

No figure. Something changes at nine o’clock that the parable doesn’t point out. The dawn men had negotiated a denarius. These men are offered no figure at all: “whatever is right I will give you.” They have a promise and a person, and no number. And they go — a considerable thing for a man with nothing at home, on a stranger’s word. Every group after the first enters on the owner’s character rather than on terms; only one group has a contract.

Contract or trust. That turns out to be the difference between the men content at evening and the men bitter. A man holding a contract can feel cheated. A man trusting a person has nothing to measure the outcome against but the one who promised, and the promise was kept. The dawn workers weren’t cheated of a penny; they were simply the only men with a figure in their heads, and by evening the figure had become a grievance.

The tell. Few Christians would say they deal with God on terms, but many do. The tell is what rises when things go badly. The man on a contract says, after all these years, after all I gave up, after the way I kept myself. The man trusting a person is bewildered and frightened and keeps trusting, because his confidence was never in the arithmetic. A test: which was closer to your words the last time God didn’t do what you expected?

Not against agreements. The dawn men did nothing wrong in agreeing to a denarius; the master will honour it to the penny. The trouble comes when we carry a contract into a relationship that was never contractual and then read every kindness God shows someone else as a clause we have been denied.
verseByVerse.note: The third hour was about 9 a.m.

verseByVerse.quote: Going out again about the sixth hour and the ninth hour, he did the same. And about the eleventh hour he went out and found others standing. And he said to them, "Why do you stand here idle all day?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God goes out to the overlooked and passed-over, and no one is ever in his kingdom because he found his own way there — every worker was sought and found.

Still coming. Noon, then three, and the master keeps coming out. Then the eleventh hour, five o’clock, with the day ending at six, and men are still standing there.

The standing. They had been in that square since before dawn. Four times they had watched an employer walk in, look along the line, choose others and leave. By mid-afternoon a man has stopped arranging his face; he stays only because going home is worse.

The question. “Why do you stand here idle all day?” sounds like an accusation but isn’t; their answer satisfies him and he hires them at once. It is the question of a man who has walked up to people nobody has spoken to all day and asked what happened.

Every church has them. The man out of work so long that sympathy has run out. The believer converted at sixty who does the arithmetic on the years and concludes he has nothing to bring. The chronically ill Christian who can do none of the things his church visibly counts. The person never picked first for anything, who has built a theology out of it. If you think the useful part of your life is behind you and you arrived too late to matter, this is the hour you were hired in.

Who went out? Not one man in the parable finds his way to the vineyard. Nobody applies or knocks at the estate. Every labourer is there because the owner came down to the market and found him. So it is with salvation: “we love because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19). A test: do you see your faith as your search for God, or his search for you?
verseByVerse.note: The sixth hour was about noon, the ninth about 3 p.m., the eleventh about 5 p.m. — an hour before the day ended.

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him, "Because no one has hired us." He said to them, "You go into the vineyard too." And when evening came, the owner of the vineyard said to his foreman, "Call the laborers and pay them their wages, beginning with the last, up to the first."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God doesn’t hide his generosity to others to keep us comfortable; he lets us see it, so that what rises in our hearts can be exposed and healed.

“Because no one has hired us.” That is the whole answer, and the parable lets it stand. They weren’t lazy or hiding; they had been available since dawn, and the market had chosen others. The parable isn’t sentimental about idleness, but it refuses to blame them for what was done to them. “You go into the vineyard too” — no interview, not even a promise of what is right. There is an hour left; go and have it.

Last to first. Then the most deliberate sentence in the parable: “beginning with the last, up to the first.” Pay the dawn men first and they go home satisfied, never knowing what happened at the end of the line. The master could have bought their contentment for nothing by paying in the obvious order.

A diagnosis. He arranges for them to watch instead. That isn’t carelessness or cruelty but diagnosis. God doesn’t conceal his kindness to others to keep us comfortable. He lets us see what he has given someone else, because what rises in us then is the truest thing anyone could tell us about ourselves, and until it rises it can’t be dealt with.

When you find out. Remember that the next time you learn what someone else was given. The news didn’t reach you by accident or to make you miserable. It came the way a doctor sends a man for a scan. A test: what does your reaction to someone else’s blessing reveal about your heart?

parallels.desc: give him his wages on the same day

verseByVerse.quote: And when those hired about the eleventh hour came, each of them received a denarius. Now when those hired first came, they thought they would receive more. But each of them also received a denarius.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Eternal life is given by grace according to our need, not measured out by our output, and much of our disappointment with God is over promises he never made.
