Their arithmetic. The dawn men’s reasoning wasn’t stupid. One hour has been paid a denarius; twelve hours at that rate is twelve. They weren’t greedy, just consistent.

A day’s keep. But a denarius wasn’t lavish; it was what a family needed to reach tomorrow. The eleventh-hour man had earned about a twelfth of it, and a twelfth would have fed nobody. So the master doesn’t pay what his hour was worth; he pays what his household needs. The wage isn’t set by output but by need, and there is the shape of the gospel in a coin.

Only one wage. That is also why the dawn men can’t be given twelve. There is only one wage, and it is the whole of what the master has to give. Eternal life doesn’t come in grades; there is no larger portion of God for someone who has been at it longer, because God isn’t a quantity you accumulate. The first workers were given everything there is, the same as the last, and it felt like an insult only because they thought of it as pay.

“They thought.” “They thought they would receive more.” They supposed it; nobody had told them. The master made one promise and kept it exactly. The extra eleven denarii existed only in their heads.

Promises he never made. Much of the disappointment Christians carry with God is over things he never said. He didn’t promise that marriage would be easy because you waited, that the child raised in the faith would keep it, that years of service would be recognised, or that the diagnosis would go the other way. Somewhere along the way an arrangement got built that he was never party to, and when it didn’t come, it felt like a broken promise. A test: go through your grievance item by item and ask which of these God actually said.

verseByVerse.quote: And on receiving it they grumbled at the master of the house, saying, "These last worked only one hour, and you have made them equal to us who have borne the burden of the day and the scorching heat."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Envy takes nothing from us but our joy, turning God’s kindness to others into a grievance, and its cure begins by calling it sin.

A fair-sounding complaint. Twelve hours in the summer heat against one hour in the cool of evening, and the same pay? By human standards it sounds fair. It is the complaint of every religious person who has done the right thing for decades and then sees a late convert receive the same grace — like the elder brother watching the calf killed for the prodigal (Luke 15:28–30).

Nothing had happened to them. Their wage hadn’t been cut or their hours lengthened. The coin in their hand was the coin they had been content to work for all day. One thing changed: they saw somebody else’s pay.

The mechanism of envy. Envy has never made anyone better off, including the envious. It can’t take anything from you; it can only change how you feel about what you have, and it is very good at that. A man happy at dawn is bitter by dusk with the same denarius in his pocket.

The Christian version. Someone comes to faith at fifty and seems to have skipped the decades you spent under obedience. Someone else’s ministry flourished while yours didn’t. Someone got the marriage, the child, the health, the easier road — and where gladness should be, you notice a small, persistent coldness.

The cure. The master’s question can be borrowed: “Did you not agree with me for a denarius?” Go back to what you were actually given. Then do three things. Name it to God as sin, not as a grievance, since it always presents itself as a grievance, and that disguise is why it survives so long in respectable people. Thank him specifically for your own denarius. And pray for the person by name, asking God to give them more of the very thing you envy. It is nearly impossible, and it works. A test: whose blessing do you find hard to rejoice in?

verseByVerse.quote: But he replied to one of them, "Friend, I am doing you no wrong. Did you not agree with me for a denarius? Take what belongs to you and go. I choose to give to this last worker as I give to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God wrongs no one, and he gives freely because he wants to — but whoever insists on strict justice from God will receive exactly that.

“Friend.” It isn’t as warm as it sounds in English. Matthew uses this word as a form of address only three times: here, to the grumbler; to the guest without a wedding garment, just before he is thrown out (22:12); and to Judas in Gethsemane with the kiss on his face: “Friend, do what you came to do” (26:50). Each time it is spoken courteously to a man in the wrong. It is the word for someone you still treat civilly when both of you know what he is doing.

No case. “I am doing you no wrong. Did you not agree with me for a denarius?” Every fact is on the master’s side. The wage was named before the work, the work done, the wage paid in full and on time. The grievance isn’t that he got too little but that someone else got the same.

Take it and go. “Take what belongs to you and go.” He gets exactly what he bargained for and is dismissed with it. Nothing more is coming, because he asked for terms and has been given terms. Someone who insists on strict justice from God will receive strict justice, and it is hard to think of anything more frightening to be granted. The eleventh-hour men went home with the same coin and something the grumbler never touched: they knew it was a gift.

“I choose.” “I choose to give to this last worker as I give to you” — I will it, I want to. Not because he is obliged or the accounts require it. That is the only reason the parable gives for the eleventh-hour denarius, and no other reason is given anywhere in Scripture for why God saves anyone (Ephesians 1:5).

Still talking to him. This isn’t God turning cold. He doesn’t have the man removed or answer through the foreman. He comes to him personally, addresses him courteously, reasons step by step, and asks him two questions — more patience than the complaint deserved. A test: do you come to God asking for your rights, or for his grace?

verseByVerse.quote: "Am I not allowed to do what I choose with what belongs to me? Or do you begrudge my generosity?" So the last will be first, and the first last.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The real problem isn’t God’s generosity but our evil eye, which can turn bitter at his goodness — while grace given to one never makes it thinner for another.

An evil eye. The ESV notes that “do you begrudge my generosity?” is literally “is your eye bad because I am good?” In Scripture a good eye is generous and a bad eye grudging, unable to bear giving or seeing others given to (Deuteronomy 15:9; Proverbs 28:22). Jesus used the same picture in the Sermon: “if your eye is bad, your whole body will be full of darkness” (6:23), in a passage about money. The problem isn’t the wage; it is the eye that looked down the line.

Because I am good. Notice how the sentence runs. Not “because he is undeserving,” but “because I am good.” God’s goodness is what provoked the reaction. That goes deeper than a charge of greed: something in us can be made bitter by God being kind where we didn’t expect him to be.

His own. “Am I not allowed to do what I choose with what belongs to me?” This isn’t a God who does as he likes and calls it righteous; the master has already shown he wronged no one before he appeals to his rights. Sovereign generosity isn’t caprice. But it isn’t negotiable either (Romans 9:15–16). And grace doesn’t get thinner when shared; nobody in that line got less because someone else got something.

The brackets. “So the last will be first, and the first last” turns around the saying at 19:30, so the parable sits between brackets. It is the worked example of what Jesus said to twelve men just promised thrones who had immediately started counting.

No differences of reward? Does the one denarius mean there are no differences of reward in heaven? The wage everyone receives is eternal life, God himself, the same for all. Other texts speak of different rewards and responsibilities (Luke 19:17–19; 1 Corinthians 3:12–15), but those rewards are themselves grace, and no one in heaven will envy another.

The mercy in it. If the kingdom paid by the hour, the eleventh-hour man would have almost nothing, and the dawn man would spend eternity knowing exactly how much he had earned. Both would be unbearable. The master gives everyone the whole day’s keep and shuts the ledger, and the only man who goes home unhappy is the one who kept it open. A test: have you shut the ledger?
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that “do you begrudge” is literally “is your eye bad” — an idiom for envy.

parallels.desc: I will have mercy on whom I have mercy

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–34 — The Third Passion Prediction, the Mother's Request, and Two Blind Men
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the road to Jerusalem, Jesus gives the fullest passion prediction yet: delivered to the Gentiles, mocked, flogged, crucified, raised. Immediately the mother of James and John asks for her sons to sit at Jesus's right and left in his kingdom. Jesus corrects the request: greatness is service, and the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve and to give his life as a ransom for many. Two blind men at Jericho cry out "Son of David, have mercy on us" and receive their sight. Between the request and the healing the other ten turn on the two brothers (v. 24) — not from principle but because they wanted the same thing and were beaten to it — and Jesus answers all twelve rather than the two who asked.
verseByVerse.theology: The timing of the mother's request — immediately after the passion prediction — reveals the distance between the disciples' understanding and Jesus's reality. He has just announced crucifixion; she asks for thrones. The response of Jesus is not irritated dismissal but patient teaching: "You do not know what you are asking." The cup he must drink and the baptism he must undergo are not metaphors for achievement but for suffering. The right and left are not his to give; they are the Father's appointment. The contrast between the Gentile rulers who "lord it over" others and the Son of Man who gives his life is the most concentrated leadership theology in the Gospels. Two things guard it from becoming a slogan. Jesus does not abolish ambition: the sentence is whoever would be great among you, and only the object of the wanting is changed. And the standard is not an attitude but a cross — he does not say be like a servant, he says the Son of Man came to serve and to give his life as a ransom for many. The many of v. 28 is Isaiah's word for a multitude nobody could number (Isa 53:11-12), not a word that fences people out.
verseByVerse.examples: The two blind men at Jericho echo the two blind men of 9:27-31. The title "Son of David, have mercy on us" is the messianic title of chapter 9, and it elicits the same response: Jesus stops, asks, heals. Their sight is the last healing miracle before the triumphal entry — a fitting preparation for Jerusalem. Those who cry "Son of David" will soon hear the crowds cry "Hosanna to the Son of David." The blind who gain sight anticipate the seeing of what Jerusalem refuses to see. Matthew also asks the same question twice in this chapter, and the two answers are the spine of it: What do you want? to the mother of James and John (v. 21), and What do you want me to do for you? to the beggars (v. 32). One asks for the two best seats in the kingdom; the other asks for eyes. And in both Jericho scenes the obstacle between a needy person and Christ is the crowd already following him — as it was with the children in the previous chapter (19:13).

verseByVerse.quote: And as Jesus was going up to Jerusalem, he took the twelve disciples aside, and on the way he said to them, "See, we are going up to Jerusalem. And the Son of Man will be delivered over to the chief priests and scribes, and they will condemn him to death"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus walked toward the cross with open eyes, naming it plainly to his friends, and he was handed over both by sinful men and by God’s own plan.

Going up. This is literal. Jericho lies far below sea level in the Jordan valley, and Jerusalem high in the hills; the road climbs steeply for about fifteen miles through bare rock and ravines. They are climbing in a crowd of Passover pilgrims, and the man at the front knows exactly what waits at the top. So he takes the Twelve aside on the crowded road to tell them quietly. He doesn’t want them to hear it later or from anyone else.

More exact each time. This is the third prediction, and each is more specific. At 16:21 it was suffering and being killed; at 17:22–23, being delivered into the hands of men. Now it is condemnation by the chief priests and scribes, handing over to the Gentiles, mocking, flogging — and crucifixion, named for the first time.

Looking at it. We usually manage dread by not looking at it: keeping the appointment vague, not asking the doctor the second question, leaving the letter unopened. Jesus named what was coming, in detail, three times, to people who didn’t want to hear, and then set his face toward the hill and kept climbing (Luke 9:51). His strength for Jerusalem didn’t come from refusing to look at Jerusalem. A test: what are you refusing to face that you need to bring to God?

Delivered by whom? “The Son of Man will be delivered over.” Judas, the council and Pilate will each do it and answer for it. But Peter later says the rest: he was “delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God” (Acts 2:23). Both are true at once. Nobody forced him up that road.
verseByVerse.note: Jerusalem stands high in the hills; one always went “up” to it.

verseByVerse.quote: "and deliver him over to the Gentiles to be mocked and flogged and crucified, and he will be raised on the third day."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ suffered the full shame and pain of the cross at the hands of both Jew and Gentile, and the resurrection he always promised didn’t depend on his disciples understanding it.

The weight of the words. Mocked, flogged, crucified — familiarity has worn them smooth. “Mocked” means what Matthew later shows: a scarlet robe over a torn back, a crown of thorns, a reed for a sceptre, soldiers kneeling in mock homage before they spat (27:28–31). “Flogged” is the Roman scourge, which men sometimes didn’t survive. And crucifixion was so shameful that Cicero said the very word should be kept from Roman ears. It was the death for slaves and rebels — worth carrying nine verses on, where the same man tells his friends that whoever would be first must be a slave.

Both had a part. The chief priests and scribes condemn; the Gentiles mock, flog and crucify. Jew and Gentile, the covenant people and the nations, each contribute to the same cross. No one stands outside it, which is the point when the ransom is named in verse 28 (Acts 4:27).

The fifth verb. “And he will be raised on the third day.” Three predictions, and every one ends with resurrection, yet the disciples remember none of it. At the tomb the angel doesn’t break news but reminds: “He is not here, for he has risen, as he said” (28:6).

Not depending on us. That is a strange comfort. The men closest to him heard all three predictions and fell apart when it happened. Their failure to understand didn’t derail a single detail. He wasn’t depending on their grasp to get it done, and he isn’t depending on yours. A test: do you trust Christ’s work more than your understanding of it?
verseByVerse.note: This third prediction is the first to name crucifixion.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the mother of the sons of Zebedee came up to him with her sons, and kneeling before him she asked him for something. And he said to her, "What do you want?" She said to him, "Say that these two sons of mine are to sit, one at your right hand and one at your left, in your kingdom."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ambition for privilege can sit right beside the cross, even in a mother’s prayer, and Christ sees whose request it really is.

The request. The mother of James and John kneels and asks that her sons sit at his right and left in his kingdom — the places of highest honour, first and second minister. It comes straight after the most detailed prediction of the cross. Jesus has named crucifixion, and the family of Zebedee asks for thrones.

Mother or sons? In Mark, James and John come and ask for themselves (Mark 10:35). Which was it? Some say Matthew moved the words to their mother to spare the apostles. That is unlikely. Matthew doesn’t spare people; he records Peter called “Satan” (16:23), all the disciples fleeing (26:56), and his own name as “Matthew the tax collector” (10:3). And his own account shows the sons behind it: Jesus replies with plural verbs addressed to them, the sons answer, “We are able,” and the ten are indignant “at the two brothers” (v. 24). Both accounts are true. The sons wanted the thrones and sent their mother to ask. Matthew tells you who spoke; Mark tells you whose ambition it was. Comparing the women at the cross, she may be Salome (27:56; Mark 15:40).

Asking for them. There is something touching in a mother’s ambition for her sons, and something dangerous. Many parents pray more for their children’s success than for their faithfulness. A test: when you pray for those you love, do you ask for their prominence, or for their likeness to Christ?
verseByVerse.note: In Mark the brothers ask for themselves. Comparing the women at the cross, their mother may be Salome.

parallels.desc: the mother of the sons of Zebedee at the cross

verseByVerse.quote: Jesus answered, "You do not know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I am to drink?" They said to him, "We are able." He said to them, "You will drink my cup, but to sit at my right hand and at my left is not mine to grant, but it is for those for whom it has been prepared by my Father."
verseByVerse.commentary:
To follow Christ is to share his cup of suffering, and our place in his kingdom is the Father’s gift, not something won by lobbying — which frees us from comparison.

The cup. “Are you able to drink the cup that I am to drink?” In the prophets the cup isn’t hardship in general but God’s judgment: “in the hand of the LORD there is a cup with foaming wine… and all the wicked of the earth shall drain it down to the dregs” (Psalm 75:8); Isaiah calls it “the cup of his wrath” (Isaiah 51:17). So he isn’t asking whether they can cope with a hard road. He is telling them what he is going to Jerusalem to receive — not chiefly nails, but the wrath of God against sin, drained by one who never deserved a drop (26:39).

“We are able.” Brave, sincere, and spoken with no idea what they had volunteered for. Jesus doesn’t call them liars; they will drink his cup, though not its wrath, which he drinks alone. They drank it in two very different forms. James was the first apostle martyred, killed with the sword by Herod Agrippa (Acts 12:2). John, by early tradition, lived long and died old after exile on Patmos (Revelation 1:9). One short and violent, one long and lonely. The cup isn’t one flavour, and a Christian given the slow version shouldn’t conclude he was given the easy one.

Not mine to grant. This isn’t Jesus disclaiming authority; he will claim “all authority in heaven and on earth” (28:18). It is the Son declining to act outside the Father’s arrangement. And position in the kingdom isn’t open to lobbying. There is no queue and no case to put, and the sooner we believe that, the freer we are from exhausting comparison. It cuts the other way too: if your place can’t be secured by asking, it can’t be lost by someone else asking.

Right and left. When Jesus entered his kingdom by way of the cross, there were men on his right and left — two criminals on crosses (27:38). James and John had asked for places no one would want if they understood. A test: are you seeking a place, or willing to share his cup?
verseByVerse.note: The “cup” is an Old Testament picture of God’s judgment poured out.

verseByVerse.quote: And when the ten heard it, they were indignant at the two brothers. But Jesus called them to him and said, "You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The world’s way of power presses down on those beneath, and Jesus rejects it for everyone who follows him — the indignant as well as the ambitious.

The ten. The ten aren’t indignant from moral superiority; they are angry because two tried to get ahead first. They all wanted the same thing. So Jesus speaks to all twelve. Nobody got to hear this as advice for someone else.

Lording it over. “The rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them.” Both verbs carry a prefix meaning “down upon”: they press their lordship and authority down on those beneath. Crushing people with the weight of your position is the world’s pattern, and Jesus describes it without a flicker of admiration.

Ambition redirected. He doesn’t abolish ambition: “whoever would be great among you” lets the wanting stand and changes its object. James and John aren’t rebuked for wishing to matter, but for misunderstanding what mattering is. A Christian isn’t required to want nothing, but the right thing — a towel rather than a throne.

Authority still matters. This isn’t the abolition of authority. Jesus gave commands, appointed leaders, rebuked error and made decisions; a leader who won’t lead isn’t humble but leaves people unshepherded. Servant leadership is authority used for the good of those under it, “not domineering over those in your charge, but being examples to the flock” (1 Peter 5:3).

The worse failure. The more common failure is the man who wears “servant leader” as a title while making every decision alone, resenting challenge, and demanding loyalty from everyone beneath him. He has kept what Jesus forbade and borrowed the vocabulary of what he commanded — worse than the Gentile rulers, who at least didn’t pretend. A test: how do you use whatever authority you have — at home, at work, in church?

verseByVerse.quote: "It shall not be so among you. But whoever would be great among you must be your servant, and whoever would be first among you must be your slave," "even as the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Greatness in Christ’s kingdom is service, because the Son of Man came to serve and to give his life as a ransom, paying the price of our freedom in our place.

Servant and slave. “It shall not be so among you.” A servant waits at table, doing unglamorous work for others’ comfort. A slave owns no rights at all — not his time, preferences, reputation or plans for the afternoon. Jesus uses both, in ascending order, the opposite of the way careers usually travel.

Tests of a servant. A servant is available; he doesn’t control his diary as a master does. He does work no one sees or thanks him for, and keeps doing it. He can be interrupted. And the sharpest test: you can tell a servant by how he behaves when he is treated like one. Anyone can use the language while quietly requiring deference; the truth shows when the deference isn’t given.

A ransom. And this isn’t mere advice, because the standard is a cross: “even as the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” A ransom was the price paid to free a slave or a captive. The word “for” here means “in place of”: his life given instead of ours. The ransom isn’t paid to Satan, as some early writers speculated, but satisfies the justice of God. And “many” echoes Isaiah’s servant, who would “make many to be accounted righteous” and “bore the sin of many” (Isaiah 53:11–12).

For many, or for all? “Many” isn’t a word that shuts people out; in Hebrew idiom it means the multitude, and Paul moves between “the many” and “all” freely (Romans 5:15–19). But a real question lies underneath. Scripture says the ransom is “for many,” and elsewhere that Christ “gave himself as a ransom for all” (1 Timothy 2:6). Many believers read the “all” texts to mean Christ died to make salvation possible for every person. The Reformed answer is that a ransom isn’t an offer but a payment: money laid down for prisoners doesn’t make them releasable; it releases them. If Christ’s death only made salvation possible for all and certain for none, it would be a ransom paid that might leave the captive in his cell. So we hold that the cross actually secured the freedom of those it was given for — a people purchased, not merely an opportunity: “the church of God, which he obtained with his own blood” (Acts 20:28; cf. Ephesians 5:25). The “all” of 1 Timothy 2 means all kinds of people, Jew and Gentile, kings and slaves. Those who read it otherwise are brothers, and the disagreement should be held with respect.

Not a gate to check. This doctrine has been used to frighten people it was meant to comfort. No one is ever asked to work out first whether he is one of the many. The invitation is unrestricted: “let the one who desires take the water of life without price” (Revelation 22:17). You discover you were among the many the way the eleventh-hour workers found they were in the vineyard: by coming when called and being handed the wage. It is the discovery afterward that the price of your freedom was paid before you thought to ask. A test: have you come to him?
verseByVerse.note: A ransom was the price paid to free a slave or captive.

parallels.desc: he bore the sin of many

verseByVerse.quote: And as they went out of Jericho, a great crowd followed him. And behold, there were two blind men sitting by the roadside, and when they heard that Jesus was passing by, they cried out, "Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David!" The crowd rebuked them, telling them to be silent, but they cried out all the more, "Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Desperate need cries out to Christ and won’t be silenced, and the people most likely to stand in the way are often those already following him.

Two, or one? Matthew has two blind men; Mark names one, Bartimaeus (Mark 10:46). This is Matthew’s habit, as at the tombs of the Gadarenes (8:28): Mark and Luke fix on the one memorable man, while Matthew notes there were two. One never denies a second.

Leaving or entering Jericho? Matthew and Mark place it as Jesus left Jericho; Luke as he drew near (Luke 18:35). One likely explanation is that there were two Jerichos about a mile apart: the ruined old city of Joshua’s day and the new Jericho Herod had built nearby. Leaving one and approaching the other, both descriptions could be true of one moment. Other explanations have been offered; none requires a contradiction.

The crowd. It isn’t officials or Romans who tell them to be quiet, but the crowd following Jesus up the road. Matthew has shown this once already, when the disciples turned away the families with children (19:13). Twice in two chapters the obstacle between a needy person and Christ is the group already committed to him.

Who learned to keep quiet? Every congregation has ways of signalling that some people make things difficult: the man whose questions hold everything up, the woman whose crisis has gone on too long, the family with loud children, the person whose need is chronic and won’t turn into a testimony. Nobody says “be quiet.” The crowd probably thought it was helping, keeping the road clear for an important man. A test: who has learned to keep their voice down in your church, and who taught them?

All the more. The rebuke made them louder. They had nothing left to lose and knew exactly how much they needed. But persistence isn’t a lever that moves a reluctant God; Jesus is never reluctant in this story. Persistence in prayer is what real need looks like from outside. They kept calling because they had no alternative and had worked out who was passing by.

Son of David. Two men who could see nothing shouted the one true title on that road — “Son of David,” the King promised to David (2 Samuel 7:12–13) — while a crowd with perfect eyesight told them to stop. Within days Jerusalem would ring with the same title, and soon after with something else entirely.
verseByVerse.note: Jericho lay about 15 miles east of Jerusalem, near the Jordan. Mark names one of the men, Bartimaeus.

verseByVerse.quote: And stopping, Jesus called them and said, "What do you want me to do for you?" They said to him, "Lord, let our eyes be opened."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ stops for the needy even under the greatest pressure, and his question “What do you want me to do for you?” shows what we really ask for when we pray.

He stopped. He is in a column of pilgrims going up to the Passover where he will be killed. He has just described what waits at the top. The crowd is large and moving and has tried to silence these men. And he stops. The procession waits while the Son of David attends to two men everyone had classed as an interruption. If you want to know what he is like under the greatest pressure anyone has ever known, the answer is: he stops.

The same question twice. Matthew puts the same question twice in one chapter. To the mother of James and John: “What do you want?” (v. 21). To two beggars: “What do you want me to do for you?” Same questioner, same courtesy, two very different answers. One asks for the two best seats in the kingdom. The other asks for eyes.

A good request. The mother asked for something that would put her sons above the others. The blind men asked for something they couldn’t get anywhere else or pretend to have. It wasn’t modest; opening blind eyes was something the Old Testament reserved for God: “the LORD opens the eyes of the blind” (Psalm 146:8). It was enormous, and simply honest.

What would you ask? If he stopped, called you and asked what you want him to do for you, what would actually come out? Most of us would hear ourselves asking for something nearer the thrones than the eyes: for the situation to go our way, for the person wrong about us to be proven wrong, for the recognition or the outcome. That isn’t a reason to despair but a reason to ask him for better wants, which is itself a prayer of the second kind.

Why ask? He could see they were blind; so could the whole road. He asks anyway, because he won’t treat a man as a case to process when he can treat him as a person to speak to. A test: what do you truly want Christ to do for you?

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus in pity touched their eyes, and immediately they recovered their sight and followed him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ’s compassion moves him to touch and heal, and those whose eyes he opens follow him even on the road to the cross.

Pity first. Matthew tells us what moved before what happened: “Jesus in pity” — the word used of his compassion for crowds like sheep without a shepherd (9:36) and for the hungry four thousand (15:32). The compassion comes before the healing.

He touched them. He didn’t have to. He healed a centurion’s servant at a distance (8:13) and a Canaanite woman’s daughter by a word (15:28). So the touch wasn’t for the miracle but for the men. Two beggars who had spent the morning being told to be quiet, and the first thing that happens is a pair of hands on their faces. Whatever they had been in that town — a fixture, a noise, something to step around — they weren’t that to him.

And followed him. Followed him where? Up the road he had just described: to a flogging and a cross. These are the last people Jesus heals before Jerusalem, and they use their new eyes to follow him into the passion. The Twelve, told three times, were arguing about seats; the crowd was going up for a festival. Two beggars, blind an hour before, saw who he was and went with him.

One movement. The chapter opens with a landowner who walks down to the market himself at dawn and goes back at nine, noon, three and five for men nobody had chosen. It closes with the Son of Man stopping a procession on the way to his own death because two beggars the crowd had silenced were crying for mercy. The parable said that is what the owner of the vineyard is like; the Jericho road shows him doing it (Luke 19:10). A test: now that he has opened your eyes, are you following him?

20.theology: The atonement as ransom. Matthew 20:28 is Matthew’s clearest statement of substitutionary atonement. The word “ransom” (lytron) carries the weight of a payment that secures release — it is used in the Septuagint for the price paid to redeem a slave or a firstborn. Jesus applies it to his own death: he gives his life as the price that sets the many free from their captivity to sin, death, and judgment. Reformed theology has always insisted that the atonement is primarily objective — it actually accomplishes something in the divine court (the cancellation of debt, the satisfaction of justice) — before it is subjective (inspiring us, moving us, transforming us). The ransom is paid; the captives are free.
20.examples:
Then: James and John wanted the best seats. They had left everything (19:27) and felt entitled to the premium return. Jesus redefines the currency: greatness is measured in service and suffering, not in position and honour. The Twelve would spend the rest of their lives learning this.

Now: The parable of the workers challenges every theology of spiritual merit — the idea that longer service, greater sacrifice, or more faithful obedience earns a greater share of God’s favour. Grace cannot be earned; it can only be received. The workers who grumble are those who have forgotten that any wage at all is mercy. The appropriate response to grace is gratitude, not calculation.

21.title: The King Enters Jerusalem
21.text: <sup>1</sup>Now when they drew near to Jerusalem and came to Bethphage, to the Mount of Olives, then Jesus sent two disciples, <sup>2</sup>saying to them, “Go into the village in front of you, and immediately you will find a donkey tied, and a colt with her. Untie them and bring them to me. <sup>3</sup>If anyone says anything to you, you shall say, ‘The Lord needs them,’ and he will send them at once.” <sup>4</sup>This took place to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet, saying, <sup>5</sup>“Say to the daughter of Zion, ‘Behold, your king is coming to you, humble, and mounted on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a beast of burden.’” <sup>6</sup>The disciples went and did as Jesus had directed them. <sup>7</sup>They brought the donkey and the colt and put on them their cloaks, and he sat on them. <sup>8</sup>Most of the crowd spread their cloaks on the road, and others cut branches from the trees and spread them on the road. <sup>9</sup>And the crowds that went before him and that followed him were shouting, “Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest!” <sup>10</sup>And when he entered Jerusalem, the whole city was stirred up, saying, “Who is this?” <sup>11</sup>And the crowds said, “This is the prophet Jesus, from Nazareth of Galilee.” <sup>12</sup>And Jesus entered the temple and drove out all who sold and bought in the temple, and he overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those who sold pigeons. <sup>13</sup>He said to them, “It is written, ‘My house shall be called a house of prayer,’ but you make it a den of robbers.” <sup>14</sup>And the blind and the lame came to him in the temple, and he healed them. <sup>15</sup>But when the chief priests and the scribes saw the wonderful things that he did, and the children crying out in the temple, “Hosanna to the Son of David!” they were indignant, <sup>16</sup>and they said to him, “Do you hear what these are saying?” And Jesus said to them, “Yes; have you never read, “‘Out of the mouth of infants and nursing babies you have prepared praise’?” <sup>17</sup>And leaving them, he went out of the city to Bethany and lodged there. <sup>18</sup>In the morning, as he was returning to the city, he became hungry. <sup>19</sup>And seeing a fig tree by the wayside, he went to it and found nothing on it but only leaves. And he said to it, “May no fruit ever come from you again!” And the fig tree withered at once. <sup>20</sup>When the disciples saw it, they marveled, saying, “How did the fig tree wither at once?” <sup>21</sup>And Jesus answered them, “Truly, I say to you, if you have faith and do not doubt, you will not only do what has been done to the fig tree, but even if you say to this mountain, ‘Be taken up and thrown into the sea,’ it will happen. <sup>22</sup>And whatever you ask in prayer, you will receive, if you have faith.” <sup>23</sup>And when he entered the temple, the chief priests and the elders of the people came up to him as he was teaching, and said, “By what authority are you doing these things, and who gave you this authority?” <sup>24</sup>Jesus answered them, “I also will ask you one question, and if you tell me the answer, then I also will tell you by what authority I do these things. <sup>25</sup>The baptism of John, from where did it come? From heaven or from man?” And they discussed it among themselves, saying, “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say to us, ‘Why then did you not believe him?’ <sup>26</sup>But if we say, ‘From man,’ we are afraid of the crowd, for they all hold that John was a prophet.” <sup>27</sup>So they answered Jesus, “We do not know.” And he said to them, “Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things. <sup>28</sup>“What do you think? A man had two sons. And he went to the first and said, ‘Son, go and work in the vineyard today.’ <sup>29</sup>And he answered, ‘I will not,’ but afterward he changed his mind and went. <sup>30</sup>And he went to the other son and said the same. And he answered, ‘I will, sir,’ but did not go. <sup>31</sup>Which of the two did the will of his father?” They said, “The first.” Jesus said to them, “Truly, I say to you, the tax collectors and the prostitutes go into the kingdom of God before you. <sup>32</sup>For John came to you in the way of righteousness, and you did not believe him, but the tax collectors and the prostitutes believed him. And even when you saw it, you did not afterward change your minds and believe him. <sup>33</sup>“Hear another parable. There was a master of a house who planted a vineyard and put a fence around it and dug a winepress in it and built a tower and leased it to tenants, and went into another country. <sup>34</sup>When the season for fruit drew near, he sent his servants to the tenants to get his fruit. <sup>35</sup>And the tenants took his servants and beat one, killed another, and stoned another. <sup>36</sup>Again he sent other servants, more than the first. And they did the same to them. <sup>37</sup>Finally he sent his son to them, saying, ‘They will respect my son.’ <sup>38</sup>But when the tenants saw the son, they said to themselves, ‘This is the heir. Come, let us kill him and have his inheritance.’ <sup>39</sup>And they took him and threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. <sup>40</sup>When therefore the owner of the vineyard comes, what will he do to those tenants?” <sup>41</sup>They said to him, “He will put those wretches to a miserable death and let out the vineyard to other tenants who will give him the fruits in their seasons.” <sup>42</sup>Jesus said to them, “Have you never read in the Scriptures: “‘The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone; this was the Lord’s doing, and it is marvelous in our eyes’? <sup>43</sup>Therefore I tell you, the kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a people producing its fruits. <sup>44</sup>And the one who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces; and when it falls on anyone, it will crush him.” <sup>45</sup>When the chief priests and the Pharisees heard his parables, they perceived that he was speaking about them. <sup>46</sup>And although they were seeking to arrest him, they feared the crowds, because they held him to be a prophet.
21.overview:
Chapter 21 is the hinge between the Galilean ministry and the Passion Week. Jesus enters Jerusalem not as a military conqueror on a warhorse but as a humble king on a donkey, fulfilling Zechariah 9:9 with deliberate precision. The crowds shout “Hosanna to the Son of David!” — they are celebrating a political liberation that is not coming. Jesus has a different kind of liberation in mind.

The chapter is structured around three confrontational actions: the entry (vv. 1–11), the temple cleansing (vv. 12–17), and the cursing of the fig tree (vv. 18–22), sandwiched around a series of parables and controversies. The fig tree and the temple interpret each other: Israel, like the fig tree, has leaves of religious activity but no fruit. The temple establishment has turned the Father’s house of prayer into a market. Jesus’ authority is challenged (vv. 23–27); he responds with the parable of the two sons (vv. 28–32) and the parable of the tenants (vv. 33–46), both of which declare that the kingdom will be taken from the current tenants and given to a people who produce its fruit.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — The Triumphal Entry, Cleansing of the Temple, and the Withered Fig Tree
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus sends for a donkey and her colt, enters Jerusalem to the crowd's Hosannas, cleanses the temple of money-changers and dove-sellers, heals the blind and lame in the temple, and returns to Bethany. The next morning he curses a fig tree that has leaves but no fruit; it withers immediately. He teaches the disciples about faith that moves mountains. In between, children run about the temple courts shouting the same Hosanna, the chief priests object to what they are saying, and Jesus answers them out of Psalm 8 (vv. 15-16).
verseByVerse.theology: The triumphal entry deliberately fulfills Zechariah 9:9: the king who comes humble and mounted on a donkey, not a warhorse. Jesus is not claiming the military kingship Israel wanted; he is claiming the humble-servant kingship Zechariah foresaw. The Hosanna (Hebrew: save now!) from Psalm 118:25-26 is the pilgrims' greeting to the coming king. The crowd who shouts it does not fully understand what they are saying; they are speaking more truly than they know. "Hosanna to the Son of David" is the church's cry from that day to this. Two things the section does that are easily missed. Hosanna is not a cheer but a prayer — hoshia-na, save now — and the crowd prayed it with the wrong emergency in mind, wanting Rome dealt with while he came for something they had not thought to mention. And the psalm they sang is the psalm he quotes back in the temple: the pilgrims shout Psalm 118:26 on the way in (v. 9), and Jesus quotes Psalm 118:22, the rejected stone, to the men who run the place (v. 42). Between two verses of one psalm lies the whole week.
verseByVerse.examples: The cleansing of the temple is an act of prophetic judgment: the court of the Gentiles (the only place where non-Jews could pray) has been turned into a market. The money-changers and dove-sellers served legitimate temple functions, but their location in the court of the Gentiles prevented the very prayer the temple was meant to facilitate. Jesus quotes Isaiah 56:7 — "a house of prayer for all nations" — and Jeremiah 7:11 — "a den of robbers." He restores the temple to its purpose as a place of prayer and healing, then leaves it to be destroyed (ch. 24). The withered fig tree is a living parable of Israel's fruitlessness: outward leaves of religious activity, no fruit of genuine repentance. Three notes on that sign. It belongs to a recognised prophetic genre — Jeremiah smashing a jar, Ezekiel lying beside a brick, Ahijah tearing a cloak — and it is worth observing that in a ministry of raising the dead and healing all who came, the only thing Jesus ever destroyed was a plant, by a roadside, where nobody was hurt. The charge against the tree is precise: not barrenness but advertising, since a fig in full leaf out of season is making a claim that can be checked from the road. So the guard matters for the anxious reader — this condemns pretence, not weakness, and the same Gospel says a bruised reed he will not break (12:20). The children of vv. 15-16, meanwhile, get Psalm 8 quoted in their defence, and the rest of that verse — to still the enemy and the avenger — tells the chief priests which part of the psalm they are standing in.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when they drew near to Jerusalem and came to Bethphage, to the Mount of Olives, then Jesus sent two disciples, saying to them, "Go into the village in front of you, and immediately you will find a donkey tied, and a colt with her. Untie them and bring them to me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus comes to Jerusalem as her King on purpose, arranging every detail of the entry himself — nothing in the week ahead simply happens to him.

The threshold. Bethphage, on the Mount of Olives, was the last village before the city. At the threshold, the first thing Jesus does is stop the party and send two men for an animal.

The one ride. For three years he walked everywhere — Galilee, Tyre and Sidon, Caesarea Philippi, the long climb from Jericho — and the Gospels never mention him riding. The one time he lets himself be carried is the short way into his own capital, as her king.

The right hill. Zechariah said that on the day of the LORD “his feet shall stand on the Mount of Olives” (Zechariah 14:4). Jesus doesn’t stumble into fulfilment. He stops at the right hill, sends for the right animal, and rides down it.

A royal mount. This isn’t a story about a man too poor for a horse. In Israel the donkey could be a royal mount. When David settled the succession, he had Solomon set on the king’s own mule and led down to Gihon, and the people shouted, “Long live King Solomon!” until the earth split with the noise (1 Kings 1:33–40). A king’s son, a royal beast, a descent from a hill, a shouting crowd: the last coronation procession Israel had seen looked like this one.

He is setting it up. Mark tells us the colt had never been ridden (Mark 11:2), and an unbroken colt in a shouting crowd with cloaks flying would normally bolt; it carried him. And the instructions are exact: a donkey tied, a colt with her, in the village ahead, found “immediately.” Whether by earlier arrangement or direct knowledge, Matthew doesn’t say. What is plain is that he is not a victim of events. A test: do you trust that Christ is in control of what lies ahead of you?
verseByVerse.note: Bethphage was a village on the Mount of Olives, just east of Jerusalem, near Bethany.

verseByVerse.quote: "If anyone says anything to you, you shall say, 'The Lord needs them,' and he will send them at once." This took place to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet, saying,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord of all things comes owning nothing and asks for the loan of a donkey, and simple willingness to give him what he asks is part of how his purposes are fulfilled.

“The Lord needs them.” No name, no message about who is asking, no promise to return the animals. “The Lord” is the whole of his credentials, and it is enough.

Needs. The one through whom all things were made, walking toward the city where he will be crowned and killed, sends two friends to borrow transport. It is the quiet condescension that runs through the whole story: no house of his own, a borrowed upper room for the supper, a tomb cut for someone else, and at the end only the clothes soldiers gambled over. He owns everything, and arrives asking for a colt (2 Corinthians 8:9).

“To fulfill.” Matthew steps out of the story to say what is happening: “This took place to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet.” He has used that formula many times since chapter 1, and by now we know what he means — not just a prediction ticking over, but a pattern long written arriving at what it was shaped for (see on 2:15). The words were on a scroll for five hundred years; now they are hoofbeats on a road.

A nameless owner. Matthew doesn’t say whether the owner had been spoken to in advance. What he reports is the result: he sent them at once. Somewhere in that village is a man who lost the use of his donkey for an afternoon and never appears again, and the King’s entry waited on his willingness. A test: when the Lord asks for something of yours, do you send it at once?

verseByVerse.quote: "Say to the daughter of Zion, 'Behold, your king is coming to you, humble, and mounted on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a beast of burden.'" The disciples went and did as Jesus had directed them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ is a gentle King who comes in peace, with all his strength under control, and he came not to deal with Rome but with sin — at the cost of himself.

Humble. The word is the one used of the meek who inherit the earth (5:5) and that Jesus used of himself: “I am gentle and lowly in heart” (11:29). It doesn’t mean weak. It means strength under control — and that is the King riding down the hill.

The donkey is his policy. The next verse of Zechariah explains it: “I will cut off the chariot from Ephraim and the war horse from Jerusalem; and the battle bow shall be cut off, and he shall speak peace to the nations” (Zechariah 9:10). The animal isn’t just a note of humility; it is his programme. He rides what you ride when the war horses have been abolished, and the sentence ends with the nations — whose only court in the temple he is about to clear.

Not a Roman triumph. A Roman triumph had a fixed shape: the general in a chariot, the spoils carried before him, captured enemies in chains behind, and sacrifices at the end. This King has no chariot, no spoils, and no prisoners, having spent three years setting them free. At the end of his route there is a sacrifice — and it is him.

The crown in an unwanted form. This is sometimes preached as the moment Jesus finally accepted the crown. He did, in the one form nobody wanted. The crowd wanted a king to deal with Rome; he came to deal with what they hadn’t asked him to touch. He didn’t correct the volume, only the meaning, by choosing his transport.

Ordinary obedience. “The disciples went and did as Jesus had directed them.” They weren’t asked to understand Zechariah, only to fetch a donkey, and they did. A great deal of obedience is that size. A test: what small thing has Christ asked of you today?
verseByVerse.note: A king riding a donkey came in peace, not on a warhorse. Matthew mentions both the donkey and her colt.

parallels.desc: your king comes, humble and mounted on a donkey
say to the daughter of Zion

verseByVerse.quote: They brought the donkey and the colt and put on them their cloaks, and he sat on them. Most of the crowd spread their cloaks on the road, and others cut branches from the trees and spread them on the road.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The crowd welcomes Jesus with homage fit for a king, and even the details of the scene match what the prophet foretold.

Homage. Spreading cloaks on the road was homage to a king; it was done for Jehu when he was proclaimed king (2 Kings 9:13). Branches added festive and royal celebration. “Most of the crowd” joins in, publicly and unmistakably. They welcome him as king even if they don’t understand what kind of king he is.

Two animals? Matthew mentions the donkey and her colt, where Mark, Luke and John mention only the colt Jesus rode; and he says they put their cloaks “on them, and he sat on them.” Critics ask whether Jesus rode two animals at once, and whether Matthew misread Zechariah 9:9, where Hebrew poetry names “a donkey” and “a colt” in parallel lines as one animal described twice. Neither charge holds. There were two animals, and Matthew notices what the others pass over: an unbroken colt is steadier with its mother walking beside it. “He sat on them” most naturally means the cloaks: they threw garments over both animals, and he sat on the garments. Far from misunderstanding the parallelism, Matthew — steeped in the Scriptures — saw the scene match even the doubled wording of the prophet and recorded it.

What would you lay down? The crowd gave their cloaks to be trampled for a king. Christ asks more than our coats; he asks for ourselves (Romans 12:1). A test: what have you laid at his feet?
verseByVerse.note: Spreading cloaks on the road was a gesture of homage to a king.

verseByVerse.quote: And the crowds that went before him and that followed him were shouting, "Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! Hosanna in the highest!" And when he entered Jerusalem, the whole city was stirred up, saying, "Who is this?" And the crowds said, "This is the prophet Jesus, from Nazareth of Galilee."
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Hosanna” is a cry for God to save, and the crowd prayed the right prayer for the wrong rescue — while Jesus came to save from something far deeper than Rome.

Save now. “Hosanna” isn’t a cheer, though it became one. It means “save, we pray,” a cry addressed to God, from the psalm pilgrims sang on the way to the feast: “Save us, we pray, O LORD!… Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD!” (Psalm 118:25–26). The crowd was praying at the top of its voice.

The wrong emergency. Ask that crowd what they wanted saving from and they would have said Rome — the garrison, the taxes, the humiliation of occupation. It was a real grievance, and he did nothing about it. He had come to deal with something they hadn’t mentioned, and the rescue they asked for was smaller than the one he carried up the hill (1:21). They were more right than they knew and less right than they thought — the usual condition of anyone praying.

Two verses of one psalm. The crowd shouts Psalm 118:26 on the way in. Before the chapter ends, Jesus quotes Psalm 118:22 at the temple leaders: “The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone” (v. 42). Between those two verses lie the rejection, the trial and the cross.

The city shook. “The whole city was stirred up” — the word for an earthquake. Jerusalem shakes when he enters it, the earth shakes when he dies (27:51), and again at the tomb on the third day (28:2). Three tremors, and only the city’s is caused by people. “Who is this?” is the right question, and “the prophet Jesus, from Nazareth of Galilee” is true and far too small.

Same crowd, Sunday and Friday? It is often said that the crowd shouting “Hosanna” on Sunday shouted “Crucify” on Friday. The text doesn’t clearly support that. This crowd is largely pilgrims who came up the road with him, many from Galilee. The crowd at the trial gathered early in the city, and “the chief priests and the elders persuaded the crowd to ask for Barabbas” (27:20). The truth is less tidy and worse: when it mattered, the people who cheered him weren’t to be found, and a smaller crowd that had been worked on was. A test: will you stand with Christ when it costs you, or only when the crowd is cheering?
verseByVerse.note: “Hosanna” means “save, we pray,” and had become a shout of praise.

parallels.desc: blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus entered the temple and drove out all who sold and bought in the temple, and he overturned the tables of the money-changers and the seats of those who sold pigeons. He said to them, "It is written, 'My house shall be called a house of prayer,' but you make it a den of robbers." And the blind and the lame came to him in the temple, and he healed them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ comes as Lord of the temple to cleanse it for prayer and healing, and he himself is the true temple — God with us, the sacrifice, and the way our prayers reach the Father.

The market. Money-changers exchanged coins into the currency accepted for the temple tax; pigeon-sellers supplied the sacrifice the poor could afford. Both services had a place, but the trade filled the outer court, the one place Gentiles could pray, and the poor were being fleeced. Jesus drives it out, quoting Isaiah — “My house shall be called a house of prayer” (Isaiah 56:7, which adds “for all peoples”) — and Jeremiah’s charge of a “den of robbers” (Jeremiah 7:11): people using worship as a hiding place while they exploit others.

The blind and the lame. Then at once “the blind and the lame came to him in the temple, and he healed them.” The space is restored to its purpose. If zeal clears a space and nothing tender happens in it, it has done the wrong half of the scene.

The true temple. The temple was where God dwelt among his people, where sacrifice was offered, and through which prayer went up. The man standing among the overturned tables is Immanuel, God with us (1:23); days from now he will offer the sacrifice that ends all others; and he is the one through whom prayer reaches the Father (John 14:13–14). John records him saying, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19), and adds, “he was speaking about the temple of his body” (John 2:21). So when the building fell in AD 70, the people of God lost nothing they hadn’t already been given in Christ.

One cleansing or two? John places a cleansing at the start of Jesus’ ministry (John 2:13–22); Matthew, Mark and Luke place it in the last week. Some think there was one, and John arranged his Gospel by theme. But the details suggest two: in John, oxen, sheep and a whip of cords, and a demand for a sign; here, doves and money-changers, and a question about authority. The trade would have grown back, and Jesus confronted the temple both when he began and when he finished. Either way, the meaning is untouched. Mark adds that he looked around on the first evening and cleansed it the next day (Mark 11:11, 15); Matthew, as with the fig tree, tells it compactly.

Does this justify angry protest? “Jesus flipped tables” is often used to excuse the furious post or the scorching email. But this is the owner arriving in his own house, with an authority that belongs to him alone. And notice what moved him: not a slight to himself — he had been mocked for chapters without overturning anything — but the poor being fleeced and the Gentiles crowded out. Anger that flares when I am disrespected and stays seated when the weak are exploited isn’t this anger (see on 5:21–22).

Selling in church? A church foyer isn’t the temple. What Jesus condemned was exploitation and crowding out prayer. A bookstall isn’t wrong in itself; the test is whether anyone is being fleeced and whether business is getting in the way of worship. A test: is anything in your church — or your heart — crowding out prayer?
verseByVerse.note: The trading happened in the outer court, the only place Gentiles could pray. Pigeons were the sacrifice the poor could afford. Money-changers exchanged coins into the currency accepted for the temple tax.

parallels.desc: a house of prayer for all peoples
pigeons for those who cannot afford a lamb

verseByVerse.quote: But when the chief priests and the scribes saw the wonderful things that he did, and the children crying out in the temple, "Hosanna to the Son of David!" they were indignant, and they said to him, "Do you hear what these are saying?" And Jesus said to them, "Yes; have you never read, 'Out of the mouth of infants and nursing babies you have prepared praise'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The same works of Christ that move children to praise make the proud indignant, and God draws praise from the smallest voices to silence his enemies.

In the temple courts. This isn’t on the road, where a crowd can be dismissed as excited pilgrims, but inside the temple, where the chief priests are in charge — and the noise is from children, shouting “Hosanna to the Son of David!” at the man who has just overturned the furniture.

The content offends. The leaders don’t say “keep them quiet” but “Do you hear what these are saying?” Children are calling him Son of David, and he isn’t correcting them.

Same evidence, opposite responses. What prompted the shouting was “the wonderful things that he did.” The priests saw the same things: the blind receiving sight in their own courts. The same evidence produced worship in children and indignation in men trained to interpret it.

Psalm 8. Jesus quotes the psalm in its Greek form: “Out of the mouth of infants and nursing babies you have prepared praise.” The Hebrew has “established strength,” and continues “because of your foes, to still the enemy and the avenger” (Psalm 8:2). He doesn’t need to say that line aloud to men who knew the psalter; he has told them which part of the psalm they are standing in.

Not a sneer at learning. This is the Lord who thanked the Father for hiding these things “from the wise and understanding” and revealing them “to little children” (11:25). The problem with these men wasn’t that they had studied, but that their study had become the property of their position, so that a conclusion costing them the position had become unthinkable. A child had nothing to lose by saying “Son of David.” And “have you never read” is the question Jesus keeps putting to professional readers of Scripture (12:3; 19:4; 21:42; 22:31) — not about ignorance, but about refusing to be governed by what they know. A test: is there a truth you know but won’t let govern you?
verseByVerse.note: Jesus quotes the psalm in its Greek form.

parallels.desc: out of the mouth of babies and infants

verseByVerse.quote: And leaving them, he went out of the city to Bethany and lodged there. In the morning, as he was returning to the city, he became hungry.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The King of Israel had no bed in his own city and felt real hunger, showing both his rejection and his true humanity.

Where the King slept. On the evening of his entry as king, where did he sleep? Not in a palace or the temple precincts. He walked about two miles back over the Mount of Olives in the dark to Bethany, home of Martha, Mary and Lazarus (John 11:1, 18). The city that shook at his arrival in the morning didn’t offer him a bed at night.

Every night. He did this each night that week. It was prudent: Jerusalem at Passover was crowded and watched, and a man who sleeps outside the walls is harder to arrest in the dark. But it was more than tactics. He didn’t live in the city he came to save; he came in each morning to teach and left each evening, and his last night near it he would spend awake in a garden on that same hillside.

He became hungry. Early morning, two miles uphill on an empty stomach. This is the man who fed five thousand and four thousand, and who refused to turn stones into bread in the desert when far hungrier (4:2–4). The power was never absent; it simply wasn’t for himself. The Gospels aren’t embarrassed by his hunger. It is the incarnation showing at an ordinary hour: he got tired, slept in a boat, wept at a grave, and was hungry on the way to work (Hebrews 4:15).

Toward the tree. And it is the hunger that takes him to the fig tree. The sign that follows doesn’t begin as a lesson looking for an illustration, but with a hungry man walking toward a tree that looked from the road as though it had fruit. A test: do you believe Christ understands your weariness and need from the inside?
verseByVerse.note: Bethany was about two miles east of Jerusalem, home of Mary, Martha and Lazarus.

verseByVerse.quote: And seeing a fig tree by the wayside, he went to it and found nothing on it but only leaves. And he said to it, "May no fruit ever come from you again!" And the fig tree withered at once. When the disciples saw it, they marveled, saying, "How did the fig tree wither at once?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The withered fig tree is a prophetic sign of God’s judgment on religion that has leaves without fruit — a warning against pretence, not against weakness.

Why curse a tree? It is the obvious question. On the surface, a hungry man finds no breakfast and kills the tree. But this isn’t temper; it is a prophet’s sign-act, a genre Israel knew well. Jeremiah smashed a clay jar before the elders (Jeremiah 19); Ezekiel lay on his side beside a brick drawn with the city (Ezekiel 4); Ahijah tore a new cloak into twelve pieces (1 Kings 11:30–31). The prophets acted their message when words stopped landing. So Jesus, the morning after clearing the temple, does to a tree what he is about to say about the house on the hill. And in a life spent raising the dead and healing all who came, the one thing he destroyed in a sign of his own was a plant by the road, where no one was hurt.

The fig and Israel. The fig tree was a prophetic picture of Israel: “there are no grapes on the vine, nor figs on the fig tree; even the leaves are withered” (Jeremiah 8:13). Everyone on that road had the association ready.

Leaves that advertise. Mark notes “it was not the season for figs” (Mark 11:13). A fig tree in leaf normally carries early green fruit; a tree in full leaf makes a claim that can be checked from the road. This one had leaves and nothing else. It wasn’t quietly failing; it was advertising — like the temple, full of noise and sacrifice, while the poor were fleeced and the Gentiles crowded out.

“At once.” Matthew has it wither immediately; Mark has the disciples notice it the next morning (Mark 11:20–21). Matthew tells the episode in one piece, as he often compresses (cf. 9:18). The two don’t collide: Matthew says when the tree died, Mark when the disciples saw it.

Pretence, not weakness. This will frighten the wrong reader first — the tender Christian who audits himself and finds little fruit. But the tree was judged not for smallness or slowness but for displaying what it didn’t have. The same Gospel says of Christ, “a bruised reed he will not break, and a smoldering wick he will not quench” (12:20). He is fierce with pretence and gentle with frailty. A test: is there a gap between what you show and what is real?
verseByVerse.note: Mark adds that “it was not the season for figs”; leaves on a fig tree normally promise early fruit. The fig tree was a prophetic picture of Israel.

parallels.desc: no figs on the fig tree

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus answered them, "Truly, I say to you, if you have faith and do not doubt, you will not only do what has been done to the fig tree, but even if you say to this mountain, 'Be taken up and thrown into the sea,' it will happen. And whatever you ask in prayer, you will receive, if you have faith."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Faith in God can remove what seems immovable for the sake of his kingdom, and prayer offered for his purposes will never lack his supply.

A question about their future. They ask how the tree withered; he tells them what they will be doing. They wanted the mechanics; he gives them a mission.

This mountain. He stands on the road over the Mount of Olives with the temple mount in view across the valley. The Mount of Olives is the hill Zechariah says will split on the day of the LORD (Zechariah 14:4); the temple mount is what the withered tree has just pictured. We aren’t told which he meant. Either way, the immovable thing in view is a religious system soon to be rubble, and he tells fishermen and tax collectors that obstacles that size can be told to move.

What they actually moved. None of them ever withered a tree. But within a generation these provincial nobodies, with no money, standing or army, had carried the gospel into the great cities between Jerusalem and Rome against the opposition of both the council and the empire. Most were executed for it, and it didn’t slow down. That is the mountain, and it went into the sea.

Anything I ask? “Whatever you ask in prayer, you will receive, if you have faith.” Is this a promise that anything asked with enough faith will be given? No. Prayer is answered according to God’s will: “if we ask anything according to his will he hears us” (1 John 5:14). Wrong motives aren’t rewarded (James 4:3), and Paul’s prayer for healing was answered no (2 Corinthians 12:8–9). Faith is trust in God, not confidence in a particular outcome (see on 17:20). In context, it is the assurance that the work he gives will never fail for lack of supply, so they may ask boldly for it.

What are you asking for? We come asking whether we have enough faith for what we want. The passage asks what we are asking for. Much of our praying would need no mountain moved, only a modest tidying of circumstances. These men were told to expect the impossible because they had been given something impossible to do. A test: are you praying for anything that only God could do for his kingdom?

parallels.desc: ask in faith, with no doubting

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–46 — Authority Questioned: Three Parables of Judgment
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chief priests and elders challenge Jesus's authority: by what authority do you do these things? Jesus answers with a counter-question about John's baptism that they refuse to answer, then tells three parables of judgment: the two sons (the one who refused then obeyed vs. the one who agreed but didn't), the wicked tenants who killed the vineyard owner's son, and the implied parable of the rejected cornerstone from Psalm 118. The parables systematically indict the religious leadership of Israel for rejecting God's messengers and the Son himself. The counter-question is not a diversion: John had already answered the authority question in public, so to ask whether John was from heaven is to hand it back in the one form they cannot answer safely. And the verdict between the parables is the sharpest sentence in the chapter — the tax collectors and the prostitutes go into the kingdom ahead of them (vv. 31-32).
verseByVerse.theology: The authority question and Jesus's counter-question about John expose the leaders' bad faith: they do not want to know the source of Jesus's authority; they want to discredit him publicly. Their refusal to answer John's question (whether from heaven or from men) reveals that they are governed by crowd opinion rather than truth-seeking. Jesus therefore refuses to answer them directly — but he answers indirectly and devastatingly through the three parables. The wicked tenants is the most explicit: they will kill the son, and the vineyard will be given to others who will produce its fruits. Two details carry the tenants parable. Jesus quotes Isaiah's Song of the Vineyard almost item for item (Isa 5:1-2) and then changes it: in Isaiah the vine is at fault, here the vine is fine and the tenants are the problem — the indictment is narrowed off the nation and onto its leaders. And the tenants do not kill the son by mistake. This is the heir — recognition is the motive, which is why unbelief in this chapter is never a shortage of information. Note also 2 Chr 36:15-16, which is this parable written four centuries early: God sent persistently by his messengers, and they kept mocking them, until there was no remedy.
verseByVerse.examples: The rejected cornerstone from Psalm 118:22 — the same psalm shouted at the triumphal entry — completes the argument. The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone; what the religious establishment rejects, God establishes as the foundation of his kingdom. The chief priests and Pharisees understood that he was speaking about them — and they wanted to arrest him but feared the crowds. The rejection is comprehensive; the judgment is announced; the crowds are the only restraint preventing its immediate human execution. Two applications. Verse 43's taken away from you is about tenancy, not race — the vineyard is re-let, and the people it was first let to were Jews to a man (see the verse-by-verse on vv. 43-44). And verse 45 is the most sobering sentence here for anyone who reads the Bible well: they perceived that he was speaking about them. The parables landed perfectly, were understood completely, and produced not repentance but an arrest plan. Understanding the text is not the goal, and it is possible to be an excellent reader of Scripture and be destroyed by what you have correctly understood.

verseByVerse.quote: And when he entered the temple, the chief priests and the elders of the people came up to him as he was teaching, and said, "By what authority are you doing these things, and who gave you this authority?" Jesus answered them, "I also will ask you one question, and if you tell me the answer, then I also will tell you by what authority I do these things."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ often answers our questions by pointing us back to the evidence we have already refused, because the real issue is not information but willingness.

An official question. “The chief priests and the elders of the people” is an official delegation, and their question is the one the council existed to ask. Israel’s law required testing anyone who spoke as a prophet (Deuteronomy 18:20–22). On the face of it, they are doing their job.

“These things.” In a day he has ridden into the city like a king, cleared the temple court, healed in the sanctuary, and let children call him Son of David. Every act was one of ownership. Now the administrators ask on what basis he behaved like the proprietor of the building they ran.

A counter-question. Answering a question with a question was ordinary rabbinic practice, not evasion, and he attaches a promise: answer mine and I will answer yours. And his question is the authority question in another form. John was the one man in Israel who had already answered it publicly. He had said the one coming after him was so great that “I am not worthy to carry” his sandals (3:11), and he had baptized Jesus when the voice from heaven spoke (3:16–17). If John was from heaven, they already had their answer and had been refusing it.

Back to what you know. Christ doesn’t always answer the question we put; he often answers the one underneath it, or points to evidence we have declined to look at. Someone who says he would believe if God only made it clear often has something specific in view he has decided not to act on. The Lord’s habit is to send him back there first. A test: is there something God has already shown you that you haven’t acted on?

verseByVerse.quote: The baptism of John, from where did it come? From heaven or from man?" And they discussed it among themselves, saying, "If we say, 'From heaven,' he will say to us, 'Why then did you not believe him?' But if we say, 'From man,' we are afraid of the crowd, for they all hold that John was a prophet."
verseByVerse.commentary:
When the question in our mind shifts from “What is true?” to “What will this cost me?”, we are no longer seeking truth — and fear of people takes control.

The minutes of the huddle. Matthew takes us inside a private conversation of Israel’s most senior religious men, deciding what to say about a prophet of God. Two options, each weighed only for its cost: if we say heaven, he will ask why we didn’t believe; if we say man, we fear the crowd. Not one word about whether John was in fact from heaven. The question of truth never comes up.

Wrong or corrupt. That is the difference between a man who is mistaken and a man who is corrupt. Being wrong about John would have been correctable. These men weren’t weighing evidence badly; they had stopped weighing it and were running a different calculation, competently.

Afraid of the crowd. These men could summon the temple guard, hold a trial before dawn, and get a Roman governor out of bed. Yet they feared ordinary people, and the fear governed them. Matthew says it again twenty verses later (v. 46). The guardians of Israel’s conscience took their instructions from Israel’s mood (Proverbs 29:25).

The quiet calculation. The test isn’t whether you have ever told a lie, but whether you notice when the question in your mind silently changes from what is true to what it will cost me to say. It happens in a staff room when someone mocks Christians and you decide in a second and a half this isn’t the moment; when a group settles on an unfair view of someone you know; in families over things done years ago. It is so fast it doesn’t feel like a decision.

Not a call to blurt. Prudence isn’t cowardice; Jesus told us to be “wise as serpents and innocent as doves” (10:16). The difference is what sits in the driver’s seat. Wisdom decides how and when to say the true thing. In this huddle, safety was deciding the content. A test: when did fear last decide what you said?
verseByVerse.note: “From heaven” means from God.

verseByVerse.quote: So they answered Jesus, "We do not know." And he said to them, "Neither will I tell you by what authority I do these things. What do you think? A man had two sons. And he went to the first and said, 'Son, go and work in the vineyard today.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those who refuse the light they already have forfeit further light, yet Christ keeps calling them to see themselves and turn.

“We do not know.” Four words, false, and everyone knew it. These were the men whose office was to know — to judge true and false, prophet and fraud. And the subject wasn’t obscure: “Jerusalem and all Judea… were going out to him” (3:5). Half the country had an opinion about John; its official guardians declared they hadn’t formed one.

A lie and a confession. What they meant was: we have an answer and can’t afford it. That is worse than ignorance. Ignorance can be cured by information; this can be cured only by repentance.

Forfeiting an answer. “Neither will I tell you.” He doesn’t scold or argue; he declines, and the declining is the judgment. To someone who won’t act on what he has, more light isn’t a kindness but only more to answer for: “to the one who has, more will be given… but from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away” (13:12).

“If only it were clearer.” People often say sincerely that they would believe if the evidence were clearer. It is worth asking gently what they would do if it were clear. If the honest answer is that little would change, the difficulty was never the evidence. These men had watched a prophet and seen wonders in their own courts.

Still patient. And immediately he tells them a story: “What do you think? A man had two sons.” They refused his question and he won’t answer theirs, but he isn’t finished with them. Three parables follow, each aimed at them, each giving them a way to see themselves and turn. He is more patient with them than they deserve, and far more patient than they will be with him. A test: are you waiting for more light, or refusing the light you have?

verseByVerse.quote: "And he answered, 'I will not,' but afterward he changed his mind and went. And he went to the other son and said the same. And he answered, 'I will, sir,' but did not go."
verseByVerse.commentary:
What counts with God isn’t the right words but actually going where he sends — and a bad start is never a settled verdict for anyone who turns and obeys.

Which son am I? Jesus asks the question himself, so it is meant for every reader, not only for the men in front of him.

The second son. Most people who read a commentary are in more danger of being the second son. He doesn’t refuse. He isn’t rude or rebellious. He says the right thing, in the right tone, with the right title — “I will, sir” — and everyone would have thought well of him. His failure is invisible until you look at the vineyard. That is much respectable Christianity: a yes given years ago, the language still fluent, the vineyard unvisited (7:21).

The first son. He isn’t a model of manners; he was insolent, and Jesus doesn’t pretend otherwise.
