What commends him isn’t candour about his reluctance — plenty are candidly disobedient and stay that way — but that “he changed his mind and went.” The parable doesn’t care which son felt better about himself, only who ended up in the field.

A question with a date. Not “did I once say yes,” but: since I last said yes to God about something specific, have I actually gone? There is usually one thing in view — a conversation to have, a debt to repay, a habit to end, a person to forgive, money to give. You will know it, because it came to mind before this sentence finished.

The better news. The first son’s story means a bad start isn’t a settled verdict. Nothing stops someone who said no this morning from being in the vineyard by the afternoon, and the father in this parable doesn’t demand a speech first. He wants a son in the field. If you have been the second son for twenty years, the way out isn’t despair or a better speech but a change of direction today, in one thing. A test: what has God told you to do that you said yes to and haven’t done?

verseByVerse.quote: "Which of the two did the will of his father?" They said, "The first." Jesus said to them, "Truly, I say to you, the tax collectors and the prostitutes go into the kingdom of God before you. For John came to you in the way of righteousness, and you did not believe him, but the tax collectors and the prostitutes believed him. And even when you saw it, you did not afterward change your minds and believe him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Repentant sinners enter the kingdom ahead of the religious who refuse to believe, yet even for the proud the door is still being held open.

Self-sentenced. They answer correctly — “The first” — and so pass sentence on themselves, as they will again with the tenants (v. 41). The parable was too plain to get wrong and too small to feel dangerous.

Tax collectors and prostitutes. Hear it as they heard it. Tax collectors were collaborators who bought the right to take Rome’s money from their neighbours and kept the surplus. Prostitutes were beyond the edge of respectable society, many driven there by a man who discarded them or by hunger. Jesus names these two groups, in the temple, to the highest religious authorities in the nation, and puts them in front.

Ahead of you. “The tax collectors and the prostitutes go into the kingdom of God before you.” He doesn’t say they go in and you stay out, but that they are going in ahead of you. A queue is something you can still join. Even at the sharpest moment, the door isn’t shut in their faces; it is held open while they are told who is walking through first.

You did not believe him. “John came to you in the way of righteousness, and you did not believe him.” Not that they disliked his style, but that they didn’t believe. And the knot is tied with one word. The first son “changed his mind” and went (v. 29); of them Jesus says, “you did not afterward change your minds” (v. 32). He has made them praise the hero and then handed them the hero’s verb with a “not” in front of it.

Even when you saw it. They watched collaborators pay money back and ruined women come up from the Jordan new, and it moved them not at all. There is a settled state in which fresh evidence stops working as evidence. It isn’t reached by one bad decision but by a long series of moments when the honest answer was known and not acted on (Hebrews 3:13).

Astonishing mercy. Held together, the sentence is astonishing rather than merely severe. The worst news a religious man could hear is that the door is open to the very people he would cross the street to avoid — and nothing in the sentence stops the high priest from joining them. A test: are there people you think are further from God than you who may be entering ahead of you?

parallels.desc: the tax collectors baptized, the Pharisees refusing

verseByVerse.quote: "Hear another parable. There was a master of a house who planted a vineyard and put a fence around it and dug a winepress in it and built a tower and leased it to tenants, and went into another country. When the season for fruit drew near, he sent his servants to the tenants to get his fruit."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has given his people every advantage and asks for the fruit his vineyard exists to produce — and he holds its leaders especially answerable.

Isaiah’s song. Within five words every listener recognised it: a vineyard, a fence, a winepress, a tower — Isaiah’s Song of the Vineyard almost item for item (Isaiah 5:1–2). And Isaiah had said who the vineyard was: “the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isaiah 5:7). The chief priests knew how it ended — the hedge removed and the vineyard trampled — and let him tell it.

The change. In Isaiah the fault is in the vine, which yields wild grapes. Here the vine isn’t blamed; the fault is the tenants. Jesus narrows the prophets’ indictment from the people to the men given charge of them. That was a far more dangerous parable to tell in the temple, and for an ordinary Israelite in the crowd, more merciful.

A going concern. A fence against animals, a winepress cut into the rock, a watchtower: a fully equipped estate, the work done before the tenants arrive. Every advantage they have came from the man they are about to rob (Romans 9:4–5).

Taking sides. Absentee landlords leasing estates to tenant farmers were a real grievance in that country, and Jesus uses it on purpose. The crowd’s sympathy is with the tenants — until the tenants start killing people. It is the same move as with the two sons: get the audience to take a side, then show them which side they took.

His fruit. The owner sends not for rent in coin but for “his fruit,” what the vineyard exists to produce. He is asking a vineyard to be a vineyard. That is the question this whole chapter puts — to the fig tree in leaf, to the busy temple, to the men in charge: not whether the operation is busy, but whether anything is growing (John 15:8). A test: if God came looking for fruit in your life today, what would he find?
verseByVerse.note: The setting echoes Isaiah’s song of the vineyard, where the vineyard is Israel. Absentee landlords commonly leased land to tenant farmers.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the tenants took his servants and beat one, killed another, and stoned another. Again he sent other servants, more than the first. And they did the same to them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God has sent messenger after messenger to his rebellious people in astonishing patience, but his patience is not indifference and it does not last forever.

A summary, not exaggeration. “They beat one, killed another, and stoned another.” The listeners needed no explanation; they knew what happened to God’s messengers. Jeremiah was beaten and put in the stocks by the chief officer of the temple and later dropped into a muddy cistern (Jeremiah 20:2; 38:6). Zechariah son of Jehoiada was stoned in the court of the temple and died saying, “May the LORD see and avenge!” (2 Chronicles 24:20–22) — a killing Jesus will name later (23:35). Uriah fled to Egypt, was brought back, and struck down with the sword (Jeremiah 26:20–23).

Written long before. Israel’s history had summed it up already: “The LORD, the God of their fathers, sent persistently to them by his messengers, because he had compassion on his people and on his dwelling place. But they kept mocking the messengers of God, despising his words and scoffing at his prophets, until the wrath of the LORD rose against his people, until there was no remedy” (2 Chronicles 36:15–16). That is this parable, written centuries before it was told.

The sending. The emphasis isn’t on the violence but on the sending: “Again he sent other servants, more than the first.” As a landlord’s strategy it is absurd; no owner whose staff are being killed sends a larger unarmed party. As history it is the patience of God across centuries — after Elijah, Amos; after Amos, Hosea; then Isaiah, Micah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel — each sent into a country that knew what it did to the last.

Both halves. The patience is real and almost unbelievable. And the Chronicler’s last clause is real too: “until there was no remedy.” Patience isn’t indifference, and it isn’t permanent (2 Peter 3:9–10). Whoever reads the long delay as proof that nothing will ever be said has misread what the parable does next, because after all the servants, one more figure stands at the gate. A test: are you presuming on God’s patience?

verseByVerse.quote: "Finally he sent his son to them, saying, 'They will respect my son.' But when the tenants saw the son, they said to themselves, 'This is the heir. Come, let us kill him and have his inheritance.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God sent his own Son last of all, and the deepest unbelief isn’t confusion about who he is but a clear refusal of his rightful claim.

Finally. “Finally he sent his son.” The word sits there like a door closing. After this there is no one else to send, and everyone in that court could feel the story running out of servants (Hebrews 1:1–2).

“They will respect my son.” Doesn’t God know what they will do? He does; Jesus has told his disciples in detail that he will be handed over and crucified (16:21; 20:18–19). But this is a parable, speaking as a father speaks. It isn’t a statement about the limits of God’s foreknowledge but a way to make us feel the size of what is about to be done. The owner sends his boy to men who have killed his staff, and the sentence lets you hear him hoping.

Because they knew. Then the most frightening line: “This is the heir. Come, let us kill him and have his inheritance.” They don’t kill him by mistake; they kill him because they know who he is. Recognition is the motive. With the heir gone, the estate is theirs. Jesus is telling the men who will sit at his trial that they won’t condemn him out of ignorance.

Not a lack of information. We like to think of unbelief as a failure of information: if people only understood, if the case were better made. Sometimes it is. But this chapter says its deepest form isn’t confusion but a clear-eyed calculation that this man’s claim is incompatible with keeping what I have, and a decision to keep it (John 3:19). The tenants’ problem wasn’t that they didn’t know whose vineyard it was. It was that they did.

They did it. Within days, “the chief priests and the elders of the people gathered in the palace of the high priest… and plotted together in order to arrest Jesus by stealth and kill him” (26:3–4). The parable wasn’t a warning about something that might happen. They walked out and did it. A test: what claim of Christ on your life are you resisting because of what it would cost you?

parallels.desc: God has spoken by his Son

verseByVerse.quote: "And they took him and threw him out of the vineyard and killed him. When therefore the owner of the vineyard comes, what will he do to those tenants?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ was rejected and killed outside the city, and in that very act he was placed where the sacrifice for sin belonged; we must let the parable judge us, not only others.

Out, then killed. “They took him and threw him out of the vineyard and killed him.” Normally you would kill a man and then dispose of the body. Here he is put outside first and killed outside. Matthew’s readers knew why. Jesus was condemned in the city and crucified outside its wall. Hebrews makes the point: “Jesus also suffered outside the gate,” as the bodies of the sin offerings were burned outside the camp (Hebrews 13:11–12). The tenants threw the son over the wall to be rid of him, and so put him exactly where the sacrifice belonged.

Finish the story. “When therefore the owner of the vineyard comes, what will he do to those tenants?” For the second time in a short while, he invites them to judge a case that is their own. It is the method Nathan used when he told David about a poor man’s lamb, and the king pronounced sentence on himself (2 Samuel 12:1–7).

A mirror, not a snare. This isn’t a trap set to destroy them but a mirror set where they can’t avoid it. Everything in this chapter has been an attempt to get these men to see themselves while there is still time: a question about John, two sons, and now tenants. He isn’t steering them toward the sentence but toward recognition, the only thing that could save them.

About somebody else. The danger isn’t confined to Jerusalem. You can read a passage attentively, form a confident judgment about the people in it, and never notice the judgment applies to you. These men understood the parable perfectly (v. 45). They simply assumed, until the last second, that it was about someone else. A test: when you read Scripture, do you ask first how it applies to others, or to you?
verseByVerse.note: Jesus was crucified outside the city walls.

verseByVerse.quote: They said to him, "He will put those wretches to a miserable death and let out the vineyard to other tenants who will give him the fruits in their seasons." Jesus said to them, "Have you never read in the Scriptures: 'The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone; this was the Lord's doing, and it is marvelous in our eyes'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The stone the builders rejected became the cornerstone — the rejection of Christ was itself the Lord’s doing, the marvellous way God brought salvation out of the worst thing men ever did.

Their own verdict. They answer at once, with relish: “He will put those wretches to a miserable death.” The Greek has a hard little wordplay, bad men badly. They see clearly that such tenants deserve destruction and the vineyard should go to others — the verdict Jesus is about to pronounce on them.

Psalm 118 again. “Have you never read in the Scriptures…?” He quotes the psalm with which the chapter began. The crowd sang verse 26 on the way in: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD.” Now he quotes verse 22: “The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.” Between those verses lies the whole week: the welcome, the refusal, the trial, the cross and the empty tomb.

The builders. These men were the builders, the professionals whose standing rested on knowing what belonged in the building and what should be thrown off the site. They inspected one stone and discarded it, and it turned out to be the stone the whole structure would rest on. They were experts, they examined him, and they got it exactly wrong.

The Lord’s doing. Then the clause that turns tragedy into wonder: “this was the Lord’s doing, and it is marvelous in our eyes.” Not that God salvaged something from a disaster; the rejection itself was the Lord’s doing. The builders threw the stone away and, in that act, laid the foundation of a building they didn’t know was going up. That doesn’t excuse them; they knew what they did. Both are true, as Peter said at Pentecost: delivered up “according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God,” and killed “by the hands of lawless men” (Acts 2:23).

For the rejected. That is the deepest comfort for anyone whose life contains a rejection that can’t be undone. The stone didn’t become the cornerstone in spite of being thrown away; it became the cornerstone by being thrown away. That can’t be turned into a technique or promised cheaply to someone still bleeding. But it happened once, publicly, in the most important week in history: the worst thing men ever did was the thing God was doing (Genesis 50:20). The children in verse 15 had it right — it is a wonder. A test: do you trust that God can bring good even out of the rejection you have suffered?

verseByVerse.quote: "Therefore I tell you, the kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a people producing its fruits. And the one who falls on this stone will be broken to pieces; and when it falls on anyone, it will crush him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The kingdom is taken from faithless leaders and given to a people who bear its fruit — Jew and Gentile who receive the Son — and Christ is either our cornerstone or the stone that crushes us.

Taken and given. “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a people producing its fruits.” The stone then becomes a warning: those who stumble over it are broken, recalling Isaiah’s stone of stumbling (Isaiah 8:14–15), and those on whom it falls are crushed, recalling Daniel’s stone that shatters the kingdoms (Daniel 2:34–35, 44). The same Christ who is the cornerstone for believers is the crushing stone for those who reject him (1 Peter 2:7–8).

Has God finished with the Jews? This verse has been used, in very dark centuries, to teach that God finished with the Jewish people that week and handed their inheritance to the Gentiles, and terrible things were done in the name of that idea. Look at who is addressed. Not a race in the abstract, but the men in front of him: “the chief priests and the Pharisees… perceived that he was speaking about them” (v. 45). They are the tenants, and it is the tenancy that is revoked. The vineyard isn’t destroyed; it is re-let.

Who received it? The people producing its fruit began as a community of Jews — the apostles, the three thousand at Pentecost, Paul and the first generation of the church. Whatever this verse announces, it can’t mean excluding Jewish people, since it was first handed to them. Paul asks the question directly: “has God rejected his people? By no means! For I myself am an Israelite” (Romans 11:1). The church of Jew and Gentile is now the one people of God, and Jews are welcomed into it by faith in their Messiah, as Paul hoped for many of his own people (Romans 11:23–26).

Verse 44. The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit verse 44. Many think it original, since it fits Isaiah and Daniel, but nothing in the argument depends on it.

A warning to us. This isn’t a transfer of favour from one race to another but a warning about tenancy, and it points at the reader first. Paul warned the Gentile church in the same breath not to grow smug: “So do not become proud, but fear” (Romans 11:20). A church that keeps the leaves and yields no fruit has been told in this very chapter what happens to such trees. A test: is your church bearing the fruit of the kingdom, or only the leaves?
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts omit verse 44.

parallels.desc: the stone that breaks the kingdoms

verseByVerse.quote: When the chief priests and the Pharisees heard his parables, they perceived that he was speaking about them. And although they were seeking to arrest him, they feared the crowds, because they held him to be a prophet.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Understanding the Bible is not the same as submitting to it, and those ruled by fear of people are never truly free.

The parables worked. “They perceived that he was speaking about them.” There was no failure of communication. The question about John, the two sons and the tenants all landed. Jesus got through completely.

Understanding without repentance. That is the most sobering sentence in the chapter, because perfect understanding produced no repentance. They saw themselves in the story, recognised the verdict, knew who the son was — and went out to plan the murder. Understanding the text isn’t the goal, and it isn’t even a reliable step toward it. You can be an excellent reader of Scripture and be destroyed by what you have correctly understood (James 1:22). These men would have passed any exam on the parable of the tenants.

Ruled by the crowd. “They feared the crowds.” It is the same fear that shaped their answer about John (v. 26) and will keep them from arresting him openly at the feast (26:5). They had the offices, the titles, the temple and the guard, and their diary was set by a crowd they despised. They weren’t free men.

A thin wall. The crowds “held him to be a prophet” — the estimate given at the entry (v. 11), true and inadequate, and for now the only thing between Jesus and arrest. It was thin, and both sides knew it. A crowd that thinks you a prophet can be persuaded otherwise in days by men who work at it, and Matthew tells us when: “the chief priests and the elders persuaded the crowd to ask for Barabbas” (27:20). The restraint was a delay, not a reprieve.

Where it ends. The chapter closes where it opened, on who this is: a crowd that half knows, a leadership that fully knows and won’t have it, and a King who spends the day telling the truth in stories while his arrest is being planned. He doesn’t run, and he doesn’t soften it. A test: has your understanding of Christ led you to bow to him?

21.theology: Christ as the true Temple. The temple cleansing in Matthew 21 points to one of the great themes of biblical theology: Jesus as the replacement and fulfilment of the temple. The temple was the place where God dwelt with his people, where sacrifice was made, where prayer ascended. Jesus embodies all three functions: he is Emmanuel — God dwelling with his people; he is the Lamb whose self-offering ends the sacrificial system; he is the mediator through whom prayer reaches the Father (John 14:13–14). John’s Gospel makes this explicit (“the temple he had spoken of was his body”, John 2:21). The destruction of the Jerusalem temple in AD 70 was the confirmation that the type had given way to the antitype.
21.examples:
Then: The crowds welcomed Jesus with genuine excitement and completely wrong expectations. They wanted a Maccabean king who would drive out Rome; they got a crucified Servant who would drive out death. The Palm Sunday crowd’s theology is a warning: it is possible to praise Jesus enthusiastically while fundamentally misunderstanding who he is and what he has come to do.

Now: The fig tree is the perennial warning against fruitless religion — maintaining the form of Christian practice without the substance of faith, repentance, love, and transformed life. The church with its worship services, theological conferences, and evangelical brands may be full of leaves. The question Jesus asks of every institution and every individual is the same: where is the fruit?

22.title: The Great Banquet and the Hard Questions
22.text: <sup>1</sup>And again Jesus spoke to them in parables, saying, <sup>2</sup>“The kingdom of heaven may be compared to a king who gave a wedding feast for his son, <sup>3</sup>and sent his servants to call those who were invited to the wedding feast, but they would not come. <sup>4</sup>Again he sent other servants, saying, ‘Tell those who are invited, “See, I have prepared my dinner, my oxen and my fat calves have been slaughtered, and everything is ready. Come to the wedding feast.”’ <sup>5</sup>But they paid no attention and went off, one to his farm, another to his business, <sup>6</sup>while the rest seized his servants, treated them shamefully, and killed them. <sup>7</sup>The king was angry, and he sent his troops and destroyed those murderers and burned their city. <sup>8</sup>Then he said to his servants, ‘The wedding feast is ready, but those invited were not worthy. <sup>9</sup>Go therefore to the main roads and invite to the wedding feast as many as you find.’ <sup>10</sup>And those servants went out into the roads and gathered all whom they found, both bad and good. So the wedding hall was filled with guests. <sup>11</sup>“But when the king came in to look at the guests, he saw there a man who had no wedding garment. <sup>12</sup>And he said to him, ‘Friend, how did you get in here without a wedding garment?’ And he was speechless. <sup>13</sup>Then the king said to the attendants, ‘Bind him hand and foot and cast him into the outer darkness. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.’ <sup>14</sup>For many are called, but few are chosen.” <sup>15</sup>Then the Pharisees went and plotted how to entangle him in his words. <sup>16</sup>And they sent their disciples to him, along with the Herodians, saying, “Teacher, we know that you are true and teach the way of God truthfully, and you do not care about anyone’s opinion, for you are not swayed by appearances. <sup>17</sup>Tell us, then, what you think. Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not?” <sup>18</sup>But Jesus, aware of their malice, said, “Why put me to the test, you hypocrites? <sup>19</sup>Show me the coin for the tax.” And they brought him a denarius. <sup>20</sup>And Jesus said to them, “Whose likeness and inscription is this?” <sup>21</sup>They said, “Caesar’s.” Then he said to them, “Therefore render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.” <sup>22</sup>When they heard it, they marveled. And they left him and went away. <sup>23</sup>The same day Sadducees came to him, who say that there is no resurrection, and they asked him a question, <sup>24</sup>saying, “Teacher, Moses said, ‘If a man dies having no children, his brother must marry the widow and raise up offspring for his brother.’ <sup>25</sup>Now there were seven brothers among us. The first married and died, and having no offspring left his wife to his brother. <sup>26</sup>So too the second and third, down to the seventh. <sup>27</sup>After them all, the woman died. <sup>28</sup>In the resurrection, therefore, of the seven, whose wife will she be? For they all had her.” <sup>29</sup>But Jesus answered them, “You are wrong, because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. <sup>30</sup>For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven. <sup>31</sup>And as for the resurrection of the dead, have you not read what was said to you by God: <sup>32</sup>‘I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’? He is not God of the dead, but of the living.” <sup>33</sup>And when the crowd heard it, they were astonished at his teaching. <sup>34</sup>But when the Pharisees heard that he had silenced the Sadducees, they gathered together. <sup>35</sup>And one of them, a lawyer, asked him a question to test him. <sup>36</sup>“Teacher, which is the great commandment in the Law?” <sup>37</sup>And he said to him, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind. <sup>38</sup>This is the great and first commandment. <sup>39</sup>And a second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. <sup>40</sup>On these two commandments depend all the Law and the Prophets.” <sup>41</sup>Now while the Pharisees were gathered together, Jesus asked them a question, <sup>42</sup>saying, “What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is he?” They said to him, “The son of David.” <sup>43</sup>He said to them, “How is it then that David, in the Spirit, calls him Lord, saying, <sup>44</sup>“‘The Lord said to my Lord, “Sit at my right hand, until I put your enemies under your feet”’? <sup>45</sup>If then David calls him Lord, how is he his son?” <sup>46</sup>And no one was able to answer him a word, nor from that day did anyone dare to ask him any more questions.
22.overview:
Chapter 22 is a day of public controversy in Jerusalem. The religious establishment sends wave after wave of opponents — Pharisees, Herodians, Sadducees — each with a question designed to trap Jesus. He answers all of them and turns the final question back on his attackers, leaving them silenced. Matthew arranges the chapter as a trial in which the judge is the one in the dock: every party that challenges Jesus is exposed by his answers, and the final question — “Whose son is the Christ?” — reveals that the Messiah is not merely David’s descendant but David’s Lord.

The chapter opens with the parable of the wedding banquet, which recapitulates the entire history of Israel’s rejection of God’s invitations and the extension of grace to the Gentile roads and byways. “Many are called, but few are chosen” is not a statement about the inefficacy of the gospel but about the mystery of election: the call goes out wide; the choice of God secures who will respond. The banquet hall will be full — but with those God has chosen, not those who presumed on their invitation.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — The Parable of the Wedding Banquet and the Question about Taxes
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus tells the parable of the wedding banquet: a king invites guests to his son's wedding, they refuse and some kill his servants, the city is destroyed, and the hall is filled instead with whoever is found at the road junctions, both bad and good. One guest is discovered without a wedding garment and is cast out. Then the Pharisees and Herodians, in an alliance of convenience, try to trap him on the Roman poll tax; he asks for a coin, and answers that what bears Caesar's image goes to Caesar and what bears God's image goes to God. They marvel, and leave him.
verseByVerse.theology: The invitation is free, finished and urgent. Everything is ready is perfect tense throughout — the oxen are already slaughtered, nothing is pending, and the only thing outstanding is attendance. And the guests who refuse had already accepted, since invitations in that world went out twice; they are the second son of 21:30 again, whose word and whose feet have parted company. Grace then reaches the road junctions and gathers both bad and good with no screening at the door, which is the Gentile mission in parabolic form. But grace is not universalism: the king walks the room, and the man without the garment is speechless because nothing had been withheld from him — he had declined what was offered, not failed to manufacture what was required. On the tax, Jesus neither divinises Caesar nor anarchises the gospel. The coin bears Caesar's image and may be returned to him; the image on the man is God's, and that Caesar may never have.
verseByVerse.examples: Notice what the first guests were doing instead: one went to his farm, another to his business. Not vice, not blasphemy — a field that needed walking and a shop that needed running. The most effective rival to God in most lives has never been wickedness but respectable occupation, and it works because nobody has to defend it. Indifference and violence end in the same place in this parable, which should sober anyone who has assumed that not being hostile is the same as being safe; nobody here is condemned for opposing the king, only for not turning up. The tax scene has its own sting: asked for a coin, they produced one — in the temple, from men professing scruples about Caesar's tribute, a denarius inscribed Tiberius Caesar, son of the divine Augustus and Pontifex Maximus. It is easy to hold a principled objection while living comfortably inside the thing, and be unaware of the gap. The test is not what you would say if asked, but what turns up when somebody says: show me. And verse 22 names the most respectable way of rejecting Christ — they marvelled, and they left him.

verseByVerse.quote: And again Jesus spoke to them in parables, saying, "The kingdom of heaven may be compared to a king who gave a wedding feast for his son,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s kingdom is a royal wedding feast in honour of his Son, so to refuse the invitation is to pass a verdict on the Son himself.

Whose wedding. “A king who gave a wedding feast for his son.” A royal wedding was the occasion when a king put his whole house on display — herds slaughtered, cellars opened, days of celebration at his expense — all to honour his son. Declining such an invitation wasn’t a social lapse but a public verdict on the son.

Isaiah’s feast. Behind the image stands Isaiah: “On this mountain the LORD of hosts will make for all peoples a feast of rich food, a feast of well-aged wine” (Isaiah 25:6). The prophet’s picture of the end isn’t a courtroom or a cloud but food, company and wine kept for a great occasion — and alongside it, “He will swallow up death forever; and the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from all faces” (Isaiah 25:8). A test: is that what you look forward to?

Already accepted. Invitations in that world probably went out twice: a first notice in advance, then servants sent when the food was on the table to say, “Come, it is ready.” So those who refuse aren’t strangers turning down a stranger; they had said yes and are simply being called to keep their word. It is the second son again, who said “I will, sir” and didn’t go (21:30) — not a rebel, but a respectable person whose word and feet have quietly parted company.

The same as Luke’s banquet? Most likely not. The shape is like the great banquet of Luke 14:16–24, but here there is a king, his son’s wedding, murdered servants, a burned city and a guest without a garment. Jesus taught similar themes on different occasions.

A story for enemies. He tells this in the temple to the men who questioned his authority, days before they killed him. A story gets past defences an argument would only harden — and leaves a man who won’t have it holding nothing but an anecdote about catering.
verseByVerse.note: A royal wedding feast could last a week.

parallels.desc: the marriage supper of the Lamb

verseByVerse.quote: and sent his servants to call those who were invited to the wedding feast, but they would not come. Again he sent other servants, saying, "Tell those who are invited, See, I have prepared my dinner, my oxen and my fat calves have been slaughtered, and everything is ready. Come to the wedding feast."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything needed for our welcome is already done, so the gospel’s only remaining word to us is “Come.”

Not willing. “They would not come” — they weren’t willing. Not that they couldn’t or were prevented. The obstacle in this parable is never circumstance but the will, and Matthew says so before any excuse is offered (John 5:40).

He sends again. A slighted monarch would usually strike back. This king sends another delegation with a warmer message — the pattern of the previous parable, servants and then more servants (21:34–36), and of every prophet God sent to a people who had mistreated the last.

Everything is ready. “I have prepared my dinner, my oxen and my fat calves have been slaughtered, and everything is ready.” Done, finished, complete; nothing is pending. And without refrigeration, meat already killed can’t be put back. The king is committed and has made himself vulnerable to their refusal before they refuse.

The gospel invitation. That is the shape of the gospel. The church isn’t sent to persuade God to be gracious or to ask people to help him prepare. It is sent to say it is finished and the only thing outstanding is coming. What remained to be done when Jesus told this would be done within the week, and he would cry from the cross, “It is finished” (John 19:30).

Waiting for what? Many who aren’t at the feast think they are waiting for something: to understand more, to feel differently, to get part of their life straight first, to become the kind of person who belongs. Read the message again. There is nothing on the list. The oxen are killed, the tables laid, and the only word left is “Come.” A test: what are you waiting for?
verseByVerse.note: Guests were invited ahead of time and then summoned when the meal was ready.

verseByVerse.quote: But they paid no attention and went off, one to his farm, another to his business, while the rest seized his servants, treated them shamefully, and killed them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The commonest way to refuse God isn’t hostility but busyness with good things, and indifference ends in the same place as open rebellion.

Too busy. “They paid no attention and went off, one to his farm, another to his business.” They made light of it. Nobody argues or sends a reason. They just have something on.

A farm and a shop. Not vice or blasphemy or a rival religion, but a field to walk and a business to run — legitimate things a responsible man should attend to, and the reason he wasn’t at the wedding. God’s most effective rival in most lives isn’t wickedness but respectable occupation, and it works because no one has to defend it. A man who misses the feast for a mistress knows he has done something; a man who misses it for the farm has merely been busy (Luke 8:14).

Indifference. Indifference can be more dangerous than hostility. Hostility at least concedes the matter is serious. The men who went to the farm had settled their view of a royal invitation without ever thinking about it, and would sincerely say they had nothing against the king. Their diaries had decided it years earlier.

The violent. Others “seized his servants, treated them shamefully, and killed them.” Jesus isn’t exaggerating. Within a few years Stephen was stoned in that city and James killed by Herod’s sword (Acts 7:58–60; 12:2).

The same end. The violent and the busy are dealt with together and end in the same place: outside, with the feast going on without them. Anyone who assumes that not being hostile is the same as being safe should take note. No one in this story is condemned for opposing the king, but for not coming. A test: what is your farm, your business, that keeps you from coming?

parallels.desc: the servants in the vineyard beaten and killed

verseByVerse.quote: The king was angry, and he sent his troops and destroyed those murderers and burned their city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God’s patience has an end, and those who murder his messengers and refuse his Son will face his just anger — a warning that leaves no one, Gentile or Jew, room for smugness.

Not over a snub. Read carelessly, this looks like a king burning a town over a declined invitation. But the men in verse 6 seized the king’s envoys, humiliated and killed them. In the ancient world, murdering a royal embassy was an act of war. The king responds to murder by people who held their land from him.

The sentence had a date. Within forty years Jerusalem rose against Rome, and in AD 70 Titus took it after a terrible siege, burned the temple and levelled the city. Jesus says it plainly two chapters later: “there will not be left here one stone upon another” (24:2). Some suggest this verse was written in after the event. It needn’t have been; a man who predicted the destruction openly that same week could allude to it here.

No satisfaction. This verse has been quoted with satisfaction by Christians about Jewish people for centuries, and that satisfaction is a blasphemy. It is addressed to the tenants, the leadership (21:45), not to a race. The same speaker wept over this city: “How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!” (23:37). And the church in Jerusalem was made up of Jewish believers, who had been warned to flee (Luke 21:20–21). No Gentile Christian may feel comfortable reading it.

Patience has an end. What it says without apology is that patience ends. That isn’t cruel. A God who could be refused forever without consequence wouldn’t be a God who cared; the anger here exists because the invitation, the son and the murders were all real. A test: are you treating God’s invitation as though it will always be open?
verseByVerse.note: Many see here a pointer to the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to his servants, "The wedding feast is ready, but those invited were not worthy. Go therefore to the main roads and invite to the wedding feast as many as you find."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The King’s invitation goes out to the unlikely and undeserving — people at the road junctions with no claim at all — which is the story of every Gentile believer.

Not worthy. “Those invited were not worthy.” Worthiness here has nothing to do with merit. The first guests weren’t disqualified for failing a standard but for not coming. Those who fill the hall aren’t more deserving; they are simply willing to walk through a door. The only unworthiness that matters is refusal, and the only worthiness on offer is an empty stomach.

The main roads. The servants go where the streets leave town and meet the highway — junctions and edges, where people are passing through and belong to no one. There was no second tier on the guest list. Whoever stood at a road junction on the afternoon of a royal wedding was brought in.

The reversal. The first group had covenant standing, ancestral promise and a reserved place. The second had no pedigree, no claim and no reason to think a palace had anything to do with them. And they aren’t let in at the back to watch; they are guests at the wedding of the king’s son, at the same tables.

You at the junction. That is the Gentile mission in one sentence, and the story of most readers. If you aren’t Jewish, you are the person at the road junction, with no ancestral claim on the God of Israel and no grounds for complaint if the servants had walked past you (Ephesians 2:12–13). Paul never quite got over it, and neither should we.

A test for a church. The king’s instruction isn’t “invite those likely to accept” or “those who will fit in,” but “invite… as many as you find.” A church that looks like a careful selection from one part of one town hasn’t been to the main roads; it has been to the people it already knew.

parallels.desc: we are turning to the Gentiles

verseByVerse.quote: And those servants went out into the roads and gathered all whom they found, both bad and good. So the wedding hall was filled with guests.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nothing is required to get into the King’s feast, yet something is required to be there — the bad are welcomed, but they aren’t left as they were.

Bad and good. “Both bad and good.” Matthew puts the bad first. It isn’t an apology for the standard of guest; it is the point. The servants gathered everyone they found, and no one at the door was assessed.

No screening. We don’t really believe it. There is no check on a man’s history, no discreet enquiry, no probation. The hall filled with a crowd that wouldn’t have been admitted to any other event in the kingdom.

A full house. “So the wedding hall was filled with guests.” The room the first guests left empty didn’t stay empty. The king had determined there would be a full house, and there was.

Not “stay as you are.” This verse invites the reading “come as you are and stay as you are.” But the next verse is about a man who came as he was and wasn’t clothed, and the king who welcomes the bad without a question at the door also walks the room. Both halves are in the story: nothing is required to get in, and something is required to be there. The bad are brought in; they aren’t left as they were found (1 Corinthians 6:9–11).

What it does to a church. If the servants are doing their work, the hall will contain people whose lives are visibly a mess, before they are tidy. A congregation with no such people hasn’t been more faithful than the parable, only more selective. The early church — Jew and Gentile, slave and owner, the respectable and the notorious at one table — baffled the world around it. That wasn’t a lapse in standards; it was the servants doing as they were told. A test: would the messy feel welcome in your church?

parallels.desc: the net gathers fish of every kind

verseByVerse.quote: But when the king came in to look at the guests, he saw there a man who had no wedding garment. And he said to him, "Friend, how did you get in here without a wedding garment?" And he was speechless.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Being inside the church isn’t the same as being clothed by the King, and no one will have any excuse for refusing the righteousness he freely provides.

The king inspects. “When the king came in to look at the guests.” Everything so far has been about getting people through the door. Now the host walks the room, and one man is found who doesn’t belong.

Inside. The man is inside. He got past the servants, took a place among the guests, and no one challenged him. Whatever is wrong wasn’t detectable at the door; it is detected by the king (7:21–23).

“Friend.” The courteous, cool word Matthew uses only three times in address: to the grumbling labourer (20:13), here, and to Judas in Gethsemane (26:50). Each time to someone in the wrong, and each time polite.

Speechless. “How did you get in here without a wedding garment?” It is an enquiry, and he can’t meet it; he was silenced, as though muzzled. If he had been poor he could have said so; if overlooked, he could have said that. His silence is the admission.

The garment. It is often said hosts provided robes at the door. The evidence for that custom is thin. But the parable’s own logic points the same way: a man brought in off a road junction at an hour’s notice couldn’t be blamed for his clothes unless something had been made available. He is speechless because nothing was withheld. Scripture’s own pictures line up: “he has clothed me with the garments of salvation; he has covered me with the robe of righteousness” (Isaiah 61:10); and the bride “was granted” to clothe herself in fine linen (Revelation 19:8). The garment is the righteousness God gives in Christ and the holy life that always comes with it. No one in that hall wove his own clothes.

A believer who lost his salvation? Some read it that way. More likely he was a professing guest who never put on what the king provided — someone who came in on his own terms. Those whom God truly clothes he keeps: “no one will snatch them out of my hand” (John 10:28; cf. Philippians 1:6). A test: are you trusting your own clothes, or Christ’s righteousness?
verseByVerse.note: The wedding garment stands for the fitting clothing the host requires — the righteousness God gives and the life that matches it.

parallels.desc: clothed with the garments of salvation
fine linen, the righteous deeds of the saints

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king said to the attendants, "Bind him hand and foot and cast him into the outer darkness. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth." For many are called, but few are chosen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Final exclusion awaits those who refuse the King’s provision, and though many are called, the chosen are those God himself brings in — a truth meant to comfort, not to frighten, those who come.

The outer darkness. “Bind him hand and foot and cast him into the outer darkness.” It is the darkness outside the lit hall, and in Matthew it means final exclusion from the kingdom (8:12; 25:30): “weeping and gnashing of teeth,” grief and bitter regret without end. And it falls not for some dramatic wickedness but for refusing the King’s provision.

Called and chosen. “For many are called, but few are chosen.” The gospel invitation goes out genuinely and widely to all; those who actually come are those God has chosen and draws. The outward call goes to everyone without distinction; God’s inward call secures the response of his own (Romans 8:28–30; 2 Thessalonians 2:13). Some, especially in the Arminian tradition, read “chosen” as simply those who respond rightly: many are invited, few accept on the king’s terms. The Reformed reading is the more likely, since Scripture elsewhere makes God’s choosing the ground of a right response. In practice both agree: those who end up inside are those the king has clothed.

“What if I’m not chosen?” The doctrine raises a fear: if only the chosen are saved and I can’t see the list, what peace can I have? That fear has kept people from Christ, a bitter irony, since the doctrine was given to settle fear. No one in Scripture is told to establish that he is elect before coming. In this very parable the servants are given an invitation, not a list of names.

The floor, not the door. Paul writes about election to churches — people already inside — to explain how they got there and assure them they will be kept. It is the floor under the house, not the door. Someone standing outside trying to read the foundations before stepping through has mistaken what the doctrine is for. Look at Christ, the mirror in which we see our election, as Calvin taught. The promise has no small print: “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37).

If you want to come. So: if you want to come, come. And take the wanting as encouragement, because you didn’t manufacture it. No one draws himself toward God unaided (John 6:44); the desire to be at the feast is a sign that the One who chooses is already at work. The man without the garment wasn’t refused a ticket he couldn’t obtain; he declined what was offered. Nobody at that table earned his clothes, and nobody outside was refused a set. A test: have you come?

verseByVerse.quote: Then the Pharisees went and plotted how to entangle him in his words. And they sent their disciples to him, along with the Herodians, saying, "Teacher, we know that you are true and teach the way of God truthfully, and you do not care about anyone's opinion, for you are not swayed by appearances."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Enemies of Christ unite in strange alliances, and flattery is often a trap that uses our reputation to steer us into a fall.

A snare. “The Pharisees went and plotted how to entangle him in his words” — the word for a fowler’s snare, hidden, baited, and sprung by the bird’s own movement. Matthew tells us the intention first, so we can’t mistake what follows for a discussion.

A strange alliance. Pharisees regarded Roman rule as a defilement and the tribute as a humiliation. Herodians depended on Rome’s goodwill for everything they had. On the question about to be asked, they held opposite views. They agreed only that this man must be finished. Hostility to Christ has always been an efficient organiser of people who can’t otherwise share a room (Psalm 2:2). And the Pharisees “sent their disciples” — the younger men sent to do the work while the seniors kept their distance.

True words, false heart. “Teacher, we know that you are true and teach the way of God truthfully, and you do not care about anyone’s opinion.” Every clause is accurate. They describe him perfectly and don’t believe a word of it.

How flattery works. Scripture treats flattery as an attack, not a lapse of taste: “a flattering mouth works ruin” (Proverbs 26:28). The aim isn’t to please him but to build a box out of his reputation: we have said in public you fear no one, so prove it by answering recklessly. Praise a man for courage loudly enough and he may do something foolish to keep the compliment.

Recognising it. It still arrives dressed as respect. “You’re the only one here who says what he really thinks.” “You’re not afraid of this, like the others.” “I knew you’d understand — you’ve always been more open-minded.” Each holds a door open in a particular direction, and the compliment is the hinge. A test: is the praise describing you, or steering you — and did it arrive just before a request?
verseByVerse.note: The Herodians supported Herod’s family and Roman rule; the Pharisees resented Rome. Their alliance was a trap.

verseByVerse.quote: "Tell us, then, what you think. Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Some questions are built so that any answer offends someone, and the questioner wants the offence, not the truth.

A deadly question. The tax was the Roman poll tax, a denarius a year on every head in the province, introduced when Judea came under direct Roman rule in AD 6. The amount wasn’t the sting. A census had counted God’s people like Caesar’s cattle, and paying was a yearly admission of who owned the land. When it began, Judas the Galilean led a revolt against it and perished with his followers, as Gamaliel later reminded the council (Acts 5:37).

Either way, a witness. Say yes, and the crowds who had shouted “Hosanna” hear their Son of David endorse the tribute, with Pharisees there to make sure they hear it. Say no, and it is sedition, with Herodians there to make sure Pilate hears it. Either answer had its witnesses ready.

A question of conscience. “Is it lawful?” — does God’s law permit it? Framed that way, it looks like a scruple rather than a snare, and refusing to answer would look like dodging a religious duty. They aren’t asking what is wise; they are asking him to rule.

Still in use. Almost every generation produces a question designed so that a Christian must offend one group or the other, where the questioner wants the offence, not the answer. “Tell us, then, what you think” is often the most hostile sentence in the room. What Jesus does next isn’t a dodge or a compromise: he refuses the false choice and answers a larger question. A test: when you are handed a trap question, do you answer the trap, or seek the deeper truth?
verseByVerse.note: This was the poll tax paid directly to Rome, bitterly resented. “Yes” would anger the people; “no” would be treason.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus, aware of their malice, said, "Why put me to the test, you hypocrites? Show me the coin for the tax." And they brought him a denarius.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ sees through flattery to the heart, and he exposes the gap between our professed scruples and how we actually live.

He saw their malice. “But Jesus, aware of their malice.” The flattery didn’t work at all. They told him he wasn’t swayed by appearances, and then found that he wasn’t. He calls them “hypocrites” to their faces before answering a word.

Show me. “Show me the coin for the tax.” He doesn’t have one; he asks them. And they produce it, in the temple precincts. Men presenting themselves as troubled in conscience about paying Caesar’s tax have the coin in a purse on the temple mount and hand it over without a flicker.

What was on it. A denarius of Tiberius bore the emperor’s head and an inscription calling him son of the divine Augustus, and on the reverse the title “high priest.” So in the temple of the living God, men who claimed scruples handed Jesus a coin proclaiming another man son of a god and chief priest. They had carried it all morning. Their objection to Rome hadn’t reached their pockets.

Principle and purse. It is easy to hold a principled objection to something while living comfortably inside it, and to be unaware of the gap. These men weren’t consciously lying about their scruples; they had simply never let scruple and purse meet. A test: it isn’t what you would say if asked, but what turns up when someone says, “Show me.”
verseByVerse.note: The denarius was a silver coin, a day’s wage for a labourer.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jesus said to them, "Whose likeness and inscription is this?" They said, "Caesar's." Then he said to them, "Therefore render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Give the state what it rightly claims, but give God yourself, because you bear his image — and when the two clash, we must obey God rather than men.

Whose image? “Whose likeness and inscription is this?” “Caesar’s.” The coin bears Caesar’s image, so give it back to him; don’t make a religion of resenting it. But you bear God’s image (Genesis 1:27), so render yourself to God. Civil government has real authority in its sphere; God’s authority is ultimate and total. The answer neither makes Caesar divine nor makes the gospel anarchy.

When they collide. What do I do when Caesar commands what God forbids, or forbids what God commands? The apostles answered before the same council. Ordered to stop preaching, Peter said, “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29), and took the flogging. So did the Hebrew midwives who wouldn’t kill the boys (Exodus 1:17), the three young men who wouldn’t bow to the statue (Daniel 3:16–18), and Daniel at his open window.

Two guards. First, the exemption is narrow. Paul wrote, “Let every person be subject to the governing authorities” (Romans 13:1), and Peter, “Honor the emperor” (1 Peter 2:17), under Nero, who would kill them both. A government being unjust, corrupt or hostile isn’t in itself grounds for disobedience. The line is crossed not when the state is wicked but when it requires you to be. Second, the manner. Those examples disobeyed openly and bore the cost — no rebellion, plotting or contempt. Christian disobedience isn’t refusing the state’s authority to punish but refusing to sin, with the punishment accepted.

Everything. Under it lies something more radical than a tidy division of spheres. Caesar may have your taxes, your obedience in his own sphere, your honour and your prayers. He may never have the thing that bears the other image. That isn’t a small reservation; it is everything. Tyrants have found that Christians will give them the coin all day and won’t give them that. A test: have you given God yourself?
verseByVerse.note: The coin bore the emperor’s head — probably Tiberius — and an inscription calling him son of the divine Augustus.

parallels.desc: be subject to the governing authorities

verseByVerse.quote: When they heard it, they marveled. And they left him and went away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Admiring Christ without following him is the most respectable way of rejecting him, and admiration that refuses to become allegiance doesn’t stay neutral for long.

They marveled. Matthew has sounded this note for two chapters. The chief priests saw his wonderful works and were indignant (21:15); Jesus called the rejected stone “marvelous in our eyes” (21:42); now his opponents marvel at an answer they can’t fault. Three marvels, and none ends in worship.

They left him. Not the argument — him. They came with a question, received a better answer than any of them could produce, were genuinely impressed, and walked away from the person. Nothing had happened to them.

The respectable rejection. This is the most respectable way of rejecting Christ, and the commonest, and the special danger of people who read commentaries. You can find Jesus intellectually magnificent — enjoy how he handles opponents, admire the answer about Caesar, recommend the passage to others — and not have moved an inch. Admiration is comfortable. It costs nothing, flatters the admirer, and can last a lifetime.

By Thursday. A simple test: when you finished the last passage you read, did anything change by Thursday? Not whether you agreed or found it striking, but whether you did anything, stopped anything, said anything to anyone, asked anyone’s forgiveness (James 1:22–24).

Where it goes. “They left him and went away” — and they will come back, not with questions but looking for false witnesses against him (26:59). A test: has your admiration of Christ become obedience?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–46 — Resurrection, the Great Commandment, and David's Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Three delegations in succession, and then Jesus asks a question of his own. The Sadducees construct a levirate-marriage absurdity with seven brothers to make resurrection look ridiculous, and are told they know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God — the resurrection proved out of the Torah they accepted, from the present tense of one verb at the burning bush. The crowd is astonished. The Pharisees regroup and send a lawyer to ask which commandment is greatest, and receive the Shema and Leviticus 19:18, on which the whole Law and Prophets hang. Then Jesus asks whose son the Christ is, quotes Psalm 110, and nobody is able to answer him a word or dares question him again.
verseByVerse.theology: Two failures are named in one sentence and almost every serious error in the church lands under one of them: you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. The Sadducees had the Torah by heart, which is what makes the first charge devastating — knowing the Scriptures is not the same as having them. And they believed in God while not believing he could do anything, which is a God cut down to the size of arrangements we already understand. The resurrection argument turns on covenant: God binds himself by name to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob and says I am, not I was, six hundred years after Abraham died. He does not attach his name to dust. Then the double love command, where the verb is krematai — the Law and Prophets hang on two pegs, so the 613 commandments are not separate obligations but the outworking of two. And Psalm 110 closes the sequence: the Christ is David's son according to the flesh and David's Lord according to his eternal nature, which is Matthew's own first chapter put as a riddle (1:23).
verseByVerse.examples: Like angels in heaven needs its guard: it does not mean we become angels or lose our bodies. The comparison is made in one respect only, and the sentence names it — angels do not marry. On the tender question every widow and every married reader brings here, see the verse-by-verse on vv. 29-30: what ends is the institution, not the love. Notice also the woman in the Sadducees' story, whom nobody in it notices — she has buried seven husbands and appears purely as a question of ownership, and Jesus's answer incidentally gives her back what their question took away. As yourself in v. 39 is a measure, not a recommendation of self-esteem: you never have to be reminded to take an interest in your own toothache, and that automatic attention is the standard. Test it where it bites — when something goes wrong for you the mind supplies context, and when it goes wrong at somebody else's hands the mind supplies character. And v. 33 is a warning laid inside a victory: astonishment is not allegiance, and within three days a crowd in this city would be shouting for Barabbas.

verseByVerse.quote: The same day Sadducees came to him, who say that there is no resurrection, and they asked him a question, saying, "Teacher, Moses said, 'If a man dies having no children, his brother must marry the widow and raise up offspring for his brother.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Those with most to lose in this world often find the arguments against a world to come most persuasive, and doubts about the resurrection rest on a false picture of it.

The Sadducees. They were the aristocratic, priestly party: the high priest was one of them, they controlled the temple and its revenues, and held real power in Jerusalem. They rejected the Pharisees’ oral traditions and gave the five books of Moses the highest place. They denied the resurrection, and with it angels and spirits (Acts 23:8), and they had made their working arrangement with Rome.

Why it fits. Those things fit together. A party with wealth, office and influence in this world has the least incentive to believe in a world to come. If this life is where the accounts are settled, they have already won, and a coming judgment can only threaten. Theology is rarely held in a vacuum: the men whom the resurrection would cost most found the arguments against it most persuasive (Luke 16:31).

Why they are here. They had watched Jesus clear the temple courts, and the temple was theirs. This isn’t an enquiry but the men whose market he overturned coming back with a clever question.

The law of the brother. Their premise is the levirate law (Deuteronomy 25:5–6): if a married man died without a son, his brother was to marry the widow, and the first son would carry the dead man’s name and inheritance. It protected widows from destitution and kept the family line and land intact; Ruth’s story shows its spirit. Their question will try to make resurrection look absurd by assuming it means simply resuming this life. A test: do your doubts about eternity arise from evidence, or from what belief would cost you?
verseByVerse.note: The Sadducees, the priestly party, rejected the Pharisees’ oral traditions and probably held the five books of Moses above the rest of Scripture and denied the resurrection. The law of levirate marriage kept a dead man’s name alive.

parallels.desc: Sadducees say there is no resurrection

verseByVerse.quote: "Now there were seven brothers among us. The first married and died, and having no offspring left his wife to his brother. So too the second and third, down to the seventh."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Clever arguments against God often hide a false premise, and they can treat real suffering people as mere counters in a debate.

A debating case. Seven brothers, seven marriages, seven funerals, no children. It isn’t a real case brought for a ruling; it is a constructed puzzle, piled high so the doctrine looks ridiculous.

The hidden premise. The logic runs: if your doctrine is true, this absurd situation follows; it is absurd; so your doctrine is false. Everything depends on the hidden premise — that resurrection means resuming this life exactly as it was, with the same contracts and property law. Jesus will deny the premise, which is usually where such arguments really break.

The woman. Nobody in the story notices her. She is the only person in it who has suffered anything. She buried seven husbands, was handed from brother to brother as a legal obligation, bore no children in a society where a childless widow had no protection, and died after a life of accumulating grief. In the argument she is only a difficulty — whose wife will she be? The question is about the men.

Her dignity restored. They took a law meant to protect destitute widows and used it to mock the one hope that could comfort such a woman. And Jesus’ answer gives her back what their question took: in the resurrection she isn’t the seventh brother’s property or the first brother’s widow. She is herself, before God.

People as illustrations. It isn’t the main point, but it isn’t nothing. People who use others as counters in an argument rarely notice. A test: in your debates, do you remember that the people involved are real?

verseByVerse.quote: "After them all, the woman died. In the resurrection, therefore, of the seven, whose wife will she be? For they all had her."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The life to come isn’t this life improved but this life transformed, real and bodily, yet beyond anything we can extrapolate from here.

“They all had her.” The word is the word for having something as one’s own, and the assumption is baked into the question. Seven men had a claim; the resurrection would produce a dispute; so it can’t be true. The argument is only as good as its picture of the age to come, and the picture is this one with the wrinkles ironed out.

Heaven improved. That error isn’t confined to Sadducees. Ask most people, Christians included, what they expect of heaven and you will hear the present world improved: the same house without the mortgage, the same work without Monday, the same relationships without friction. It is natural, since this world is all the material we have. But it is extension, not transformation, and the New Testament never describes the age to come that way.

Why heaven sounds boring. That is why heaven strikes many people as faintly dull. If the hope is just this life continued forever, honest reflection finds the prospect wearying, and the fault is in the picture, not the hope. Paul answers the same confusion with a seed: “what you sow is not the body that is to be, but a bare kernel” (1 Corinthians 15:37). Continuous, the same life, and not remotely predictable from the seed. No one holding an acorn would guess an oak.

Both halves. The resurrection body is neither a ghost nor a repeat. It is real and recognisable — the risen Christ ate fish before his friends and showed Thomas his scars (Luke 24:42–43; John 20:27) — and also transformed past anything we can imagine (1 Corinthians 15:42–44). Drop the first and you get a spiritual mist Scripture never promises; drop the second and you get the Sadducees’ question, which has no answer.

Imagination and unbelief. These men weren’t short of intelligence but of any category for a God who does genuinely new things. So the only future they could imagine was a copy of the past, and quite reasonably they found it absurd. A test: does your hope of heaven stir you, or only bore you?

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus answered them, "You are wrong, because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God. For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like angels in heaven."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Error about eternity comes from not knowing the Scriptures or the power of God; in the resurrection marriage gives way to something greater, and no good love is lost.

“You are wrong.” No diplomatic opening. “You are wrong” — deceived, led off the road — said publicly to the party that ran the temple.

Two errors. “You know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God.” Almost every serious error lands under one of these. These men knew the Torah by heart, which makes the first charge devastating: knowing the words isn’t the same as knowing what they say. And the second is worse: they believed in God and didn’t believe he could do anything. A God who can’t raise the dead has been cut down to the size of arrangements we already understand.

The premise denied. “In the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage.” The man’s part and the woman’s part in that world’s arrangements are simply absent. Their puzzle isn’t solved; it stops applying.

Like angels — how? “Like angels in heaven” is often misread. We don’t become angels; Scripture never suggests humans are turned into a different kind of creature, and the idea that the dead get wings has no footing here. Nor do we become bodiless. The likeness is in one respect only: angels don’t marry.

Will I be with my spouse? A married or widowed reader can’t help asking. What ends is the institution — the exclusive covenant “till death us do part,” given for this age and the raising of families; in the resurrection there is no death to guard against and no children to bear. But love isn’t abolished; it is perfected. You won’t know your beloved less, but far more, in a love with nothing left to fear or forgive. Marriage was always a signpost, a picture of Christ and his church (Ephesians 5:32), and when the marriage supper of the Lamb comes (Revelation 19:7–9), the picture gives way to what it was painting. We aren’t told every detail. It is enough that nothing good is lost there; it is taken up, deepened and made everlasting. A test: is your hope fixed on the Bridegroom himself?

verseByVerse.quote: "And as for the resurrection of the dead, have you not read what was said to you by God: 'I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob'? He is not God of the dead, but of the living."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God binds himself by covenant to his people by name, and the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob doesn’t leave his own to the grave.

From Moses. The Sadducees gave the five books of Moses the highest authority, and the clearest statements of resurrection stand later, in Isaiah and Daniel (Isaiah 26:19; Daniel 12:2). Jesus doesn’t appeal to those. He goes to Exodus, to the burning bush, and argues on the ground they acknowledged.

A covenant, not a tense. “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” God said this to Moses centuries after the patriarchs had died. The Hebrew has no verb at all — literally “I, the God of Abraham” — so the argument doesn’t rest on the tense of a verb. It rests on the covenant. God had bound himself by name to these three men as persons, not to an idea. A God who ties his own name to a man and then lets him end as dust would have broken his covenant; the relationship would be a memorial, not a bond. “He is not God of the dead, but of the living” (cf. Luke 20:38, “for all live to him”). If the LORD is still the God of Abraham at the bush, Abraham is still there to have a God.

Said to you. “Have you not read what was said to you by God.” Not to Moses long ago, but to you. Jesus tells men in Jerusalem that a sentence spoken at a bush in the desert was addressed to them. Scripture isn’t only a record that God once spoke; it is God speaking now (Hebrews 3:7).

Three flawed names. God might have called himself by any title — maker of heaven and earth, the God who parts seas. What he chose, at the bush and through the rest of the Bible, was the God of three men. One lied about his wife twice; one was a passive father who favoured the wrong son; one cheated his brother and limped after wrestling God. He took their names into his own and kept them there, and on that basis Jesus tells a hostile court that the grave doesn’t get them. A test: do you believe God has bound his name to you in Christ?
verseByVerse.note: Jesus answers from the books of Moses, the part of Scripture the Sadducees held highest.

parallels.desc: the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob

verseByVerse.quote: And when the crowd heard it, they were astonished at his teaching.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Being astonished by Jesus isn’t the same as following him; the question is whether anything changes after we are moved.

Astonished. The word means to be struck out of oneself, knocked sideways. Matthew uses it of the Sermon on the Mount (7:28), of Nazareth (13:54), of the disciples on the rich man (19:25), and here. These people have been hit by something.

Who they are. Not the Sadducees, now silent, nor the Pharisees about to regroup, but the ordinary crowd in the temple courts: pilgrims, tradesmen, families. They have watched their teachers beaten by a Galilean and are delighted.

A warning in a victory. Read it with some sadness. Matthew has shown us where this crowd’s astonishment goes. Within days a crowd at the governor’s residence, worked on by the men who have just lost this argument, will shout for a murderer to be freed instead of him (27:20–23).

Astonishment isn’t allegiance. You can enjoy Jesus enormously — relish his answers, enjoy seeing pomposity dismantled, leave a service genuinely moved — and still be one of the crowd rather than a disciple. In this Gospel the difference between the two is almost never the intensity of the reaction, but whether anyone follows him out of the building.

A fair test. Nothing here is against being moved; the Psalms are full of it. But ask what last moved you deeply, and what it changed. If it was a very good hour and nothing came of it, that isn’t a reason to despair but a reason to ask him for more than astonishment.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the Pharisees heard that he had silenced the Sadducees, they gathered together. And one of them, a lawyer, asked him a question to test him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Opposition to Christ isn’t a set of convictions that a better argument could change, but a settled hostility that survives every argument — yet God can bring glory from a hostile question.

They regrouped. The Pharisees’ rivals have just been publicly beaten on the very point the Pharisees held: the resurrection, defended from the Torah. They might have been delighted. Instead they close ranks and send another questioner. Opposition to Christ isn’t a set of convictions a better argument might correct but a disposition that survives every argument, including the ones it wins.

Gathered together. “They gathered together” echoes Psalm 2, where “the rulers take counsel together, against the LORD and against his Anointed” (Psalm 2:2). The early church prayed that psalm and named those in it: Herod, Pilate, the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel, gathered against God’s holy servant Jesus (Acts 4:25–27). The men in the temple court are standing inside a psalm whose verdict is that “He who sits in the heavens laughs” (Psalm 2:4).

Testing him. A lawyer — an expert in the law — asks “to test him,” the word used of the devil in the wilderness (4:1) and of the Pharisees on divorce (19:3). Matthew has been keeping a list of those who came to test Jesus.

Glory from bad motives. What follows is the greatest answer about the law ever given, drawn out by a man who didn’t want to know. God has never been kept from saying something glorious by the poor motives of whoever asked. A test: do you come to Christ’s word wanting to learn, or to argue?
verseByVerse.note: A lawyer was an expert in the law of Moses.

verseByVerse.quote: "Teacher, which is the great commandment in the Law?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Treating God’s commands as a list to manage leaves the self in charge, but Christ’s answer takes the whole person and leaves nothing to do the managing.

Weighing the commands. Teachers in Jesus’ day debated which commandments were heavy and which light, and Jesus himself spoke of “the weightier matters of the law” (23:23). Later rabbinic tradition counted 613 commandments in the Torah. So the question was real.

A trap with three jaws. But in this mouth it is a trap. Name one commandment great and you imply the others are small. Name one linked to a party and you offend the rest. Refuse and you aren’t the teacher you claim to be.

An inventory. Underneath sits an assumption: the law is an inventory of separate items that could be sorted by importance, so a careful man could work out where to spend his attention. That leaves the man himself intact. However scrupulous he becomes, he is managing a portfolio.

No one left to manage. Jesus doesn’t refuse to rank or pick a safe item from the middle. He names what every command is made of, and takes the question out of the man’s competence altogether. You can’t manage a portfolio of loving God with all your heart; nothing is left over to do the managing.

Your list. Most Christians have a working list of what really matters and what is “technically” commanded, never written down or defended aloud, and usually shaped to be keepable. A test: what is on your list, and what have you left off because it couldn’t be kept?
verseByVerse.note: Later rabbis counted 613 commandments in the law; teachers debated which were weightiest.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to him, "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind. This is the great and first commandment."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The great commandment calls for love of God with all that we are; it exposes our failure, sends us to Christ who kept it for us, and grows in us as we look at his love.

All of you. Jesus quotes Deuteronomy 6:5, the heart of Israel’s daily confession. Heart, soul, mind: every faculty directed wholly to God. This is first because all other obedience flows from it.

Three words or four? Matthew has heart, soul and mind; Mark has four, “heart… soul… mind… strength” (Mark 12:30); Luke the same four in another order (Luke 10:27); Deuteronomy has “heart… soul… might.” The list isn’t an inventory dividing a person into drawers but a Hebrew way of saying all of you; the terms overlap and pile up. Jesus gives the sense of a text everyone knew, and every version agrees: the list has no edge you can stand outside.

“I don’t love God like that.” That is the honest difficulty, and you can’t command a feeling. The objection is half right. Biblical love is never less than feeling — the Psalms are full of thirst and longing — but it is chiefly a settled direction of the whole person, which is why it can be commanded. So the question “Do I love God?” isn’t answered by taking your emotional temperature. Jesus answers it: “If you love me, you will keep my commandments” (John 14:15). Obedience isn’t a substitute for love; it is love’s most reliable evidence, available on days when feeling isn’t.

How it grows. Not by working on the love directly, which is like trying to feel warm by concentrating. Love is a response: “We love because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19). The way to love God more is to look longer at what he has done, which is why the church puts the cross at the centre of worship. In practice: Scripture read slowly, the Lord’s Supper, singing with others, remembering particular mercies — and obeying meanwhile. Feelings often follow the feet.

Christ who kept it. A lawyer asks for the greatest command, and Jesus gives him the one no one in the room had kept for an hour.
