You are commanded to love God with all your heart and soul and mind; you haven’t; and the one telling you so did, all the way to the cross, in your place. Start there, and loving becomes possible, because it is no longer the price of anything. A test: are you looking long enough at his love to love him back?

parallels.desc: love the LORD your God with all your heart

verseByVerse.quote: "And a second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. On these two commandments depend all the Law and the Prophets."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Love of neighbour stands beside love of God, and the whole of Scripture hangs on these two; giving others the attention we give ourselves is far harder, and truer, than being nice.

Like it. “And a second is like it” — of the same kind. He doesn’t say the second is nearly as important but puts love of neighbour in the same category as love of God.

Hangs on two pegs. “On these two commandments depend all the Law and the Prophets” — hang, as a door on hinges. Everything Moses wrote and the prophets thundered is suspended from two pegs. The many commands aren’t separate obligations but love of God or love of neighbour taking particular shapes (Romans 13:9–10).

As yourself. This isn’t a command to self-esteem, to love yourself first and pass on the surplus. It names a measure chosen because no one needs persuading of it. Nobody has to remember to care about his own toothache, his own future, being cold, or being treated unfairly. That automatic, ever-present attention to your own case is the standard: give the same to the person next to you.

The same excuses. When something goes wrong for you, the mind supplies context at once: I was tired, it was difficult, anyone would have. When the same happens at someone else’s hands, it supplies character: he is careless, she is like that. Loving your neighbour as yourself means giving him the same generous supply of excuses you make for yourself. It would reshape most families and churches within a fortnight.

Who is my neighbour? The command comes from Leviticus 19:18, applying first to fellow Israelites and then, in the same chapter, to the foreigner: “you shall love him as yourself” (Leviticus 19:34). When a lawyer asked Jesus this, he told of the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:25–37): your neighbour is anyone in need you can help. And Jesus has said it includes enemies (5:43–48).

Inseparable. “If anyone says, ‘I love God,’ and hates his brother, he is a liar” (1 John 4:20). The love of God isn’t a private arrangement between a man and heaven that leaves the people in his house untouched. It comes down the stairs, or it was never on the roof. A test: whom do you need to give the benefit of the doubt you give yourself?

verseByVerse.quote: Now while the Pharisees were gathered together, Jesus asked them a question, saying, "What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is he?" They said to him, "The son of David."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A correct answer about Jesus isn’t the same as a living faith; we must follow the truth far enough to see who is asking.

His question. All day he has answered questions: the tax, the resurrection, the great commandment. Now, with the Pharisees gathered, he puts one question of his own, and it is the only one in the chapter that finally matters: “What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is he?”

The same question. At Caesarea Philippi he asked twelve friends, “Who do you say that I am?” (16:15). Here, among the men arranging his death, he asks it about the Messiah in the abstract. It is the question this Gospel has been walking toward since the genealogy, and everyone in Matthew ends up answering it: Peter, the high priest, Pilate, the centurion at the cross.

True and stopped short. “The son of David.” It is right — the orthodox answer any student would give, the title the blind men shouted on the Jericho road (20:30; cf. 2 Samuel 7:12–16). They aren’t caught in an error but in an answer that is true and has stopped short.

A correct position. That is the danger exposed here, and it isn’t unbelief. You can hold a completely correct doctrine about Jesus Christ and get no further than the doctrine. These men could have passed an exam on the Messiah’s lineage; what they couldn’t do was follow their own answer far enough to notice who was asking. Jesus doesn’t correct their answer; he asks them to keep reading. A test: has your right doctrine about Christ brought you to bow before him?

verseByVerse.quote: He said to them, "How is it then that David, in the Spirit, calls him Lord, saying, 'The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, until I put your enemies under your feet'?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
David, speaking by the Spirit, called the Messiah his Lord, showing that the Christ is far more than David’s descendant — he shares God’s throne.

My Lord. Jesus cites Psalm 110:1, one of the Old Testament verses most often quoted in the New (Acts 2:34–35; Hebrews 1:13). David calls the Messiah “my Lord,” an address no Israelite king would use of his own descendant. And this Lord is enthroned at God’s right hand, ruling until all enemies are subdued. So the Messiah must be more than David’s heir; he must share God’s own rule.

Did David write it? The argument rests on David being the author, and much modern scholarship assigns Psalm 110 to a later court poet writing of a king, in which case there is no puzzle. Three things weigh against that. The psalm’s heading reads “A Psalm of David,” the oldest testimony we have. These hostile experts, eager to catch him in a mistake, could have answered in one sentence — “David didn’t write that psalm” — and none did: “no one was able to answer him a word” (v. 46). Their silence shows what everyone took for granted.

His word on it. And for a Christian the third settles it. Jesus stakes a public argument about his own identity on David’s authorship, saying David spoke “in the Spirit.” He could have argued from other texts. A Lord who built his case on a premise he knew to be false wouldn’t be worth trusting on anything else. A test: do you take Scripture as Christ took it — as God’s Spirit speaking through its human authors?
verseByVerse.note: Psalm 110:1 is among the Old Testament verses most often quoted in the New.

verseByVerse.quote: "If then David calls him Lord, how is he his son?" And no one was able to answer him a word, nor from that day did anyone dare to ask him any more questions.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Christ is both David’s son and David’s Lord, truly man and truly God; when arguments are exhausted, every mouth must end in one kind of silence or another.

The riddle. “If then David calls him Lord, how is he his son?” Inside their framework there is no answer. A descendant isn’t his ancestor’s lord; the more royal the ancestor, the more absurd the reversal. Either David spoke carelessly, or the Messiah is more than the last and greatest king in a line.

The answer. There is one arrangement in which both are true, which the church took centuries to state carefully: Christ is David’s son by human descent and David’s Lord in his eternal nature — one person, truly man and truly God (Romans 1:3–4). The son of Mary who grew tired on the road to Jerusalem is the same person who was at the Father’s right hand before David was born. Matthew has said it since chapter 1, where the son of David is also “Immanuel… God with us” (1:23).

Silence. “No one was able to answer him a word, nor from that day did anyone dare to ask him any more questions.” The controversies are over. What follows isn’t debate but the woes of chapter 23 and the long discourse of chapters 24–25. The next time these men speak in his presence, they will be seeking witnesses against him (26:59). When argument is exhausted, what remains isn’t agreement but the plot.

Three silences. This chapter shows different kinds of silence. The man without the wedding garment was speechless because he had no defence (v. 12). These men are silent because they won’t say what they can see. And there is the silence of someone who stops arguing because he has understood who he is talking to. One day “every knee should bow” (Philippians 2:10). The only question left is which kind of quiet a person ends in, and Jesus stood in that court answering delegation after delegation to give the men before him time to choose the right one. A test: have you stopped arguing with Christ and bowed?

22.theology: Election and the free offer of the gospel. The parable of the wedding banquet and the phrase “many are called, but few are chosen” bring together two truths that Reformed theology has always insisted must be held together. The general call of the gospel goes out to all people without exception — “Go therefore to the main roads and invite as many as you find.” This is the free and genuine offer of the gospel, and it must be preached without restriction. At the same time, the effectual call of God draws the chosen to the feast. Both are real; both are necessary. The preacher does not know who the elect are; he simply opens the banquet doors as wide as the gospel goes and trusts God with the result.
22.examples:
Then: The religious leaders tried to trap Jesus with politics (tribute coin), doctrine (resurrection), law (greatest commandment). He answered all three with Scripture, clarity, and a question they could not answer. The one they thought to judge was the judge.

Now: The same four questions are still asked of Christians today — political, doctrinal, ethical, and Christological. The answers Jesus gives are still sufficient. Render to Caesar what is Caesar’s; God claims your whole self made in his image. The resurrection is secured by the living God who keeps covenant. Love God with everything; love your neighbour as yourself. And the Christ is both Son of David and Lord of David — the God-man who saves.

23.title: Woe to You, Scribes and Pharisees
23.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Jesus said to the crowds and to his disciples, <sup>2</sup>“The scribes and the Pharisees sit on Moses’ seat, <sup>3</sup>so do and observe whatever they tell you, but not the works they do. For they preach, but do not practice. <sup>4</sup>They tie up heavy burdens, hard to bear, and lay them on people’s shoulders, but they themselves are not willing to move them with their finger. <sup>5</sup>They do all their deeds to be seen by others. For they make their phylacteries broad and their fringes long, <sup>6</sup>and they love the place of honor at feasts and the best seats in the synagogues <sup>7</sup>and greetings in the marketplaces and being called rabbi by others. <sup>8</sup>But you are not to be called rabbi, for you have one teacher, and you are all brothers. <sup>9</sup>And call no man your father on earth, for you have one Father, who is in heaven. <sup>10</sup>Neither be called instructors, for you have one instructor, the Christ. <sup>11</sup>The greatest among you shall be your servant. <sup>12</sup>Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted. <sup>13</sup>“But woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you shut the kingdom of heaven in people’s faces. For you neither enter yourselves nor allow those who would enter to go in. <sup>15</sup>Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you travel across sea and land to make a single proselyte, and when he becomes a proselyte, you make him twice as much a child of hell as yourselves. <sup>16</sup>“Woe to you, blind guides, who say, ‘If anyone swears by the temple, it is nothing, but if anyone swears by the gold of the temple, he is bound by his oath.’ <sup>17</sup>You blind fools! For which is greater, the gold or the temple that has made the gold sacred? <sup>18</sup>And you say, ‘If anyone swears by the altar, it is nothing, but if anyone swears by the gift that is on the altar, he is bound by his oath.’ <sup>19</sup>You blind men! For which is greater, the gift or the altar that makes the gift sacred? <sup>20</sup>So whoever swears by the altar swears by it and by everything on it. <sup>21</sup>And whoever swears by the temple swears by it and by him who dwells in it. <sup>22</sup>And whoever swears by heaven swears by the throne of God and by him who sits upon it. <sup>23</sup>“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you tithe mint and dill and cumin, and have neglected the weightier matters of the law: justice and mercy and faithfulness. These you ought to have done, without neglecting the others. <sup>24</sup>You blind guides, straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel! <sup>25</sup>“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you clean the outside of the cup and the plate, but inside they are full of greed and self-indulgence. <sup>26</sup>You blind Pharisee! First clean the inside of the cup and the plate, that the outside also may be clean. <sup>27</sup>“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful, but within are full of dead people’s bones and all uncleanness. <sup>28</sup>So you also outwardly appear righteous to others, but within you are full of hypocrisy and lawlessness. <sup>29</sup>“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you build the tombs of the prophets and decorate the monuments of the righteous, <sup>30</sup>saying, ‘If we had lived in the days of our fathers, we would not have taken part with them in shedding the blood of the prophets.’ <sup>31</sup>Thus you witness against yourselves that you are sons of those who murdered the prophets. <sup>32</sup>Fill up, then, the measure of your fathers. <sup>33</sup>You serpents, you brood of vipers, how are you to escape being sentenced to hell? <sup>34</sup>Therefore I send you prophets and wise men and scribes, some of whom you will kill and crucify, and some you will flog in your synagogues and persecute from town to town, <sup>35</sup>so that on you may come all the righteous blood shed on earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah the son of Barachiah, whom you murdered between the sanctuary and the altar. <sup>36</sup>Truly, I say to you, all these things will come upon this generation. <sup>37</sup>“O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it! How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing! <sup>38</sup>See, your house is left to you desolate. <sup>39</sup>For I tell you, you will not see me again, until you say, ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.’”
23.overview:
Chapter 23 opens the fifth and final discourse of Matthew — and the most sorrowful. It begins with a warning to the crowds and disciples about the Pharisees (vv. 1–12), then delivers seven woes against the scribes and Pharisees (vv. 13–36), and closes with a lament over Jerusalem (vv. 37–39) that is one of the most heartbreaking passages in all of Scripture. The woes are not vindictive; they are diagnostic. Jesus names the disease precisely so that it can be seen for what it is: a religion of external performance concealing internal corruption, a leadership that burdens rather than shepherds, a tradition that has become a wall keeping people out of the kingdom.

The lament over Jerusalem (“O Jerusalem, Jerusalem”) reveals the heart behind the woes. Jesus does not pronounce judgment with cold severity; he pronounces it with the grief of a hen who would have gathered her chicks but could not because they would not come. The image is maternal, tender, aching. The holy Judge is also the loving Shepherd who weeps over the city he must judge. Both are true: God is not willing that any should perish, and God judges unrepentant hardness of heart. The cross, which is days away, is where both truths converge.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — Seven Woes: The Hypocrisy of Scribes and Pharisees (Part One)
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus turns from silencing his opponents to warning the crowds about them, and this is his last public address in Matthew. He concedes the office before he indicts the men: the scribes and Pharisees sit on Moses' seat, so what they read from it binds Israel even when their lives do not match it. Then the indictment — burdens tied on other people's shoulders and not lifted with a finger, phylacteries widened and fringes lengthened to be seen, titles and seats and greetings craved — followed by the levelling of the disciples under one Teacher and one Father. The first three woes follow: shutting the kingdom in people's faces, making converts twice as much children of hell, and the whole scribal machinery of binding and non-binding oaths.
verseByVerse.theology: The chapter begins with a distinction the church has needed ever since: the authority of a pulpit is borrowed, every word of it. When a man sits on Moses' seat and reads out what God has said, the hearer is bound and the messenger's hypocrisy does not release him; when he steps off that seat, the conscience is free. So do and observe whatever they tell you is not a blank endorsement of Pharisaic teaching, which this same Gospel calls leaven (16:12) and says made void the commandment of God (15:6). On titles, the reason given is Christological rather than merely moral: no disciple is to be called rabbi because the seat is occupied — there is one Teacher, and he names him as the Christ. And the first woe is the head of all seven. The other six describe men damaging themselves; this one describes men standing in a doorway between other people and the kingdom, and it is put first for that reason.
verseByVerse.examples: The burdens are worth making concrete: thirty-nine categories of forbidden Sabbath work, each subdivided, down to whether a chair might be dragged in case dragging scratched a furrow. None of it was invented by wicked men; it was produced by serious people trying to be careful, which is how such systems are always produced. And the same tradition supplied the devices by which those who knew it could live within it — so the men who designed the yoke were the ones least troubled by it. Matthew makes the contrast with the same noun: heavy burdens here (phortia), and my burden is light at 11:30 (phortion). The phylacteries and fringes were both commanded, and Jesus wore the fringes himself (9:20) — the objection is to the width and the length, which is why this woe cannot be legislated against. The test that gets underneath it is not what you do but who is watching: take something genuinely good in your religious life, suppose it were certain nobody would ever know of it, and see what quietly deflates.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Jesus said to the crowds and to his disciples, "The scribes and the Pharisees sit on Moses' seat,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Note who is being spoken to, because it is not who we assume. Jesus said to the crowds and to his disciples. The scribes and Pharisees are talked about in the third person for most of the first twelve verses — he is warning the congregation about its clergy, in public, in the temple, with the clergy standing there listening. That is a considerable thing to do, and it is worth registering that he did it openly rather than privately.

Moses' seat was a real piece of furniture. Excavations of ancient synagogues at Chorazin and elsewhere have turned up the stone chair set at the front, facing the congregation, from which the Law was expounded once it had been read standing. The teacher sat down to interpret. Our own word cathedral comes from the Greek for that chair — the church eventually named its largest buildings after a seat.

And Jesus begins by conceding the seat. Before a syllable of criticism he grants that these men occupy a genuine office and that what is read from that chair binds Israel. He does not start a reform movement by declaring the institution void; he separates the chair from the men in it, which is a distinction the next verse turns into a working principle and which the history of the church has repeatedly needed.

One more thing about the placing of this chapter. This is the last time in Matthew that Jesus addresses a public crowd. From the end of it he goes out of the temple, sits down on the Mount of Olives, and everything after that is spoken to disciples in private (24:3) until he answers the high priest under oath. So these are his final public words, delivered in the temple courts, days before he is killed by the men he is describing — and he spends them warning ordinary people about their religious leaders and then weeping over the city.

Which sets the tone for what follows, and the tone is easy to get wrong. Seven woes are coming, in the harshest language he ever used. They are not delivered to a hostile deputation in a corner. They are delivered to the flock, about the shepherds, by someone who is about to die for both.
verseByVerse.note: “Moses’ seat” stands for the authority to teach the law; synagogues may have had a stone chair for the teacher.

verseByVerse.quote: "so do and observe whatever they tell you, but not the works they do. For they preach, but do not practice."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gap between proclamation and practice is the essence of hypocrisy. Jesus commands submission to correct teaching even when the teacher's life is inconsistent — truth is not invalidated by the messenger's failure. But he exposes the fatal credibility gap: those who preach repentance without practicing it, who demand righteousness they themselves do not embody. It has been called the most uncomfortable verse in the Bible for preachers, and it is: every man who stands up to explain God's word stands under this indictment the moment his pulpit and his life diverge.

But there is a difficulty here that a careful reader will not get past, and it is worth stopping for. "Do and observe whatever they tell you" — whatever? This is the same Gospel in which Jesus tells the disciples to beware of "the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees," and Matthew explains that he meant their teaching (16:12); the same Gospel in which their tradition is said to have made void the commandment of God (15:6); and in this very chapter he is about to call their instruction on oaths the reasoning of blind fools (vv. 16-22). So he cannot be handing them a blank endorsement, and it will not do to quietly insert the word "correct" into his sentence and move on.

The answer is in the clause just before it: they "sit on Moses' seat." That seat is the point. The authority in the room is not theirs; it is Moses' — that is, the Scripture they are reading out. When they open the Law and tell Israel what God has said, the people are bound, and the messenger's hypocrisy does not release them, because the word is God's and not his. When they leave that seat and start building fences and loopholes of their own, they have stepped off the only ground that gave them a claim on anyone's conscience. Jesus is not commanding obedience to Pharisees; he is commanding obedience to Moses, even from the mouth of a Pharisee.

And that principle has never stopped being useful. The authority of any pulpit is borrowed, every word of it. A congregation is bound to the Word that is read to them, not to the man who reads it — which protects them in both directions at once: from the preacher whose life is worse than his sermon, and from the preacher whose opinions have quietly replaced it. Listen for Moses' seat. Where the man is on it, obey God. Where he has wandered off it, you are free, and so is your conscience.

parallels.desc: you who teach others, do you not teach yourself?

verseByVerse.quote: "They tie up heavy burdens, hard to bear, and lay them on people's shoulders, but they themselves are not willing to move them with their finger."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Put some weight in the burden, because in the abstract it stays abstract. The written Law said: remember the Sabbath day and do no work. The oral tradition then took that and specified. Thirty-nine categories of prohibited labour, each subdivided: how far a man might walk, how much he might carry and in which hand, whether a lamp could be moved, whether a chair could be dragged across a floor since dragging might scratch a furrow and furrowing is ploughing. Whether you could lift your own child. Whether a woman might look in a mirror in case she saw a grey hair and pulled it out, which would be reaping. None of that is caricature, and none of it was invented by wicked men; it was produced by serious people trying to be careful. That is exactly how such systems are always produced.

And then: they themselves are not willing to move them with their finger. The phrase is not only about laziness. The same tradition that generated the rules generated the devices for living with them — legal arrangements by which a courtyard could be declared a single household so that carrying within it was permitted, and similar provisions for a journey. Men who knew the system intimately could move within it. The ones crushed by it were the ones who only knew that they were failing.

Which is why the contrast Jesus draws is exact, and Matthew has laid it out with the same noun. Here the scribes tie up heavy burdens — phortia barea. Twelve chapters earlier he had said: come to me, all who labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest; take my yoke upon you, for my burden is light — phortion elaphron (11:28-30). Two men in one Gospel offering to load your shoulders, using the same word for what they put there, and the only question is whose you carry.

Every generation of the church rebuilds some version of this, and it is never built by cynics. It is built by earnest people extrapolating from real commands, and it always lands on the same people. God says pray; the tradition specifies the hour, the method and the minimum. God says give; the tradition supplies the percentage and the tone in which failure is discussed. God says teach your children; the tradition produces a schooling decision that sorts the faithful from the rest. Not one of those additions is wicked. Together they produce a Christian who is quietly certain he is behind and does not know where the line is.

And here is the tell, which is the second half of the verse. Look at who is setting the standard, and ask whether the standard happens to be achievable by someone with his life. A man with a study, a quiet house and no shift work will describe an early-morning devotional discipline as the mark of a serious believer. He is not lying, and he has never once tried it with a newborn, two jobs and a bus at six. The burden is real; the man laying it on has simply never had to move it with his finger.

parallels.desc: a yoke our fathers could not bear

verseByVerse.quote: "They do all their deeds to be seen by others. For they make their phylacteries broad and their fringes long, and they love the place of honor at feasts and the best seats in the synagogues"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The diagnosis is in a single phrase: to be seen by others. The Greek is theathenai, from the root that gives us theatre, and it is the same charge Jesus had already made at length in the Sermon on the Mount — beware of practising your righteousness before other people in order to be seen by them (6:1), where the word is the same. This chapter is not introducing a new sin. It is showing what happened to men who had been doing it for thirty years.

The two examples are chosen because both are commanded. Phylacteries were the tefillin: small leather cases holding parchment strips of Scripture, bound to the forearm and the forehead in obedience to a plain instruction — you shall bind them as a sign on your hand, and they shall be as frontlets between your eyes (Deut 6:8). Specimens have been recovered from the caves at Qumran and they are tiny, the writing minute. To make yours broad was to enlarge the case so that it could be identified across a courtyard. And the fringes were the tzitzit of Numbers 15:38-40, the tassels with a blue cord, worn as a reminder of the commandments. Jesus wore them himself — it was the fringe of his garment that the haemorrhaging woman reached for in the crowd (9:20). He is not objecting to the tassel. He is objecting to the length.

That is the awkward genius of this woe, and it is what makes it inescapable. There is nothing here that could be forbidden. You cannot legislate against a wide phylactery, because the phylactery is commanded and the width is a matter of taste. Everything visible in this verse is defensible, and the whole of it is rotten, and the difference lies entirely in an invisible motive that no synagogue committee could ever have assessed.

Then the seats, which are the same appetite with the religion stripped off: the place of honour at feasts and the best seats in the synagogues. The first is the couch nearest the host, from which precedence descended in order down the table, so that everyone in the room could read the seating and know the rankings. The second is the bench at the front of the synagogue, facing the congregation — the seat in which you spend the service being looked at, with your back to the scrolls.

The test that gets underneath this is not a question about what you do but about who is watching while you do it, and it can be run in about ten seconds. Take some part of your religious life that is genuinely good — a discipline, a habit of giving, a service you perform, something you know about the Bible. Now suppose it were absolutely certain that nobody would ever find out about it. Not concealed, simply never mentioned, for the rest of your life. Does it survive at full strength, or does something in it quietly deflate? Whatever deflates was the part being worn broad.
verseByVerse.note: Phylacteries were small leather boxes holding verses of Scripture, strapped to the forehead and arm. Fringes were the tassels on a garment’s corners.

parallels.desc: bind them on your hand and between your eyes

verseByVerse.quote: "and greetings in the marketplaces and being called rabbi by others. But you are not to be called rabbi, for you have one teacher, and you are all brothers."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Greetings in the marketplaces sounds harmless until you know what a greeting cost in that culture. There were protocols: you rose when a teacher passed, you greeted him first and waited to be answered, you used his title, you gave way in the street. A recognised rabbi walking from his house to the temple could be publicly acknowledged twenty times before he arrived, and every one of those small deferences was visible to everybody in the square. It was not vanity in the private sense. It was a daily, structured, public administering of status, and men came to need it the way they needed breakfast.

And rabbi itself means, quite literally, my great one. That is what the word says. Every use of it was a small sentence about the relative size of two people.

Now notice the reason Jesus gives for forbidding it to his disciples, because it is not the reason we would give. He does not say: because titles are worldly, or because leadership is dangerous, or because you should think less of yourselves. He says for you have one teacher — and two verses later he names him: the Christ. He is not making a point about humility here. He is making a point about himself. The seat is occupied. The reason no disciple may be called rabbi is that the position of Teacher in this community is filled, permanently, by the man saying so.

And you are all brothers. Which follows exactly: if there is one Teacher and everybody else is a learner, then the only relation left among the learners is siblinghood. Not equality of gift or of office — Matthew's Gospel ends with commissioned apostles, and the New Testament has elders and overseers with real authority — but equality of standing. The senior man and the newest convert are at the same distance from the chair.

Guard it from becoming a rule about vocabulary, because that misses it twice over. Paul calls himself a teacher without embarrassment, the New Testament names offices, and Jesus himself is addressed as Teacher throughout this Gospel without correction. What is forbidden is the appetite, not the noun. And it is worth saying that the appetite survives the abolition of the noun perfectly well: congregations that pride themselves on having no titles, where everyone is on first-name terms, routinely develop an informal pecking order that is felt by everyone, written down nowhere, and considerably harder to challenge than a formal one. A hierarchy you can name can be questioned. The other kind just is.

So the test is not what people call you. It is what happens inside when the deference does not arrive — when the newcomer does not know who you are, when your opinion is passed over, when somebody less experienced is asked instead. The Pharisees' problem was not that they were called rabbi. It was that by this point in their lives they could not have done without it.
verseByVerse.note: “Rabbi” means “my great one,” a title of respect for a teacher.

parallels.desc: not many of you should become teachers

verseByVerse.quote: "And call no man your father on earth, for you have one Father, who is in heaven. Neither be called instructors, for you have one instructor, the Christ."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The prohibition on "father" and "instructor" extends the same principle: no human being should occupy the place of ultimate spiritual authority that belongs to God alone. This does not forbid calling one's parent "father" or acknowledging a mentor's role, but it prohibits the spiritual inflation of human authority into a surrogate for divine fatherhood. The Reformation recovered this principle against medieval ecclesiastical structures that made the Pope a spiritual father in an absolute sense. All human teaching is derivative; only Christ is the instructor of the soul.

But the prohibition exists to protect something, and the something is named in the same breath: you have one Father, who is in heaven. That is not a technicality about address. It is the relationship this whole Gospel has been putting in front of us — Matthew calls God your Father again and again, feeding the birds and clothing the grass and knowing what you need before you ask (6:8, 26, 30), seeing in secret (6:6), giving good things to those who ask him (7:11). Every one of those sentences would be weakened if there were an intermediate father standing in the room. The command is jealous on the reader's behalf, not on God's.

And the second title is worth noticing for its rarity. Instructor here is kathegetes, a word that occurs nowhere else in the New Testament — the guide who goes ahead and shows the way. Jesus uses it once, of himself, in the same sentence in which he forbids anyone else to take it.

Which means the danger this verse addresses is not confined to one church's vocabulary, and Protestants should be slow to feel comfortable here. The thing forbidden is a human being occupying the place where God belongs, and it arrives just as easily without a title. It is the pastor whose approval has quietly become the measure of whether you are acceptable. The mentor whose opinion functions as your conscience, so that you cannot tell whether you believe something or he does. The teacher, dead or living, whose books you cannot disagree with — and there is a peculiarly modern form of this in the preacher heard weekly through headphones and never once able to be questioned. None of those men is called father. Every one of them can end up sitting in the chair.

The test is not what you call anyone. It is what happens when the man you respect most is wrong. If you can see it, say it, and go on loving him, he is a brother and a teacher. If the possibility cannot be entertained, then whatever his title, the seat is occupied.

This verse is often thrown across the table between Protestants and Roman Catholics, so it is worth handling honestly. It cannot be a flat ban on the word "father," or Scripture would contradict itself: Paul calls Abraham "the father of us all" (Rom 4:16), speaks of "our fathers" in the wilderness (1 Cor 10:1), and calls himself the spiritual father of those he led to Christ — "I became your father in Christ Jesus through the gospel" (1 Cor 4:15; cf. Philem 10). Stephen addresses the Sanhedrin as "fathers" (Acts 7:2). So the Bible plainly permits both the natural word and the affectionate sense of a spiritual mentor. What Jesus forbids is the thing behind the title in these Pharisees — the arrogating to a man of the place that belongs to God alone, as though a human being were the source of one's spiritual life or the required channel of grace. A Protestant does well, then, not to major on the mere word a Catholic uses for his priest, but on the real question: is any man treated as the indispensable mediator between the soul and God? For there Scripture is jealous — "there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus" (1 Tim 2:5). Honour your teachers; love your fathers in the faith; but keep the throne of the heart for the one Father in heaven and the one Teacher, his Son.

parallels.desc: have we not all one Father?
one God, the Father, and one Lord

verseByVerse.quote: "The greatest among you shall be your servant. Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The kingdom inverts the world's hierarchy. Status is gained through service, not self-promotion. This is not merely an ethical principle but a reflection of the gospel itself: the Son of God humbled himself to a servant's death (Phil. 2:5–8) and was exalted to the highest name. The divine order — humility before exaltation — governs both Christ's own story and the pattern for all who follow him. The reversal is certain, and it runs in both directions: the man who takes the lowest place will be raised, and the man who takes the highest will find it was never his to take.

There is a trap in this chapter, and this is the verse where a reader falls into it. You have just been shown seven portraits of religious pride, and if the reading has gone well you are now feeling rather pleased at having recognised them. That is the whole difficulty with humility: it is the one virtue that evaporates the moment you notice you have it. Anyone who has tried to be humble knows the loop — you succeed, you observe your success, and the success is gone.

Which is why it repays attention that Jesus does not actually command a feeling here. He does not say feel lowly. He states how God deals with people — the self-exalting are brought down, the self-humbling lifted — and, in the verse before it, he gives the mechanism: the greatest among you shall be your servant. Humility is not a mood to be worked up. It is a position to be taken, and positions can be taken on days when the mood is entirely absent.

That makes it practical in a way that introspection never is. You cannot decide to feel small. You can decide to do the job nobody wants and not mention that you did it; to let someone else be right about something that does not matter; to leave out the detail of the story that would have impressed the table; to take the seat further down; to ask a question instead of delivering a verdict. None of that requires you to have achieved the correct inner state first, and — this is the point — the state tends to arrive later, quietly, by the back door, in people who stopped monitoring for it.

Most self-examination about humility is simply pride holding a mirror. The deeper cure is not thinking less of yourself but thinking about yourself less, which happens only when something better has your attention. Notice where this chapter finally goes: not to a call for us to be humbler, but to a man standing over a city that is about to kill him, saying how often would I have gathered your children (v. 37). Spend long enough looking at that and the arithmetic of who ranks where in the room stops being interesting.

And take the promise as it stands, without turning it into a technique. It does not say that humility earns exaltation, which would make it one more way of climbing. It says God does the lifting — and he has never once been fooled about which of the two he is looking at.

verseByVerse.quote: "But woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you shut the kingdom of heaven in people's faces. For you neither enter yourselves nor allow those who would enter to go in."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two words in this verse need their meaning back before the woe can land.

Woe is ouai, and it is not a curse. It is the sound a person makes over a disaster — the prophets' cry, closer to alas than to damn you. Isaiah stacked six of them and then turned the seventh on himself (Isa 5:8-22; 6:5). It carries warning and grief in one syllable, and if you read these seven as a man losing his temper you will not be able to account for verse 37, where the same voice breaks.

Hypocrite is hypokrites, and in ordinary Greek it meant an actor — the man on stage speaking through a mask. That is the whole charge in a word. Not that these men were worse than other men, but that there was a face and there was a man behind it, and the two were not the same. Jesus uses the word of them repeatedly in this chapter and it is worth hearing the theatre in it every time.

Then the first woe, which is the head of all seven: you shut the kingdom of heaven in people's faces. The image is of a doorway with men standing in it. And these were the very men entrusted with the keys — Jesus had put that image on the table already, giving the keys of the kingdom to Peter and to the church (16:19), and Luke records the same charge in sharper form: you have taken away the key of knowledge (Lk 11:52). The men appointed to open the door had positioned themselves in the gap.

Read the last clause slowly, because there is a detail in it that is easily missed and is heartbreaking: nor allow those who would enter to go in. Those who would enter. People were trying. There were men and women in Israel who wanted in, who had heard John, who had followed the crowds out to hear this Galilean, who were reaching for something — and the professionals stood in the way. That is why this woe comes first and why it is the worst. The other six describe men damaging themselves. This one describes men damaging somebody else's only chance.

Which is also why this chapter should frighten anyone who teaches, leads, hosts, parents or explains. The office is not the danger; standing in the doorway is. And the modern forms of it — the unwritten requirements, the tidying-up expected before belonging rather than after — are set out where Jesus turns the whole list back on the reader (see on vv. 33-34). What matters here is the weight: of the seven things he could have put first, he put this one.
verseByVerse.note: A woe is a solemn lament and warning of judgment, used by the prophets.

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you travel across sea and land to make a single proselyte, and when he becomes a proselyte, you make him twice as much a child of hell as yourselves."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A reader with an open Bible will find a gap here, and it should be explained rather than stepped over. Most modern versions print no verse 14, or bracket it with a footnote. The missing words are: Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you devour widows' houses and for a pretence you make long prayers; therefore you will receive the greater condemnation.

The facts are these. The sentence is absent from the oldest and best copies of Matthew, including Sinaiticus and Vaticanus, and it appears in later manuscripts in two different positions — some put it before verse 13, some after. Wandering like that is a classic sign of an insertion: a sentence that belongs somewhere does not move about. And there is an obvious source, because the words stand undisputed in Mark and Luke, where Jesus says exactly this about the scribes who devour widows' houses and make long prayers (Mk 12:40; Lk 20:47). This is the fourth time we have met the same movement of a scribe's hand in this Gospel — Luke carried into 18:11, Mark into 17:21, Luke's weather saying into 16:2-3 — and it is always the same instinct: a copyist who knew the other Gospels well and could not bear a gap.

So the words are the Lord's and their home is Mark and Luke. Nothing is lost. And the charge itself is worth a moment, because it names a real and documented abuse: religious men acting as guardians and trustees of widows' estates, taking their fees out of the administration, and covering the arrangement with a reputation for lengthy prayer. It is the combination that is deadly. The long prayers were not a distraction from the fees; they were the security on which the fees depended.

Then the woe Matthew did write. You travel across sea and land to make a single proselyte. Jewish missionary effort in that period was real and energetic — Josephus records synagogues full of interested Gentiles, and the book of Acts is full of the God-fearers it produced. This is not sarcasm about effort. The effort was genuine, expensive, and sincere.

Which makes the verdict the most disturbing sentence in the chapter: you make him twice as much a child of hell as yourselves. Not as bad. Twice as bad. Anyone who has watched a convert to a cause knows why: the man who has crossed over has staked something on it, has argued with his family about it, and will hold the position with a fierceness the people born into it never needed. Zeal passed on without truth does not arrive diluted. It arrives concentrated.

And this is where the woe stops being about first-century synagogues. Evangelism is not automatically good, and enthusiasm is not a virtue in itself. It matters enormously what a convert is converted to, and it is entirely possible to work hard, travel far, spend money and win somebody sincerely into a system that leaves them further from God than they were on the day you met them. Guard the point at both ends, though: this cannot be an argument against mission, since the same Gospel closes with a command to make disciples of all nations (28:19). The Lord who says this woe gave that commission. The question he is raising is not whether to go, but what they find when they arrive.
verseByVerse.note: The ESV notes that some manuscripts add verse 14, a woe about devouring widows’ houses and long prayers for a pretence. A proselyte was a Gentile convert to Judaism.

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to you, blind guides, who say, 'If anyone swears by the temple, it is nothing, but if anyone swears by the gold of the temple, he is bound by his oath.' You blind fools! For which is greater, the gold or the temple that has made the gold sacred?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The system Jesus is describing sounds absurd until you see what it was for. An oath sworn by the temple did not bind; an oath sworn by the gold of the temple did. So a man could stand in the street, invoke the sanctuary of God with every appearance of solemnity, satisfy the person he was dealing with, and walk away holding no obligation whatever — and he had broken no rule. The whole elaborate machinery existed to make it possible to sound bound without being bound.

That is worth stating plainly because it is the most sophisticated form dishonesty ever takes. These men had not abolished truth-telling; they had built a technically defensible system on top of it, with published rules, so that deceit could be practised by the scrupulous. The person being deceived hears an oath. The person swearing it knows which oath he chose. Nobody has lied, and somebody has been robbed.

Then the argument, and it is one sentence long: which is greater, the gold or the temple that has made the gold sacred? The gold in that building was ordinary metal until it was brought inside; the temple did not derive its holiness from the gold. They had the logic exactly upside down, and once the question is asked the system collapses, which is why he asks it rather than arguing.

But most readers will trip over something else in these verses, and it deserves an answer. He calls them blind fools — and this is the same Gospel in which he said that whoever says to his brother You fool! is liable to the hell of fire (5:22), using that same word, more. So has he broken his own commandment?

No, and the reasons matter. What 5:22 forbids is contemptuous anger against a brother: the word thrown in a quarrel to dismiss another human being as worthless. That is not what is happening here. This is a judicial pronouncement by the one appointed to judge, delivered publicly about men holding public office, and it is a statement of fact rather than an insult — they were teaching, and they could not see. And the biblical fool is not a man of low intelligence; from the Psalms onward he is a moral category, the man who has arranged his thinking so as not to have to reckon with God: the fool says in his heart, there is no God (Ps 14:1). These men were formidably clever. That is precisely what made them blind.

May a Christian swear an oath in court or make marriage vows? Yes. Jesus is exposing the evasions of those who used oaths to deceive, not forbidding every solemn oath. God himself swears (Heb 6:13–17), Paul calls God to witness (2 Cor 1:23), and Jesus answered under oath before the high priest (26:63–64). Some Christians, especially in the Anabaptist tradition, refuse all oaths on the basis of 5:34. The more likely reading is that lawful oaths and vows are permitted; what is forbidden is casual or evasive swearing.

Which leaves the practical caution exactly where the chapter puts it. Jesus can say this because he reads hearts and will judge them; we cannot and will not, and this Gospel has already told us to take the log out of our own eye first (7:3-5). The right use of a verse like this is not to acquire vocabulary.
verseByVerse.note: These rules let a man decide which of his oaths were binding.

verseByVerse.quote: "And you say, 'If anyone swears by the altar, it is nothing, but if anyone swears by the gift that is on the altar, he is bound by his oath.' You blind men! For which is greater, the gift or the altar that makes the gift sacred?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He runs the same argument a second time with a different pair of objects, and the repetition is deliberate: this is not one odd ruling but a settled habit of mind. An oath by the altar does not bind; an oath by the gift lying on the altar does. Same structure, same inversion, same result.

And now the pattern is visible enough to name, because it is the same in both cases and it explains everything else in this chapter. Look at which item they treated as weighty. Gold over the temple. The gift over the altar. In each pair the thing they took seriously is the thing that can be weighed, counted, valued and carried; the thing they treated as nothing is the thing that gives it meaning and cannot be quantified at all. Gold has a market price; a sanctuary does not. A gift has a value the donor knows to the shekel; an altar's holiness cannot be entered in a ledger.

That is the deep logic of the whole Pharisaic project, and it accounts for the rest of the woes without further explanation. Tithed dill can be measured, so it received meticulous attention; justice and mercy and faithfulness cannot, so they were neglected (v. 23). The outside of a cup can be inspected; greed cannot (v. 25). A phylactery's width is a fact; the motive behind it is not (v. 5). Give a religious man a system and he will gravitate, irresistibly and without noticing, toward the parts of it that can be assessed — because those are the parts at which he can succeed, and the parts by which he can be seen to have succeeded.

Which is a live danger and not a historical curiosity, because the measurable is genuinely easier to care about. Attendance can be counted; love for the people attending cannot. Bible chapters read can be logged; whether they changed anything cannot. Doctrinal precision can be examined line by line; whether a man is kind to his wife at nine on a Tuesday night cannot. Nobody decides to prefer the countable. It simply offers the one thing the heart wants, which is a score.

And notice the second charge in the address: you blind men. Twice in four verses he calls them blind guides, and the phrase is a contradiction he intends. A guide is defined entirely by his ability to see the road. A blind guide has not merely failed at a job; he is an impossibility being paid a salary — and the people behind him are the ones who will end up in the ditch.

parallels.desc: whatever touches the altar shall become holy

verseByVerse.quote: "So whoever swears by the altar swears by it and by everything on it. And whoever swears by the temple swears by it and by him who dwells in it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having taken the system apart, he puts the truth in its place, and it is very short: whoever swears by the altar swears by it and by everything on it. And whoever swears by the temple swears by it and by him who dwells in it.

The principle underneath is that you cannot detach a thing from the God who gives it meaning. There is no such thing as invoking the altar and not the One the altar was built for; the altar is not an object with religious associations, it is a place where God has put his name. Swear by the temple and you have named its resident, whether you intended to or not. The Pharisaic system depended on being able to reach for the sacred and leave God out of it, and Jesus's answer is that there is no such transaction available anywhere in creation.

That is worth grasping as more than a ruling about oaths, because it undoes a habit far wider than theirs. A great deal of religion consists of handling holy things at arm's length from the one who made them holy — going through a liturgy without addressing anyone, treating a building as sacred while its Lord is not consulted, valuing the Bible as an object and not reading it, taking bread and wine as a custom. In each case the article is being invoked and the Person edited out. Jesus says the editing does not work. What is holy is holy because of somebody, and touching it touches him.

And it puts these verses exactly where the Sermon on the Mount already stood. There he had said: do not swear at all, not by heaven or by earth or by your own head, but let your yes be yes and your no be no (5:34-37). At first sight this is a different teaching; in fact it is the same one arriving from the other side. If every oath invokes God, then the whole apparatus of graded oaths is not merely dishonest, it is unnecessary — because a Christian who understands that every word he speaks is spoken in God's hearing has no use for a device that makes some of his words more binding than others. You do not need a mechanism for occasional truthfulness if you have stopped operating a distinction between the words that count and the words that do not.

Which is the question these verses put, and it is not really about swearing. Do you have two registers? Most people do: statements made where it matters, carefully, and statements made in passing that were never meant to be held to — the promise to a child, the assurance given to end a conversation, the commitment made because it was easier than declining. The Pharisees had codified that instinct and published the rules. The instinct itself needs no code. It arrives free with the human heart.

parallels.desc: a place for you to dwell in forever

verseByVerse.quote: "And whoever swears by heaven swears by the throne of God and by him who sits upon it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The last step closes every remaining exit. Swear by heaven, and heaven is God's throne, and the throne has somebody sitting on it. There is nowhere left. You cannot reach for the sanctuary without reaching for its resident, nor for the altar without its consecration, nor for the sky without the One enthroned in it. Every available object in the universe turns out to belong to him, which means every oath is sworn in his hearing whether or not his name is used.

And that is a far larger statement than the oath debate that produced it. There is no neutral ground anywhere. The distinction most of us actually live by — that some parts of life are religious and the rest are simply life, so that words spoken in church carry a weight that words spoken in the car do not — is the same distinction these men had built into a system, and it does not exist. A man is never off the record. There is no room in the house and no hour of the week in which he is speaking merely to other people.

Which sounds oppressive and is meant to be liberating, and the difference lies in who is on the throne. If the constant hearer were an inspector, the doctrine would be unbearable. Jesus has just spent this chapter describing men for whom God had become exactly that — an auditor to be satisfied and, where possible, out-manoeuvred — and their religion had rotted under the weight of it. The One who hears everything is the Father who feeds the birds and counts the hairs on a head (6:26; 10:30), and who is described three times in the Sermon as the one who sees in secret and rewards it (6:4, 6, 18). The same total attention that makes hypocrisy impossible makes hiddenness safe.

So the practical fruit of this teaching is not more careful oaths but plainer speech, and the tells of the alternative are worth knowing because they are so respectable. The sentence that is accurate and designed to mislead. The commitment worded loosely enough to be escaped later. The silence held while somebody forms a false impression you could correct in four words. The technically true answer to a question you knew was really asking something else. Not one of those is a lie by the rules, and every one of them is an oath sworn by the gold rather than by the temple.

The cure Jesus gives is almost embarrassingly simple, and it is the hardest discipline in ordinary Christian life: let your yes be yes. Say the thing you mean, in words that can only mean it, and then do it — and if you cannot say it, decline. A man who lives that way needs no oaths, and after a while people stop asking him for any.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–39 — Seven Woes Concluded and the Lament over Jerusalem
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The last four woes drive from the outside inward: tithed garden herbs while justice, mercy and faithfulness are neglected; a cup scoured outside and full of plunder within; whitewashed tombs; and monuments built to murdered prophets by men arranging a murder. Then the language hardens further — serpents, brood of vipers, fill up the measure of your fathers — and the blood of the righteous from Abel to Zechariah is laid on that generation. And then the voice breaks: O Jerusalem, Jerusalem… how often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing. The chapter ends not on desolation but on a single word: until.
verseByVerse.theology: Woe and lament sit in one chapter and must be held together, because each without the other is a distortion. Woe is ouai, the prophets' cry of grief rather than a curse, and it is aimed with precision: not at sinners — no harsh word in this Gospel ever falls on a prostitute, a tax collector or a dying thief — but at men shutting the door on them. Severity toward a shepherd fleecing the flock is mercy toward the flock. Then the remedy, which is the most important clause here for anyone who reads the seven and wants out: first clean the inside of the cup and the plate, that the outside also may be clean. The order is the whole difference between the gospel and moralism, and the promise is that the outside follows. It is also the one thing no one can do for himself, which is why the honest response is David's after his worst year: create in me a clean heart (Ps 51:10). And the measure of v. 32 explains the patience of God — judgment waited four hundred years for the Amorites' cup to fill (Gen 15:16) — without promising that the delay is permanent.
verseByVerse.examples: Two images repay their background. The gnat and the camel is a joke: straining wine through cloth to catch an unclean insect was ordinary practice, the camel was the largest unclean animal in the country, and in Aramaic the words chime — qalma and gamla. And the whitewashed tombs were limed before Passover not for beauty but as a warning, since touching a grave barred a pilgrim from the feast for seven days (Num 19:16); the mark meant to keep people away was what made them gleam. Which makes the charge worse than inconsistency: such men are contagious, and their respectability is the danger. The seventh woe is the one to watch for while reading this chapter — if we had lived in the days of our fathers is the cheapest sentence in the world, because the sins of a previous age are labelled and ours are still disguised as normal life. Everyone is certain he would have hidden Jews in 1942. The certainty costs nothing and is almost always false. The seven translated into their modern forms, and the guard on whether we may speak as Jesus does here, are set out in the verse-by-verse on vv. 33-34.

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you tithe mint and dill and cumin, and have neglected the weightier matters of the law: justice and mercy and faithfulness. These you ought to have done, without neglecting the others. You blind guides, straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Start with what is actually being praised, because this woe is almost always quoted as though tithing herbs were the sin. It was not. The Law required a tenth of the produce of the land, and whether kitchen herbs grown in a few feet of soil fell under the requirement was genuinely disputed; these men tithed them in case. That is not hypocrisy, it is scruple, and Jesus explicitly does not withdraw it: these you ought to have done, without neglecting the others. He is not asking for less carefulness about small things. He is asking why the carefulness stopped where it did.

Because the omissions are named, and they are not small: justice and mercy and faithfulness. Micah had put the same three together and called them the whole of what God wants — to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God (Mic 6:8) — and the men counting cumin seeds had let all three go. It is a very particular kind of failure: not a collapse into obvious wickedness, but a religion that had become entirely accurate about everything that could be checked and had quietly dropped everything else.

Then the image, which is a joke, and it survives translation badly. Straining wine through a cloth to remove insects was ordinary practice, because winged insects were unclean (Lev 11:20-23) and a scrupulous man did not want to swallow one. The camel was the largest unclean animal in the country. So the picture is a man holding his cup up to the light, filtering it with great care to catch anything the size of a pinhead, and then swallowing a camel whole. And in Aramaic the two words chime — qalma, a gnat or louse, and gamla, a camel — so the sentence was a pun as well as an accusation. Jesus was funny, and the men he was talking to will not have found it funny at all.

Which gives a test that requires nothing but honesty and about a minute. Make two lists. The first is what you are meticulous about in your Christian life — the things you would notice immediately if they slipped, the standards you hold, the points on which you are reliably careful. The second is what you are relaxed about, the areas where you have made a settled peace with a certain amount of failure. Now read the two lists against the three words in this verse. Justice: whether the people who depend on you are dealt with fairly. Mercy: whether anyone gets a second chance from you. Faithfulness: whether you can be relied on when it costs. If those three keep turning up on the second list while the first list is full of things that can be counted, this woe has your name on it.

Should Christians tithe? Jesus was speaking to Jews still under the law, before the cross, so this verse does not bind Christians to the tenth. The New Testament calls for generous, cheerful, proportionate giving (1 Cor 16:2; 2 Cor 8–9), and many Christians find the tenth a useful starting point rather than a law. What Jesus says applies to everyone: careful giving is good, but it must go together with justice, mercy and faithfulness.

And the reason it is a woe rather than advice is worth noting. A man in this condition is not miserable. He is doing well by his own measurements and has the receipts. That is why somebody had to say it out loud to him.
verseByVerse.note: The law required a tithe of produce; the Pharisees extended it to kitchen herbs. Both gnats and camels were unclean; wine was strained through cloth to remove insects.

parallels.desc: a tithe of the seed of the land
do justice, love kindness, walk humbly

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you clean the outside of the cup and the plate, but inside they are full of greed and self-indulgence. You blind Pharisee! First clean the inside of the cup and the plate, that the outside also may be clean."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He is using their own argument against them. There was a live dispute in the schools about exactly this — whether a vessel's outer surface could be ritually clean while its interior was unclean, and how far the uncleanness of the contents travelled. The Shammaites and Hillelites took different views. So the image is not a homely illustration Jesus reached for; it is a technical question these men had argued about, and he answers it in a way none of them expected by applying it to the men holding the cups.

Then look at what he says is inside, because the words are stronger than most translations let on. Greed is harpage, from the verb meaning to seize and carry off — it is the word for plunder, not for a general acquisitiveness. And self-indulgence is akrasia, the absence of self-control, appetite with nothing holding it. So the cup is not full of vague worldliness. It is full of what they had taken from people and what they could not stop themselves wanting. The widows' houses of the disputed verse fourteen were in there.

And then the remedy, which is the most important sentence in the chapter for anybody who reads the woes and wants out: first clean the inside of the cup and the plate, that the outside also may be clean.

Notice the order and notice the promise. The order is inside first — which is precisely the order no religion of performance can manage, because a system can only ever reach the outside. And the promise is that the outside follows. He does not say clean the inside and then also work on the outside; he says deal with the inside and the outside will be clean. That is the whole difference between the gospel and moralism in one clause. Moralism scrubs the exterior and hopes something happens within. Christ starts at the centre and lets the surface take care of itself.

Which raises the obvious difficulty: how does a man clean his own inside? He cannot, and that is not a discouragement but the doorway. It is the thing David asked for after the worst year of his life, when the outside had been managed for months and the inside was rotten: behold, you delight in truth in the inward being… create in me a clean heart, O God (Ps 51:6, 10). He does not offer to do it. He asks. The one thing needed is the one thing that has to be given, and the men in this chapter never asked because they never believed the inside was the problem.

So the woe is severe and the cure is available in the same breath, and the cure was already standing in front of them holding a cup.

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you are like whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful, but within are full of dead people's bones and all uncleanness. So you also outwardly appear righteous to others, but within you are full of hypocrisy and lawlessness."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The image needs its background or it loses most of its force. Tombs in that country were limewashed each spring before Passover, and the reason was not decoration. Contact with a grave made a man ceremonially unclean for seven days (Num 19:16), which would have barred him from the feast — and with tens of thousands of pilgrims walking in from every direction, many of them at night, an unmarked tomb beside a road was a serious hazard. The whitewash was a warning sign. It was put there so that people would know to keep away.

And the effect, in spring sunshine on the hills around Jerusalem, was that the tombs gleamed. A thing painted to say danger ended up being the most striking object in the landscape. That is the irony Jesus is standing on, and it is sharper than the usual reading of the verse: it is not merely that these men looked good and were rotten inside. It is that what made them look impressive was the very marking that should have warned people off.

Which turns the accusation from inconsistency into something worse. A whitewashed tomb is not just a disappointing object; it is contagious. Touch it and you cannot go to the feast. So the charge against these men is not simply that their outsides and insides did not match. It is that contact with them left people unfit for the presence of God, and that the very respectability which drew people toward them was the thing that made them dangerous. The safest-looking men in the city were the ones you could not afford to touch.

Then the two words in the verdict, and the second is the one that lands. Hypocrisy we expect by now. Lawlessness we do not: anomia, actual violation of God's law. He is not saying they kept the law with wrong motives. He is saying that underneath the performance there was no keeping of it at all. And Matthew has used that word before, in the most frightening paragraph in the Sermon on the Mount, spoken to men who had prophesied and cast out demons in his name: I never knew you; depart from me, you workers of lawlessness (7:23). The same noun. It is possible to have a ministry and be described by that word.

One thing must be said before leaving this verse, because it is what keeps the passage from being merely an attack on a party. What Jesus describes here is not a rare condition peculiar to first-century Judaism; it is the natural state of the human heart wherever religion is available and regeneration is not. These men are not uniquely wicked. They are uniquely exposed, by someone who could see inside the cup. Anyone who reads this and feels safe has misunderstood which end of the sentence he is standing at, and the seventh woe — which is next — is aimed precisely at him.
verseByVerse.note: Tombs were whitewashed so that passers-by would not touch them by accident and become unclean.

parallels.desc: whoever touches a grave is unclean

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you build the tombs of the prophets and decorate the monuments of the righteous, saying, 'If we had lived in the days of our fathers, we would not have taken part with them in shedding the blood of the prophets.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The seventh woe is the cleverest and the most frightening, because on the surface these men are doing something admirable. They are restoring the graves of murdered prophets and putting up monuments to the righteous. Herod had built on a grand scale over the tombs of the patriarchs, and there was a real and reverent practice of maintaining such places. Nobody watching would have called it sin.

And they say the right thing about it: if we had lived in the days of our fathers, we would not have taken part with them in shedding the blood of the prophets. That sentence is the woe. It is not a lie exactly — they meant it — and it is the purest self-deception in the Gospels, because the men saying it were at that moment arranging the death of the greatest prophet who ever came, and the arrangement did not feel to them like killing a prophet. It felt like protecting the nation from a dangerous Galilean.

That is the mechanism, and it is worth being exact about it, because everyone alive uses it. The sins of a previous generation are visible to us in a way our own never are, for a reason that has nothing to do with our virtue: theirs have been sorted, labelled, and agreed upon, and ours are still disguised as normal life. Nobody in history has ever committed a sin that looked to him like the thing later ages would condemn. It looked like common sense, or necessity, or the way things are done, or a hard decision taken responsibly.

Which makes the counterfactual the cheapest currency there is. Everyone is certain he would have hidden Jews in 1942, freed his slaves in 1850, spoken up when the others stayed quiet. The certainty costs nothing, cannot be tested, and is almost certainly false — because the people who did not do those things were not monsters; they were ordinary, respectable, churchgoing people to whom the wrong of it was somehow not apparent. If you want to know what you would have done then, the only available evidence is what you are doing now about the things your own age finds it convenient not to see. And you will not be able to name those easily, which is the point.

There is a version of this available to the most careful Bible reader, and this chapter is where it becomes visible. You can read Matthew 23 with real attention, recognise every one of the seven, feel the force of them — and locate them all in other people, or in a previous century, or in a different sort of church from yours. That is precisely what the men decorating the tombs were doing. They had a whole theology of what went wrong last time, and they used it to be sure of themselves this time.

The honest thing to do with this woe is therefore not to admire its aim. It is to ask what living correction you are currently resisting — whose voice, in your church or your family, you have quietly filed under difficult, unbalanced, or not to be taken too seriously. It is always easier to build a monument to a dead prophet than to listen to a live one, and it has the additional advantage of being extremely good for your reputation.

verseByVerse.quote: "Thus you witness against yourselves that you are sons of those who murdered the prophets. Fill up, then, the measure of your fathers."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Thus you witness against yourselves. He takes the sentence they were proud of and turns it over. By saying our fathers they had claimed the lineage — and a lineage cannot be claimed selectively. They wanted the descent for the dignity of it and had assumed the guilt could be left in the previous generation. Jesus points out that they have just identified themselves, out of their own mouths, as the sons of the men who did the killing.

Then comes one of the most terrible sentences in the Bible: Fill up, then, the measure of your fathers.

Read carefully, because it is not a command to sin, and it is not sarcasm either. It belongs to a form of speech Scripture uses when God addresses the settled and determined — the moment at which he stops arguing and says, in effect, proceed. It is the voice of let the evildoer still do evil at the end of Revelation (22:11), and of the hardening of Pharaoh after Pharaoh had hardened himself several times over. There is nothing in the universe more frightening than God ceasing to obstruct a man. He is not being given permission. He is being left alone.

And the measure is worth understanding, because it explains something about God that puzzles everybody. The image is a vessel filling drop by drop, and Scripture uses it explicitly: God told Abraham that his descendants would not possess Canaan for four hundred years, because the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete (Gen 15:16). Judgment waited four centuries for a cup to fill. That is what the patience of God actually is — not indifference, not the absence of a reckoning, but a delay with a limit built into it. Every unpunished generation was being given time. The time was real, and so was the cup.

Which is the answer to a question honest people ask in both directions. To the person who concludes from the delay that nothing is ever going to be said: the measure explains the silence, and it does not promise that the silence is permanent. To the person frightened by the severity of it: notice that the delay was four hundred years long, and that the same chapter which announces the cup full ends a few verses later with a man weeping over the city and saying how often would I have gathered your children.

See too what this tells us about the man speaking. He knows what they are going to do to him. He is not walking toward the cross in hope that it can still be avoided or in ignorance of who will arrange it; he is standing in front of the men who will do it, describing it, days in advance, and then going up the hill anyway. Nobody took his life. He knew the measure was full, and he stayed.

parallels.desc: which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute?

verseByVerse.quote: "You serpents, you brood of vipers, how are you to escape being sentenced to hell? Therefore I send you prophets and wise men and scribes, some of whom you will kill and crucify, and some you will flog in your synagogues and persecute from town to town,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Serpents" and "brood of vipers" — language John the Baptist also used (3:7) — identifies the leaders with the ancient adversary, the deceiver of Eden. Hell (Gehenna, the valley of Hinnom) is not hyperbole but judicial reality. Even now Jesus sends messengers — apostles, teachers — knowing they will be killed, because God's way of dealing with sin is to send grace into the midst of it. The future persecutions described here are fulfilled in Acts and the apostolic letters. Which shows that the cross is not the end of God's sending but the beginning of a wider one: therefore I send you prophets, said on the way to Calvary.

Many readers reach this verse and flinch. You serpents, you brood of vipers — from the man who said love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, turn the other cheek; who called himself gentle and lowly in heart (5:44, 39; 11:29). Is this the same person? And may I speak like this? Both questions deserve an answer, because the chapter is unreadable without one.

Start by noticing the pattern of his severity, which is not random at all. Look at who never gets spoken to this way: the prostitute at the Pharisee's house, the tax collector up a tree, the woman taken in adultery, the thief dying beside him, Peter after he denied him three times. Not one harsh word to any of them. Now look at who does get it — and at the charge in the first woe: you shut the kingdom of heaven in people's faces (v. 13). The ferocity is not aimed at sinners; it is aimed at men who are standing in the doorway keeping sinners out. He is tender with the broken and terrible toward the proud who break them, and the two are not in tension — they are the same love facing two different directions. Severity toward a shepherd who is fleecing the flock is mercy toward the flock. A father who spoke gently to the man harming his children would not be gentle; he would be indifferent.
