Then the redistribution, which offends most modern readers on first hearing: take the talent from him and give it to him who has the ten. It is not a reward for being rich. The master is doing what any sensible owner does with a resource that is producing nothing — moving it to where it will be used. The talent was never the servant's property. It was capital on loan, and capital that is not working gets reassigned.

Which contains a sober principle about opportunity. What God entrusts is not held on indefinite terms regardless of use. A gift left buried long enough is not merely wasted; it is eventually taken up by somebody else, and the work gets done — the master's estate does not suffer for one servant's caution. The loss in this parable is not the master's. It is entirely the servant's.

verseByVerse.quote: "'For to everyone who has will more be given, and he will have an abundance. But from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away. And cast the worthless servant into the outer darkness. In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
To everyone who has, more will be given. Read as economics it is monstrous, and it has occasionally been quoted that way, as though Jesus were endorsing the accumulation of wealth. He is stating a law about capacity, and it is one every person has already observed. A language used is a language kept and a language neglected is gone in a decade. A muscle worked grows and a limb in plaster wastes in six weeks. A friendship maintained deepens and one left alone quietly dissolves without anyone deciding to end it. Use enlarges, disuse shrinks, and this is true of every good thing God gives, including grace.

So the sentence is not about the rich getting richer. It is about the difference between a gift that has been exercised and a gift that has been buried, and the fact that the gap between them widens by itself, every year, without anyone intending it.

Then the word the master uses for the third servant: worthless — achreios, useless, of no service. Not thief. Not traitor. Not enemy. The judgment falls on a man whose distinguishing characteristic is that nothing whatever happened because of him. He did no harm and no good; the estate was exactly as it would have been had he never been born into it. That is the whole charge, and it is heavier than it sounds.

Which is the second of the chapter's three warnings, and the three are carefully different. The first parable condemns a woman who lacked something invisible. The second condemns a man who did nothing with something valuable. And the third, shortly, will condemn people who did not notice somebody in front of them. Not one of the three is condemned for an act of wickedness. All three are condemned for an absence, and between them they cover most of the ways a respectable person is actually lost.

Does the parable teach salvation by works? No. The one-talent servant’s problem is not that he earned too little but that he did not know or trust his master; he thought him a hard man (v. 24). He represents nominal religion that never knew the Lord. The fruit of the faithful servants is the evidence of a living faith, not the payment for salvation (cf. Jas 2:26).

And may a Christian invest and receive interest? The law forbade charging interest to a poor fellow Israelite (Exod 22:25), which is a different thing from investment. The parable uses ordinary business as a picture and does not teach investment ethics, but it does not condemn a fair return. The point is that God expects his gifts to be used, not buried.

The consignment to outer darkness is the same formula that closed the previous chapter (24:51), and it is Matthew's settled language for exclusion. What is new here is the ground of it. The man is not thrown out for what he did to the master. He is thrown out for what he declined to do for him, having been handed a fortune and an absence long enough to use it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 31–46 — The Judgment of the Nations
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The Olivet Discourse closes with the Son of Man enthroned in his own glory, all the nations gathered, and the flock parted as a shepherd separates sheep from goats at evening. Both groups are judged by the same six items — food, drink, welcome, clothing, a visit in sickness, a visit in prison — and both are astonished, the sheep because they cannot remember doing any of it and the goats because they never noticed the chance. The King's ground in each case is the same: as you did it to one of the least of these, you did it to me. Note that this is no longer a parable; it is a description.
verseByVerse.theology: Who are the least of these my brothers? The narrower reading observes that in Matthew my brothers nearly always means Jesus' disciples, and that the least echoes the little ones and sent messengers of ch. 10, so the nations are judged by their response to the King through his despised people. The broader reading takes it of any suffering person. The first is probably the passage's own point; the principle underneath it is true wherever need is found. Either way the doorway is guarded before a single deed is named: the sheep inherit — nobody earns an inheritance — a kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world, that is, before any of these people existed and before there was anything to reward. The works are produced as evidence, never as the purchase price. Note also the asymmetry at v. 41: the blessing is by my Father and the curse is attributed to nobody, and the fire was prepared for the devil and his angels, not for human beings. And at v. 46 one adjective governs both destinies, which is why the punishment cannot quietly expire unless the life does too.
verseByVerse.examples: Everything on the King's list is a service to somebody who cannot repay it and mostly cannot even report it — which is precisely why it is the list. Prison is the sharpest case: Roman prisons did not feed their inmates, so a man without visitors went hungry, and carrying food through that door announced publicly that you were associated with a criminal. The modern equivalents are the illness where the cards stop after three weeks, the man whose trouble is his own fault, and the visit to someone with dementia who will not remember by teatime that you came. Note what the goats' defence actually admits: we would have, had we recognised you. Their service was available to importance and not to need, and they state it themselves in front of the assembled nations. So the test is whether the trouble you take over a person varies with what that person can do for you. And the sheep could not produce a list of their own good deeds — which is worth weighing by anyone who could.

verseByVerse.quote: "When the Son of Man comes in his glory, and all the angels with him, then he will sit on his glorious throne. Before him will be gathered all the nations, and he will separate people one from another as a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Something changes at this verse and it is easy to read past. The two preceding passages began the kingdom of heaven will be like and it will be like a man going on a journey. This one does not. It begins when the Son of Man comes in his glory, and it never stops being a description. There is a comparison inside it — sheep and goats — but the frame is not a parable at all. He has stopped illustrating and started announcing.

And notice whose glory it is. Earlier in the Gospel the Son of Man was coming in the glory of his Father (16:27); here it is his glory, and his throne, and the angels are his attendants. This is the Son of Man of Daniel 7, who came to the Ancient of Days and was given dominion — and who is now seated, with every nation of every century assembled in front of him, doing what only God does in the Old Testament, which is judge the earth.

Then the image, and it is more ordinary than it looks. Sheep and goats grazed together in the same mixed flock all day, which is exactly how a Palestinian shepherd worked. They were separated in the evening, because goats needed shelter from the cold night and sheep did not. So the separation was a routine, daily, entirely unremarkable operation, performed at speed by a man who could tell one animal from another at a glance without breaking stride.

That is the concrete comfort buried in a terrifying scene. The sorting of the human race looks, from where we stand, like an impossible task — billions of people, mixed motives, hidden hearts, hypocrites indistinguishable from saints. This chapter has already twice insisted that the difference cannot be seen from outside. To the shepherd it is the work of an evening. He does not investigate; he recognises.

And all the nations — panta ta ethne — settles the scope beyond argument. Not Israel, not the church, not the religious. Every people group and every individual within them, including everyone who never heard of this scene and everyone who was confident it would not happen. Nobody is outside the summons, and the shepherd is the man who was crucified.
verseByVerse.note: Sheep and goats often grazed together in mixed flocks and had to be separated.

parallels.desc: the Son of Man given dominion
all the holy ones with him
I judge between sheep and sheep, rams and male goats

verseByVerse.quote: "And he will place the sheep on his right, but the goats on the left."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A small piece of local colour makes the picture sharper. The sheep of that country were predominantly white and the goats predominantly black or dark brown, so once the flocks were parted the two groups were visibly, unmistakably distinct from a distance — two blocks of colour where a moment before there had been one mingled crowd.

Right and left are not arbitrary. In that world the right hand was the place of honour and favour, and this Gospel has already used it at its highest pitch: sit at my right hand, until I put your enemies under your feet, the psalm Jesus quoted against the Pharisees three chapters ago (22:44; Ps 110:1). To be placed at the King's right is to be given the position of the honoured.

But the important thing is what the separation does and does not do. It does not create the difference. Nothing happens in this scene to make one animal a sheep and another a goat; the shepherd sorts what is already the case, and the sorting is a revelation rather than a verdict reached on the evidence of the day.

Which is the third time this chapter has said the same thing in three different pictures. Five girls out of ten had a flask, and nobody could tell which. Three servants received the same trust from the same master, and only the reckoning showed what each had done with it. Now one flock grazes together until evening. In every case the division runs through the middle of a group that looked uniform, and in every case it becomes visible only at the end.

That is precisely what Jesus said earlier about the wheat and the weeds — leave them growing together until the harvest, because pulling at them now uproots both (13:29-30). The present church is a mixed flock, and it is meant to be, and no amount of vigilance will sort it. Two things follow, and they are both freeing. You are not the shepherd, and the responsibility for identifying goats has never once been given to you. And the only animal in the flock whose position you have any business examining is the one you are standing in.
verseByVerse.note: The right hand was the place of honour.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then the King will say to those on his right, 'Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. For I was hungry and you gave me food, I was thirsty and you gave me drink, I was a stranger and you welcomed me,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before a single deed is mentioned, the question of how anybody gets to the right hand has already been settled twice over in one sentence — and it is worth slowing down, because this is the passage most often produced as proof that heaven is earned.

The first word is inherit. Nobody has ever earned an inheritance. It is the one form of getting that depends entirely on whose family you belong to, and a man who worked twice as hard as his brother does not thereby inherit twice as much. The verb settles the matter before the list of works begins.

The second is prepared for you from the foundation of the world. The kingdom being handed over was ready before the universe was made — which is to say, before the first sheep gave the first cup of water, before any of these people existed, and before there was anything whatever to reward. The works in this passage are named in the courtroom as evidence. They are nowhere named as the purchase price, and the timing makes it impossible that they could be.

Then the list starts, and the striking thing about it is how ordinary it is. Hungry, and you gave me food. Thirsty, and you gave me a drink. A stranger, and you took me in. Not one item on the list requires money, training, gifting, a platform, an organisation, or any particular ability. A child could do most of it. The kingdom's evidence turns out to be bread, water and an opened door.

Note the third one especially, because it is the one modern readers skate over. I was a stranger and you welcomed me — xenos, the outsider, the person with no claim on you and no connection to you, who does not belong and whom nobody would blame you for ignoring. Hospitality to people who already matter to us is a pleasure, not a virtue. This is the other kind, and it costs an evening and a certain amount of social awkwardness, and it is on the list the King reads out at the end of the world.

parallels.desc: share your bread with the hungry
chosen before the foundation of the world

verseByVerse.quote: "'I was naked and you clothed me, I was sick and you visited me, I was in prison and you came to me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The list continues: clothing the naked, visiting the sick, coming to those imprisoned. These works represent costly, inconvenient, personally engaged care — not institutional programs from a safe distance but the presence of one person with another in their suffering. "You visited me" (epeskepsasthe) carries the force of the shepherd searching for the sheep, the God who sees and comes. The prison visit is perhaps the most striking: it requires entering a place of shame and social stigma. The extent of Christian mercy is meant to match the extent of human need, and these verses define that need comprehensively — physical, social, relational, communal.

Every word of this passage is aimed at the people doing the visiting. But there is somebody else standing in the scene, and the chapter never turns to speak to them — so it is worth doing here.

If you are the one who is ill, or hungry, or out of work, or alone in a hospital bay, or inside a prison of some kind — a literal one, or the sort made of illness or shame or debt or a house nobody calls at — then read what the King actually says about you. He does not say, I saw what they did for you. He says they did it to me.

That claim runs in both directions, and both matter. Where you were visited, Christ counts it as a visit paid to himself. And where you were not — the phone that did not ring, the church that meant to come and did not, the friends who found your trouble awkward and drifted — he counts that as a neglect of himself, and he says so in front of the assembled nations. He is not a spectator of your situation. He has stepped into it and put his own name on it.

Two things follow for anyone in that position. Your circumstances are not invisible to heaven, however invisible they feel from the ward or the flat or the cell; the King has made his identification with people in exactly your position the criterion by which he sorts the human race, which is not the behaviour of someone who has overlooked you. And the kindness you have received was never charity handed down to you from above. It was Christ being served in you — which quietly reverses the whole transaction, and may matter a great deal to someone who has always hated being helped.

He also knows the ground he is standing on. He was hungry for forty days in a wilderness, thirsty on a cross, a stranger with nowhere to lay his head, stripped bare in front of a crowd at his execution, and led away under armed guard. There is not one category on this list that he has not personally occupied. He is not describing a class of people he has heard about.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then the righteous will answer him, saying, 'Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you, or thirsty and give you drink? And when did we see you a stranger and welcome you, or naked and clothe you?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The most remarkable thing in this scene is not the King's verdict. It is that the people being commended do not recognise the evidence.

Lord, when did we see you hungry and feed you? This is not modesty and it is not a polite deflection of praise. They are asking a real question, because they genuinely do not have the memory. They are being shown a record they cannot recall compiling, and their reaction is bewilderment.

Which tells us something exact about how those acts were done. Nothing was filed. There was no ledger, no mental note, no quiet satisfaction stored away for later — because a man who is keeping account can always produce the account, and these people cannot produce anything. The deeds went out of their minds within the week, the way it does when you help somebody for the ordinary reason that they needed help and you were there.

So there is a test in this, and it is uncomfortable in an unusual direction. Could you produce a list? Most people, asked what they have done for the poor or the sick or the stranger, can retrieve two or three examples fairly quickly — and the retrieval is the problem, not the deeds. The ones commended here could not have answered that question. What they had done had never been converted into evidence about themselves.

One guard, because this can be twisted into a reason to stop planning any good at all, on the grounds that self-consciousness spoils it. It does not follow. A man may deliberately set aside a Saturday to visit a prison, plan it in his diary, and arrange the transport; the deliberateness is not the trouble. The trouble is keeping the receipt. Do it on purpose, and then let it go — and if in forty years you find you cannot remember much of it, you are in the company of the people standing at the King's right hand and asking him what he is talking about.

One more thing about their question, which becomes visible only when the chapter is read whole. Listen to how they address him: Lord, when did we see you hungry? Now listen to the five shut outside the wedding: Lord, lord, open to us (v. 11). And in a few verses, the goats: Lord, when did we see you hungry? — the same word, in the same chapter, from all three groups. Everybody in Matthew 25 calls him Lord. Nobody in this chapter is condemned for failing to, and nobody is saved for managing it, which is exactly what he had said at the close of the Sermon: not everyone who says to me, Lord, Lord, will enter the kingdom of heaven (7:21). The title is the one thing the whole chapter holds in common.

verseByVerse.quote: "'And when did we see you sick or in prison and visit you?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The last two on the list are the costliest, and it is worth being specific about why, because they are the two most easily left to somebody else.

Visiting the sick is unpleasant in ways nobody admits. There is a risk of catching whatever it is. There is nothing to achieve — you cannot fix anything, and you will leave having accomplished nothing measurable. You will not know what to say, and much of what you do say will be wrong. And illness is dull; the third visit is harder than the first, and the twentieth is when almost everybody stops.

The prison visit is harder still, and in the ancient world it carried a weight that has been lost. Roman prisons did not feed their inmates properly. A prisoner ate what his family and friends carried in to him, which meant that a man with no visitors did not merely feel forgotten — he went hungry, and could die of it. You came to me was not a courtesy in that world. It was a supply line. And to be seen carrying food through that door was to announce publicly that you were associated with a criminal, which many were not willing to do.

The modern equivalents are not hard to find and are usually going unattended right now. The long illness, where the cards stop after the third week and the casseroles after the second month, and the person is still ill in the second year. The man whose troubles are his own fault, where visiting looks like approval. The relative in a secure ward. And most purely of all, the visit to someone with advanced dementia — who will not recognise you, cannot thank you, will not remember by teatime that you came, and cannot tell anybody you were kind. There is no possible return on that visit of any kind whatever.

Which is exactly why it appears on this list. Everything the King names here is a service rendered to somebody who cannot repay it and mostly cannot even report it. That is the whole class of action he has chosen to identify himself with, and it is the class of action the world has no way of noticing.

verseByVerse.quote: "And the King will answer them, 'Truly, I say to you, as you did it to one of the least of these my brothers, you did it to me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The most remarkable claim in the passage: the King identifies himself with the suffering recipients of mercy. "My brothers" — in Matthew, this term refers primarily to Jesus' disciples (12:48–50; 28:10), suggesting the primary referent is the persecuted missionary community. But the Christological claim is broader: Jesus is present in human suffering in a way that makes care for the least a direct encounter with him. This does not collapse the distinction between Christ and humanity; it shows that his lordship reaches us through his identification with the vulnerable. To ignore them is to ignore him; to serve them is to serve him.

It is worth being clear about the debate here, because much hangs on it. Who are "the least of these my brothers"? Two readings compete. The narrower one, favoured by many careful interpreters, notes that in Matthew "my brothers" nearly always means Jesus' disciples (12:49-50; 28:10), and that "the least" echoes the little ones and the sent messengers of chapter 10, where receiving a disciple with a cup of cold water is receiving Christ (10:40-42). On this reading the nations are judged by how they treated Christ's people — especially his persecuted missionaries — which is really a judgment on how they received the gospel those people carried. The broader reading takes "the least" as any suffering human being, so that Christ is met in every hungry, sick, or imprisoned person on earth. The wisest course honours both. The passage's first point is almost certainly the narrower one: a watching world will be sorted by its response to the King through his often-despised people. But the principle underneath it — that the King so identifies with the lowly that what is done to them is done to him — is gloriously true wherever human need is found, and Scripture everywhere commands mercy to all (Gal 6:10; Luke 10:25-37). So the text is not a licence to reduce the gospel to social work, nor an excuse to spiritualise away the plain call to feed and clothe and visit. And guard the doorway: even here the sheep "inherit" a kingdom "prepared from the foundation of the world" (v. 34) — their mercy is the fruit and proof of grace already given, never the price that buys heaven. They are surprised by their own good works precisely because those works flowed from a renewed heart, not a calculating one.

parallels.desc: not ashamed to call them brothers

verseByVerse.quote: "Then he will say to those on his left, 'Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry and you gave me no food, I was thirsty and you gave me no drink,"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Set the two sentences side by side, because the asymmetry between them is deliberate and it is the most merciful thing in the passage.

To the right: Come, you who are blessed by my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. To the left: Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.

Two differences. The blessing is attributed — blessed by my Father; the curse is attributed to nobody. And the kingdom was prepared for you, while the fire was prepared for someone else entirely. Hell, on the King's own account, was not built with human beings in mind. It was made for the devil and his angels, and the people going there are going somewhere that was never designed for them, having attached themselves to its original occupant. Heaven is a home prepared for guests. Hell is not, and even in the sentence of condemnation Jesus takes the trouble to say so.

Then the charge sheet, and it is the same list as before with every verb negated. What is striking is what is not on it. Nobody is accused of beating a prisoner, or turning a hungry man away from the door, or mocking the sick. There is no cruelty in the indictment at all. The whole case against them is a series of things that did not happen.

That deserves a guard, because it can crush the wrong reader. Anyone who has ever failed somebody in trouble — and everybody has, and most of us can name them — will read this and hear a sentence passed on himself. But what is being described here is not an instance. It is a life: a settled pattern with no exceptions in it, running to the end, in a person who produces at the judgment not one occasion when he did otherwise. And the sheep are not presented as people who never failed anybody either. They are simply people in whom something was true, and it showed, and they did not know it was showing.

parallels.desc: the devil thrown into the lake of fire

verseByVerse.quote: "'I was a stranger and you did not welcome me, naked and you did not clothe me, sick and in prison and you did not visit me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the fourth time the list has been recited in ten verses — spoken to the sheep, queried by the sheep, spoken to the goats, and about to be queried by the goats. Six items, four times over. Nobody talks like that by accident. It is repetition used as a hammer, and by the end of the passage a hearer could recite the six in order, which is presumably the intention.

And what is being condemned, said as plainly as possible, is indifference. Not malice. The goats did not hate the stranger; they had no particular feelings about him at all. They did not refuse the sick man; they simply never went. Every charge in this list is an absence rather than an act, and the King treats those absences as the moral equivalent of a verdict.

Which is worth understanding rather than merely deploring, because nobody walks past need by deciding to. The mechanisms are entirely respectable. There is busyness, which is real and not an excuse anyone invents. There is distance, so that the need is known about rather than seen, and known-about need has never moved anybody. There is the reasonable assumption that somebody else is handling it, that there are agencies and professionals and a pastoral team. There is fatigue, because the need is endless and a person cannot weep at every item on the news. And there is the small, quiet postponement — not now, not this week — which is the wicked servant's sentence from the previous chapter in a gentler key.

Not one of those is wickedness. Together they are how a life ends up with nothing on the list, and how a person arrives at the judgment genuinely puzzled about what he is supposed to have done wrong.

So the practical question this verse puts is not whether you are a cruel person. Almost nobody reading it is. The question is whether anything at all has been costing you lately — an evening, a Saturday, a sum of money you noticed spending, a friendship with somebody who cannot do a thing for you in return. If the honest answer is nothing, that is worth knowing now, while the list can still be added to.

verseByVerse.quote: "Then they also will answer, saying, 'Lord, when did we see you hungry or thirsty or a stranger or naked or sick or in prison, and did not minister to you?' Then he will answer them, saying, 'Truly, I say to you, as you did not do it to one of the least of these, you did not do it to me.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The goats ask the same question the sheep asked, and it looks at first like the same bewilderment. It is not, and the difference is buried in what their question actually claims.

Lord, when did we see you hungry or thirsty or a stranger or naked or sick or in prison, and did not minister to you? The implication is unmistakable, and they mean it sincerely: we would have. Had we recognised you, we would have acted. We are not the sort of people who leave the Lord of glory standing in the road.

And that is a confession, though they do not hear themselves making it. They are saying that their service was available — but it was available to importance. Show them a King and they would have moved; show them a hungry nobody and they had other things on. Which is precisely the accusation, stated by the defendants in their own defence. The sheep never asked who the person was. The goats would have needed to know.

Then the King's reply strips the last cover away: as you did not do it to one of the least of these, you did not do it to me. Note that my brothers does not appear in this second version; it is simply the least of these. Whatever weight that carries for the debated question of who the brothers are (see on v. 40), the point being pressed here is the identification itself, and it is total. There is no gap between the two. Doing nothing for the one was doing nothing for him, and no further step of reasoning is offered or needed.

So the test the passage leaves is a simple and searching one, and it can be run on any ordinary week. Does the amount of trouble you take over a person vary with what that person can do for you? Everybody's does to some extent, and the goats' mistake was not that theirs did but that theirs did entirely. The King has arranged the final examination so that the people who cannot repay you are the ones he is standing behind, and he has told us in advance, which means the arrangement is not a trap. It is an invitation with the answers printed.

parallels.desc: whoever oppresses a poor man insults his Maker

verseByVerse.quote: "And these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The parallelism is exact and sobering: the same adjective ("eternal") governs both punishment and life, ruling out any interpretation that makes the punishment temporary or the life exhaustible. Both are equally permanent, equally real, equally the consequence of relationship — or its absence — with the Son of Man. The Olivet Discourse ends here: the King has spoken, the judgment is certain, the separation is coming, and the call of chapters 24–25 is to live now in light of that final day.

The argument in that first sentence deserves to be named, because it is answering something. Two alternatives to everlasting punishment are held today by people who love the Bible. Universalism says that all will be saved in the end, the fire being purifying rather than final. Annihilationism, or conditional immortality, says the lost are not tormented for ever but are finally destroyed — they cease to exist. That second view is not a fringe position; John Stott held it tentatively and with evident sorrow, and others of real godliness have followed him. It should be argued with, not sneered at.

But it must be argued with, and this verse is where the argument lands, because Jesus puts both destinies in one sentence under one adjective: eternal punishment, eternal life. The word need not by itself mean unending — it can carry the sense of "belonging to the age to come" — and that is precisely why the force here is not the bare word but the balance. Whatever weight you give it on the right-hand side, you must give it on the left, for it is the same word in the same breath about the same day. If the punishment quietly runs out, so does the life. The sentence ties the two together with one knot, and there is no way to loosen it at one end only.

Which leaves the question underneath, the one that is really being asked when people press these alternatives: how can a God of love do this? Two things are worth holding. The first is who is speaking. More is said about judgment by Jesus than by anyone else in Scripture — the outer darkness, the closed door, the fire prepared for the devil are all his images, not some later hardening of a gentler message. And this is the same voice that broke over Jerusalem two chapters ago, how often would I have gathered your children, and that within days would be nailed to a cross precisely so that people would not have to hear the words in verse 41. The doctrine did not reach us from hard men. It came from the tenderest voice in the Bible, and it cost him everything to open a way out of it.

Is eternal punishment really everlasting? Some evangelicals hold that the lost will finally cease to exist, and they have reasons: Scripture speaks of the wicked as destroyed and perishing (10:28; Phil 3:19; 2 Thess 1:9), fire consumes, and death is the wages of sin. The more likely reading is that the punishment is conscious and unending. Jesus sets eternal punishment side by side with eternal life in the same sentence, so that if one ends, so does the other; he speaks of fire that is not quenched (Mark 9:48), and Revelation says the smoke of their torment goes up forever and ever (Rev 14:11). This is the hardest truth in Scripture, and it is meant to send us to Christ, who bore judgment for all who come to him.

The second is how a Christian should carry it. Not with relish, ever — "As I live, declares the Lord GOD, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked" (Ezek 33:11), and any believer who finds this doctrine comfortable has not understood it. Nor with speculation: Scripture pictures the same reality as fire and as darkness, which cannot both be photographs, and the pictures are given to tell us that the loss is total, not to furnish a map. What we are told is enough, and it is the ground of urgency in mission. If it is true, no one who believes it can be casual about the person sitting next to them.

parallels.desc: some to everlasting life, some to everlasting contempt

25.theology: Faith and works in the final judgment. The parable of the sheep and goats is sometimes misread as teaching salvation by charity. It teaches the opposite: those who are blessed by the Father (elect from the foundation of the world, v. 34) demonstrate their status through the fruit of mercy. Works do not earn salvation; they reveal it. James and Paul are not in contradiction: Paul says we are justified by faith alone (Rom 3:28); James says a faith without works is dead (Jas 2:26). Matthew 25 stands with James: the living faith that justifies is the faith that produces mercy. The absence of mercy is evidence not of an imperfect Christian but of a heart that has never truly encountered the merciful King.
25.examples:
Then: The early church was remarkable for its care of the poor, the sick, the orphan, and the widow — in a culture that largely left the vulnerable to die. Pagans observed and were astonished. The church was not performing charity as a strategy; it was loving Christ in the face of the neighbour. The Roman emperor Julian complained: “The godless Galileans feed not only their own poor but ours also.”

Now: The parable of the talents is a rebuke of every Christian who sits on their gifts out of fear — fear of failure, fear of criticism, fear of the cost. Every person reading these words has been entrusted with something by the master: a relationship, a skill, a platform, a message, an opportunity. The question at the end will not be “how much did you have?” but “what did you do with what you were given?” Faithfulness, not magnitude, is the measure.

26.title: The Last Supper and Gethsemane
26.text: <sup>1</sup>When Jesus had finished all these sayings, he said to his disciples, <sup>2</sup>“You know that after two days the Passover is coming, and the Son of Man will be delivered up to be crucified.” <sup>3</sup>Then the chief priests and the elders of the people gathered in the palace of the high priest, whose name was Caiaphas, <sup>4</sup>and plotted together in order to arrest Jesus by stealth and kill him. <sup>5</sup>But they said, “Not during the feast, lest there be an uproar among the people.” <sup>6</sup>Now when Jesus was at Bethany in the house of Simon the leper, <sup>7</sup>a woman came up to him with an alabaster flask of very expensive ointment, and she poured it on his head as he reclined at table. <sup>8</sup>And when the disciples saw it, they were indignant, saying, “Why this waste? <sup>9</sup>For this could have been sold for a large sum and given to the poor.” <sup>10</sup>But Jesus, aware of this, said to them, “Why do you trouble the woman? For she has done a beautiful thing to me. <sup>11</sup>For you always have the poor with you, but you will not always have me. <sup>12</sup>In pouring this ointment on my body, she has done it to prepare me for burial. <sup>13</sup>Truly, I say to you, wherever this gospel is proclaimed in the whole world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her.” <sup>14</sup>Then one of the twelve, whose name was Judas Iscariot, went to the chief priests <sup>15</sup>and said, “What will you give me if I deliver him over to you?” And they paid him thirty pieces of silver. <sup>16</sup>And from that moment he sought an opportunity to betray him. <sup>17</sup>Now on the first day of Unleavened Bread the disciples came to Jesus, saying, “Where will you have us prepare for you to eat the Passover?” <sup>18</sup>He said, “Go into the city to a certain man and say to him, ‘The Teacher says, My time is at hand. I will keep the Passover at your house with my disciples.’” <sup>19</sup>And the disciples did as Jesus had directed them, and they prepared the Passover. <sup>20</sup>When it was evening, he reclined at table with the twelve. <sup>21</sup>And as they were eating, he said, “Truly, I say to you, one of you will betray me.” <sup>22</sup>And they were very sorrowful and began to say to him one after another, “Is it I, Lord?” <sup>23</sup>He answered, “He who has dipped his hand in the dish with me will betray me. <sup>24</sup>The Son of Man goes as it is written of him, but woe to that man by whom the Son of Man is betrayed! It would have been better for that man if he had not been born.” <sup>25</sup>Judas, who would betray him, answered, “Is it I, Rabbi?” He said to him, “You have said so.” <sup>26</sup>Now as they were eating, Jesus took bread, and after blessing it broke it and gave it to the disciples, and said, “Take, eat; this is my body.” <sup>27</sup>And he took a cup, and when he had given thanks he gave it to them, saying, “Drink of it, all of you, <sup>28</sup>for this is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins. <sup>29</sup>I tell you I will not drink again of this fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new with you in my Father’s kingdom.” <sup>30</sup>And when they had sung a hymn, they went out to the Mount of Olives. <sup>31</sup>Then Jesus said to them, “You will all fall away because of me this night. For it is written, ‘I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.’ <sup>32</sup>But after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee.” <sup>33</sup>Peter answered him, “Though they all fall away because of you, I will never fall away.” <sup>34</sup>Jesus said to him, “Truly, I tell you, this very night, before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times.” <sup>35</sup>Peter said to him, “Even if I must die with you, I will not deny you!” And all the disciples said the same. <sup>36</sup>Then Jesus went with them to a place called Gethsemane, and he said to his disciples, “Sit here, while I go over there and pray.” <sup>37</sup>And taking with him Peter and the two sons of Zebedee, he began to be sorrowful and troubled. <sup>38</sup>Then he said to them, “My soul is very sorrowful, even to death; remain here, and watch with me.” <sup>39</sup>And going a little farther he fell on his face and prayed, saying, “My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will.” <sup>40</sup>And he came to the disciples and found them sleeping. And he said to Peter, “So, could you not watch with me one hour? <sup>41</sup>Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak.” <sup>42</sup>Again, for the second time, he went away and prayed, “My Father, if this cannot pass unless I drink it, your will be done.” <sup>43</sup>And again he came and found them sleeping, for their eyes were heavy. <sup>44</sup>So, leaving them again, he went away and prayed for the third time, saying the same words again. <sup>45</sup>Then he came to the disciples and said to them, “Sleep and take your rest later on. See, the hour is at hand, and the Son of Man is betrayed into the hands of sinners. <sup>46</sup>Rise, let us be going; see, my betrayer is at hand.” <sup>47</sup>While he was still speaking, Judas came, one of the twelve, and with him a great crowd with swords and clubs, from the chief priests and the elders of the people. <sup>48</sup>Now the betrayer had given them a sign, saying, “The one I will kiss is the man; seize him.” <sup>49</sup>And he came up to Jesus at once and said, “Greetings, Rabbi!” And he kissed him. <sup>50</sup>Jesus said to him, “Friend, do what you came to do.” Then they came up and laid hands on Jesus and seized him. <sup>51</sup>And behold, one of those who were with Jesus stretched out his hand and drew his sword and struck the servant of the high priest and cut off his ear. <sup>52</sup>Then Jesus said to him, “Put your sword back into its place. For all who take the sword will perish by the sword. <sup>53</sup>Do you think that I cannot appeal to my Father, and he will at once send me more than twelve legions of angels? <sup>54</sup>But how then should the Scriptures be fulfilled, that it must be so?” <sup>55</sup>At that hour Jesus said to the crowds, “Have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs to capture me? Day after day I sat in the temple teaching, and you did not seize me. <sup>56</sup>But all this has taken place that the Scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled.” Then all the disciples left him and fled. <sup>57</sup>Then those who had seized Jesus led him to Caiaphas the high priest, where the scribes and the elders had gathered. <sup>58</sup>And Peter was following him at a distance, as far as the courtyard of the high priest, and going inside he sat with the guards to see the end. <sup>59</sup>Now the chief priests and the whole council were seeking false testimony against Jesus that they might put him to death, <sup>60</sup>but they found none, though many false witnesses came forward. At last two came forward <sup>61</sup>and said, “This man said, ‘I am able to destroy the temple of God, and to rebuild it in three days.’” <sup>62</sup>And the high priest stood up and said, “Have you no answer to make? What is it that these men testify against you?” <sup>63</sup>But Jesus remained silent. And the high priest said to him, “I adjure you by the living God, tell us if you are the Christ, the Son of God.” <sup>64</sup>Jesus said to him, “You have said so. But I tell you, from now on you will see the Son of Man seated at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven.” <sup>65</sup>Then the high priest tore his robes and said, “He has uttered blasphemy. What further witnesses do we need? You have now heard his blasphemy. <sup>66</sup>What is your judgment?” They answered, “He deserves death.” <sup>67</sup>Then they spit in his face and struck him. And some slapped him, <sup>68</sup>saying, “Prophesy to us, you Christ! Who is it that struck you?” <sup>69</sup>Now Peter was sitting outside in the courtyard. And a servant girl came up to him and said, “You also were with Jesus the Galilean.” <sup>70</sup>But he denied it before them all, saying, “I do not know what you mean.” <sup>71</sup>And when he went out to the entrance, another servant girl saw him, and she said to the bystanders, “This man was with Jesus of Nazareth.” <sup>72</sup>And again he denied it with an oath: “I do not know the man.” <sup>73</sup>After a little while the bystanders came up and said to Peter, “Certainly you too are one of them, for your accent betrays you.” <sup>74</sup>Then he began to invoke a curse on himself and to swear, “I do not know the man.” And immediately the rooster crowed. <sup>75</sup>And Peter remembered the saying of Jesus, “Before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times.” And he went out and wept bitterly.
26.overview:
Chapter 26 is the most theologically dense chapter in Matthew. In a single evening Jesus institutes the Lord’s Supper, reveals his betrayer, predicts Peter’s denial, agonises in Gethsemane, is arrested by a crowd with swords, and is condemned by the Sanhedrin. Every scene is simultaneously the action of history and the fulfilment of Scripture: Judas’ betrayal for thirty pieces of silver (Zech 11:12–13), the scattering of the disciples (Zech 13:7), the suffering servant (Isa 53), the enthroned Son of Man (Dan 7:13).

Gethsemane is the chapter’s theological centre. Jesus does not walk to the cross with stoic detachment; he falls on his face and prays that the cup might pass. His agony is real — the weight of the wrath of God against sin, the drinking of the cup of Jeremiah 25 and Isaiah 51, the bearing of the curse. And then: “not as I will, but as you will.” This is the most perfect prayer ever prayed — complete honesty about human desire, complete submission to divine will. The cross is not the defeat of the Son; it is the triumph of obedience.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–46 — The Plot, the Anointing, the Last Supper, and Gethsemane
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jesus finishes the last of his five discourses and immediately names the day of his own execution. The council meets to arrange it and rules out Passover; a woman in a leper's house breaks a year's wages over his head and is scolded for waste; Judas goes out and lets the priests set a price. In a borrowed upper room Jesus keeps the Passover with the twelve, names his betrayer, and gives them bread and a cup as his body and his blood of the covenant. Then the Hallel, the walk to Gethsemane, the prediction that all of them will fall away, and a night on the ground in an olive grove asking for the cup to pass.
verseByVerse.theology: The section's engine is the difference between what appears to be happening and what is happening. The council schedules the arrest for after the feast and he dies during it; Judas names no price and lets them value the Son of God at the compensation rate for a gored slave (Ex 21:32; Zech 11:12-13); the disciples see waste where Jesus sees a burial anointing. At the table the new covenant is inaugurated in the words of Sinai with one word changed — my blood of the covenant (Ex 24:8) — and Jeremiah's promise of forgiveness is attached to a cup. Gethsemane then shows that the atonement was not endured from behind any protective screen: Matthew's verb for his distress is the strongest available in the Greek of the period, and the cup is the Old Testament cup of wrath (Isa 51:17; Ps 75:8). He asked three times for it to pass, was refused, and got up and went to meet the betrayer.
verseByVerse.examples: Three things in this section are unusually usable. The woman's jar had to be broken to be poured, so the extravagance was decided before a drop touched him — and the test she leaves is whether anything in your Christian life has lately been indefensible on grounds of usefulness. You always have the poor with you is quoted to excuse doing nothing, and it is a quotation of Deuteronomy 15:11, where the permanence of poverty is the stated reason for permanent open-handedness; he quotes the middle of the verse and lets the table supply the end. And Gethsemane is the passage for anyone in real mental anguish: he said out loud how bad it was, asked friends to stay near him, asked three times for it to be lifted, and fell on his face — and what heaven sent was not the removal of the cup but strength to drink it. That is very often the shape of the answer, and it is not a lesser one.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jesus had finished all these sayings, he said to his disciples, "You know that after two days the Passover is coming, and the Son of Man will be delivered up to be crucified."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Matthew has used this formula four times already, at the close of each great block of teaching (7:28; 11:1; 13:53; 19:1). Here he uses it for the fifth and last time, and he adds one word: when Jesus had finished all these sayings. All of them. The teaching is over. From this sentence to the end of the book he does almost nothing but suffer.

And the first thing he does with the silence is name the date of his own execution. You know that after two days the Passover is coming, and the Son of Man will be delivered up to be crucified. Nobody speaks like that. Men who expect to be killed may say so in general terms; they do not hand their friends a timetable with the method on it. He has told them three times already that this was coming (16:21; 17:22-23; 20:18-19), each time in more detail, and now he gives them the day.

Note which day. Not merely Friday, but Passover — the feast that commemorated a night when the blood of a lamb on a doorpost turned away a judgment that would otherwise have fallen on the household inside. Israel had kept that meal every year for something like fourteen centuries, and every year it pointed at something. He arranges to die during it.

Then the verb: will be delivered up — paradidotai, handed over. It is passive, and the passive hides a great deal. Judas hands him over to the priests; the priests hand him over to Pilate; Pilate hands him over to be crucified. But Paul reaches behind all three: he who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Rom 8:32). The chain of betrayals runs all the way back, and at the top of it the Father is handing over the Son, and the Son is walking toward the date he has just announced.

Which sets the terms for everything that follows, and it is worth fixing in mind now, because the next fifty verses will show him bound, struck, spat on, and led about by men who appear to be running the operation. Not one of them surprises him. He named the week.
verseByVerse.note: Passover recalled Israel’s rescue from Egypt, when the blood of a lamb protected each household. Jerusalem swelled with pilgrims for the feast.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the chief priests and the elders of the people gathered in the palace of the high priest, whose name was Caiaphas, and plotted together in order to arrest Jesus by stealth and kill him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two meetings are held in these opening verses, and Matthew sets them side by side deliberately. In the first, a man speaks openly to his friends about his own death. In the second, a group of powerful men meet behind a closed door to arrange it.

Caiaphas is worth knowing. He held the high priesthood from about AD 18 to 36 — an extraordinary run, when his predecessors had lasted a year or two apiece and were removed by the Roman governor at will. He was also the son-in-law of Annas, the previous holder, and between them that family kept the office in its own hands for decades. A man does not survive eighteen years in a post held at Rome's pleasure without being an exceptional political operator. That is who is chairing this meeting: not a fanatic, but a manager, protecting an arrangement that worked.

And the arrangement is what is really being defended. John records Caiaphas making the case in plain words a few weeks earlier — if we let him go on, the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation, and it is better that one man die for the people (Jn 11:48-50). Read as politics that is not even unreasonable. It is the calculation any careful administrator makes: one life against a national catastrophe. He is not cackling. He is managing risk.

Which is the thing worth pausing over. The men who killed Jesus were not monsters and did not think of themselves as opposing God. They were the responsible party, the ones who held things together, doing what responsible people do when something destabilising appears — containing it. Every one of them could have given a reasoned account of his conduct, and several would have described it as a painful duty.

David had already described this scene: the kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers take counsel together, against the LORD and against his Anointed (Ps 2:2). The psalm's next line is what the conspirators never suspect. He who sits in the heavens laughs. Not because their power is imaginary — they will use it, and it will hurt — but because the meeting they think they are convening to end this man's work is the meeting at which his work begins.
verseByVerse.note: Caiaphas was high priest from about AD 18 to 36; his father-in-law Annas had held the office before him.

verseByVerse.quote: But they said, "Not during the feast, lest there be an uproar among the people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
One sentence of minutes from that meeting survives, and it is the most quietly devastating verse in the chapter. Not during the feast, lest there be an uproar among the people.

The concern is crowd control. Jerusalem at Passover was not the city of ordinary weeks; pilgrims poured in from across the empire, and the population may have swelled several times over. Josephus, counting lambs, arrives at figures for the festival crowds that are almost certainly inflated but tell you how the thing felt: the city was packed, tense, and full of men who had come to celebrate a national deliverance from a foreign power while a foreign power watched from the fortress. A popular teacher arrested in front of that congregation could have set the whole place alight, and the Roman garrison was reinforced at festivals for exactly that reason. So: wait until the pilgrims go home.

They did not wait. Within about seventy-two hours Jesus is dead, and he dies at Passover, on the one occasion in the calendar the council had specifically ruled out. The single scheduling decision these men made is the single thing they did not get.

And consider what had to happen for their plan to fail in exactly that way. They needed someone inside the group, willing, who knew where he went at night — and while they were still saying not during the feast, Judas was on his way to them. Nobody arranged that in the room. The council set a date and a man they had never met unset it, for money, of his own free will, for his own reasons.

Which is how providence appears to work almost everywhere in Scripture: not by suspending anybody's freedom but by employing it. Caiaphas made a calculation and meant it; Judas made a choice and meant it; and the outcome was that the Lamb of God was killed during the feast of the lamb, at the hour appointed before the world was made. No one in that room was overruled. They were simply used, and the used never notice.

verseByVerse.quote: Now when Jesus was at Bethany in the house of Simon the leper, a woman came up to him with an alabaster flask of very expensive ointment, and she poured it on his head as he reclined at table.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Notice first whose house this is. Simon the leper — and the name has stuck to the man, which means everyone knew what he had been. A leper's house was a place no respectable person entered and no respectable person ate in. Either Simon had been healed, presumably by the man now reclining at his table, or the house still carried the name of its ruined owner. Either way, the last meal of hospitality Jesus receives before his death is taken in a house that religious Jerusalem would have crossed the road to avoid.

Then the flask. Alabaster was the standard container for costly perfume, sealed at the neck; nard was imported from the mountains of northern India, carried overland for months, and John prices this one at three hundred denarii — very nearly a labouring man's wages for a year. Whatever the woman's circumstances, this was not a gift she could repeat. It may well have been everything she had, or a family inheritance, or the security a woman without a husband kept for a disaster.

And to use it she had to break the neck of the flask. That is the detail to hold. A sealed alabaster jar cannot be opened by halves; there is no pouring out a measured portion and keeping the rest for later. She broke it, which means that before a drop touched him she had already decided that none of it was coming back. The extravagance was not in the gesture. It was in the decision that preceded the gesture, taken while the jar was still whole in her hands.

Then she poured it on his head. Anointing the head is not what you do to a guest — that is a courtesy of oil, a small thing. Pouring a flask over the head is what Samuel did to David and what was done to Israel's kings and priests at their installation. In a leper's house, at a private supper, an unnamed woman performs a coronation.

Is this the same anointing as Luke 7? No. Luke’s story is set earlier, in Galilee, in the house of Simon the Pharisee, with a sinful woman. This is the anointing at Bethany that John also records (John 12:1–8), where the woman is Mary, Lazarus’s sister. John dates the meal six days before Passover; Matthew and Mark place the story here to set it beside the plot against Jesus. John mentions his feet, Matthew his head; she anointed both.

She had understood something the men around that table had not, though he had told them three times. The one in front of her was going to die, he was the anointed King, and the moment for arithmetic had passed. It is a striking fact about this Gospel that the person who reads the situation correctly, when the twelve cannot, is a woman whose name Matthew does not even record.
verseByVerse.note: John names the woman as Mary, sister of Martha and Lazarus. Alabaster was a soft stone used for perfume flasks; Mark and John say the ointment was pure nard, worth about a year’s wages.

parallels.desc: a different anointing, by a sinful woman in Galilee

verseByVerse.quote: And when the disciples saw it, they were indignant, saying, "Why this waste? For this could have been sold for a large sum and given to the poor."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The objection is unanswerable, which is what makes it dangerous. Three hundred denarii would have fed a great many hungry people in a city with a great many hungry people in it. Nobody at that table was wrong about the arithmetic, and if the question were put in a church meeting today it would carry the room.

The word they use is worth having: eis ti hē apoleia hautē — why this destruction, this ruin, this loss. It is the language of an asset written off. They are looking at an act of worship and seeing a balance sheet with a hole in it, and they are genuinely indignant, and their indignation has a moral shape to it. That is precisely the trouble. Bad motives are easy to identify; this is a good motive standing in the wrong place, which is much harder to see and impossible to argue with.

John tells us that at least one of them had a private reason — Judas kept the money bag and helped himself (Jn 12:6) — but there is no sign the rest were dissembling. They meant it. Which is worse, in a way: the eleven who loved him could look at the most beautiful act recorded in the Gospels and see waste.

So it is worth asking what kind of religion cannot recognise worship when it is standing in front of it. It is the religion that has learned to justify everything by usefulness — where the question asked of any expenditure of time or money or attention is what does it achieve, and where a thing done simply because Christ is worth it has no category to sit in. Such a faith is often very active and very defensible and it can run a long time without anyone noticing what has gone out of it.

The test is not hard to apply. Has anything in your Christian life recently been indefensible on the grounds of usefulness — money given that bought nothing, a morning spent on something with no outcome, a cost incurred purely because he was worth the cost? If everything you do for God can be justified in a report, something has quietly happened. There were twelve men in that room who could have written the report, and one woman who broke a jar, and only one of them was commended.
verseByVerse.note: John says the complaint came from Judas.

verseByVerse.quote: But Jesus, aware of this, said to them, "Why do you trouble the woman? For she has done a beautiful thing to me. For you always have the poor with you, but you will not always have me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He defends her, and he defends her against his own men. That is worth registering before anything else. Eleven of them are ranged on one side of the room with an argument that sounds like conscience, one woman is on the other with an empty jar, and he takes her side.

She has done a beautiful thing to me. The word is kalon, which in Greek means noble and fine as much as lovely — not merely a pleasing gesture but an act of moral excellence. He is not being gallant about a well-meant mistake. He is saying she got it right and they got it wrong.

Then the sentence that has done more damage than almost any other in this Gospel: you always have the poor with you. It has been quoted for centuries to explain why nothing much can be done about poverty — as though Jesus were shrugging, as though the permanence of the problem excused the effort. That reading is not merely wrong; it is the precise reverse of the sentence he is quoting.

Because he is quoting. Deuteronomy 15 is the law of the sabbatical year, and its argument runs like this: there will be no poor among you if you keep the commandment, and then, realistically, there will never cease to be poor in the land — and therefore, you shall open wide your hand to your brother, to the needy and to the poor (Deut 15:4, 11). The permanence of poverty is stated in Scripture as the reason for permanent generosity, not as an excuse for resignation. Every Jew at that table knew the verse and knew how it ended. He quotes the middle of it and lets them supply the rest.

So what he actually says is: you will have the poor to serve for the rest of your lives and the obligation never lapses — and you will not always have me. There is a window here, a few days wide, that will not come again. This woman has understood that and you have not.

Which is a lesson about timing rather than about priorities in the abstract. There are things that can be done at any point and things that can only be done now, and the second kind are usually the ones that look least urgent. The visit to a dying man can be made this week or not at all. The word of thanks to someone old can be said now or said at a funeral to people who cannot hear it. Care for the poor is a lifelong duty precisely because the poor will still be there. Some things will not be.

parallels.desc: there will never cease to be poor in the land

verseByVerse.quote: "In pouring this ointment on my body she has done it to prepare me for burial. Truly, I say to you, wherever this gospel is proclaimed in the whole world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He tells them what she has done, and it is not what she thought she was doing. In pouring this ointment on my body she has done it to prepare me for burial. Whether the woman understood that is not said and probably not; she came to honour him, and he receives it as embalming. Corpses in that country were anointed with spices before being wrapped, and he is telling a room full of men who will not accept that he is going to die that his body has now been prepared for the grave.

There is a bitter footnote to that. When the women came to the tomb on the Sunday morning with their spices, intending to do this properly, they were too late — he was not there. The women's spices on Sunday morning came too late; the anointing he accepted for his burial was this one, poured out in love before he died, given days early by a woman who was being told off for it at the time.

Then the promise, and it is the largest one he ever attaches to a private act: wherever this gospel is proclaimed in the whole world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her. He is standing in a leper's house in a village outside Jerusalem, two days from execution, with a movement of eleven frightened men and one traitor, and he says: this will be told everywhere on earth.

It has been. The sentence is self-fulfilling every time the passage is read, and it is being fulfilled now, in this room, on this page, in a language she never heard of, two thousand years after she broke the jar. There is no other promise in the Gospels that a reader can verify in the act of reading it.

And notice what he does not do. He does not give her name. Matthew never tells us who she was; John identifies her as Mary of Bethany, but in this Gospel the most universally commended human act is performed by a woman with no name in the text — in memory of her, and we do not know who she is. That is its own kind of comfort for anybody whose best work has gone unrecorded and unattributed. He remembers what she did. He was not depending on Matthew to keep the record.
verseByVerse.note: Bodies were anointed with spices for burial; Jesus would be buried in haste.

verseByVerse.quote: Then one of the twelve, whose name was Judas Iscariot, went to the chief priests and said, "What will you give me if I deliver him over to you?" And they paid him thirty pieces of silver.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Matthew's placing is deliberate and merciless. A woman has just poured out a year's wages on him and been called beautiful for it; the very next sentence has a man walking out to find a price for him. Extravagance and calculation, side by side, and the calculation is being done by one of the twelve.

Look at how he opens the negotiation: What will you give me if I deliver him over to you? He does not name a figure. He asks them to. A man selling something valuable states his price; a man who has decided to sell and does not much care what he gets asks what is on offer. Judas let the buyers set the value, and they did.

Thirty pieces of silver. It is not a random sum, and every Jew present would have known where it came from. In the law of Exodus, if an ox gores a slave to death, the owner pays the slave's master thirty shekels of silver (Ex 21:32). That is the compensation rate for a dead slave — not the price of a person but the damages payable for one. Zechariah then uses the same figure with heavy irony: the LORD's shepherd asks his wages, is weighed out thirty pieces of silver, and is told by God to throw the lordly price to the potter in the house of the LORD (Zech 11:12-13). Judas will do exactly that in the next chapter.

So the amount is a message, whether or not the priests intended it. They valued the Son of God at the insurance payout for a gored slave. And he accepted the figure without negotiating.

What is unnerving about Judas is not that he was a monster but that nobody could see it. He had been on the road for three years. He had heard every sermon in this book from the front, watched the blind receive sight and the dead get up, been sent out to preach and given authority over unclean spirits with the others (10:1-4), and held the common purse because the group trusted him with money. When Jesus said at the table that one of them would betray him, not one of the eleven turned and looked at Judas. They all asked whether it was themselves. Three years at close quarters and he had not given himself away to a single one of them.
verseByVerse.note: Thirty shekels of silver was the price the law set for a slave gored by an ox.

parallels.desc: thirty pieces of silver, the shepherd’s wages

verseByVerse.quote: And from that moment he sought an opportunity to betray him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
From that moment he sought an opportunity. The word is eukairian — a good moment, the right time. It is the language of a man waiting for a gap in a diary.

That is the sentence to sit with, because it rules out the reading that would make Judas easier to live with. This was not a flash of rage, or a moment of madness, or a man swept away by an impulse he could not control and regretted by morning. He made a decision, and then he went back to work. He ate with them. He walked with them. He kept the money bag and presumably kept it honestly enough that nobody noticed anything. He sat through the supper and dipped his hand in the same dish. And underneath all of it, day after day, he was watching for a convenient evening.

Sin that has become patient is a different order of thing from sin that erupts. The eruption at least announces itself and can be repented of the same night. This is a settled purpose, carried quietly, in ordinary company, requiring the man to be pleasant at breakfast — and every day he sustained it made the next day easier, because a decision that has been lived with for days has stopped feeling like a decision at all. It has become a fact about him.

And that is how most serious wrong actually gets done. Not in the moment of temptation, where everybody expects the danger to be, but in the long quiet stretch afterwards, when the thing has been decided and is merely awaiting a convenient hour. The affair that has not happened yet but has been agreed to in the mind. The resignation letter written and saved. The lie that will be told when the question finally comes. Judas had weeks in which nothing had happened yet and everything had already happened.

What makes the picture unbearable is that during those weeks he was being loved. He was given the morsel at the table, addressed as friend in the garden, and asked a direct question that would have let him stop. He was still inside the circle, still being reached for. He was simply waiting for a good moment.

verseByVerse.quote: Now on the first day of Unleavened Bread the disciples came to Jesus, saying, "Where will you have us prepare for you to eat the Passover?" He said, "Go into the city to a certain man and say to him, 'The Teacher says, My time is at hand. I will keep the Passover at your house with my disciples.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jesus' foreknowledge — sending disciples to an unspecified man in the city — again demonstrates his sovereign command of events. "My time is at hand" (kairos) is the appointed moment in salvation history, not a tragic accident. He is not surprised by what approaches; he has been moving toward it since Galilee. The Passover preparation is itself loaded with significance: they are about to eat the meal that commemorates Egypt's slavery and the redemption by blood — and Jesus will transform it into the memorial of the ultimate redemption. Every detail of the Last Supper is dense with the typological richness of the exodus.

A well-known difficulty stands over this verse, and a reader who has John open will meet it at once. Matthew, Mark and Luke all present this meal plainly as the Passover — the disciples ask where to prepare it, and they prepare it. But John seems to put the whole thing a day earlier: on the morning of the crucifixion the leaders will not enter Pilate's headquarters "so that they would not be defiled, but could eat the Passover" (John 18:28), and John calls that day "the day of Preparation of the Passover" (John 19:14) — as though the meal were still ahead and Jesus died at the hour the lambs were being killed. Which is it?

Two answers carry real weight, and neither requires anyone to have got it wrong. The first is that Preparation (paraskeuē) is simply the ordinary Greek word for Friday — it is still the word for Friday in Greek today — so "the day of Preparation of the Passover" most naturally means the Friday of Passover week, not the day before the meal. On the same reading, "eat the Passover" in John 18:28 refers to the festival meals that ran through the whole seven-day feast (the chagigah offerings), not to the lamb eaten the previous night; a man defiled that morning would have been barred from those, which is exactly what worried them. The second answer is that the day itself was reckoned differently by different Jews — there is evidence that Galileans and Judeans, and Pharisees and Sadducees, did not begin the day at the same hour — so Passover was legitimately kept on two consecutive evenings, and a city swollen with pilgrims accommodated both. Jesus, a Galilean, keeps it with his disciples on the earlier evening; the Judean leadership keeps it on the later one.

What should be resisted is the tidy modern suggestion that John simply moved the date to make a theological point. He is the most precise of the four about hours and feasts, and the suggestion asks us to believe he preferred a symbol to the truth. Besides, the symbol was never his to invent. Whichever reckoning is right, both accounts land in the same place: the Lamb was killed at Passover. It was John's own Gospel that opened with "Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world" (John 1:29), and Paul says it without a trace of hesitation — "Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed" (1 Cor 5:7). The meal in the upper room and the death outside the wall are the same feast seen from its two ends: the supper he gave them, and the sacrifice he became.
verseByVerse.note: Unleavened Bread was the week-long feast that began with Passover; lambs were sacrificed at the temple that afternoon.

verseByVerse.quote: And the disciples did as Jesus had directed them, and they prepared the Passover. When it was evening, he reclined at table with the twelve.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two ordinary sentences, and it is worth slowing down over how ordinary they are. Somebody had to buy the lamb and take it to the temple to be killed. Somebody carried the carcass back, and someone else swept the room for leaven, and set out the bitter herbs and the unleavened bread and the wine, and arranged the cushions. It was a domestic evening's work, of the kind done in tens of thousands of houses in that city that week, and the men doing it had no idea they were preparing the most consequential meal in human history.

When it was evening, he reclined at table with the twelve. Reclining is the posture of a free man at a feast — Jews ate the Passover lying on the left side, propped on an elbow, precisely because slaves ate standing and this was the meal of a liberated people. He takes that posture on the last night of his life, hours before he is bound.

And notice: with the twelve. All twelve. Judas is at the table with his fee already agreed. Jesus reclines at a feast of freedom beside the man arranging his arrest.

The new covenant is going to be inaugurated in this room, and the room is a borrowed one, up a flight of stairs, in a house belonging to a man Matthew does not name. Not the temple, where the sacrifices were; not a court, where covenants were witnessed; not before the council, who would have been the obvious parties to such a thing. Thirteen men round a table, one of whom is a traitor, in someone else's dining room.

That is worth remembering by anybody who has felt that his own church is too plain a place for anything eternal to be happening in. The bread on the table in the upper room was the same bread everybody else in Jerusalem was eating that night. God has a settled habit of doing the largest things in the least impressive rooms, with ordinary objects, in front of people who are not concentrating.
verseByVerse.note: The Passover was eaten after sunset, reclining.

verseByVerse.quote: And as they were eating, he said, "Truly, I say to you, one of you will betray me." And they were very sorrowful and began to say to him one after another, "Is it I, Lord?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He waits until they are eating. As they were eating, he said, Truly, I say to you, one of you will betray me. Not before the meal, when it would have ended it; not after, when they were leaving. In the middle, with food in front of them and the man in question within arm's reach.

The setting is the whole weight of it. Sharing a meal in that culture was not a casual arrangement; to eat at a man's table was to be in covenant with him, under his protection, committed to his interests. David had felt the same wound and written it down: even my close friend in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, has lifted his heel against me (Ps 41:9). Betrayal from a stranger is a misfortune. Betrayal from a man with your bread in his mouth is something else.

Then the disciples' response, and the Greek is sharper than the English. Is it I, Lord? — meti ego, kyrie. Greek marks the expected answer, and meti expects the answer no. They are saying: it isn't me, is it, Lord? Which is exactly how a man asks a question he badly wants a particular answer to.

And notice what they did not do. Eleven men, told there is a traitor at the table, and not one of them turns and looks at anybody else. There is no accusation, no glance down the table, no comparing of notes. Each asks about himself, one after another. It would have been the most natural thing in the world to start theorising about which of the others it was, and nobody does.

That instinct is worth borrowing, because it is rarer than it looks. The ordinary response to hearing that something is badly wrong in a group is to work out who is responsible, and it can be done with real solemnity and mistaken for discernment. These men had lived with each other for three years and knew each other's weaknesses; any one of them could have made a case against two or three of the others. Told that one of them was capable of the worst thing imaginable, every single one of them thought first of himself — and eleven of them were wrong about it, and were right to ask.

verseByVerse.quote: He answered, "He who has dipped his hand in the dish with me will betray me. The Son of Man goes as it is written of him, but woe to that man by whom the Son of Man is betrayed! It would have been better for that man if he had not been born."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He who has dipped his hand in the dish with me. At the Passover meal a common bowl of sauce stood on the table and everyone dipped into it, so the answer identifies nobody in particular — all twelve had dipped. It is not a name. It is a restatement of the horror: the man who will do this is a man whose hand has been in the same bowl as mine tonight.

Then two sentences set side by side that no theologian has ever fully prised apart.
